profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-11-22T06:15:12.52+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into $lang.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.
5. The target language is $lang.
Input text:

p.seg: The Dào,
covers heaven and bears up earth,
extends to the four directions,
splits open the eight extremes,
so high it has no summit,
so deep it cannot be fathomed,
enveloping heaven and earth,
endowing and receiving the formless.
From its source, springs bubble forth,
empty, yet gradually filling;
gushing and rushing,
turbid, yet gradually clearing.
Thus, planted, it fills heaven and earth;
spread horizontally, it pervades the four seas;
applied endlessly,
it knows no dawn or dusk.
Unfurled, it shrouds the six directions;
rolled up, it does not fill a single grasp.
Contracted, yet able to expand;
obscure, yet able to shine;
weak, yet able to be strong;
soft, yet able to be hard.
Spanning the four dimensions, it embraces Yīn and Yáng;
encompassing the cosmos, it illuminates the three lights.
Very soft and smooth,
very fine and subtle.
Because of it, mountains are high,
abysses are deep,
beasts run,
birds fly,
the sun and moon are bright,
the stars and calendar move,
the qílín swims,
the fènghuáng soars.
The Two Sovereigns of high antiquity,
grasped the handle of the Dào,
stood at the center,
their spirit roaming with transformation,
thereby pacifying the four quarters.
Therefore, heaven could revolve and earth stand still,
turning like a wheel without ceasing,
water flowing without stop,
sharing beginning and end with the myriad things.
Winds rise and clouds steam forth,
and no affair goes unanswered;
thunder peals and rain falls,
responding together endlessly.
Ghosts emerge and spirits enter;
dragons rise and luán birds gather;
like a potter's wheel spinning, like a hub turning,
revolving and starting anew.
Already carved, already polished,
they return again to simplicity.
Acting through non-action,
they harmonize with the Dào;
speaking through non-speech,
they connect with virtue;
serene and joyful without arrogance,
they attain harmony;
embracing the myriad differences,
they accommodate their natures;
their spirit lodges in the tip of an autumn hair,
yet expands to the totality of the cosmos.
Their virtue envelops heaven and earth and harmonizes Yīn and Yáng,
regulates the four seasons and tunes the five phases.
Breathing upon and nurturing,
the myriad things and all living beings,
moistening the plants and trees,
soaking the metals and stones,
the birds and beasts grow large,
their fine fur glossy,
their wings and feathers vigorous,
their antlers and horns grow,
no beast's fetus is miscarried,
no bird's egg fails to hatch,
fathers have no worry of losing sons,
elder brothers have no grief of mourning younger brothers,
children are not orphaned,
women are not widowed,
rainbows do not appear,
malevolent stars do not travel,
such is the effect of embodying virtue.
The supreme Dào above,
generates the myriad things but does not possess them,
completes transformations and forms but does not dominate them.
Creeping things and those that breathe through beaks,
flying insects and wriggling creatures,
rely on it to be born,
yet none know to be grateful;
rely on it to die,
yet none can resent it.
Those who benefit from it cannot praise it,
those who use it and fail cannot blame it.
It gathers and stores up, yet does not grow richer;
it distributes and bestows, yet does not become poorer.
Coiled and continuous, it cannot be exhausted;
fine and subtle, it cannot be labored over.
Piled up, it grows no higher;
cast down, it sinks no lower;
increased, it does not become more numerous;
decreased, it does not become fewer;
chopped, it does not become thin;
slain, it is not mutilated;
chiseled, it is not made deep;
filled, it is not made shallow.
Vague and indistinct,
it cannot be given form;
indistinct and vague,
its use is inexhaustible;
dark and obscure,
it responds to the formless;
deep and penetrating,
it does not move in vain.
It rolls and unfurls with hardness and softness;
it bends and rises with Yīn and Yáng.
In ancient times, when Féng Yí and Dà Bǐng drove,
they mounted thunder chariots,
harnessed six cloud-steeds,
roamed the faint mists,
galloped through the indistinct and vague,
traversed the distant and ever higher to reach the extremes,
passed through frost and snow leaving no tracks,
shone upon by sunlight casting no shadow,
riding the whirlwind, embracing the sheep's horn, they ascended,
charting the rivers and mountains,
treading and leaping over Kūnlún,
pushing open the Chānghé gates,
entering the celestial gate.
The charioteers of later ages,
even with light carriages and fine horses,
strong whips and sharp goads,
could not compete with them for the lead.
Therefore, the great person
is placid without thought,
tranquil without worry;
taking heaven as his canopy,
earth as his carriage;
the four seasons as his horses,
Yīn and Yáng as his drivers;
riding the clouds, scaling the heavens,
keeping company with the Creator.
Releasing his will, relaxing his pace,
he gallops across the great expanse.
He can walk when it is time to walk,
and run when it is time to run.
He commands the Rain Master to sprinkle the road,
orders the Wind Earl to sweep the dust.
He uses lightning as his whip,
thunder as his chariot wheels.
Above, he wanders the wilds of the high empty voids;
below, he emerges from the gate of the boundless margins.
His vision scans everywhere, illuminating all,
yet he remains guarded in his completeness.
He traverses the four corners,
yet returns again to the pivot.
Therefore, taking heaven as a canopy,
then nothing is left uncovered;
taking earth as a carriage,
then nothing is left unborne;
taking the four seasons as horses,
then nothing is left unguided;
taking Yīn and Yáng as drivers,
then nothing is left unprepared for.
Thus, he is swift yet not shaken,
travels far yet is not wearied,
his four limbs are not taxed,
his hearing and sight are not impaired,
and yet he knows the shapes and boundaries of the eight cords and nine fields—
Why is this?
Because he holds the handle of the Dào,
and roams in the land of the boundless.
Therefore, the affairs of the world cannot be forced;
one must follow their natural course and guide them.
The transformations of the myriad things cannot be fully explored;
one must grasp their essential direction and return to it.
Now, when mirror and water come into contact with forms,
they employ no cunning or artifice,
yet square, round, curved, and straight cannot escape them.
Therefore, the echo does not deliberately respond,
the shadow does not deliberately appear;
calling out and its faint answer,
silently, it is so of itself.
Humans are born tranquil—
this is the nature of Heaven.
Stirred, and only then acting—
this is the injury to nature.
this is the movement of awareness.
Awareness interacts with things,
and likes and dislikes are born therefrom.
Likes and dislikes take form,
and awareness is seduced by externals;
unable to return to oneself,
the Heavenly principle is extinguished.
Thus, those who have attained the Way
do not let human concerns alter Heaven's course;
outwardly they transform with all things,
yet inwardly do not lose their true nature.
Though possessing nothing, they supply all needs;
though ever active, they remain anchored.
Whether large or small, long or short,
each thing has its proper place;
even when myriad things surge forth
in tumultuous chaos,
their inherent order is never lost.
Therefore, such rulers dwell above yet people feel no burden,
stand ahead yet none are harmed;
all under Heaven turn to them,
while treacherous evils fear them.
Because they contend with nothing,
nothing can contend with them.
One who fishes by the river
may spend days without filling a basket,
even with sharp hooks, barbed points,
fine lines, and fragrant bait,
aided by the skills of Zhān Hé and Juān Xuān—
still cannot compete with net fishing.
An archer drawing the Wūhào bow,
nocking Qíwèi arrows,
possessing the prowess of Yì and Péng Méngzǐ
to shoot flying birds
cannot match the catcher's net in bounty.
Why is this?
Because their tools are too limited.
Were the whole sky their cage,
the rivers and seas their net,
how could any fish or bird escape?
Thus, arrows are inferior to tethered lines,
lines to nets, nets to formless imagery.
To abandon the great Way for petty techniques
is no different from ordering crabs to catch mice
or toads to seize fleas—
incapable of stopping treachery and evil,
chaos only grows fiercer.
When Gǔn of Xià built nine-ren walls,
the nobles rebelled,
and distant lands grew sly.
Yǔ, knowing the realm's disloyalty,
tore down walls, filled moats,
distributed wealth,
burned armor and weapons,
and governed with virtue—
then distant lands submitted,
border tribes offered tribute,
and at Túshān he gathered nobles,
ten thousand states bearing jade and silk.
So when cunning lurks in the heart,
purity is tainted,
divine virtue incomplete;
if one lacks self-awareness,
how can they win distant hearts?
Thus, hard leather breeds sharp weapons,
high walls invite battering rams;
like pouring boiling water on flames,
chaos only intensifies.
Whipping a biting dog
or lashing a kicking horse
to train them
—even Yī Yǐn or Zào Fǔ would fail.
But remove the urge to harm,
and you can tail a hungry tiger,
let alone tame dogs or horses!
Hence, followers of the Way rest without exhaustion,
while manipulators toil fruitlessly.
Harsh laws and cruel punishments
build no kingly legacy;
frequent use of whip and spur
wins no long-distance race.
Lí Zhū's sharp eyes
spot a needle tip a hundred paces away,
yet cannot see fish in deep pools.
Shī Kuàng's keen ears
distinguish eight winds' harmonies,
yet cannot hear beyond ten lǐ.
Thus, relying on one person's ability
cannot manage three mǔ of land.
Following cosmic principles,
aligning with nature's course,
even the whole world becomes orderly.
So when Yǔ dredged rivers,
he took water as his guide;
when Shénnóng sowed grains,
he learned from sprouting stalks.
Duckweed roots in water,
trees root in soil,
birds soar through void,
beasts tread on solid ground,
jiāolóng dwell in water,
tigers and leopards haunt mountains—
this is Heaven and Earth's nature.
Rubbing wood ignites fire,
metal meeting fire flows liquid;
round things tend to roll,
hollow things float—
this is nature's inclination.
So when spring winds arrive, sweet rain falls,
nurturing all things:
birds brood eggs,
mammals carry young,
plants bloom splendidly,
creatures lay eggs or bear live young—
none see how it's done,
yet the work is complete.
Autumn winds bring frost,
cutting growth, causing withering;
eagles and falcons strike fiercely,
insects hide dormant,
plants sink roots deep,
fish and turtles gather in depths—
none see how it's done,
yet life vanishes unseen.
Dwellings in trees are nests,
in water are caves;
beasts have lairs,
people have houses;
plains suit oxen and horses,
boats require abundant water;
the Xiōngnú produce felted furs,
Gān and Yuè weave grass linen—
each creates what it needs
against drought or damp,
each adapts to its environment
to ward off heat and cold;
all find their proper place,
each thing serves its function.
From this we see:
all things follow nature's course;
what need have sages to interfere?
South of Jiǔyí Mountains,
land tasks are few, water tasks many,
so people cut hair, tattoo bodies
to resemble scaled creatures,
wear short pants without leggings
for wading ease,
roll short sleeves
for paddling convenience—
this is adaptation.
North of Yànmén Pass,
the Dí tribe eats no grain,
values youth over age,
prizes strength and courage,
never unstring bows,
never unsaddle horses—
this is suitability.
So when Yǔ visited the naked country,
he removed his clothes to enter,
donned them to leave—
this is adaptation.
Those who transplant trees
and disrupt their yīn-yáng nature
will see them wither.
Thus, oranges planted north of the river
turn into trifoliate oranges;
mynahs cannot cross the Jì River,
raccoon dogs die past the Wèn River—
form and nature cannot be changed,
habitat cannot be shifted.
Therefore, those who comprehend the Way
return to clarity and stillness;
those who understand things
end in non-action.
Nurturing nature with calm,
housing spirit with detachment,
they enter the gate of Heaven.
What we call "Heaven"
is purity, simplicity,
straightforward and spotless,
never mixed with adulteration.
What we call "human"
involves twisted wisdom, cunning artifice,
crafty deceptions
used to navigate worldly affairs
and mingle with customs.
Thus, oxen having cloven hooves and horns,
horses growing manes and solid hooves
is Heaven's doing.
Bridling horses' mouths,
piercing oxen's noses
is human doing.
Following Heaven
means roaming with the Way;
following human ways
means mingling with worldly customs.
One cannot discuss the vastness of the ocean with a well fish,
for it is confined to narrow limits;
one cannot speak of cold with a summer insect,
for it is bound by its season;
one cannot discourse on the ultimate Way with a provincial scholar,
for he is constrained by custom
and restricted by his teachings.
Thus, the sage does not let human concerns disrupt Heaven,
nor let desires disturb his true nature.
Without planning, he acts appropriately;
without speaking, he is trusted;
without pondering, he attains;
without acting, he accomplishes.
His essence penetrates the spiritual storehouse,
and he companions with the Creator.
Expert swimmers may drown;
skilled riders may fall.
Each, through their own expertise,
brings disaster upon themselves.
Hence, those who force things never succeed,
and those who contend for profit never prosper.
In ancient times, with the strength of Gònggōng,
he struck Mount Bùzhōu,
causing the earth to tilt southeast.
Contending with Gāoxīn to become emperor,
he sank into the depths,
his clan destroyed,
his lineage cut off without sacrifice.
King Yì of Yuè fled to mountain caves,
but the Yuè people smoked him out,
leaving him no choice.
From this we see
that attainment lies in timing,
not in contention;
order lies in the Way,
not in sagehood.
Earth remains low,
not contending for height,
thus secure and without peril;
water flows downward,
not contending to lead,
thus swift and never delayed.
When Shùn tilled at Lìshān,
after a year, farmers vied for rocky fields,
yielding fertile land along boundaries;
when he fished by the river,
after a year, fishermen contended for rapid streams,
ceding deep pools and bends.
At that time,
he spoke no words,
gave no signals with his hands,
yet held profound virtue in his heart,
and his influence spread like divinity.
Had Shùn lacked this intent,
even with eloquent persuasion door to door,
he could not have transformed a single person.
Thus, the Way of non-action
is vast and magnificent indeed!
To pacify the Sānmiáo,
make the Yǔ people pay homage,
relocate the Luǒguó,
and incorporate the Sùshèn,
without issuing commands
yet changing customs and traditions—
is this not solely through mental influence?
How could laws, punishments,
or penalties achieve this?
Therefore, the sage cultivates the root within,
without adorning the branches without,
preserves his spirit and energy,
sets aside cunning and artifice,
serenely inactive yet nothing left undone,
tranquilly ungoverning yet all in order.
What is called non-action
is not acting before things;
what is called all-action
is following what things do.
What is called ungoverning
is not altering nature;
what is called all-governing
is according with how things interact.
All things have their origin,
but only he knows to guard the root;
all affairs have their source,
but only he knows to guard the gate.
Thus, he exhausts the inexhaustible,
reaches the boundless,
illuminates things without confusion,
responds without exhaustion—
this is called heavenly understanding.
Hence, those who attain the Way
have weak wills but strong actions,
empty minds yet fitting responses.
What is meant by weak will
is pliability, quietude,
concealed in timidity,
acting as if incapable,
serenely without worry,
moving never missing the moment,
circling and revolving with all things,
not leading the way,
but responding when stirred.
Thus, the noble must take humility as their title,
and the high must have the low as their foundation.
Embrace the small to contain the large,
control the external from within,
practice softness yet be firm,
use weakness to achieve strength,
transforming and adapting,
grasping the Way of Oneness,
and correcting the many with the few.
What is meant by strong action
is meeting change and handling emergencies,
repelling troubles and overcoming difficulties,
with strength that never fails,
enemies none unconquered,
adapting to transformations and timing,
so none can harm him.
Therefore, those who desire firmness
must guard it with softness;
those who desire strength
must preserve it with weakness.
Accumulate softness, and it becomes firm;
accumulate weakness, and it becomes strong.
Observe what is accumulated,
and know the direction of fortune and misfortune.
Strength overcomes those inferior to oneself,
but meets its match with equals;
softness surpasses those superior to oneself,
its power immeasurable.
Thus, an army too strong will be destroyed,
a tree too rigid will break,
hard leather will crack,
teeth harder than the tongue
wear out first.
Hence, the soft and weak
are the trunk of life,
while the hard and strong
are companions of death.
Those who lead first
walk the path to hardship;
those who act after
find the source of success.
How do we know this is so?
Generally, people live to seventy years,
yet their choices and actions
bring daily and monthly regrets,
until death.
Thus, Qú Bóyù at fifty
saw forty-nine years of errors.
Why?
Because the pioneer's way is hard to know,
while the follower's is easy to improve.
If the first climbs high,
the latter follows by pulling up;
if the first descends low,
the latter treads upon him;
if the first falls into a pit,
the latter learns from it;
if the first fails utterly,
the latter avoids it.
From this we see
the pioneer is the target for the latter's arrows.
Like the spearhead and its butt,
the blade faces danger while the butt remains unharmed—
why?
Because it relies on a rear position, shielded.
This is commonly seen by ordinary folk,
yet even the wise cannot avoid it.
What is meant by 'latter'
is not stagnation and inaction,
nor congealment and immobility,
but valuing accord with principle and timeliness.
Holding the Way's principles to couple with change,
the former can control the latter,
and the latter can control the former.
Why so?
By not losing what controls others,
others cannot control him.
The moment shifts and turns,
allowing not a breath's pause.
Act too early, and you overshoot;
act too late, and you miss.
The sun revolves, the moon circles,
time does not linger with man.
Thus, the sage does not prize a foot-long jade,
but values every inch of shadow,
for time is hard to gain and easy to lose.
When Yǔ raced with time,
he did not stop for lost shoes,
nor turn back for a caught hat—
not contending to be first,
Therefore, the sage guards the path of clarity and embraces the feminine principle,
adapting to changes through following the natural course,
always remaining behind and not taking the lead.
Soft and weak through tranquility,
serene and peaceful through stability,
they can overcome the mighty and wear down the hard,
with none able to contend with them.
Of all things under heaven,
none is softer and weaker than water,
yet it is vast beyond limits,
deep beyond measure,
extending endlessly to the infinite,
stretching far into the boundless,
its loss and gain,
reaching the immeasurable.
Rising to the sky, it becomes rain and dew;
descending to the earth, it brings moisture and nourishment.
Without it, all things cannot live;
without it, all affairs cannot succeed.
It envelops all living beings
without partiality,
its moisture reaches even the tiniest insects
without seeking reward,
enriching the world without exhaustion,
bestowing virtue upon the people without cost.
Its movement cannot be exhausted,
its subtlety cannot be grasped.
Strike it—it leaves no wound;
pierce it—it suffers no injury;
chop it—it does not break;
burn it—it does not ignite.
Flowing and yielding,
twisting and turning in complexity,
it cannot be scattered.
It can penetrate metal and stone;
its strength sustains the world.
Moving in the realm of the formless,
soaring above the ethereal regions,
winding through rivers and valleys,
surging across the vast wilderness.
In surplus or shortage,
it takes and gives with heaven and earth,
bestowing upon all things without preference.
Thus, it is neither selfish nor public,
surging and vibrating,
merging with the vastness of heaven and earth.
It has no left and no right,
coiling and intertwining,
enduring with all things from beginning to end.
This is called the ultimate virtue.
The reason water can achieve its ultimate virtue in the world
lies in its softness and smoothness.
Hence, Lǎodān's words say:
"The softest thing in the world
gallops through the hardest.
It emerges from non-existence,
enters without a gap.
Thus, I know the benefit of non-action."
The formless
is the great ancestor of things;
the soundless
is the great origin of sounds.
Its child is light,
its grandchild is water,
both born from the formless!
Light can be seen but not held;
water can be followed but not destroyed.
Thus, among things with form,
none is more noble than water.
From birth to death,
from non-being to being,
from being to non-being,
it thus declines and becomes humble.
Therefore, clarity and tranquility
are the pinnacle of virtue;
softness and weakness
are the essence of the Dào;
emptiness, non-being, and serene joy
are the function of all things.
Responding solemnly to stimuli,
profoundly returning to the root,
one merges into the formless.
What is called the formless
refers to the One.
What is called the One
is that which has no equal under heaven.
Loftily standing alone,
solidly dwelling in solitude,
it connects above to the nine heavens,
penetrates below through the nine fields.
Round, yet not fitting a compass;
square, yet not fitting a square;
vast and merged into one,
layered without root,
embracing heaven and earth,
serving as the gateway to the Dào.
Profound and obscure,
pure virtue alone remains,
giving without exhaustion,
used without toil.
Thus, looking at it, one sees no form;
listening to it, one hears no sound;
following it, one grasps no substance.
From the formless, forms are born;
from the soundless, the five tones resound;
from the tasteless, the five flavors take shape;
from the colorless, the five colors are formed.
Hence, being is born from non-being,
substance emerges from emptiness.
When the world is its sphere,
name and substance coexist.
The number of musical tones is no more than five,
yet the variations of the five tones
are too many to hear entirely.
The blends of flavors are no more than five,
yet the transformations of the five flavors
are too many to taste entirely.
The number of colors is no more than five,
yet the variations of the five colors
are too many to behold entirely.
Thus, in music,
when the tonic is established, the five tones take form;
in flavors,
when sweetness is established, the five flavors are balanced;
in colors,
when white is established, the five colors are completed;
in the Dào,
when the One is established, all things are born.
Therefore, the principle of the One
extends throughout the four seas;
the understanding of the One
reaches the limits of heaven and earth.
In its wholeness,
it is pure like unworked wood;
in its dispersion,
it is mixed like turbid water.
Turbid, it slowly clears;
empty, it slowly fills.
Calm, it resembles the deep abyss;
floating, it resembles drifting clouds.
Seemingly non-existent, yet present;
seemingly lost, yet existing.
The totality of all things
passes through a single opening;
the root of all affairs
emerges from a single gate.
Its movement is formless,
its transformations like the divine;
its path leaves no trace,
always behind yet arriving first.
Therefore, in governing, the ultimate person
conceals their keenness,
extinguishes their embellishments,
follows the Dào and discards cleverness,
sharing with the people in commonality.
They remove temptations,
eliminate desires,
and cast aside worries.
By simplifying what they guard, they gain clarity;
by reducing what they seek, they attain fulfillment.
Those who rely on ears and eyes for hearing and seeing
toil their bodies without true understanding;
those who use knowledge and scheming to govern
strain their minds without achieving merit.
Hence, the sage unifies measures and follows the path,
not altering what is appropriate,
not changing what is constant,
applying standards and following guidelines,
flexibly adapting as fitting.
For joy and anger
are deviations of the Dào;
worry and sorrow
are losses of virtue;
likes and dislikes
are faults of the heart;
desires and cravings
are burdens on nature.
In humans, great anger damages the yīn,
great joy harms the yáng;
weakened qì causes loss of voice,
fear and terror lead to madness;
worry and sorrow breed resentment,
and illness accumulates;
excessive likes and dislikes
bring disaster in their wake.
Thus, when the heart knows neither sorrow nor joy,
it is the perfection of virtue;
when it is connected yet unchanging,
it is the perfection of tranquility;
when desires and cravings are not harbored,
it is the perfection of emptiness;
when there are no preferences or aversions,
it is the perfection of equanimity;
when it does not mingle with external things,
it is the perfection of purity.
One who can achieve these five states
will penetrate divine clarity.
To penetrate divine clarity
is to attain what lies within.
Therefore, governing the external from within,
no task will be neglected;
if one can grasp it internally,
then one can manage the external.
When the inner is attained, the five viscera are calm,
thoughts and worries are balanced,
sinews and strength are firm,
ears and eyes are sharp and clear,
penetrating without confusion,
strong without breaking,
without great excess
and without falling short,
dwelling in smallness without feeling constrained,
dwelling in greatness without feeling hollow,
the soul is not restless,
the spirit is not troubled,
serene and solitary,
one becomes a leader of the world.
The great path is level and broad, not far from oneself; seeking what is near, one goes and returns again.
When stimulated, it can respond;
when pressed, it can move;
profound and boundless,
its transformations have no form.
Leisurely and unrestrained,
like an echo to a sound or a shadow to a form;
ascending heights and overlooking below,
never losing what one holds;
treading danger and walking risks,
never forgetting the mysterious support.
The great path is level and broad,
not far from oneself;
seeking what is near,
one goes and returns again.
If one can preserve this,
their virtue remains undiminished.
Amid the myriad things in confusion,
they transform along with them;
listening to the world,
it is like riding with the wind at one's back—
this is called ultimate virtue.
Ultimate virtue brings joy.
The ancients lived in caves yet their spirit was not lost;
in decadent times, some hold power over ten thousand chariots yet grieve daily.
From this, it is evident
that sageliness lies not in governing others,
but in attaining the Way;
joy lies not in wealth and honor,
but in the harmony of virtue.
Knowing to value oneself and regard the world as small
brings one close to the Way.
What is called joy—
must it necessarily mean residing in Jīngtái or Zhānghuá,
roaming Yúnmèng or Shāqiū,
listening to the "Jiǔsháo" or "Liùyíng" with the ears,
savoring rich and fragrant flavors,
galloping on smooth roads,
angling and hunting for sùshuāng birds to be called joy?
What I call joy
is when a person attains what they truly should attain.
Those who attain what they should
do not take extravagance as joy,
nor frugality as sorrow;
they close with yīn,
and open with yáng.
Thus, Zǐxià's heart was conflicted and he grew thin,
but when the Way prevailed, he grew stout.
The sage does not let the body be enslaved by things,
nor let desires disrupt harmony;
thus, their joy is not excessive,
their sorrow is not despondent.
Though the myriad directions change in a hundred ways,
wavering and unsettled,
I alone resolutely discard things
and emerge together with the Way.
Therefore, having self-contentment,
beneath tall trees,
within empty caves,
is sufficient to satisfy the spirit.
Without self-contentment,
even taking the world as one's home,
and the myriad people as servants,
is insufficient to nurture life.
One who can reach the state of no-joy
will find joy in everything;
joy in everything is the ultimate joy.
Erecting bells and drums,
arranging pipes and strings,
spreading felt mats and cushions,
adorning with plumes and ivory,
listening with the ears to the seductive music of Zhāogē's northern outskirts,
matching it with delicate beauties,
setting out wine and feasts,
continuing day and night,
shooting high-flying birds with strong crossbows,
chasing cunning hares with hounds—
this kind of joy,
blazing and dazzling,
entices as if by some lure.
But when the carriages are unhitched and horses rested,
the wine stopped and music cleared away,
the heart suddenly feels as if something is lost,
melancholy as if bereft.
Why is this?
It is because joy does not come from within to the external,
but from the external to the internal.
When the music plays, there is delight;
when the tune ends, there is sorrow.
Sorrow and delight alternate and generate each other,
the spirit becomes confused and disturbed,
unable to find peace even for a moment.
Examining the cause, one cannot grasp its form,
and daily it harms life,
losing what one should attain.
Therefore, if the internal is not attained within,
but one relies on the external for adornment,
it does not penetrate the skin,
does not permeate the marrow,
does not remain in the heart and mind,
does not settle in the five viscera.
Thus, what enters from the outside,
having no master within, does not stay.
What emerges from within,
finding no response outside, does not proceed.
Therefore, hearing good words and clever plans,
even fools know to delight in them;
hearing of ultimate virtue and noble conduct,
even the unworthy know to admire them.
Many delight in them,
but few apply them;
many admire them,
but few practice them.
Why is this so?
Because they cannot return to their innate nature.
If the inner self is not opened and one forces learning,
it enters the ear
but does not lodge in the heart.
How is this different from a deaf person singing?
Imitating what others do
brings no personal joy;
sound comes from the mouth
but scatters and fades.
The heart
is the master of the five viscera,
controlling the four limbs,
circulating blood and vital energy,
galloping through the realm of right and wrong,
and entering and exiting the gateway of all affairs.
Thus, without attaining the heart
yet having the ambition to govern the world
is like having no ears yet wanting to tune bells and drums,
or no eyes yet wanting to enjoy patterns and colors—
it is surely beyond one's capacity.
Therefore, the world is a divine vessel,
not to be acted upon;
those who act ruin it,
those who hold onto it lose it.
Xǔ Yóu regarded the world as small and did not exchange himself for Yáo,
because his will transcended the world.
Why is this so?
Because he followed the world to govern the world.
The essence of the world
lies not in others but in oneself,
not in other people but in one's own person.
If the self attains it, then the myriad things are complete.
Penetrating the discourse on mental cultivation,
then desires, preferences, and aversions are externalized.
Thus, there is no particular joy and no particular anger,
no particular pleasure and no particular pain;
the myriad things merge mysteriously,
without wrong or right;
transformation and nurturing shine mysteriously,
living as if dead.
The world is also what I possess,
and I am also what the world possesses;
between the world and me,
how could there be any separation?
Those who possess the world—
must they necessarily grasp power and hold authority,
wield the handle of life and death,
and enforce their commands?
What I call possessing the world,
does not mean this,
but rather self-attainment.
With self-attainment, the world also attains me.
When I and the world mutually attain each other,
we eternally possess one another;
how could there be any failure to accommodate within this relationship?
What is called self-attainment
is the full realization of one's person.
With the full realization of one's person, one becomes one with the Dào.
Therefore, even when roaming by riverbanks and seashores,
galloping on swift horses,
raising emerald canopies,
with eyes viewing the music of "Plume Dances" and "Martial Manifestations",
ears hearing magnificent, extraordinary, stirring and resonant sounds,
promoting the grand music of Zhèng and Wèi,
continuing the lingering style of "Stirring Chǔ",
shooting high-flying birds at marshy shores,
chasing running game in parks and preserves,
these are what cause ordinary people to become dissolute and indulgent,
yet when a sage dwells among them,
it is insufficient to disturb his essence and spirit,
confuse his vital energy and will,
or make his heart fearful and lose its innate nature.
Dwelling in impoverished remote villages,
beside mountain streams and valleys,
hidden within thickets and undergrowth,
in a room of surrounding earthen walls,
thatched with raw reeds,
with a蓬door and jar window,
twisted mulberry as the pivot,
leaking above and damp below,
moisture soaking the northern chamber,
snow and frost accumulating,
soaking the water plants and rushes,
wandering freely within vast marshes,
and roaming beside mountain cliffs,
these are what cause ordinary people to become haggard and dark-skinned,
sorrowful and unable to fulfill their aspirations,
yet when a sage dwells among them,
he does not become distressed, haggard, resentful or discontent,
nor lose that by which he finds self-contentment.
Why is this?
Because within he is connected to the celestial mechanism,
and does not lose his will and virtue due to honor or disgrace, poverty or wealth, toil or ease.
Therefore, the cawing of crows,
the chirping of magpies,
do they ever change their sounds because of cold or heat, dryness or dampness?
Thus, one who has attained the Dào is already settled,
and does not await the shifting of the myriad things,
nor determines his self-attainment
based on momentary changes.
What I call attainment
is the condition of innate nature and destiny, dwelling in their proper place.
Now innate nature and destiny,
emerge together with the form from their source;
when the form is complete, innate nature and destiny are formed,
and when innate nature and destiny are formed, likes and dislikes arise.
Therefore, scholars have fixed principles,
women have unchanging conduct,
compasses and squares cannot make them round or square,
hooks and cords cannot make them curved or straight.
As for heaven and earth's eternity,
climbing a hill cannot make it taller,
dwelling in low ground cannot make it shorter.
Therefore, those who have attained the Dào,
are undaunted in poverty,
unelated in success,
unafraid in high position,
steady when holding fullness,
fresh without being flashy,
enduring without changing,
unscorched when entering fire,
unwetted when entering water.
Therefore, they are honored without relying on power,
wealthy without relying on riches,
strong without relying on force,
peaceful, empty, and flowing downward,
soaring with transformation.
If it be so,
they hide gold in mountains,
conceal pearls in deep waters,
do not profit from goods and wealth,
do not covet power and fame.
Therefore, they do not consider comfort as joy,
nor deprivation as sorrow,
nor honor as security,
nor disgrace as danger.
Form, spirit, vital energy, and will
each dwell in their proper place,
following heaven and earth's actions.
Now the form is the dwelling of life;
vital energy is the fullness of life;
spirit is the governor of life.
If one loses its position, the other two are harmed.
Therefore, the sage causes each to dwell in its position,
maintain its function,
and not interfere with one another.
Thus, if the form
dwells where it is not at ease,
it deteriorates;
if vital energy is used
where it should not be full, it leaks;
if spirit acts
where it is not appropriate, it becomes obscured.
These three
must be carefully guarded.
Now all things under heaven, from insects and tiny creatures,
to crawling and moving beings,
all know what they like, dislike, benefit, and harm them - why?
Because their innate nature is present within them and does not depart;
if suddenly removed,
their flesh and bones would become disordered.
Now the reason people can see clearly,
hear keenly,
their physical bodies can resist,
and all joints can bend and stretch,
their perception can distinguish black and white,
see ugly and beautiful,
and their knowledge can differentiate same and different,
clarify right and wrong - why?
Because vital energy fills them,
and spirit directs them.
How do we know this is so?
Whenever a person's will
is fixed on something
and the spirit is tied to it,
when walking,
he may stumble into pits,
bump into straight trees
without realizing it,
not see when beckoned,
not hear when called.
It's not that his eyes and ears have left him,
yet he cannot respond - why?
Because his spirit has lost its guard.
Therefore, when focused on the small, he forgets the large;
when focused on the inside, he forgets the outside;
when focused on above, he forgets below;
when focused on left, he forgets right.
When there is nothing it does not fill,
then there is nowhere it is not present.
Therefore, those who value emptiness
take the tip of a hair as their dwelling.
Now when madmen cannot avoid the danger of water and fire
or overcome the perils of ditches and gullies,
is it because they lack form, spirit, vital energy, and will?
Rather, they use them differently.
Having lost their proper positions to guard,
and separated from their inner and outer dwellings,
therefore their actions cannot be appropriate,
their movements cannot hit the mark,
throughout life moving withered forms through gates of connected ridges and arranged terraces,
and stumbling into filthy pits and trap-filled gullies,
although born equal to others,
they cannot avoid being ridiculed by people - why?
Because form and spirit have lost each other.
Therefore, when spirit is the master,
the form follows and benefits;
when the form is the controller,
the spirit follows and is harmed.
Greedy and desirous people,
obscured by power and profit,
seduced by fame and position,
hoping with extraordinary wisdom
to establish themselves high in the world,
then their essence and spirit daily diminish and drift farther away,
long immersed and not returning,
with forms closed and centers blocked,
then spirit has no way to enter.
Thus, the world constantly has the affliction of blindness, delusion, and self-loss.
This is like the grease candle,
where the more fiercely it burns, the quicker it consumes itself.
Now essence, spirit, vital energy, and will,
when tranquil and full, daily grow stronger;
when agitated and depleted, daily grow older.
Therefore, the sage nurtures his spirit,
harmonizes and softens his vital energy,
levels and calms his form,
and with the Dào sinks or floats, lowers or raises,
leisurely lets it go,
urgently uses it.
When letting it go, it's like dropping clothes;
when using it, it's like releasing a trigger.
Being thus,
then the transformations of the myriad things are all encountered,
and the changes of all affairs are all responded to.
There are those that have a beginning,
those that have not yet begun to have a beginning,
and those that have not yet begun to have that which has not yet begun to have a beginning.
There are those that have existence,
those that have non-existence,
and those that have not yet begun to have existence or non-existence.
What is called having a beginning refers to
when vitality is pent up and not yet released,
buds and sprouts are just emerging,
without distinct forms or boundaries,
wriggling imperceptibly,
about to generate life but not yet forming into categories of things.
Having not yet begun to have a beginning means
the celestial qi begins to descend,
the terrestrial qi begins to ascend,
yīn and yáng intertwine and merge,
roaming and competing freely throughout the cosmos,
imbued with virtue and harmony,
flourishing profusely,
about to interact with things but not yet showing signs of manifestation.
Having not yet begun to have that which has not yet begun to have a beginning means
heaven contains harmony but has not yet descended it,
earth embraces qi but has not yet uplifted it,
in a state of emptiness and solitude,
desolate and vast,
without any semblance,
where qi converges and profoundly penetrates the obscure darkness.
Having existence refers to
the myriad things in their full array,
with roots, stems, branches, and leaves,
lush and verdant,
resplendent and dazzling,
insects flying and creeping creatures moving,
crawling and breathing,
tangible and measurable in quantity.
Having non-existence means
looking but not seeing its form,
listening but not hearing its sound,
touching but not grasping it,
gazing but not reaching its limit,
expansive and boundless,
vast and immense,
immeasurable and unquantifiable, yet connecting with light and radiance.
Having not yet begun to have existence or non-existence means
enveloping heaven and earth,
molding and transforming the myriad things,
profoundly penetrating the混沌 and obscure,
deep, broad, and immense,
with no outside,
even when dissected to the finest detail,
with no inside,
existing without spatial confines, giving rise to the root of existence and non-existence.
Having not yet begun to have that which has not yet begun to have existence or non-existence means
before heaven and earth separated,
before yīn and yáng divided,
before the four seasons were distinguished,
before the myriad things were born,
tranquil and calm like a vast ocean,
silent and clear,
with no visible form,
as if light and radiance inquired into non-being,
retreating in self-loss,
saying:
"I can grasp non-being,
but cannot grasp the non-being of non-being.
When it comes to the non-being of non-being,
how can the utmost subtlety ever reach this!"
The great clod burdens me with form,
toils me with life,
eases me with old age,
rests me with death.
What makes my life good
is also what makes my death good.
Storing a boat in a ravine,
or a mountain in a marsh,
people call it secure.
However,
at midnight, a strong man might carry it away,
and the sleeper would not know.
Though hiding small or large things appropriately,
they can still be lost.
If one hides the world in the world itself,
then there is nowhere for it to be lost.
How can things be said to lack great transformation?
Merely being cast into human form is already a joy.
Beings like humans
undergo countless changes without ever reaching an end.
Worn out and renewed again,
the joy of it
is beyond calculation!
It is like a dream:
dreaming of being a bird flying in the sky,
or a fish diving in the depths.
While in the dream,
one does not know it is a dream;
only upon waking does one realize it was a dream.
There will be a great awakening,
and then we will know that this present life is a great dream.
Before I was born,
how could I know the joy of life?
Now that I am not yet dead,
how can I know that death is not joyful?
In the past, Gōngniú Āi fell ill and transformed,
turning into a tiger in seven days.
His brother entered through the door to check on him,
and the tiger pounced and killed him.
Thus, when his patterns became those of a beast,
his claws and teeth changed,
his will and heart altered,
his spirit and form transformed.
While he was a tiger,
he did not know he had once been human;
while he was human,
he did not know he would become a tiger.
The two states alternate and clash,
each content in its formed state.
Cunning or dull-witted,
right and wrong without origin,
who knows where they begin!
Water facing winter congeals into ice,
ice meeting spring melts into water.
Ice and water transform before us,
as if moving in cycles,
who has time to ponder their sorrows or joys!
Thus, when the body is harmed by the harshness of heat, cold, dryness, or dampness,
the body may wither but the spirit remains strong;
when the spirit is injured by the troubles of joy, anger, thought, or worry,
the spirit may be exhausted while the body remains intact.
Hence, when a worn-out horse dies,
its skin peels off like a dry husk;
when a vigorous dog dies,
its flesh is still moist when cut.
Therefore, those who die of injury have restless ghosts,
while those who die in their time have tranquil spirits.
These are cases where body and spirit do not perish together.
The sage uses the mind,
relying on nature and leaning on spirit,
supporting each other to achieve completion.
Thus, they do not dream in sleep,
and do not worry when awake.
The ancients dwelled in混沌 darkness,
with spirit and qi not agitated outwardly,
the myriad things serene and tranquil in joy,
and even baleful stars and disruptive energies all dissipated,
unable to cause harm.
In that era,
the people were carefree,
unaware of east or west,
strolling with food in their mouths,
playing with full bellies,
sharing in celestial harmony,
feeding on earthly virtue,
not blaming each other with cunning or disputes over right and wrong,
in a vast and boundless state,
this was called great order.
Then those in high positions
guided and employed them
without corrupting their nature;
pacified and cared for them
without altering their virtue.
Thus, without spreading benevolence and righteousness, the myriad things multiplied;
without imposing rewards and punishments, all under heaven submitted.
Such a way can bring great beauty to flourish,
but is hard to measure with calculations.
Therefore, daily accounts may fall short,
but yearly accounts show surplus.
Fish forget each other in rivers and lakes,
humans forget each other in the way and its arts.
The true people of old,
standing on the foundation of heaven and earth,
centered and leisurely,
embracing virtue and basking in harmony,
while the myriad things rise like swirling dust,
who would bother to engage in human affairs,
troubling their life and nature with external things!
The Way possesses its warp and woof, its ordered structure,
attaining the Way of Oneness,
it connects a thousand branches and ten thousand leaves.
Thus, the noble have means to carry out commands,
the lowly have means to forget their baseness,
the poor have means to delight in their tasks,
the distressed have means to abide in peril.
When the great cold arrives,
frost and snow descend,
only then do we know the luxuriance of the pine and cypress.
Confronting difficulties and treading on danger,
with benefit and harm arrayed before one,
only then do we know that the sage does not stray from the Way.
Therefore, one who can bear the great circle treads the great square,
one who mirrors the great clarity sees the great brightness,
one who establishes great peace abides in the great hall,
one who can wander in the obscure and dark shares the same light as the sun and moon.
Thus, using the Way as a fishing rod,
virtue as the line,
rites and music as the hook,
benevolence and righteousness as the bait,
cast it into the river,
float it upon the sea,
the myriad things teem and swarm,
which is not possessed by it!
Those who rely on the arts of tiptoeing and leaping,
lifting and pulling in the human realm,
probing and stirring the customs of the age,
groping and dragging the subtleties of things,
may still indulge their intentions,
fulfill their desires,
how much more so those who embrace the Way of rare treasures,
forget liver and gall,
cast aside ears and eyes,
alone float and roam beyond the realm of fixed directions,
not entangled with things in mutual decay,
inwardly leaning in the formless domain, harmonizing with heaven and earth!
If so,
they still their keen hearing and clear vision and embrace the great simplicity,
regarding benefit and harm as dust and grime,
death and life as day and night,
thus, though the eyes behold the forms of jade carriages, curved ivory,
the ears hear the sounds of "White Snow",
"Clear Horn",
these cannot disturb their spirit.
Climbing thousand-ren gorges,
facing cliffs that dizzy gibbons,
is not enough to disrupt their harmony.
It is like the jade of Zhōngshān,
fired with furnace charcoal,
for three days and three nights its color and luster do not change.
Then it is the essence of heaven and earth in utmost virtue.
Therefore, life is not enough to compel them,
how could benefit move them;
death is not enough to restrain them,
how could harm frighten them.
Understanding the distinction between life and death,
penetrating the changes of benefit and harm,
even with the greatness of all under heaven,
to exchange for a single hair on the shin,
nothing weighs on their will.
Nobility and baseness to the self,
are like the seasonal blowing of the条风 (east wind);
slander and praise to oneself,
are like the passing of a single mosquito or horsefly.
Holding to pure whiteness without blackening,
acting with purity without adulteration,
dwelling in profound darkness without obscurity,
resting in the heavenly balance without falsity,
Ménmén,
Zhōnglóng mountains cannot confine them,
only embodying the Way ensures不败 (not failing),
rushing rapids, swirling depths,
the depths of Lǚliáng cannot detain them,
the stone crevices of Tàiháng,
Fēihú,
Gōuzhù's perils cannot trouble them.
Therefore, while the body dwells above rivers and seas,
the spirit wanders below the Weique (towered gates).
Without attaining the one source,
who could reach this!
Therefore, dwelling with the utmost person,
makes families forget poverty,
makes kings and dukes disregard their nobility and wealth and delight in lowliness,
the brave see their vigor decline,
the greedy see their desires dissolve.
Sitting without teaching,
standing without discussing,
those who go empty return full,
thus without speaking, they can infuse others with harmony.
Therefore, the utmost Way is non-action,
now a dragon, now a snake,
expanding and contracting, coiling and stretching,
changing with the times.
Externally following the current,
internally preserving their nature,
ears and eyes not dazzled,
thoughts and plans not entangled.
Where their spirit dwells,
is in simplicity, roaming the great clarity,
guiding and shielding the myriad things,
all beauties sprout and grow.
Therefore, those who force their spirit find it departing,
those who rest their spirit find it abiding.
The Way emerges from one source,
penetrates the nine gates,
disperses through the six thoroughfares,
established in the realm without boundaries,
silent and desolate in emptiness and nothingness.
It does not act upon things,
yet things act by means of it.
Therefore, in undertaking affairs and following the Way,
it is not the Way that acts,
nor the Way that bestows.
What heaven covers,
earth supports,
the six directions encompass,
yin and yang breathe upon,
rain and dew moisten,
the Way and virtue uphold,
all these are born of one parent and pass through one harmony.
Thus, the locust tree and the orange and pomelo join as brothers,
the Yǒumiáo and Sānwēi connect as one family.
When the eyes watch the flight of swans,
the ears listen to the sounds of lutes and zithers,
yet the mind is at the passes of Yànmén,
within one body,
the spirit divides and separates,
within the six directions,
one movement covers thousands and tens of thousands of miles.
Therefore, viewing from their differences,
liver and gall are as distant as Hú and Yuè;
viewing from their similarities,
the myriad things are one circle.
The hundred schools differ in doctrines,
each has its origin,
as for Mò,
Yáng, Shēn,
Shāng in governance,
they are like one rib of a cover,
or one spoke of a wheel,
having them completes the count,
lacking them does not harm the function.
Yet they themselves think they exclusively possess it,
not comprehending the reality of heaven and earth.
Now when the smith casts vessels,
the metal leaps and dances in the furnace,
there must be waves and spills, some cast aside,
where it falls and congeals,
also takes the form of things.
Though their forms may have minor completeness,
yet they cannot be preserved like the Nine Tripods of the Zhōu house,
how much less compared to the standard forms?
Their distance from the Way is also great!
Now the myriad things with their sparse leaps and branching lifts,
the hundred affairs with their stems, leaves, and twining branches,
all originate from one root,
and branch out to thousands and tens of thousands.
Thus, there is that which receives,
but not that which bestows.
What is received is not bestowed, yet nothing is not received.
Nothing is not received,
like the dense gathering of encircling clouds,
widely nurturing and abundant, becoming rain,
soaking the myriad things without sharing their wetness.
Now the skilled archer has the measure of a standard,
as the craftsman has the rules of compass and square,
these all have something attained to reach the marvelous.
Yet Xīzhòng cannot become Féng Méng,
Zàofǔ cannot become Bólè,
this is because they understand one corner,
and do not penetrate the boundaries of all directions.
Now dyeing black with niè (black dye) yields black darker than niè,
dyeing blue with lán (indigo) yields blue bluer than lán.
Niè is not the black,
blue is not the lán,
here, though encountering their source, they cannot transform again.
Why is this?
To illustrate their transformation and increasing thinness.
How much more so for that which has never had niè or lán to create and transform it,
its transforming,
even engraving metal and stone,
writing on bamboo and silk,
how can they fully record its number!
From this perspective,
all things are born from existence,
and both small and large move with ease.
The tip of an autumn hair,
though it sinks into the infinitesimal, returns to the great;
the thickness of a reed stalk,
though it penetrates the void
and returns to the massive and solid.
As for what lacks the minuteness of an autumn hair
or the thickness of a reed stalk,
reaching everywhere without boundaries,
extending to the limitless,
with nothing to obstruct or hinder it—
its subtlety and profound mystery,
its stirring of all things,
its molding and transforming—
how could the space between heaven and earth suffice to describe it!
A swift wind can topple trees
but cannot pluck a single hair;
from the height of a cloud-capped tower,
one who falls may break their spine and shatter their skull,
yet a mosquito or midge can flutter safely there.
Sharing the workings of heaven with worms and grubs,
receiving form within the same circle,
those that are light, subtle, and minute
can still escape with their lives—
how much more so what has not yet taken form?
From this perspective,
the formless giving birth to the formed
is also clear.
Therefore, the sage lodges their spirit in the numinous chamber
and returns to the beginning of all things,
seeing into the dark and obscure,
listening to the soundless,
in the darkness alone perceiving dawn,
in the silence alone finding illumination.
Their use lies in not using,
and through not using, they can then use it;
their knowing lies in not knowing,
and through not knowing, they can then know it.
If heaven were not stable,
the sun and moon would have nothing to rest upon;
if earth were not stable,
plants and trees would have nothing to root in;
if what one stands on within oneself is not tranquil,
right and wrong would have no form.
Thus, only with a true person can there be true knowledge.
If what one holds is unclear,
how can one know whether what I call knowing is not unknowing?
Now, accumulating kindness and deep厚,
piling up love and layering grace,
using reputation and splendor to nurture and comfort the common people,
making them joyful,
so that they delight in their nature—
this is benevolence.
Achieving great deeds,
establishing illustrious fame,
embodying the roles of ruler and minister,
rectifying the distinctions above and below,
clarifying closeness and distance,
equalizing noble and base,
preserving endangered states,
continuing severed lineages,
resolving entanglements and managing complexities,
restoring destroyed clans,
establishing heirs for those without—
this is righteousness.
Closing the nine orifices,
concealing the heart's intentions,
discarding cleverness,
returning to无知,
wandering aimlessly beyond the dust of the world,
and drifting idly in the work of non-action,
embracing yin and exhaling yang,
so that all things harmonize and unite—
this is virtue.
Thus, the Way scatters and becomes virtue,
virtue overflows and becomes benevolence and righteousness,
and with the establishment of benevolence and righteousness, the Way and virtue are abandoned.
A tree of a hundred arm-spans,
cut down and made into a sacrificial vessel,
carved with chisels and knives,
adorned with blues and yellows,
decorated with brilliant patterns,
featuring dragons, snakes, tigers, and leopards,
curved into intricate designs—
yet if one section is left broken in a ditch,
comparing the sacrificial vessel to the broken piece in the ditch,
there is a distinction in ugliness and beauty,
but in losing the nature of the wood,
they are equal.
Therefore, those whose spirit has strayed speak flowery words,
and those whose virtue is dissipated act falsely.
When the utmost essence is lost within,
and speech and action are displayed outwardly,
this inevitably leads to the self being enslaved by things.
Those who pursue or reject false actions
seek essence outwardly;
essence can be depleted,
yet actions have no end,
thus confusing the mind and muddying the spirit,
and bewildering their root.
What they hold within is unstable,
and outwardly they are swept away by worldly customs;
the missteps they take are already decided,
and inwardly they muddy their clarity and brightness,
thus hesitating to the end,
without a moment of peace and tranquility.
Therefore, the sage cultivates the art of the Way within
and does not adorn themselves with benevolence and righteousness outwardly,
unconcerned with the delights of ears and eyes,
but roaming in the harmony of spirit and essence.
If so,
they probe down to the triple springs below,
seek up to the nine heavens above,
expand horizontally through the six directions,
and penetrate all things—
this is the roaming of the sage.
As for the true person,
they move and dissolve in the utmost emptiness,
and roam in the wilds of extinction and oblivion,
riding Feīlián and followed by Dūnyǔ,
galloping in outer realms,
resting in inner spaces,
illuminating the ten suns and commanding wind and rain,
employing Léigōng as a minister,
directing Kuāfù as a servant,
taking Fúfēi as a concubine,
and making Zhīnǚ their wife—
in the space between heaven and earth,
what could possibly detain their will!
Thus, emptiness and nothingness
are the abode of the Way,
and simplicity and ease
are the essence of the Way.
When people trouble their spirit and harass their essence,
scheming with cleverness and seeking outwardly,
they all lose their numinous brightness and depart from their dwelling.
Thus, the freezing borrow extra clothing from spring,
and the heat-stricken yearn for cool wind in autumn—
those who are ill within will surely show signs outwardly.
When the ash tree has verdant shade,
and the snail's slime cures eye ailments,
these are all medicines for the eyes.
If someone seeks these things without cause,
they must have something obscuring their sight.
What the sage uses to startle the world,
the true person has never bothered with;
what the worthy use to rectify the世俗,
the sage has never observed.
In a puddle left by a cow's hoof,
there is no carp a foot long;
on a small mound of a hill,
there is no timber of ten feet.
Why is this so?
Because their domain is too narrow
to contain anything vast and great.
How much more so for what is wrapped in nothingness!
This makes the potential of mountains and abysses far-reaching.
When people are constrained by the world,
their form is bound and their spirit leaks away,
so they cannot avoid emptiness.
If I can be tethered and bridled,
it must be that my fate lies outwardly.
In the age of perfect virtue,
people rested peacefully in the realm of boundless chaos,
and wandered freely in the vast expanse of the universe,
holding heaven and earth in their hands while entrusting all things to their natural course,
taking the primordial mist as their guiding pillar,
and floating aimlessly in the realm without boundaries.
Thus, when the sage breathed the energies of yīn and yáng,
all living beings looked up with reverence,
admiring his virtue and harmonizing with it.
At that time,
no one governed or managed,
yet everything separated and concealed itself, forming naturally,
in a state of primal simplicity and vastness,
where unadulterated innocence remained intact,
blending into a unified whole,
and all things flourished abundantly.
Hence, even with the wisdom of Yì, there was no use for it.
As the world declined,
reaching the time of Fúxī shì,
his way was obscure and indistinct,
embodying virtue and harmony,
yet his influence was profound and intense,
and knowledge began to sprout faintly and vigorously,
with everyone seeking to shed their childlike ignorance,
awakening to observe the space between heaven and earth,
thus their virtue became fragmented and could not unite.
By the time of Shénnóng
and Huángdì,
they analyzed and distinguished the great ancestors,
comprehended the workings of heaven and earth,
followed the nine orifices,
emphasized the nine mounds,
upheld yīn and yáng,
balanced hardness and softness,
branching out and connecting like leaves,
for all things and myriad clans,
establishing order and structure for each,
at which point the people gazed in awe and wonder,
all straining to listen and watch intently,
thus there was governance but no harmony.
Descending further to the eras of Kūnwú
and Xiàhòu,
desires became entangled with material things,
senses were lured by external temptations,
and the innate nature lost its proper state.
Extending to the Zhōu dynasty,
purity was diluted and simplicity scattered,
diverging from the way through artifice,
practicing virtue with frugality,
and cunning schemes began to emerge.
As the Zhōu house declined and the kingly way was abandoned,
the Rú and Mò schools started to debate the way in rows,
dividing followers and disputing.
Then, with broad learning, they doubted the sages,
used flowery falsehoods to intimidate the masses,
with music and dance,
embellishing the "Shī"
and "Shū",
to buy fame and reputation under heaven.
They elaborated on rituals of ascent and descent,
adorned with ceremonial robes and caps,
gathering crowds insufficient to exhaust their variations,
accumulating wealth inadequate to cover their expenses,
thus the people began to strive and stretch,
each wanting to exercise their cunning artifices,
seeking to fit into the world like a peg in a hole and scrambling for fame and profit,
so the masses wandered into the marshes of excess and disorder,
losing the root of the great ancestor.
The reason the world loses its innate nature,
is due to a gradual decline that made it so,
a process that has been long in the making.
Therefore, the learning of the sage
aims to return nature to its origin,
and let the mind wander in emptiness.
The learning of the enlightened person
seeks to connect nature with the vast expanse,
and awaken in solitude and silence.
As for the learning of the vulgar world, it is not so;
it plucks at virtue and uproots nature,
internally distressing the five organs,
externally exhausting the ears and eyes,
then begins to stir up the finest details of things,
shaking and discarding rén, yì, lǐ, and yuè,
flaunting actions and wisdom across the world,
to attract fame and reputation in society.
This is what I am ashamed of and will not do.
Thus, rather than possessing the world,
it is better to have understanding;
rather than having understanding,
it is better to wander through the beginnings and ends of things,
and comprehend the boundary between being and non-being.
Therefore, if the whole world praises him, he is not encouraged;
if the whole world blames him, he is not discouraged;
settled in the realm of life and death,
and penetrating the principle of honor and disgrace,
even if blazing fires and floods spread across the world,
his spirit remains undiminished within his breast.
If so,
he views the space under heaven
as no more than flying feathers or floating dust,
who would busily bother with material affairs?
Water's nature is truly clear, but soil muddies it;
human nature is tranquil, but desires disrupt it.
What humans receive from heaven—
the ears and eyes for sounds and sights,
the mouth and nose for flavors and smells,
the skin for cold and warmth—
their inherent tendencies are the same,
yet some connect with divine clarity,
while others cannot avoid folly or madness.
Why is this?
Because what controls them differs.
Thus, the spirit is the deep pool of wisdom;
when the spirit is clear, wisdom is bright.
Wisdom is
the storehouse of the heart;
when wisdom is impartial, the heart is calm.
No one uses flowing water as a mirror,
but still water for reflection,
because of its stillness;
no one views their form in crude iron,
but in a bright mirror,
because of its smoothness.
Only when smooth and still
can it reveal the nature and essence of things.
From this perspective,
what is used must rely on what is not used;
thus, an empty room generates brightness,
and auspiciousness dwells there.
A clear mirror cannot be soiled by dust and grime;
a clear spirit cannot be disturbed by desires.
If the essence and spirit have already strayed outward,
and one tries to bring them back through effort,
this is to lose the root
and seek it in the branches.
Without harmony between inner and outer, yet wanting to engage with things,
dimming one's profound light to seek knowledge through ears and eyes,
is to abandon clarity
and follow darkness,
this is called losing the way.
When the heart focuses on something, the spirit sighs and resides there;
returning to emptiness, it dissolves and extinguishes,
this is the wandering of the sage.
Therefore, in ancient times, to govern the world,
one must comprehend the essence of innate nature.
Their actions and measures may not be the same,
but their alignment with the way is one.
Not wearing fur in summer
is not out of frugality,
but because heat is abundant on the body.
Not using a fan in winter
is not out of disdain,
but because coolness is sufficient for comfort.
The sage eats according to his appetite,
clothes himself according to his form,
moderating only for himself—
how could greedy and corrupt thoughts arise?
Thus, those who can possess the world
are surely those who do not act for the sake of the world;
those who can have fame and reputation
are surely those who do not strive to seek it.
The sage has a means of attainment;
once attained, the heart of desires is externalized.
The disciples of Kǒng
and Mò
all taught the ways of rén and yì to the world,
yet they could not avoid weariness.
They themselves could not practice it,
let alone those they taught?
Why is this?
Because their way is external.
Trying to return to the root through the branches,
even Xǔ Yóu could not accomplish it,
how much less the common people!
If one truly comprehends the essence of innate nature,
then rén and yì will naturally adhere,
and choices of pursuit or avoidance cannot disturb the heart!
If the spirit has nothing to conceal,
the heart has nothing to carry,
penetrating and unobstructed,
serene and free of affairs,
with no stagnation,
empty and still in waiting,
then power and profit cannot tempt,
eloquent debaters cannot persuade,
music and beauty cannot corrupt,
the attractive cannot seduce,
the wise cannot sway,
the brave cannot intimidate—
this is the wanderings of the True Person.
In such a state,
they mold and transform all things,
companion with the Creator,
between heaven and earth,
within the cosmos,
none can cut short or obstruct.
That which transforms life does not die,
and that which transforms things does not change;
their spirit passes through Líshān
and Tàiháng without difficulty,
enters the four seas and nine rivers without getting wet,
dwells in narrow confines without being blocked,
spans between heaven and earth without gaps.
One who fails to understand this,
even if their eyes count thousands of sheep in a herd,
their ears distinguish the eight winds' harmonies,
their feet tread the dance of "Yáng'ē",
and their hands follow the rhythms of "Lǜshuǐ",
their wisdom encompassing heaven and earth,
their brightness illuminating sun and moon,
their arguments unraveling linked rings,
their words polishing jade and stone,
still brings no benefit to governing the world.
Tranquil serenity and quiet calm
are means to nurture one's nature;
harmony, joy, emptiness, and non-being
are means to cultivate virtue.
When the external does not disturb the internal,
then nature attains its proper state;
when nature does not stir harmony,
then virtue rests securely in its place.
Nourishing life to manage the world,
embracing virtue to complete one's years—
this may be called embodying the Dào.
In such a case,
blood vessels have no congestion,
the five organs have no stagnant energy,
fortune and misfortune cannot disturb,
blame and praise cannot soil,
thus one can reach the ultimate.
Without the right era,
who can succeed?
Having the right person but not meeting the right time,
even they cannot escape,
how much more so without the Dào?
Moreover, in human disposition,
ears and eyes respond to stimulation,
the heart-mind knows worry and joy,
hands and feet scratch itches
and avoid cold and heat—
these are how we interact with things.
When bees and scorpions sting fingers, the spirit cannot remain calm;
when mosquitoes and gadflies bite skin, the nature cannot stay peaceful.
The coming of worry and harm
disturbs the human heart—
not merely the sting of bees and scorpions or the bite of mosquitoes and gadflies—
yet wanting tranquil emptiness and non-being,
how can one achieve it?
One who examines the tip of an autumn hair with their eyes
cannot hear the sound of thunder;
one who harmonizes with the tones of jade and stone with their ears
cannot see the form of Tài Shān.
Why so?
When focused on the small, the large is forgotten.
Now when all things come,
plucking at our nature,
snatching away our disposition,
like a spring's source,
even if we wish not to receive,
how can we avoid it?
Consider tree planters:
watering them with fresh water,
enriching them with fertile soil,
ten people nurturing them,
but one person uproots them—
then surely no sapling remains,
how much more when a whole country cuts them down?
Even wanting long life,
how could it be possible?
Now a basin of water in the courtyard,
cleared all day,
may not reflect eyebrows and lashes;
but cloud it with one stir,
and it cannot show square or round.
The human spirit is easily clouded, hard to clear—
much like the basin of water.
With a whole world stirring and disturbing it,
how can it have even a moment's calm?
In the age of highest virtue in ancient times,
traders found convenience in their shops,
farmers enjoyed their work,
officials were content in their posts,
and recluses followed their path.
At that time,
wind and rain caused no destruction,
plants and trees suffered no premature death,
the Nine Tripods were weighty,
pearls and jade were lustrous,
the Luò River yielded the "Red Text",
the Yellow River produced the "Green Chart",
thus Xǔ Yóu,
Fāng Huí,
Shàn Juǎn,
and Pī Yī could attain the Dào.
Why so?
Because the rulers of the world had hearts wishing to benefit all under heaven,
thus people found joy therein.
The talents of these four men
were not necessarily perfect,
compared to today's world,
yet none can match their brilliance—
they met the time of Táng
and Yú.
When it came to Xià Jié
and Yīn Zhòu,
burning people alive,
executing remonstrators,
creating the roasting pillar,
casting bronze columns,
cutting out wise men's hearts,
breaking scholars' shins,
mincing Guǐ Hóu's daughter,
salting Méi Bó's remains.
At that time,
Yáo Shān collapsed,
the three rivers dried up,
birds had broken wings,
beasts had crippled legs.
At that time,
were there no sages?
Yet they could not penetrate the Dào
because they did not meet the right era.
When birds fly a thousand ren high,
beasts run through thickets,
calamity still reaches them—
how much more the common registered people?
From this we see:
embodying the Dào does not depend solely on oneself,
but also connects to the era.
The city of Lìyáng,
in one night overturned and became a lake,
where the brave and strong, the wise and sagacious, perished together with the cowardly and worthless.
On the mountains of Wūshān,
when fire is set with the wind,
the precious Xià and purple zhī orchids die along with the common wormwood.
Thus, the river fish cannot see clearly,
and young crops cannot grow in season,
for such is the nature of their environment.
Hence, in an orderly age, the foolish cannot alone cause chaos;
in a chaotic age, the wise cannot alone bring order.
To be trapped in a turbid world
and blame the Way for not prevailing
is like hobbling a qíjì horse
and yet expecting it to cover a thousand miles.
Place a monkey in a cage,
and it becomes like a pig—
not that it lacks skill and agility,
but it has no means to exercise its abilities.
When Shùn tilled the land and made pottery,
he could not benefit his village;
facing south as king,
his virtue spread across the four seas.
It was not that his benevolence increased,
but his position was advantageous and influential.
The ancient sages,
their harmony and tranquility,
were innate to their nature;
their aspirations fulfilled and the Way practiced,
were matters of fate.
Thus, nature encounters fate before it can act,
and fate attains nature before it can be clear.
A Wūhào bow
or a Xīzǐ crossbow
cannot shoot without a string.
Yuè boats and Shǔ rafts
cannot float without water.
Now, with arrows and strings set above
and nets spread below,
even if one wishes to soar,
how can the situation allow it?
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
"I gather and gather the mouse-ear,
but cannot fill my slanting basket.
Alas, I think of my beloved,
and place it there on the Zhou road."
This speaks of yearning for distant ages.
Before heaven and earth took form,
it was vast and boundless,
profound and murky,
thus called the Great Beginning.
The Great Beginning produced the Void and Expanse,
the Void and Expanse produced the cosmos,
the cosmos produced the primal qi.
The primal qi had limits and boundaries;
the light and pure spread thinly to become heaven,
the heavy and turbid congealed to become earth.
The union of the subtle and pure was easy,
the congealing of the heavy and turbid was difficult,
hence heaven formed first and earth settled later.
The essence of heaven and earth merging became yin and yang;
the concentrated essence of yin and yang became the four seasons;
the dispersed essence of the four seasons became the myriad things.
The accumulated heat of yang over time produced fire;
the essence of fire became the sun;
the accumulated cold of yin over time became water;
the essence of water became the moon.
The excessive and essential qi of the sun and moon became the stars.
Heaven receives the sun, moon, and stars;
earth receives water, floods, dust, and debris.
In ancient times, Gònggōng contended with Zhuānxū to become emperor;
in anger, he struck Mount Bùzhōu,
breaking the pillars of heaven,
and severing the cords of earth.
Heaven tilted to the northwest,
so the sun, moon, and stars move there;
earth became incomplete in the southeast,
so waters, floods, dust, and debris gather there.
The way of heaven is round;
the way of earth is square.
The square governs darkness;
the round governs light.
Light
emits qi,
hence fire and the sun cast light outward;
darkness
contains qi,
hence water and the moon hold light within.
Emitting qi gives forth;
containing qi transforms;
thus yang gives and yin transforms.
The biased qi of heaven and earth,
when agitated, becomes wind;
the harmonious qi of heaven and earth,
when balanced, becomes rain.
Yin and yang pressing against each other
induce thunder,
excite into lightning,
and chaos into fog.
When yang qi prevails, it disperses as dew and rain;
when yin qi prevails, it congeals as frost and snow.
Feathered creatures,
being of the flying kind,
thus belong to yang.
Scaled and shelled creatures,
being of the hibernating kind,
thus belong to yin.
The sun,
as the master of yang,
causes beasts to shed in spring and summer,
and when the solstice comes,
deer shed their antlers.
The moon, as the source of yin,
causes fish brains to diminish as it wanes,
and when the moon dies, snails and clams wither.
Fire flares upward,
water flows downward,
hence birds move high,
and fish move low.
Things of similar kind influence each other,
root and tip respond to one another;
thus, a yang sui mirror facing the sun ignites fire,
a fangzhu mirror facing the moon produces water,
a tiger's roar brings the valley wind,
a dragon's rise summons the radiant clouds,
qílín fighting causes eclipses of the sun and moon,
a whale's death brings forth comets,
a silkworm spinning signals the breaking of the shāng string,
a falling star foretells the bursting of the Bohai Sea.
The ruler's sentiments,
connecting upward to heaven,
thus executing tyrants brings many whirlwinds,
perverting laws brings many pests,
killing the innocent leaves the land barren,
and unenforced orders bring excessive rain.
The four seasons
are heaven's officials;
the sun and moon
are heaven's envoys;
the stars
are heaven's markers;
rainbows and comets
are heaven's taboos.
Heaven has nine fields,
nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine corners,
five hundred million miles from earth.
There are the five stars,
eight winds, ,
five offices,
six treasuries,
the Zǐ Palace,
Tàiwēi,
Xuānyuán,
Xiánchí,
four guardians,
and the Heavenly River.
What are the nine fields?
The center is called Jūntiān,
its stars Jiǎo,
Kàng, Dǐ.
The east is called Cāngtiān,
its stars Fáng,
Xīn, .
The northeast is called Biàntiān,
its stars Wěi,
Jī, Dǒu,
Qiānniú.
The north is called Xuántiān,
its stars Xūnǚ,
Xū, Wēi,
Yíngshì.
The northwest is called Yōutiān,
its stars Dōngbì,
Kuí, Lóu.
The west is called Hàotiān,
its stars Wèi,
Mǎo, Bì.
The southwest is called Zhūtiān,
its stars Zīxī,
Shēn, Dōngjǐng.
The south is called Yántiān,
its stars Yúguǐ,
Liǔ, Qīxīng.
The southeast is called Yángtiān,
its stars Zhāng,
Yì, Zhěn.
What are the Five Stars?
The East
corresponds to Wood.
Its Emperor is Tàihào,
his assistant is Gōumáng,
who holds the compass and governs spring.
Its deity is the Year Star (Jupiter),
its beast is the Azure Dragon,
its musical note is Jué,
its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
The South,
corresponds to Fire,
