its Emperor is Yándì,
his assistant is Zhūmíng,
who holds the balance and governs summer.
Its deity is the Sparkling Deluder (Mars),
its beast is the Vermilion Bird,
its musical note is Zhǐ,
its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
The Center,
corresponds to Earth,
its Emperor is Huángdì,
his assistant is Hòutǔ,
who holds the plumb line and controls the four directions.
Its deity is the Quelling Star (Saturn),
its beast is the Yellow Dragon,
its musical note is Gōng,
its days are Wù and Jǐ.
The West,
corresponds to Metal,
its Emperor is Shǎohào,
his assistant is Rùshōu,
who holds the square and governs autumn.
Its deity is the Great White (Venus),
its beast is the White Tiger,
its musical note is Shāng,
its days are Gēng and Xīn.
The North,
corresponds to Water,
its Emperor is Zhuānxū,
his assistant is Xuánmíng,
who holds the weight and governs winter.
Its deity is the Chronograph Star (Mercury),
its beast is the Dark Warrior,
its musical note is Yǔ,
its days are Rén and Guǐ.
When Tàiyīn is at the four midpoints,
the Year Star moves through three constellations;
when Tàiyīn is at the four hooks,
the Year Star moves through two constellations.
Two times eight is sixteen,
three times four is twelve,
thus in twelve years it traverses the twenty-eight constellations.
It moves one-twelfth of a degree daily,
and thirty and seven-sixteenths degrees annually,
completing a celestial cycle in twelve years.
The Sparkling Deluder always enters Tàiwēi in the tenth month to receive orders before proceeding among the constellations,
overseeing lawless states,
causing chaos and rebellion,
disease and bereavement,
famine and warfare,
appearing and disappearing irregularly,
changing its color distinctly,
sometimes visible, sometimes hidden.
The Quelling Star begins its cycle from the Dipper in the Jiǎyín epoch,
stationing in one constellation each year,
if it fails to occupy its due position,
the state loses territory;
if it occupies a position not due,
the state gains land,
and the harvest is abundant.
It moves one-twenty-eighth of a degree daily,
and thirteen and five-one hundred twelfth degrees annually,
completing a celestial cycle in twenty-eight years.
The Great White begins in the first month of the Jiǎyín epoch,
appearing in the east at dawn with the Room constellation,
for two hundred forty days before setting,
then after one hundred twenty days, appearing in the west at dusk,
for two hundred forty days before setting,
and after thirty-five days, reappearing in the east.
It rises at Chén and Xū,
and sets at Chǒu and Wèi.
If it appears or sets untimely,
or enters untimely,
the world lays down arms;
if it fails to set when due,
or fails to rise when due,
the world takes up arms.
The Chronograph Star rectifies the four seasons,
often appearing at the spring equinox in the second month near Quad
and Harness, at the summer solstice in the fifth month near Eastern Well
and Ghost,
at the autumn equinox in the eighth month near Horn
and Neck, and at the winter solstice in the eleventh month near Dipper
and Ox.
It rises at Chén and Xū,
and sets at Chǒu and Wèi,
appearing for twenty days before setting.
Observe it in the east at dawn,
and in the west at dusk.
If it fails to appear in one season,
that season is disharmonious;
if it fails to appear in all four seasons,
the world suffers great famine.
What are the Eight Winds?
Forty-five days after the winter solstice, the Tiáo Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Tiáo Wind, the Míngshù Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Míngshù Wind, the Qīngmíng Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Qīngmíng Wind, the Jǐng Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Jǐng Wind, the Liáng Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Liáng Wind, the Chānghé Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Chānghé Wind, the Bùzhōu Wind arrives;
forty-five days after the Bùzhōu Wind, the Guǎngmò Wind arrives.
When the Tiáo Wind comes, light prisoners are released,
and delays are removed.
When the Míngshù Wind comes, borders are corrected,
and fields are cultivated.
When the Qīngmíng Wind comes, silks and gifts are presented,
and envoys are sent to the feudal lords.
When the Jǐng Wind comes, ranks are conferred on the worthy,
and the meritorious are rewarded.
When the Liáng Wind comes, the earth's bounty is acknowledged,
and sacrifices are made to the four directions.
When the Chānghé Wind comes, hanging decorations are taken down,
and lutes and zithers are not played.
When the Bùzhōu Wind comes, palaces and houses are repaired,
and border walls are fortified.
When the Guǎngmò Wind comes, passes and bridges are closed,
and punishments are executed.
What are the Five Offices?
The East is for Agriculture,
the South is for the Minister of War,
the West is for Justice,
the North is for Public Works,
and the Center is for the Capital.
What are the Six Treasuries?
Zǐ-Wǔ,
Chǒu-Wèi,
Yín-Shēn,
Mǎo-Yǒu,
Chén-Xū,
and Sì-Hài are they.
Tàiwēi
is the court of Tàiyī.
Zǐgōng
is the residence of Tàiyī.
Xuānyuán
is the abode of the imperial consorts.
Xiánchí

When the Great Yin is at Jiǎzǐ,
punishment and virtue combine in the eastern palace,
always moving to the unconquered,
combining for four years then separating,
separating for sixteen years then reuniting.
The reason for separation is
that punishment cannot enter the central palace,
and moves to wood.
Where the Great Yin resides,
the day is virtue,
the hour is punishment.
Virtue doubles itself on strong days,
and moves to the unconquered on weak days.
Punishment: water hour's wood,
wood hour's water,
metal and fire stand in their places.
In moving all deities,
the Vermilion Bird is one ahead of the Great Yin,
the Hooked Array three behind,
the Dark Warrior five ahead,
the White Tiger six behind,
and the Void Star riding the Hooked Array brings heaven and earth into harmony.
For days,
Jiǎ is strong, Yǐ is weak,
Bǐng is strong, Dīng is weak,
continuing through Rén and Guǐ.
Wood is born at Hài,
flourishes at Mǎo,
dies at Wèi,
these three hours all belong to wood.
Fire is born at Yín,
flourishes at Wǔ,
dies at Xū,
these three hours all belong to fire.
Earth is born at Wǔ,
flourishes at Xū,
dies at Yín,
these three hours all belong to earth.
Metal is born at Sì,
flourishes at Yǒu,
dies at Chǒu,
these three hours all belong to metal.
Water is born at Shēn,
flourishes at Zǐ,
dies at Chén,
these three hours all belong to water.
Thus, the five elements are born at one,
flourish at five,
end at nine;
five times nine is forty-five,
so deities move every forty-five days;
with three responding to five,
thus eight moves complete the year.
When using the Great Yin,
keep punishment to the right and behind,
virtue to the left and ahead,
strike the opposing hour of the Hooked Array,
and in battle you will surely win,
in attack you will surely conquer.
To understand the way of heaven,
take the sun as the master,
in the sixth month it aligns with the heart,
circling leftward,
dividing into twelve months,
corresponding with the sun,
heaven and earth doubly harmonized,
ensuring no future calamity.

Where the Year Star resides,

its opposite is the conflict,
bringing calamity to the year.
If it should reside but does not,
moving instead to another place,
it portends the death of the ruler and the fall of the state.
When the Great Yin governs spring, it favors kindness, gentleness, and warmth;
when it governs summer, it favors generosity and clarity;
when it governs autumn, it favors preparation and military readiness;
when it governs winter, it favors fierceness, resolve, and strength.
Every three years, the seasons shift;
every six years, the norms change;
thus, every three years, there is one famine;
every six years, one decline;
every twelve years, one prosperity.

When the child generates the mother, it is called Righteousness;
when the mother generates the child, it is called Nurturance;
when child and mother harmonize, it is called Focus;
when the mother overcomes the child, it is called Restraint;
when the child overcomes the mother, it is called Distress.
Acting with Restraint leads to victory without retribution.
Engaging with Focus in affairs
brings success.
Following Righteousness in principle
establishes fame without decline.
Using Nurturance to cultivate
causes all things to thrive.
Initiating actions in Distress
leads to ruin and death.
The deities of the Northern Dipper have masculine and feminine aspects,
beginning in Zǐ in the eleventh month,
moving one celestial branch each month,
the masculine moving left,
the feminine moving right,
meeting in Wǔ in the fifth month,
planning punishments;
meeting in Zǐ in the eleventh month,
planning virtue.
The branch where the feminine resides is the aversion day,
on which no affairs should be undertaken.
The cosmos moves steadily,
the masculine knowing the feminine by sound,
thus creating extraordinary branches.
The count starts from Jiǎzǐ,
child and mother seek each other,
their meeting points are called unions.
With ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches,
a cycle of sixty days,
there are eight unions in total.
If the union falls before the year, it brings death;
if after the year, there is no calamity.

Heaven and Earth being established,

Yáng is born from Yīn,
Yīn is born from Yáng.
Yīn and Yáng intertwine,

Some die, some live,

Orifices and limbs,

Heaven has four seasons,

Heaven has twelve months,
controlling three hundred sixty days,
humans also have twelve limbs,
to operate three hundred sixty joints.
Thus, acting against Heaven's order
is opposing life itself.

To determine east and west,
first erect a gnomon in the east,
hold another gnomon ten steps back from the first,
and observe the sun rising at the northern edge.
When the sun sets directly,
erect another gnomon in the east,
using the western gnomon to observe the sun setting at the northern edge,
then fix the midpoint between the two eastern gnomons,
and the western gnomon,
thus determining true east and west.
On the winter solstice,
the sun rises in the southeast,
sets in the southwest.
At the spring
and autumn equinoxes,
the sun rises due east,
sets due west.
On the summer solstice,
it rises in the northeast,
sets in the northwest.
Then due south is determined.
To know the measurements of east-west and north-south distances,
erect four gnomons forming a one-lǐ square,
ten-some days before the spring or autumn equinox,
from the north gnomon observe the sun's first appearance and dawn,
awaiting correspondence,
correspondence means alignment with the sun.
Then use the south gnomon for observation,
using the entry number of the front gnomon as divisor,
subtract the width,
subtract the gnomon's length,
to know the east-west distance from here.
Suppose observing sunrise,
enters the front gnomon by one cùn,
then one cùn equals one lǐ.
One lǐ accumulates eighteen thousand cùn,
thus eastward from here is eighteen thousand lǐ.
Observing sunset,
enters the front gnomon by half a cùn,
then half cùn equals one lǐ.
Half cùn subtracts one lǐ,
accumulated cùn gives thirty-six thousand lǐ,
subtracted gives the westward distance from here.
Combine them,
the east-west distance in lǐ,
is the extreme diameter.
Before spring equinox and aligned,
after autumn equinox and not aligned,
this place is south.
Before autumn equinox and aligned,
after spring equinox and not aligned,
this place is north.
At equinox or solstice and aligned,
this place is the north-south center.
From the center, to know due south,
before autumn equinox and not aligned,
this place is the north-south center.
From the center, to know the north-south extremes' distances,
from the southwest gnomon observe the sun,
on summer solstice sunrise aligns with the north gnomon,
then east equals northeast gnomon,
due east eighteen thousand lǐ,
then from center north also eighteen thousand lǐ.
Double it,
the north-south distance in lǐ.
If not from the center,
adjust by the front gnomon's entry/exit number,
gnomon enters one cùn,
cùn decreases sun's proximity by one lǐ,
gnomon exits one cùn,
cùn increases distance by one lǐ.
To know the height of the sky,
set up a gnomon one zhang high,
align it due north and south a thousand li apart,
and measure their shadows on the same day.
The northern gnomon's shadow is two chi,
the southern gnomon's shadow is one chi nine cun,
meaning for every thousand li south, the shadow shortens by one cun.
At twenty thousand li south, there is no shadow,
which is directly under the sun.
With a shadow of two chi and a height of one zhang,
the ratio is one to five for southward distance versus height.
Thus, take the number of li from here to the point under the sun,
multiply it by five,
resulting in one hundred thousand li,
which is the height of the sky.
If the shadow equals the gnomon's height,
then the height equals the distance.

Encompassing within the four seas,
it is twenty-eight thousand li from east to west,
twenty-six thousand li from north to south,
with waterways of eight thousand li,
six major valleys,
six hundred famous rivers,
and land routes of three thousand li.
Yǔ then sent Tàizhāng to pace from the eastern extreme,
to the western extreme,
a distance of two hundred and thirty-three thousand five hundred li and seventy-five steps;
he sent Shùhài to pace from the northern extreme,
to the southern extreme,
a distance of two hundred and thirty-three thousand five hundred li and seventy-five steps.
All deep waters and marshes,
from three ren or more in depth,
number two hundred and thirty-three thousand five hundred and fifty-nine.
Yǔ then used fertile soil to fill the floodwaters, creating famous mountains,
and excavated the base of Kūnlún to lower the land.
Within it was a layered city ninefold,
its height ten thousand one hundred and fourteen li, two steps, and six cun,
upon which grew the Tree of Grain,
its length five xún.
Pearl trees,
jade trees,
gem trees,
and the immortal tree were to its west;
shātáng trees
and lánggān trees to its east;
crimson trees to its south;
green trees
and yáo trees to its north.
Beside it were four hundred and forty gates,
each gate spaced four li apart,
each li interval nine chún,
each chún one zhang five chi.
Beside it were nine jade wells,
guarding its northwestern corner,
with the north gate open to admit the Bùzhōu wind.
Leaning Palace,
Whirling Chamber,
Hanging Garden,
Cool Breeze,
and Fántóng were within the Kūnlún's main gate,

The pond of Shū Garden,
soaked by Yellow Water,
with Yellow Water circling three times and returning to its source,
is called White Water,
emerging from the origin of Kūnlún,
and drinking it grants immortality.
Héshuǐ emerges from the northeastern corner of Kūnlún,
pierces the Vast Sea,
and enters the Jīshí Mountain channeled by Yǔ.
Chìshuǐ emerges from its southeastern corner,
flowing southwest into the eastern part of Dān Marsh in the Southern Sea. ,
Ruòshuǐ emerges from its southwestern corner, , , (
its remnants enter the Flowing Sands) ,
crosses the Flowing Sands,
and reaches the Southern Sea.
Yángshuǐ emerges from its northwestern corner,
entering south of Yǔmín in the Southern Sea.

are the divine springs of the Emperor,
used to blend all medicines,
and moisten all things.
The hill of Kūnlún,

If one ascends double that height,

If one ascends double that height,

The beautiful things of the southwest
include the metal and stones from Huàshān.
The beautiful things of the west
include the pearls and jade from Huòshān.
The beautiful things of the northwest
include the Qiúlín and
Lánggān from Kūnlúnxū.
The beautiful things of the north
include the sinews and horns from Yōudū.
The beautiful things of the northeast
include the patterned furs from Chìshān.
The beautiful things of the central region
include Dàiyuè,
where the five grains, mulberry, and hemp grow,
and from which fish and salt emerge.
Regarding all geographical features:
east-west is the weft,
north-south is the warp;
mountains accumulate virtue,
rivers accumulate punishment;
high places foster life,
low places foster death;
hills are male,
valleys are female;
where water curves round, pearls are found;
where it bends sharply, jade is found;
clear waters hold gold,
dragon abysses hold jade essence.
The land gives birth to people according to its type;
thus, mountain qi tends to produce males,
marsh qi tends to produce females,
miasmatic qi tends to produce mutes,
windy qi tends to produce deafness,
forest qi tends to produce cripples,
woody qi tends to produce hunchbacks,
low-lying qi tends to produce swelling,
rocky qi tends to produce strength,
rugged qi tends to produce goiters,
hot qi tends to produce premature death,
cold qi tends to produce longevity,
valley qi tends to produce numbness,
hill qi tends to produce lameness,
level qi tends to produce benevolence,
mound qi tends to produce greed,
light soil tends to produce sharpness,
heavy soil tends to produce slowness,
clear waters make small sounds,
turbid waters make loud sounds,
rapid waters make people light,
slow waters make people heavy,
central soil tends to produce sages.
All reflect their qi,
all correspond to their kind.
Thus, the south has undying grass,
the north has unmelting ice,
the east has the land of gentlemen,
the west has the corpses of the punished and maimed.
Sleeping straight brings direct dreams,
when people die, they become ghosts,
magnetite flies upward,
mica attracts water,
earthen dragons summon rain,
swallows and wild geese fly in turns,
clams, mussels, pearls, and turtles
wax and wane with the moon.
Therefore, people of hard soil are firm,
people of soft soil are brittle;
people of loam are large,
people of sandy soil are fine;
people of fertile soil are beautiful,
people of barren soil are ugly.
Those who eat water are good swimmers and can endure cold,
those who eat earth have no heart but are wise,
those who eat wood are strong and explosive,
those who eat grass are good runners but foolish,
those who eat mulberry produce silk and become moths,
those who eat meat are brave and fierce,
those who consume qi are divine and long-lived,
those who eat grains are intelligent but short-lived,
those who eat nothing are deathless and godlike.
All people, birds, beasts, myriad things, and insects,
each have their means of life,
some odd, some even,
some flying, some running,
none know their true nature.
Only those who understand the Dao
can trace them to their origins.
Heaven is one, earth is two, humanity is three,
three times three makes nine.
Nine times nine is eighty-one,
one governs the sun,
the sun's number is ten,
the sun governs humans,
thus humans are born in ten months.
Eight times nine is seventy-two,
two governs even numbers,
even numbers complement odd numbers,
odd numbers govern the celestial bodies,
the celestial bodies govern the moon,
the moon governs horses,
thus horses are born in twelve months.
Seven times nine is sixty-three,
three governs the Dipper,
the Dipper governs dogs,
thus dogs are born in three months.
Six times nine is fifty-four,
four governs seasons,
seasons govern pigs,
thus pigs are born in four months.
Five times nine is forty-five,
five governs musical notes,
musical notes govern apes,
thus apes are born in five months.
Four times nine is thirty-six,
six governs pitch pipes,
pitch pipes govern elk and deer,
thus elk and deer are born in six months.
Three times nine is twenty-seven,
seven governs stars,
stars govern tigers,
thus tigers are born in seven months.
Two times nine is eighteen,
eight governs wind,
wind governs insects,
thus insects transform in eight days.
Birds and fish are both born from yin,
but belong to yang,
thus birds and fish are all oviparous.
Fish swim in water,
birds fly in clouds,
thus at the beginning of winter, swallows and sparrows enter the sea,
transforming into clams.
All living things are born into different categories:
silkworms eat but do not drink,
cicadas drink but do not eat,
mayflies neither drink nor eat,
shelled and scaly creatures eat in summer and hibernate in winter.
Swallowers have eight orifices and are oviparous,
chewers have nine orifices and are viviparous.
Four-legged creatures have no wings,
horned creatures lack upper teeth;
hornless creatures are greasy and lack front teeth,
horned creatures are fatty and lack back teeth.
Those born during the day resemble the father,
those born at night resemble the mother.
Extreme yin produces females,
extreme yang produces males.
Bears and brown bears hibernate,
migratory birds move with the seasons.
Therefore, white waters are suitable for jade,
black waters for whetstones,
blue waters for green jade,
red waters for cinnabar,
yellow waters for gold,
clear waters for turtles;
Fénshuǐ is turbid and suitable for hemp,
Jǐshuǐ is harmonious and suitable for wheat,
Héshuǐ is balanced and suitable for beans,
Luòshuǐ is light and swift and suitable for millet,
Wèishuǐ is powerful and suitable for broomcorn millet,
Hànshuǐ is stable and suitable for bamboo,
Jiāngshuǐ is fertile and benevolent and suitable for rice.
People of the central plains,
are intelligent and suited to the five grains.
The east is where rivers and valleys flow into,
and where the sun and moon rise,
its people have pointed heads and small skulls,
prominent noses and large mouths,
hawk-like shoulders and tiptoe walking,
their orifices connect to the eyes,
their tendons and qi belong there,
green color governs the liver,
they grow tall early and are knowledgeable but not long-lived;
the land is suitable for wheat,
with many tigers and leopards.
The south is where yang qi accumulates,
occupied by heat and humidity,
its people have elongated bodies and pointed upper parts,
large mouths and wide-eyed gazes,
their orifices connect to the ears,
their blood vessels belong there,
red color governs the heart,
they mature early but die young;
the land is suitable for rice,
with many rhinoceroses and elephants.
The west has high lands,
where rivers and valleys emerge,
and where the sun and moon set,
its people have square faces and slightly hunched backs,
long necks and upright walking,
their orifices connect to the nose,
their skin and hide belong there,
white color governs the lungs,
they are brave but unkind;
the land is suitable for broomcorn millet,
with many yaks and rhinoceroses.
The north is dark and obscure,
where heaven closes off,
where icy cold accumulates,
where hibernating insects lie hidden,
its people have compact bodies and short necks,
broad shoulders and low buttocks,
their orifices connect to the private parts,
their bones and frame belong there,
black color governs the kidneys,
they are simple-minded but long-lived;
the land is suitable for beans,
with many dogs and horses.
The center is accessible in all directions,
where winds and qi circulate,
and where rain and dew gather,
its people have large faces and short necks,
beautiful beards but dislike obesity,
their orifices connect to the mouth,
their skin and flesh belong there,
yellow color governs the stomach,
they are wise and sage-like and fond of governance;
the land is suitable for millet,
with many cattle, sheep, and the six domestic animals.
Wood overcomes earth,
earth overcomes water,
water overcomes fire,
fire overcomes metal,
metal overcomes wood,
thus millet sprouts in spring and dies in autumn,
beans sprout in summer and die in winter,
wheat sprouts in autumn and dies in summer,
shepherd's purse sprouts in winter and dies (
mid-) summer.
When wood is strong, water is old, fire is born, metal is trapped, earth dies;
when fire is strong, wood is old, earth is born, water is trapped, metal dies;
when earth is strong, fire is old, metal is born, wood is trapped, water dies;
when metal is strong, earth is old, water is born, fire is trapped, wood dies;
when water is strong, metal is old, wood is born, earth is trapped, fire dies.
Sounds have five tones,
with gōng as the primary.
Colors have five patterns,
with yellow as the primary.
Tastes have five variations,
with sweet as the primary.
Positions have five materials,
with earth as the primary.
Therefore, refining earth produces wood,
refining wood produces fire,
refining fire produces clouds,
refining clouds produces water,
refining water returns to earth.
Refining sweet produces sour,
refining sour produces pungent,
refining pungent produces bitter,
refining bitter produces salty,
refining salty returns to sweet.
Changing gōng produces zhǐ,
changing zhǐ produces shāng,
changing shāng produces yǔ,
changing yǔ produces jué,
changing jué produces gōng,
thus using water to harmonize earth,
using earth to harmonize fire,
using fire to transform metal,
using metal to control wood,
wood again returns to earth.
The five phases regulate each other,
thereby creating useful objects.
There are thirty-six countries overseas:
From the northwest to the southwest,
there are the Long-Legged People,
the Heavenly People,
the Sùshèn People,
the White People,
the Fertile People,
the Female People,
the Male People,
the One-Legged People,
the One-Armed People,
and the Three-Bodied People.
From the southwest to the southeast,
there are the Pigeon-Breasted People,
the Feathered People,
the Huāntóu Country People,
the Naked People,
the Sānmiáo People,
the Cross-Legged People,
the Immortal People,
the Pierced-Chest People,
the Inverted-Tongue People,
the Pig-Snouted People,
the Gouged-Teeth People,
the Three-Headed People,
and the Long-Armed People.
From the southeast to the northeast,
there are the Land of Giants,
the Land of Gentlemen,
the Black-Toothed People,
the Black-Thighed People,
the Hairy People,
and the Laboring People.
From the northeast to the northwest,
there are the Tiptoeing People,
the Gōuyīng People,
the Deep-Eyed People,
the Gutless People,
the Soft-Profit People,
the One-Eyed People,
and the Heirless People.
Luòtáng
and Wǔrén are at the northwest corner,
with Bàngyú to their south.
There are spirits, two times eight, linking arms to keep watch for the Emperor at night,
located in the southwest.
The Three Pearl Trees are in the northeast,
and there is a Jade Tree above the Chìshuǐ.
Kūnlún
and Píngqiū are in the southeast,
where there are remnant jades,
green horses,
flesh that regenerates upon sight,
yangtao,
sweet quinces,
sweet blossoms,
and where all fruits grow.
Héqiū is at the northeast corner,
with Three Mulberry Trees
and the Branchless Tree to its west,
Kuāfù
and Dāněr to its north.
Kuāfù discarded his staff,
which became the Dèng Forest.
Kūnwú Hill is in the south;
Xuānyuán Hill is in the west;
Wūxián is to its north,
standing on Mount Dēngbǎo;
Yánggǔ
and Fúsāng are in the east.
Yǒusōng is north of Bùzhōu,
with the elder daughter Jiǎndí
and the younger daughter Jiàncī.
Xīwángmǔ is by the shores of the Liúshā.
Lèmín
and Nálǘ are on the isles of the Ruòshuǐ in Kūnlún.
Sānwēi is west of Lèmín.
Xiāomíng
and Zhúguāng are on the river isle,
illuminating an area of a thousand li square.
Lóngmén is in the deeps of the river.
Tuānchí is in Kūnlún.
Xuányào,
Bùzhōu,
and Shēnchí are at the sea's edge.
Mèngzhū is in Pèi.
Shǎoshì
and Tàishì are in Jìzhōu.
Zhúlóng is north of Yànmén,
sheltered by Mount Wěiyǔ,
where the sun is not seen,
and its spirit
has a human face, dragon body, and no feet.
Hòujì's mound is west of Jiànmù,
where people die and revive,
half of them fish,
dwelling there.
Liúhuáng
and Wòmín are three hundred li to its north,
with the Dog Country to its east.
In Léizé there is a spirit,
with a dragon body and human head,
who drums its belly and plays.
The Jiāng River emerges from Mínshān,
flows east, crosses the Hàn, and enters the sea,
turns left and flows north,
reaching north of Kāimǔ,
then turns right and flows east,
arriving at the eastern extreme.
The Hé River emerges from Jīshí.
The Suī River emerges from Jīngshān.
The Huái River emerges from Tóngbó Shān.
The Jū River emerges from Yǔshān.
The Qīng Zhāng emerges from Jiélì.
The Zhuó Zhāng emerges from Fābāo.
The Jǐ River emerges from Wángwū.
The Shí, Sì,
and Yí Rivers emerge from Tái,
Tái, and Shù.
The Luò River emerges from Lièshān.
The Wèn River emerges from Fúqí,
flows west, and joins the Jǐ.
The Hàn River emerges from Bōzhǒng.
The Jīng River emerges from Mount Bóluò.
The Wèi River emerges from Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué.
The Yī River emerges from Shàngwèi.
The Luò River emerges from Xióng'ěr.
The Jùn River emerges from Huáqiào.
The Wéi River emerges from Fùzhōu.
The Fén River emerges from Yānjīng.
The Rèn River emerges from Fényíng.
The Zī River emerges from Mùyí.
The Dānshuǐ emerges from Gāodū.
The Bān River emerges from Jiāoshān.
The Gǎo and Bó Rivers emerge from Xiānyú.
The Liáng River emerges from Máolú
and Shíliáng.
The Rǔ River emerges from Měngshān.
The Qí River emerges from Dàhào.
The Jìn River emerges from Jiéchù,
and the Hé River emerges from Fēngyáng.
The Liáo River emerges from Dǐshí.
The Fǔ River emerges from Jǐng.
The Qí River emerges from Shíqiáo.
The Hūchí River emerges from Lǔpíng.
The Nítú Abyss emerges from Mánshān.
The Wéi Wetlands flow north out of Yān.
Zhūjī
and Shètí
are born of the Róng Wind;
Tōngshì
is born of the Míngshù Wind;
Chìfènruò
is born of the Qīngmíng Wind;
Gònggōng
is born of the Jǐng Wind;
Zhūbǐ
is born of the Liáng Wind;
Gāojī
is born of the Chānghé Wind;
Yúqiáng
is born of the Bùzhōu Wind;
Qióngqí
is born of the Guǎngmò Wind.
Bá gave birth to the Sea People,
the Sea People gave birth to Ruòjūn,
Ruòjūn gave birth to the Sages,
the Sages gave birth to the Common People,
all those with skin are born from the Common People.
Yǔjiā gave birth to the Flying Dragons,
the Flying Dragons gave birth to the Phoenix,
the Phoenix gave birth to the Luánniǎo,
the Luánniǎo gave birth to the Common Birds,
all those with feathers are born from the Common Birds.
Máodú gave birth to the Yìnglóng,
the Yìnglóng gave birth to the Jiànmǎ,
the Jiànmǎ gave birth to the Qílín,
the Qílín gave birth to the Common Beasts,
all those with hair are born from the Common Beasts.
Jièlín gave birth to the Jiāolóng,
the Jiāolóng gave birth to the Kūngǔn,
the Kūngǔn gave birth to the Jiànxié,
the Jiànxié gave birth to the Common Fish,
all those with scales are born from the Common Fish.
Jiètán gave birth to the Xiānlóng,
the Xiānlóng gave birth to the Xuányuán,
the Xuányuán gave birth to the Língguī,
the Língguī gave birth to the Common Turtles,
all those with shells are born from the Common Turtles.
Warmth and moisture give birth to Róng,
warmth and moisture are born from the Máofēng,
Máofēng is born from the Shīxuán,
Shīxuán gives birth to the Yǔfēng,
Yǔfēng gives birth to the Nuǎnjiè,
Nuǎnjiè gives birth to the Línbó,
Línbó gives birth to the Nuǎnjiè.
The five categories of mixed species flourish externally,
resembling their forms and multiplying.
Rìféng gave birth to Yáng'è,
Yáng'è gave birth to Qiáorú,
Qiáorú gave birth to Gànmù,
Gànmù gave birth to the Common Trees,
all trees are born from the Common Trees.
Zhāoyáo gave birth to Chéngruò,
Chéngruò gave birth to Xuānyù,
Xuānyù gave birth to Lǐquán,
Lǐquán gave birth to Huánggū,
Huánggū gave birth to the Common Grasses,
all rooted grasses are born from the Common Grasses.
Hǎilǘ gave birth to Qūlóng,
Qūlóng gave birth to Rónghuá,
Rónghuá gave birth to Biāo,
Biāo gave birth to Zǎo,
Zǎo gave birth to the Floating Grasses,
all floating, rootless plants are born from Zǎo.
The Qì of the Central Earth governs the Dusty Heaven,
the Dusty Heaven after five hundred years gives birth to Jué,
Jué after five hundred years gives birth to Huánghòng,
Huánghòng after five hundred years gives birth to Huángjīn,
Huángjīn after a thousand years gives birth to Huánglóng,
Huánglóng entering the depths gives birth to Huángquán,
the dust of Huángquán ascends to become Huángyún,
Yīn and Yáng pressing together create thunder,
stirring and rising create lightning,
the high descends to the low,
flowing water reaches its course,
and converges into the Huánghǎi.
The Qì of the Partial Earth governs the Blue Heaven,
the Blue Heaven after eight hundred years gives birth to Qīngzēng,
Qīngzēng after eight hundred years gives birth to Qīnghòng,
Qīnghòng after eight hundred years gives birth to Qīngjīn,
Qīngjīn after a thousand years gives birth to Qīnglóng,
Qīnglóng entering the depths gives birth to Qīngquán,
the dust of Qīngquán ascends to become Qīngyún,
Yīn and Yáng pressing together create thunder,
stirring and rising create lightning,
the high descends to the low,
flowing water reaches its course,
and converges into the Qīnghǎi.
The Qì of the Male Earth governs the Red Heaven,
the Red Heaven after seven hundred years gives birth to Chìdān,
Chìdān after seven hundred years gives birth to Chìhòng,
Chìhòng after seven hundred years gives birth to Chìjīn,
Chìjīn after a thousand years gives birth to Chìlóng,
Chìlóng entering the depths gives birth to Chìquán,
the dust of Chìquán ascends to become Chìyún,
Yīn and Yáng pressing together create thunder,
stirring and rising create lightning,
the high descends to the low,
flowing water reaches its course,
and converges into the Chìhǎi.
The Qì of the Weak Earth governs the White Heaven,
the White Heaven after nine hundred years gives birth to Báiyù,
Báiyù after nine hundred years gives birth to Báihòng,
Báihòng after nine hundred years gives birth to Báijīn,
Báijīn after a thousand years gives birth to Báilóng,
Báilóng entering the depths gives birth to Báiquán,
the dust of Báiquán ascends to become Báiyún,
Yīn and Yáng pressing together create thunder,
stirring and rising create lightning,
the high descends to the low,
flowing water reaches its course,
and converges into the Báihǎi.
The Qì of the Female Earth governs the Mysterious Heaven,
the Mysterious Heaven after six hundred years gives birth to Xuándǐ,
Xuándǐ after six hundred years gives birth to Xuánhòng,
Xuánhòng after six hundred years gives birth to Xuánjīn,
Xuánjīn after a thousand years gives birth to Xuánlóng,
Xuánlóng entering the depths gives birth to Xuánquán,
the dust of Xuánquán ascends to become Xuányún,
Yīn and Yáng pressing together create thunder,
stirring and rising create lightning,
the high descends to the low,
flowing water reaches its course,
and converges into the Xuánhǎi.
In the first month of spring,
Zhāoyáo points to Yín,
in the evening Shēn is at the center,
at dawn Wěi is at the center.
Its position is the East,
its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ,
its abundant virtue is in Wood,
its creatures are the scaly,
its musical note is Jué,
the pitch standard is Tàicòu,
its number is eight,
its flavor is sour,
its odor is pungent,
its sacrifice is to the Door,
offering the spleen first.
The east wind thaws the ice,
hibernating insects begin to stir and revive,
fish rise to the surface under the ice,
otters offer fish,
the wild geese fly north.
The Son of Heaven wears blue garments,
rides a blue dragon,
carries a blue jade,
raises a blue banner,
eats wheat and mutton,
drinks the water of the eight winds,
cooks with beanstalks and drills for fire,
the women of the Eastern Palace wear blue,
dress in blue colors,
play the qín and sè,
their weapon is the spear,
their domestic animal is the sheep,
he holds court in the left chamber of Qīngyáng,
to issue the spring ordinances.
He spreads virtue and bestows favors,
carries out rewards and honors,
reduces corvée and taxes.
On the day of the beginning of spring,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the three lords, nine ministers, and officials to welcome the year in the eastern suburbs,
repairs and cleans the sacrificial positions,
offers silk and prays to the ghosts and spirits,
using male animals for sacrifice.
He prohibits the cutting of trees,
forbids overturning nests,
forbids killing the pregnant and the young,
forbids taking fawns,
forbids taking eggs,
forbids gathering crowds,
forbids building city walls,
and covers exposed bones and buries decomposed corpses.
If the ordinances of summer are implemented in the first month of spring,
then wind and rain will be untimely,
grass and trees will wither early,
and the state will experience fear.
If the ordinances of autumn are implemented,
then the people will suffer great epidemics,
whirlwinds and torrential rains will arrive together,
and weeds like lí and yǒu, péng and hāo will flourish together.
If the ordinances of winter are implemented,
then floods will cause damage,
with frost, heavy hail,
and the first crops will not be harvested.
In the first month, the office is that of the Minister of Works,
its tree is the poplar.
In the mid-spring month,
the Dipper's handle points to Mǎo,
at dusk the Bow constellation is at zenith,
at dawn the Winnowing Basket constellation is at zenith.
Its position is the east,
its days are Jiǎ-Yǐ,
its creatures are scaly,
its musical note is Jué,
the pitch-pipe is Jiázhōng,
its number is eight,
its flavor is sour,
its odor is rank,
its sacrifice is to the door,
offering first the spleen.
Rainwater begins,
peach and plum trees start to bloom,
the golden oriole sings,
hawks transform into doves.
The Son of Heaven wears blue garments,
rides a blue dragon,
carries blue jade,
displays blue banners,
eats wheat and mutton,
drinks the eight-wind water,
cooks with artemisia and drills fire,
the women of the Eastern Palace wear blue,
dress in blue colors,
play the qín and sè,
their weapon is the spear,
their domestic animal is the sheep,
they hold court at the main chamber of Qīngyáng.
Order the officials
to inspect the prisons,
remove fetters,
do not flog or torture,
halt litigation,
nurture the young,
care for the orphaned and solitary,
to encourage sprouting growth.
Choose an auspicious day,
command the people to hold soil sacrifices.
In this month,
day and night are equal,
thunder begins to sound,
all hibernating insects stir and revive.
Three days before thunder,
shake bells to proclaim to the masses:
"Thunder is about to sound,
those who do not guard their comportment,
will bear children with defects,
and surely meet with misfortune."
Order the market officials,
to uniform measures,
balance scales and weights,
verify dou and tǒng vessels,
rectify steelyards and levelers.
Do not drain rivers and marshes,
do not dry up ponds,
do not burn mountains and forests,
do not undertake major works,
to hinder farming.
Sacrifices do not use live victims,
use guī and bì jades,
substitute with hides and silks.
If autumn ordinances are practiced in mid-spring,
then the state will have great floods,
cold air will repeatedly arrive,
invaders will come to attack.
If winter ordinances are practiced,
then yang energy will not prevail,
wheat will not ripen,
people will often harm each other.
If summer ordinances are practiced,
then the state will have great drought,
warm air will arrive early,
insects will cause harm.
The second month's office is the granary,
its tree is the apricot.
In the late spring month,
the Dipper's handle points to Chén,
at dusk the Seven Stars are at zenith,
at dawn the Ox constellation is at zenith.
Its position is the east,
its days are Jiǎ-Yǐ,
its creatures are scaly,
its musical note is Jué,
the pitch-pipe is Gūxiǎn,
its number is eight,
its flavor is sour,
its odor is rank,
its sacrifice is to the door,
offering first the spleen.
Paulownia begins to bloom,
field mice transform into rú quails,
rainbows first appear,
duckweed begins to grow.
The Son of Heaven wears blue garments,
rides a blue dragon,
carries blue jade,
displays blue banners,
eats wheat and mutton,
drinks the eight-wind water,
cooks with artemisia and drills fire,
the women of the Eastern Palace wear blue,
dress in blue colors,
play the qín and sè,
their weapon is the spear,
their domestic animal is the sheep,
they hold court at the right chamber of Qīngyáng.
Order the boat master to inspect boats,
five inspections and five reports,
then declare readiness to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven then first boards boats,
offers sturgeon at the ancestral temple,
then prays for grain fullness.
In this month,
vital energy is at its peak,
yang energy spreads forth,
all curled sprouts emerge,
all buds reach out,
one cannot restrain them.
The Son of Heaven orders officials,
to open granaries,
aid the poor,
relieve the destitute,
open treasuries,
distribute silks,
send envoys to feudal lords,

his weapon is the shā,
his livestock is the pig,
and he holds court in the right chamber of the Dark Hall.
He orders officials to perform the great exorcism,
with dismemberment sacrifices on all sides,
and the presentation of the earthen ox.
He commands the fishing masters to begin fishing,
and the Son of Heaven personally goes to shoot and fish,
first offering them in the ancestral temple.
He orders the people to bring out the five grains,
directs farmers to plan for paired plowing,
repair plows and shares,
and prepare field tools.
He commands the music master to hold a grand concert and then cease.
Then he orders the four inspectors
to collect firewood allocations,
to supply the fuel for the ancestral temple and the hundred sacrifices.
In this month,
the sun completes its cycle,
the moon ends its course,
the stars revolve through the heavens,
and the year is about to renew itself.
Order the farmers to rest,
with no tasks assigned.
The Son of Heaven, with his dukes, ministers, and officials, revises the state statutes,
discusses the seasonal ordinances,
to prepare for the appropriateness of the coming year.
He then commands the Grand Historian
to rank the feudal lords in order,
apportion their sacrificial animals,
to supply the offerings to the Supreme Heaven, August God, and the gods of soil and grain.
He orders the states of the same surname
to provide the animals for the ancestral temple;
from ministers and officials down to the common people,
all supply the sacrifices for the famous mountains and great rivers.
If autumn ordinances are practiced in the last month of winter,
white dew will fall early,
shelled creatures will cause calamities,
and the four borders will retreat into fortresses.
If spring ordinances are practiced,
many fetuses and young will be harmed,
the state will have many chronic illnesses,
and it is called rebellion.
If summer ordinances are practiced,
floods will ruin the state,
timely snow will not fall,
and ice will melt away.
The official of the twelfth month is the prisons,
and its tree is the oak.
The Five Regions:
The extreme of the East,
from Jiéshí past Cháoxiǎn,
piercing through the land of the Great Men,
east to the place of the rising sun,
the land of Fúmù,
the wilds of Qīngqiū where trees grow,
overseen by Tàihào
and Jūmáng,
spans twelve thousand lǐ.
Its ordinance says:
Lift all prohibitions,
open what is closed,
unblock obstructions,
clear barriers,
practice ease and leisure,
discard resentment and malice,
remit corvée and crimes,
relieve worries and hardships,
suspend punishments and penalties,
open passes and bridges,
distribute wealth,
reconcile external enmities,
pacify the four directions,
practice kindness and grace,
and restrain the violent.
The extreme of the South,
from beyond Běihùsūn,
piercing through the country of Zhuānxū,
south to the wilds of withering fire and scorching wind,
overseen by Chìdì
and Zhùróng,
spans twelve thousand lǐ.
Its ordinance says:
Ennoble the virtuous,
reward the meritorious,
benefit the worthy and good,
relieve the hungry and thirsty,
promote diligent farming,
aid the poor and destitute,
care for the orphaned and widowed,
comfort the weary and ill,
grant high emoluments,
bestow great rewards,
restore ruined ancestral temples,
establish heirs for those without,
enfeoff feudal lords,
and appoint worthy assistants.
The central extreme,
extending east from Kūnlún across both Héngshān mountains,
where the sun and moon traverse,
where the Jiāng and Hàn rivers emerge,
the land of numerous people,
suitable for the five grains,
where Lóngmén,
the Hé and Jǐ rivers interconnect,
the province where Xìrǎng soil stopped the great flood,
reaching east to Jiéshí,
governed by Huángdì
and Hòutǔ,
spans twelve thousand lǐ.
Its decree states:
Impartial without bias,
clear without harshness,
enveloping and nurturing all,
embracing everything without exception,
universal and selfless,
upright and tranquil to maintain harmony,
distribute porridge,
nourish the aged and feeble,
mourn the dead and inquire after the sick,
to escort all things to their rest.
The western extreme,
from Kūnlún across Liúshā
and Chényǔ,
west to the land of Sānwēi,
with stone walls and golden chambers,
the people who feed on qi,
the land of immortality,
governed by Shǎohào
and Rùshōu,
spans twelve thousand lǐ.
Its decree states:
Apply laws judiciously,
punish the guilty without fail,
guard against thieves and robbers,
prohibit wickedness and depravity,
organize the herds,
carefully store provisions,
repair city walls,
mend breaches,
block footpaths,
dam ditches,
halt flowing water,
block ravines and valleys,
guard the gates,
array armor and weapons,
select the hundred officials,
punish the unlawful.
The northern extreme,
from Jiǔzé to the limits of Xiàhuì's darkness,
north to the valley of Lìngzhèng,
where frozen cold and accumulated ice,
snow, hail, frost, and sleet,
and floating marshes of gathered waters lie,
governed by Zhuānxū
and Xuánmíng,
spans twelve thousand lǐ.
Its decree states:
Reinforce all prohibitions,
securely store and conceal,
repair barriers and fortifications,
mend passes and bridges,
forbid outward migration,
enact penalties and punishments,
execute the deserving,
close the gates,
conduct extensive searches for outsiders,
halt social interactions,
ban nighttime revelry,
close early and open late,
to seek out evil individuals,
once the wicked are identified,
seize them firmly.
Heaven's cycle nearly complete,
punish and kill without pardon,
even those of high and noble kinship,
judge according to the law.
Do not release water,
do not uncover stores,
do not pardon crimes.
The six harmonies:
First spring pairs with first autumn,
mid-spring with mid-autumn,
last spring with last autumn,
first summer with first winter,
mid-summer with mid-winter,
last summer with last winter.
First spring begins expansion,
first autumn begins contraction;
mid-spring starts emergence,
mid-autumn starts withdrawal;
last spring greatly emerges,
last autumn greatly withdraws;
first summer begins relaxation,
first winter begins urgency;
mid-summer reaches its full length,
mid-winter reaches its shortest;
last summer completes virtue,
last winter completes punishment.
Thus, if governance fails in the first month,
cool winds will not come in the seventh month;
if governance fails in the second month,
thunder will not cease in the eighth month;
if governance fails in the third month,
frost will not fall in the ninth month;
if governance fails in the fourth month,
cold will not freeze in the tenth month;
if governance fails in the fifth month,
hibernating insects will emerge in their homelands in the eleventh month;
if governance fails in the sixth month,
plants will not shed in the twelfth month;
if governance fails in the seventh month,
great cold will not break in the first month;
if governance fails in the eighth month,
thunder will not sound in the second month;
if governance fails in the ninth month,
spring winds will not complete in the third month;
if governance fails in the tenth month,
plants will not bear fruit in the fourth month;
if governance fails in the eleventh month,
frost and hail will fall in the fifth month;
if governance fails in the twelfth month,
the five grains will grow wild in the sixth month.
If spring follows summer's order, it brings leakage,
if it follows autumn's order, floods,
if it follows winter's order, severity.
If summer follows spring's order, winds,
if it follows autumn's order, desolation,
if it follows winter's order, obstruction.
If autumn follows summer's order, flourish,
if it follows spring's order, glory,
if it follows winter's order, waste.
If winter follows spring's order, leakage,
if it follows summer's order, drought,
if it follows autumn's order, fog.
Systems and measures:
Yīn and yáng,
the great system has six measures:
Heaven is the marking-line,
Earth is the level,
spring is the compass,
summer is the balance,
autumn is the square,
winter is the weight.
The marking-line
is to align all things.
The level
is to balance all things.
The compass
is to circle all things.
The balance
is to equalize all things.
The square
is to square all things.
The weight
is to weigh all things.
The marking-line as a measure,
straight without contention,
long without end,
enduring without decay,
distant yet not forgotten,
in virtue united with Heaven,
in brightness united with the spirits,
what it desires it obtains,
what it hates perishes,
from ancient times to now,
unshakable and firm,
its virtue profoundly dense,
vast and great to accommodate the multitude,
thus the Supreme Deity regards it as the ancestor of things.
The level as a measure,
even without peril,
uniform without bias,
broad and great to contain,
spacious and tolerant to harmonize,
soft yet not weak,
sharp yet not broken,
flowing yet not stagnant,
simple yet not foul,
issuing freely yet with order,
comprehensive yet not leaking,
level and even without error,
all things are even,
the people have no perilous schemes,
resentment and hatred do not arise,
thus the Supreme Deity regards it as the balance of things.
The compass as a standard,
Revolves without repetition,
Circular without distortion,
Gracious without indulgence,
Vast and broad,
Stirring emotions with principle,
Extending connections with discipline,
Elegant and simple,
No grievances arise,
With compass measure intact,
Vital energy is ordered.
The balance as a standard,
Leisurely yet not lagging,
Even-tempered without resentment,
Giving without claiming virtue,
Compassionate without demanding,
Constantly equalizing people's sustenance,
To supplement deficiencies,
Vigorous and radiant,
Acting only with virtue,
Nurturing growth and transformation,
All things flourish,
Producing the five grains,
Enriching the territories,
With governance unimpaired,
Heaven and earth become bright.
The square as a standard,
Solemn yet not contradictory,
Firm yet not confused,
Taking without resentment,
Internal without harm,
Awe-inspiring yet not intimidating,
Decrees executed without obstruction,
When punitive actions are justified,
Enemies are vanquished,
With square measure correct,
All punishments are accepted.
The weight as a standard,
Urgent yet not excessive,
Severe yet not cruel,
Full and substantial,
Thorough and leak-proof,
Destroying things without taking them,
Punishing crimes without pardon,
Sincere and trustworthy with certainty,
Resolute and firm,
Eliminating harsh evils,
Incapable of being bent,
Thus when winter's governance is implemented,
The weak must become strong,
The soft must become hard,
With weight measure correct,
All things are stored away.
The system of the Mingtáng,
Quietly follows the level,
Acting follows the plumb line,
Spring governed by the compass,
Autumn governed by the square,
Winter governed by the weight,
Summer governed by the balance,
Hence dryness, dampness, cold, and heat arrive in season,
Sweet rains and nourishing dew descend timely.
In ancient times, Shī Kuàng performed the music of "White Snow",
And divine beings descended for it,
Wind and rain suddenly arrived,
Duke Píng fell ill with paralysis,
And the state of Jìn suffered drought.
A common woman cried out to heaven,
Thunder and lightning struck down,
Duke Jǐng's terrace collapsed,
Limbs were injured and broken,
Seawater flooded out.
Now the blind musician and common woman,
Held low positions and humble status,
Their influence lighter than flying feathers,
Yet with focused essence and intense will,
Devoting effort and accumulating spirit,
They reached up to the Nine Heavens,
Stirring the most refined energies.
From this we see,
That heaven's punishment,
Even in empty wastelands and secluded places,
Distant and hidden,
Within layered stone chambers,
Behind boundaries and barriers,
Nowhere can one escape it
Is also clear.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Crossing at Mèngjīn,
The waves of Yáng Hóu,
Came against the current to strike,
With fierce winds and darkness,
Where men and horses couldn't see each other.
Then King Wǔ held a yellow battle-axe in his left hand,
A white yak-tail banner in his right,
Glared and commanded, saying:
"While I am here,
Who in the world dares oppose my will!"
Thereupon the wind ceased and waves calmed.
When Lǔyáng Gōng fought with Hán,
In fierce battle as sunset approached,
He raised his spear and commanded it,
And the sun retreated three zodiacal mansions for him.
Now to preserve one's nature and protect one's authenticity,
Without harming one's body,
When encountering urgent difficulties,
One's essential spirit communicates with heaven.
If one has never departed from their fundamental source,
What cannot be accomplished!
Death and life share the same domain,
Cannot be threatened or oppressed,
A single courageous warrior,
Can be the hero of three armies.
Those who merely seek fame,
And can discipline themselves
Still achieve such feats,
How much more those who govern heaven and earth,
Embrace all things, befriend creation, contain perfect harmony,
Merely temporarily inhabiting human form,
Observing the nine and penetrating the one,
Knowing what ordinary knowledge cannot know,
And whose mind has never died!
In the past, Yōngménzǐ
Gained audience with Mèngcháng Jūn through weeping,
Then expressed his thoughts and conveyed his meaning,
Pressing his chest to produce sounds,
Mèngcháng Jūn because of this
Increased his sighs and sobs,
Flowing tears uncontrollably.
When essential sincerity forms within,
And externally conveys sorrow to human hearts,
This is the untransmittable Way.
If ordinary people without their ruling spirit imitate his appearance,
They will surely be laughed at.
Thus Pú Qiězǐ snaring birds from hundred-ren heights,
And Zhān Hé attracting fish from great depths,
Both attained the Way of clarity and stillness,
The harmony of the Great Vastness.
The mutual responses among things,
Mysterious and profoundly subtle,
Knowledge cannot discuss,
Debate cannot explain.
Thus when east wind arrives, wine overflows,
When silkworms spit silk, the shāng string snaps,
Something stimulates them.
When moon's halo appears ashy, the moon's course is interrupted,
When whale dies, comet appears,
Something moves them.
Thus when sage is in position,
Embracing the Way without speaking,
Blessings reach all people.

The Way of Heaven
shows no private favoritism,
nor private rejection;
the capable have surplus,
the inept fall short;
those who follow it prosper,
those who oppose it meet misfortune.
Take for instance the pearl of Suí Hóu
or the jade of Hé Shì:
those who obtain them become wealthy,
those who lose them become poor.
The measure of gain and loss
is profound, subtle, and obscure,
difficult to comprehend through reasoning,
and cannot be explained through argumentation.
How do we know this is so?
Now, consider that Dì Huáng governs bones
while Gān Cǎo is a medicine that generates flesh.
To demand that it generate flesh because it governs bones,
or to judge its bone-governing based on flesh generation,
is like Wáng Sūn Chuò wishing to double the medicine for hemiplegia
to revive the dead —
this can be called a failure in reasoning.
If fire can char wood,
and thereby melt metal,
then the principle works;
but if because a magnet can attract iron,
one expects it to attract tiles,
it is difficult,
for things inherently cannot be judged by weight alone.
The drill's drawing fire from the sun,
the magnet's attracting iron,
Xiè's spoiling lacquer,
the sunflower's facing the sun —
even with great wisdom,
one cannot fully explain them.
Thus, the observations of ears and eyes
are insufficient to distinguish the principles of things;
the deliberations of the mind
are inadequate to determine right and wrong.
Therefore, those who rule by intellect
find it hard to maintain a state;
only those who penetrate the Great Harmony
and hold to the responses of nature
can possess it.
Thus, when Yáo Shān collapsed, the waters of Bó Luò dried up;
when Ōu Yě was born, the sword Chún Jūn was forged;
when Zhòu committed atrocities,
Zuǒ Qiáng was by his side;
with Tài Gōng in the same era,
King Wǔ's achievements were established.
From this we see
the paths of benefit and harm,
the gates of fortune and misfortune,
cannot be sought and obtained directly.
The Way and its Virtue
are like leather and hide:
distance them and they draw near,
approach them and they grow distant.
Without grasping the Way,
it is like viewing minnows.
Thus, the sage is like a mirror,
neither sending nor welcoming,
responding without storing,
thus transforming all without harm.
What is gained is thereby lost;
is what is lost not thereby gained?
Now, one who tunes strings:
strike Gōng and Gōng responds,
pluck Jué and Jué moves —
this is like tones harmonizing with the same sound.
But if one changes a single string
that does not match any of the five notes,
and upon playing it
all twenty-five strings resonate,
this is not different in sound from the start,
yet the ruler of tones has already manifested.
Thus, one who penetrates the Great Harmony
is dazed as if deeply drunk, sweetly resting
to wander within it,
unaware of how they arrived.
Pure warmth dissolves away,
dull tranquility ends,
as if never leaving the source —
this is called the Great Pervasion.
When the red chī and green qiú dragons wander Jìzhōu,
with clear skies and stable earth,
no venomous beasts arise,
no birds take flight in alarm,
they enter thickets,
feed on lush plums,
savoring sweetness,
roaming not beyond a small field's bounds,
and snakes and eels轻视 them,
thinking they cannot compete in rivers and seas.
But when black clouds gather at dawn,
yīn and yáng clash,
descending winds rise,
mixed with freezing rain,
they soar upward on whirlwinds,
shaking heaven and earth with might,
their roar echoing across the land,
while salamanders and eels bury in mud a hundred fathoms deep,
bears crawl on mountain crags,
tigers and leopards hide in dens, not daring to roar,
monkeys tumble and lose their branches,
let alone mere snakes and eels!
When the fènghuáng soars with ultimate virtue,
no thunder rolls,
no storms arise,
rivers and valleys do not swell,
grasses and trees do not sway,
yet sparrows mock it,
thinking they cannot compete within the cosmos.
But when it ascends ten thousand fathoms high,
gliding beyond the four seas,
passing Kūnlún's Shū Gardens,
drinking from Dǐzhù's rapids,
lingering at Méng Sì's isles,
wandering the borders of Jìzhōu,
treading Dū Guǎng directly,
halting at the setting sun,
bathing feathers in Ruò Shuǐ,
lodging at night in the Wind Cave,
at this time,
swans and cranes
all cower in fear and flee,
peeking by the riverbanks,
let alone mere sparrows!
This shows understanding small movements' traces
but ignorance of how great rhythms arise.
In the past, when Wáng Liáng and Zào Fǔ drove chariots,
mounting and taking the reins,
the horses aligned in harmony,
steps evenly matched,
toil and ease as one,
hearts joyful, breaths calm,
bodies nimble and light,
content in labor, eager to advance,
galloping as if vanishing,
turning left and right as if whipped,
circling like a ring —
the world deemed them skillful,
yet saw nothing noble in it.
But when Qián Jū and Dà Bǐng drove,
removing reins and bits,
discarding whips and goads,
the chariot moved of itself without shifting,
the horses ran without being driven.
Suns and moons moved with them,
stars shone in dark courses,
swift as lightning, soaring like ghosts,
advancing, retreating, bending, stretching,
with no trace of seams,
thus needing no pointing,
no shouts or scolds,
passing wild geese at Jié Shí,
surpassing kūn chickens at Gū Yú,
speeding like flight,
racing like a snapped thread,
outpacing arrows, treading wind,
chasing whirlwinds, returning to the void,
departing from Fú Sāng at dawn,
arriving at Luò Táng by sunset.
This borrows non-action to accomplish action,
not through meticulous thought
or manual dexterity;
desires take form in the breast,
and the spirit communicates with the six horses —
this is mastering without driving.
In the past, when Huáng Dì ruled the world,
assisted by Lì Mù and Tài Shān Jī,
they regulated the courses of the sun and moon,
harmonized the breaths of yīn and yáng,
moderated the measures of the four seasons,
corrected the numbers of pitch and calendar,
distinguished male and female,
separated female and male,
clarified high and low,
ranked noble and humble,
ensuring the strong did not oppress the weak,
the many did not bully the few,
people preserved their lives without premature death,
harvests ripened without disaster,
officials were upright and impartial,
high and low harmonized without fault,
laws were clear and not obscure,
advisors were just and not flattering,
farmers did not encroach on fields,
fishermen did not contend for coves,
Lost property on the road was left untouched,
markets did not engage in deceptive pricing,
city gates remained unbarred,
towns were free from thieves and robbers,
travelers from distant borders
courteously yielded wealth to one another,
dogs and pigs spat out beans and grains on the roads
without harboring resentment or strife,
thus the sun and moon shone brilliantly,
the stars did not stray from their courses,
winds and rains came in due season,
the five grains flourished and ripened,
tigers and wolves did not bite indiscriminately,
birds of prey did not strike wantonly,
phoenixes soared in courtyards,
qílín roamed the outskirts,
green dragons drew carriages,
feihuáng steeds were tamed in stables,
states such as Zhūběi and Dān'ěr
all presented their tributes.
Yet this still fell short of the Way of Fúxīshì.
In ancient times,
the four pillars collapsed,
the nine provinces split apart,
the heavens could not fully cover the earth,
the earth could not completely support all,
fires blazed uncontrollably,
floods surged unceasingly,
fierce beasts devoured innocent people,
birds of prey snatched the elderly and weak.
Thereupon Nǚwā smelted five-colored stones to mend the azure sky,
severed the legs of the giant sea turtle to set up the four pillars,
slew the black dragon to save Jìzhōu,
piled up reed ashes to halt the raging waters.
The azure sky was repaired,
the four pillars were set right,
the floodwaters dried up,
Jìzhōu was pacified,
the cunning creatures perished,
and the innocent people lived.
With backs to the square earth,
embracing the round heavens,
harmonizing with spring and summer's warmth,
restraining autumn and winter's harshness,
resting their heads on squares and sleeping on ropes,
wherever yīn and yáng were blocked or stagnant,
she opened passages to regulate them;
where perverse energies harmed beings
or injured people's accumulated wealth,
she cut them off.
In that era,
people slept soundly,
awoke serenely,
some considering themselves horses,
others thinking themselves oxen,
their gait steady,
their gaze calm,
all innocently attaining harmony,
unaware of their origins,
drifting without knowing what to seek,
spirits wandering without knowing where to go.
At this time,
birds, beasts, insects, and snakes
all concealed their claws and fangs,
hid their venom,
without any intent to seize or bite.
Examining her achievements,
they reached the nine heavens above,
penetrated the yellow earth below,
her fame spread to later generations,
her radiance illuminated all things.
Riding a thunder chariot,
harnessing yìnglóng,
with green qiú as side horses,
grasping rare auspicious signs,
seated on a vine-patterned mat,
enveloped in yellow clouds,
white chī leading ahead,
swift snakes following behind,
floating and wandering freely,
guiding ghosts and gods,
ascending the nine heavens,
paying homage to the emperor at the Spirit Gate,
resting peacefully beneath the Great Ancestor.
Yet she did not flaunt her merits,
did not proclaim her fame,
concealing the Way of the true person,
to follow the natural course of heaven and earth.
Why so?
Because her virtue connected with the heavens above,
and cunning artifice was eradicated.
By the time of Xià Jié,
the ruler was benighted and unenlightened,
the Way was neglected and uncultivated,
discarding the benevolent laws of the Five Emperors,
overthrowing the regulations of the Three Kings,
thus supreme virtue perished uncelebrated,
the imperial Way was obscured and unrevived,
actions contravened the azure heavens,
decrees defied the four seasons,
spring and autumn withheld their harmony,
heaven and earth withdrew their blessings,
rulers held positions uneasily,
ministers concealed the Way and remained silent,
officials迎合 the ruler's whims while harboring personal agendas,
alienating kin to secure their own safety,
wicked men formed cliques and conspired in secret,
standing between ruler and subject, father and son
to compete for influence,
flattering arrogant rulers to suit their desires,
creating chaos to achieve their aims,
hence ruler and minister turned against each other without affection,
kin became estranged without attachment,
altars withered and cracked,
ceremonial platforms shook and collapsed,
dogs howled in packs and plunged into deep waters,
pigs carried bedding to make nests in marshes,
beauties disheveled their hair and blackened their faces, unrecognizable,
singers swallowed charcoal to mute their voices, singing no more,
funerals lacked proper mourning,
hunts brought no joy,
the Western Elder broke his staff,
the Yellow Spirit wailed and sighed,
birds had their wings clipped,
beasts had their legs crippled,
mountains lost their towering trees,
marshes held no standing water,
foxes burrowed headfirst into dens,
horses and cattle wandered lost,
fields bore no standing grain,
roads were devoid of weeds,
accumulated metal lost its sharpness,
jade discs showed no luster,
tortoise shells for divination had no undersides,
yarrow stalks were used daily for fortune-telling.
In later ages,
the seven states of different clans,
feudal lords establishing their own laws,
each with distinct customs,
strategists scheming among them,
raised armies to clash,
attacking cities and slaughtering indiscriminately,
overthrowing the stable and endangering the secure,
digging up graves,
scattering human bones,
deploying massive assault vehicles,
erecting high fortifications,
clearing paths for battle,
paving roads to death,
confronting formidable enemies,
destroying the unrighteous,
with a hundred going forth and only one returning,
all for the sake of fleeting fame.
Thus the strong and swift-footed
became armored soldiers
deployed a thousand miles away,
while the elderly and weak at home
grieved inwardly,
laborers and stable hands,
pushing carts to deliver supplies,
on roads long and distant,
frost and snow frequently gathering,
in tattered short robes,
people exhausted and carts broken,
mud reaching their knees,
dragging each other along the roads,
struggling forward,
dying with their heads resting on cart shafts.
So-called annexation of states and territories
meant corpses lying in tens of thousands,
wrecked chariots numbering in the hundreds and thousands,
the wounded from arrows, crossbows, spears, halberds, and stones
being helped along the roads,
hence the world reached the point of using human heads as pillows,
eating human flesh,
mincing human livers,
drinking human blood,
finding it sweeter than livestock.
Therefore, since the time of the Three Dynasties onward,
the world has never been able to settle its innate nature,
find joy in its customs,
preserve its allotted lifespan,
without being cut short by human cruelty.
Why is this so?
Because feudal lords waged war with force,
and the world failed to unite as one family.
When it comes to the present era,
the Son of Heaven holds the highest position,
upholding the Way and its Virtue,
assisted by humaneness and righteousness.
Those nearby offer their wisdom,
while those afar cherish his virtue.
With a mere gesture or wave of the hand,
the four seas submit in tribute.
In spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
all present their offerings and duties.
The world merges into one,
with descendants succeeding one another.
This is how the Five Emperors welcomed Heaven's Virtue.
As for the sages,
they cannot create the times,
but when the time comes, they do not lose it.
With capable assistance,
they dismiss the beginnings of slander and flattery,
silence clever arguments,
abolish harsh laws,
remove burdensome matters,
block the traces of rumors,
close the gates of factionalism,
diminish knowledge and ability,
cultivate the Great Constant,
let go of limbs,
dull acuity and hearing,
greatly penetrate the obscure and dark,
release intentions and free the spirit,
indifferent as if without a soul,
causing all things to return to their roots.
This is to follow the path of Fúxīshì,
and return to the Way of the Five Emperors.
Qiánqiě and Dàbǐng
did not use reins or bits,
yet were renowned throughout the world for their skillful driving.
Fúxì and Nǚwā
did not establish laws and measures,
yet passed down the highest virtue to later generations.
Why is that?
Because they embodied utmost emptiness and purity,
unbothered by trivial matters.
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"Covering the pheasant but failing to catch it,
one should instead follow the wind."
Now, as for Shēn, Hán, and Shāng Yāng's methods of governance,
they uprooted and pulled out the foundations,
abandoning the essence,
without thoroughly investigating the origins of life.
How did it come to this?
They carved out the five punishments,
enacting harsh laws,
thus turning their backs on the root of the Way and its Virtue,
and contending over the minutiae like the tip of an awl or knife.
They slaughtered the common people,
exhausting more than half,
yet gleefully believing themselves to be governing well.
This is like carrying firewood to put out a fire,
or digging a hole to stop water.
If a well's surroundings grow thickets that block the jar,
or a ditch's edges sprout branches that bar the boat,
they will surely die within three months.
Why is this so?
Because they grow wildly without their roots.
The river winds nine times before flowing into the sea,
yet its current never ceases,
for it is supplied by the Kūnlún Mountains.
If floodwaters are not drained,
spreading boundlessly as far as the eye can see,
and it does not rain for ten days or a month,
they will dry up, leaving the marshes parched,
for they receive runoff without a source.
It is like when Yì requested the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ,
and Héng'é stole it to flee to the moon.
He was disconsolate as if having suffered a loss,
with no way to continue.
Why?
Because he did not know how the elixir of immortality was produced.
Therefore, begging for fire is not as good as fetching a flint,
and relying on others for water is not as good as digging a well.
In ancient times, before heaven and earth existed,
there were only images without form,
deep and dark,
vast and obscure,
chaotic and boundless,
with no one knowing its gateway.
Two deities were born in the mix,
who managed heaven and constructed earth.
Profoundly, none know their ultimate end,
vastly, none know where they rest.
Thereupon, they separated into yīn and yáng,
divided into the eight extremes,
with hardness and softness complementing each other,
and all things took form.
Turbid qi became insects,
while essential qi became humans.
Therefore, the jīngshén (essential spirit)
belongs to heaven;
and the gǔhái (bones and skeleton)
belong to earth.
When the jīngshén enters its gate,
and the gǔhái returns to its root,
what remains of me?
Hence, the sage emulates heaven and follows natural disposition,
unconstrained by customs,
unswayed by others,
taking heaven as father,
earth as mother,
yīn and yáng as the guiding principles,
and the four seasons as the framework.
Heaven is tranquil and clear,
earth stable and peaceful.
All things that lose this die,
while those that follow it live.
For tranquility and silence
are the abode of the divine intelligence;
emptiness and nothingness
are where the Dào resides.
Therefore, some who seek it externally
lose it internally;
while those who preserve it internally
gain it externally.
It is like the root and the branches:
if you pull from the root,
thousands of branches and leaves will follow without exception.
The jīngshén (essential spirit)
is received from heaven;
while the xíngtǐ (physical form)
is endowed by earth.
Hence it is said:
"The One gives birth to the Two,
the Two give birth to the Three,
the Three give birth to all things.
All things turn their backs on yīn and embrace yáng,
blending qì to achieve harmony."
Thus, it is said: in the first month, it becomes a greasy substance;
in the second month, it bloats;
in the third month, it forms a fetus;
in the fourth month, muscles develop;
in the fifth month, tendons form;
in the sixth month, bones take shape;
in the seventh month, it is fully formed;
in the eighth month, it moves;
in the ninth month, it becomes restless;
in the tenth month, it is born.
Once the xíngtǐ (physical form) is complete,
the five viscera take shape.
Therefore, the lungs govern the eyes,
the kidneys govern the nose,
the gallbladder governs the mouth,
and the liver governs the ears.
The exterior is the surface, and the interior is the inner part;
opening, closing, expanding, and contracting
each have their own order.
Thus, the roundness of the head symbolizes heaven,
and the squareness of the feet symbolizes earth.
Heaven has four seasons,
five phases,
nine divisions,
and three hundred sixty days;
humans also have four limbs,
five viscera,
nine orifices,
and three hundred sixty joints.
Heaven has wind, rain, cold, and heat;
humans also have taking, giving, joy, and anger.
Thus, the gallbladder corresponds to clouds,
the lungs to qì,
the spleen to wind,
the kidneys to rain,
the liver to thunder,
thereby correlating with heaven and earth,
with the heart as the ruler.
Therefore, the ears and eyes
are the sun and moon;
the blood and qì
are the wind and rain.
In the sun, there is the crouching crow;
in the moon, there is the toad.
If the sun and moon deviate from their course,
they are eclipsed and lose their light;
if wind and rain come at the wrong time,
they cause destruction and disasters;
if the five planets stray from their paths,
the provinces and states suffer calamity.
The Way of Heaven and Earth,
vast and immense as it is,
still moderates its brilliance,
cherishing its divine intelligence.
How can human ears and eyes long endure the toil without rest?
How can the spirit long gallop without exhaustion?
Thus, the vital energy and blood
are the splendor of humans;
and the five viscera
are the essence of humans.
When the vital energy and blood can concentrate within the five viscera without straying outward,
then the chest and abdomen are full, and desires are reduced.
With the chest and abdomen full and desires reduced,
the ears and eyes become clear,
and hearing and vision become acute.
When the ears and eyes are clear,
and hearing and vision acute,
it is called enlightenment.
When the five viscera can align with the heart without discord,
then resolute will prevails, and actions are not perverse.
With resolute will prevailing and actions not perverse,
the spirit is abundant, and the energy does not scatter.
When the spirit is abundant and the energy does not scatter, there is order;
order leads to balance;
balance leads to通畅;
通畅 leads to divinity;
with divinity, nothing is unseen in sight,
nothing unheard in hearing,
and nothing unaccomplished in action.
Thus, worries cannot enter,
and evil forces cannot assail.
Therefore, there are things sought beyond the four seas that cannot be found,
or guarded within the body that remain unseen.
Hence, those who seek much gain little,
and those who see grandly know little.
The orifices
are the windows of the spirit;
and the vital energy and blood
are the messengers of the five viscera.
If the ears and eyes indulge in the pleasures of sounds and sights,
then the five viscera become agitated and unsettled.
With the five viscera agitated and unsettled,
the vital energy and blood surge and do not rest.
With the vital energy and blood surging and not resting,
the spirit gallops outward and does not remain within.
When the spirit gallops outward and does not remain,
even if fortune or misfortune arrive
as large as a mountain,
there is no way to perceive them.
If the ears and eyes are keen, profound, and unswayed by temptations,
the will is empty, calm, joyful, and desires are reduced,
the five viscera are settled, tranquil, full, and do not leak,
and the spirit guards the body within without straying outward,
then looking back to ages past
and foreseeing events to come
would still not be enough,
let alone merely discerning fortune and misfortune!
Thus it is said:
"The farther one goes out,
the less one knows."
This speaks to how the spirit must not be allowed to stray outward.
Therefore, the five colors confuse the eyes,
making them unclear;
the five sounds clamor in the ears,
making them deaf;
the five flavors confuse the mouth,
making it impaired;
preferences and aversions disturb the heart,
causing the nature to become flighty.
These four things
are what the world uses to nurture life,
yet they all become burdens to humans.
Hence it is said:
Desires cause human energy to scatter,
and likes and dislikes cause the heart to toil.
If not quickly discarded,
the will and energy daily diminish.
Why do humans fail to live out their lifespan and instead die midway due to punishments or executions?
Why?
Because they overly cherish life.
Only by not making life a preoccupation
can one cultivate and attain life.
Heaven and Earth operate and interconnect,
and all things are unified as one.
To know the one
is to know all things;
not to know the one,
is to know nothing.
For example, I exist in the world,
also as one thing.
Do I not realize that the world prepares things with me?
Or is it that only without me are all things complete?
Then I am also a thing,
and things are also things.
Among things and things,
what basis is there to judge one another?
Even so,
when life is given to me,
what benefit does it bring?
When death is dealt to me,
what loss does it incur?
Since the Creator has made me as clay,
there is no opposing it.
How do I know that those who use acupuncture to seek life are not misguided?
And how do I know that those who hang themselves seeking death are not fortunate?
Perhaps life is but forced labor,
and death is rest?
The world is vast and obscure—
who knows?
When life is given to me, I do not forcefully seek its end;
when death is dealt, I do not forcefully seek to stop it.
I do not serve the desire for life,
nor do I refuse death out of hatred;
I do not despise being undervalued,
nor rejoice in being honored;
I follow my natural endowment and abide in it without extremes.
In life, I have a form of seven feet;
in death, I have a coffin of earth.
My life among tangible beings
is like my death submerged into the intangible.
Thus, in life, I do not increase the multitude of things,
and in death, the earth does not grow thicker;
how then can I know what to like, dislike, or what benefits and harms lie between?
The way the Creator handles things
is like a potter molding clay;
taking it from the ground to make pots and bowls
is no different from when it was still in the earth;
when the formed vessel breaks and crumbles back to its original state,
it is no different from when it was a pot or bowl.
In a village by the river,
people draw water to irrigate their gardens,
and the river does not resent it;
in a household with bitter stagnant water,
they channel it into the river,
and the stagnant water does not rejoice.
Thus, when in the river,
it is no different from watering the garden;
when in the stagnant pool,
it is no different from being in the river.
Therefore, the sage adapts to the times to secure his position,
and finds joy in his vocation in the present world.
Grief and joy
are deviations of virtue;
anger and delight
are excesses of the Way;
likes and dislikes
are burdens of the heart.
Hence it is said:
"In life, it is the movement of Heaven;
