in death, it is the transformation of things.
In stillness, one harmonizes with the virtue of Yin;
in motion, one resonates with the waves of Yang."
The spirit is serene and boundless,
not entangled with things,
and the world naturally submits.
Thus, the heart
is the master of the form;
and the spirit
is the treasure of the heart.
If the form toils without rest, it collapses;
if the essence is used without cease, it is exhausted.
Therefore, the sage values and honors them,
not daring to overstep.
One who possesses the jade of the Xiàhòu shì
stores it in a box,
treasuring it utmost.
But the value of the spirit
is not merely that of the Xiàhòu shì's jade.
Thus, the sage responds to being with non-being,
necessarily probing its principles;
receives substance with emptiness,
necessarily exhausting its details;
serene, joyful, empty, and calm,
he ends his days.
Thus, he is not overly distant
nor overly intimate,
embracing virtue and harmonizing warmth,
complying with Heaven.
He meets with the Way,
neighbors with virtue;
he does not initiate fortune,
nor precede misfortune.
His soul and spirit dwell in their abode,
and his spirit guards its root;
death and life do not alter him,
thus he is called supremely divine.
The so-called authentic person is one
whose nature is in harmony with the Way.
Thus, possessing yet appearing to have nothing,
substantial yet appearing empty,
abiding in unity without knowing duality,
cultivating the inner self without recognizing the external,
illuminated in pristine simplicity,
acting without action and returning to the unhewn,
embodying the root and embracing the spirit,
to wander within the confines of heaven and earth,
vaguely roaming beyond the dust and grime,
and drifting leisurely in the work of non-action.
Vast and expansive,
mechanical knowledge and cunning find no place in the heart.
Therefore, life and death are indeed significant,
yet they cause no change;
even if heaven and earth nurture all,
one does not cling to them.
Examining flawlessness,
and not mingling with things;
seeing the chaos of affairs,
yet able to preserve one's essence.
If so,
liver and gall are forgotten,
ears and eyes are discarded,
the mind's will is focused inward,
penetrating and connecting in oneness.
Dwelling without knowing what one does,
moving without knowing where one goes,
obliviously going forth,
suddenly coming back.
The form like a withered tree,
the mind like dead ashes.
Forgetting the five viscera,
discarding the physical form.
Knowing without learning,
seeing without looking,
accomplishing without acting,
discerning without governing.
Responding when stirred,
moving when pressed,
going forth when compelled,
like the radiance of light,
like the projection of a shadow,
taking the Way as the guideline,
acting only when conditions arise.
Holding the foundation of supreme clarity
without any attachments,
and things cannot disturb,
expansive and empty,
serene and without thoughts,
even if the great marsh burns, it cannot heat them,
even if the Yellow River and Hàn River dry up, it cannot chill them,
even if great thunder destroys mountains, it cannot startle them,
even if a great wind darkens the sun, it cannot harm them.
Thus, they regard precious pearls and jade as mere stones,
view the most honored and favored as passing travelers,
see Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī
as frightening specters.
Taking life and death as a single transformation,
regarding all things as one realm,
uniting the essence with the foundation of supreme clarity,
and wandering by the side of the indistinct region.
Having essence but not employing it,
possessing spirit but not using it,
embracing the simplicity of the great chaos,
and standing in the midst of ultimate clarity.
Therefore, in sleep they do not dream,
their wisdom does not sprout,
their earthly soul is not suppressed,
their heavenly soul does not soar.
Revolving through beginning and end,
not knowing their origins,
sweetly slumbering in the abode of great darkness,
yet awakening to see in the brightly lit universe,
resting in corners without twists and turns,
and roaming in fields without form or boundaries.
Dwelling without form,
abiding without place,
their movement has no shape,
their stillness has no substance,
existing yet as if gone,
living yet as if dead,
entering and exiting without gaps,
commanding ghosts and spirits,
sinking into the unfathomable,
entering the seamless,
transforming through different forms,
beginning and end like a circle,
none can grasp their order.
This is how the essence and spirit can ascend to the Way,
thus the wandering of the authentic person
is like blowing and breathing,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new,
the bear's stretch and the bird's extension,
the wild duck's bath and the ape's leap,
the owl's gaze and the tiger's glance,
these are for those who nurture the form,
not to disturb the heart.
Letting the spirit flow freely without losing its fullness,
day and night unharmed and harmonizing with things in springlike vitality,
this is uniting and giving birth to timeliness within the heart.
Moreover, one may have a worn form but an undiminished heart,
a decaying dwelling but an unexhausted essence.
The lame do not change their gait,
the mad do not lose their form,
the spirit is about to travel far,
who has leisure to know what it does!
Thus, the form may wear away, but the spirit never transforms;
responding to transformation with non-transformation,
through a thousand changes and ten thousand twists, it has never reached an end.
What transforms
returns to formlessness;
what does not transform
is born together with heaven and earth.
When a tree dies,
its green leaves depart.
Is what makes the tree live the tree itself?
It is like what fills the form not being the form.
Thus, what gives life never dies,
but what is born then dies;
what transforms things never transforms,
but what is transformed then transforms.
Lightening the world,
then the spirit is unburdened;
diminishing all things,
then the heart is unconfused;
equalizing life and death,
then the will is unafraid;
unifying with change,
then the vision is undazzled.
The masses consider this empty talk,
but I will cite examples to substantiate it.
The reason people delight in being rulers
is to indulge the desires of their ears and eyes,
and enjoy the comforts of their bodies.
Now, high towers and layered pavilions
are what people find beautiful,
yet Yáo's rafters were unhewn,
plain beams unadorned.
Rare delicacies and exotic flavors
are what people deem delicious,
yet Yáo ate coarse rice,
and soup of wild greens.
Embroidered silks and fox furs
are what people favor,
yet Yáo wore plain cloth to cover his form,
and deerskin to ward off cold.
The means to nurture his nature were not enriched,
but increased by the burden of heavy responsibilities,
so he relinquished the world and passed it to Shùn,
as if relieved of a heavy load.
Not merely out of polite refusal,
but truly having no use for it.
This is the means to lighten the world.
When Yǔ journeyed south to inspect the regions,
crossing the Yangtze River,
a yellow dragon bore the boat on its back,
and the people in the boat were pale with terror,
but Yǔ just laughed and declared:
"I received my mandate from heaven,
exerting myself to labor for the myriad people.
Life is but a sojourn,
death a return home,
how could this disturb my harmony!"
He regarded the dragon as a lizard,
his complexion unchanged,
and the dragon then drooped its ears, shook its tail, and fled.
Thus, Yǔ regarded things as insignificant.
When the divine shaman of Zhèng physiognomized Húzǐ Lín,
saw his signs,
and told Lièzǐ,
Lièzǐ went weeping to report to Húzǐ.
But Húzǐ held to the harmony of heaven and earth,
where name and reality do not enter,
and the mechanism springs from the heels.
Thus, Húzǐ regarded life and death as equal.
Zǐ Qiú, at fifty-four, became hunchbacked,
his spine higher than his crown, his
lower part pressing against his chin,
thighs above,
candleholder pointing skyward,
crawled to peek into a well and said:
"How great is the Creator!
Has it made me so contorted?"
Thus, he regarded change as one.
Therefore, observing Yáo's way,
we know how to lighten the world;
considering Yǔ's resolve,
we know how to diminish all things;
examining Húzǐ's discourse,
we know how to equalize life and death;
witnessing Zǐ Qiú's conduct,
we know how to unify with change.
The ultimate person leans on an unshakable pillar,
walks on unobstructed paths,
draws from an inexhaustible storehouse,
learns from an undying teacher,
and nowhere fails to accomplish,
nothing fails to penetrate.
Life cannot burden their will,
death cannot dim their spirit.
Bending and stretching, bowing and rising,
they embrace destiny and adapt flexibly.
Fortune and misfortune, benefit and harm,
in countless transformations and twists,
what can trouble their heart!
Such a person,
clings to simplicity and guards essence,
sheds their form like a cicada or snake,
wandering in the great purity,
soaring lightly alone,
suddenly entering the obscure.
Even the phoenix cannot be their mate,
let alone the quail!
How can power, status, rank, or salary sway their will!
When Yǎnzǐ swore a covenant with Cuī Zhù,
he faced death yet did not change his righteousness.
When Zhí and Huá were about to die in battle,
the ruler of Jǔ offered rich bribes to stop them,
yet they did not alter their course.
Thus, Yǎnzǐ could be moved by benevolence,
but not coerced by arms;
Zhí and Huá could be stopped by righteousness,
but not tempted by profit.
A noble person dies for righteousness,
and cannot be detained by wealth or honor;
acts for righteousness,
and cannot be threatened by death.
They simply do what is right,
and are still not constrained by external things,
how much more so one who practices non-action!
Yáo did not consider possessing the world as noble,
so he passed it to Shùn;
Prince Zhá did not consider possessing a state as honorable,
so he yielded the throne.
Zǐhǎn did not consider jade as wealth,
so he did not accept the treasure;
Wù Guāng did not let life harm righteousness,
so he threw himself into the abyss.
From this we see,
the noblest do not depend on rank,
the wealthiest do not depend on riches.
The world is the greatest thing,
yet they gave it to others;
the body is the closest thing,
yet they abandoned it in the abyss.
Beyond these,
nothing else is worth desiring.
This is called the unburdened person.
The unburdened person,
does not consider the world as noble.
Observing the discourse of the ultimate person,
deeply tracing the intent of the Way and its Virtue,
and examining below the conduct of the worldly,
one finds it truly shameful.
Thus, understanding the intent of Xǔ Yóu,
the "Golden Coffer" and
"Leopard韬" become obsolete;
Yánlíng Jìzǐ not accepting the state of Wú,
shames those who dispute over border fields;
Zǐhǎn not profiting from precious jade,
embarrasses those who fight over contracts;
Wù Guāng not being defiled by the world,
distresses those who greedily seek profit and cling to life.
Therefore, those who do not see great righteousness,
do not know that life is not worth coveting;
those who have not heard great words,
do not know that the world is not worth profiting from.
Now, the village shrine of a poor hamlet,
knocking on basins and tapping on jars,
singing in harmony,
considers itself joyful.
But try beating the great drum for them,
striking the massive bell,
and only then do they realize,
how shameful their basins and jars are.
Hiding the "Book of Songs"
and "Book of Documents",
cultivating literature and learning,
yet not knowing the essence of the ultimate discourse,
is to be among those who tap jars and knock basins.
Those who have no use for the world,
learn from the great drum.
Respectful power and substantial profit,
are what people covet.
But make them hold the map of the world in their left hand and cut their throat with the right,
and no fool would do it.
From this we see,
life is more precious than the world.
The sage's food suffices to sustain energy,
clothing suffices to cover the body,
content with their disposition, not seeking surplus,
without the world, their nature is not diminished,
with the world, they do not crave more harmony.
Having the world,
or not having the world,
is the same in substance.
Now, giving someone the Áo Granary,
or handing someone the Hé River,
when hungry, they eat from it,
when thirsty, they drink from it,
but what enters their belly is no more than a basket of food or a gourd of drink,
so their body is full, yet the Áo Granary is not reduced,
their belly is satisfied, yet the Hé River is not exhausted.
Having it does not make them fuller,
not having it does not make them hungry,
the same as guarding their granary
and owning their well.
In substance, it is one.
Great anger breaks the yin,
great joy collapses the yang,
great sorrow causes internal collapse,
great terror breeds madness.
Eliminating defilements and shedding burdens,
serene as if never departing from their origin,
this is the great penetration.
Clear eyes but not using them to see,
quiet ears but not using them to hear,
sealed mouth but not using it to speak,
entrusted heart but not using it to ponder,
abandoning cleverness and returning to great simplicity,
resting the spirit and discarding knowledge and cunning,
awake yet as if dreaming,
alive yet as if dead,
finally returning to the state before birth,
and becoming one with transformation.
Death and life,
are one body.
Now, consider the laborer,
lifting hoe and shovel,
carrying baskets of soil,
sweat streaming down,
breath panting in the throat.
At such a time,
getting to rest under a tree,
brings relief and joy.
But the peace of a mountain cave,
is not just the rest under a tree.
One ill with a tumor,
clutching the chest, pressing the belly,
kneeling and knocking the head,
curled up and moaning,
sleepless all night.
At such a time,
simply being able to lie down,
brings joy to family and siblings.
But the tranquility of a long night,
is not just the pleasure of lying down.
Therefore, knowing the vastness of the universe,
one cannot be coerced by life and death;
knowing the harmony of nurturing life,
one cannot be tempted by the world;
knowing the joy of the unborn state,
one cannot be frightened by death;
knowing that Xǔ Yóu was nobler than Shùn,
one does not covet things.
A wall standing,
is not as good as lying down,
how much more not being a wall at all!
Ice freezing,
is not as good as melting,
how much more not being ice at all!
From non-being to being,
from being to non-being,
beginning and end without a start,
none know where it sprouts.
Unless one penetrates the internal and external,
who can be without likes and dislikes?
The external beyond the external,
is the greatest;
the internal within the internal,
is the noblest;
able to know this great nobility,
where can one go and not succeed!
In a decadent age, pedantic scholars
fail to understand the essence of the heart and return to the root.
They merely carve and polish their nature,
forcibly restrain their emotions,
to interact with the world.
Thus, though their eyes desire something,
they restrain it with rules;
though their hearts delight in something,
they regulate it with rites.
They move about with measured steps,
bowing humbly with restrained demeanor,
letting meat congeal uneaten,
wine clarify undrunk.
Externally, they bind their form;
internally, they distress their virtue.
They disrupt the harmony of yīn and yáng,
and oppress the genuine nature of life,
thus becoming sorrowful individuals all their lives.
Those who comprehend the ultimate Dào are not like this:
they regulate their emotions and nature,
cultivate their mental dispositions,
nurture them with harmony,
and maintain them with appropriateness.
They delight in the Dào and forget their lowliness,
rest in virtue and forget their poverty.
If their nature lacks desire,
they lack nothing;
if their hearts lack joy,
they do nothing for joy.
What does not benefit their emotions does not burden their virtue;
what is not conducive to their nature does not disturb their harmony.
Thus, they indulge their bodies and follow their intentions,
yet their measures can serve as models for the world.
Now, the Rúists
do not address the root of desires but prohibit the desires themselves;
they do not trace the source of joy but suppress the joy itself.
This is like trying to stem the source of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers with one's hands.
Governing the people
is like rearing livestock and wild animals:
if you do not secure their enclosures,
allowing them wild ambitions,
and then tether their legs
to prevent their movement,
yet expect them to live long and die naturally,
how could it be possible!
Yán Huí,
Jì Lù,
Zǐ Xià,
Rǎn Bóniú—
these were among Confucius's accomplished disciples.
Yet Yán Yuān died young,
Jì Lù was minced in Wèi,
Zǐ Xià lost his eyesight,
Rǎn Bóniú suffered from leprosy.
All these resulted from oppressing their nature, contradicting their emotions, and failing to attain harmony.
Thus, when Zǐ Xià met Zēngzǐ,
one thin, the other plump,
Zēngzǐ asked the reason.
Zǐ Xià said:
"When I go out, I see the joys of wealth and honor and desire them;
when I come in, I see the Dào of the former kings and delight in it.
The two conflict in my heart,
hence I am thin.
When the Dào of the former kings prevails,
I become plump."
Inferring from this,
his will was not incapable of renouncing positions of wealth and honor,
nor of avoiding extravagant pleasures;
he merely oppressed his nature and suppressed desires,
defending himself with righteousness.
Though his heart was stifled and depressed,
his form and nature exhausted,
he still forced himself relentlessly,
thus unable to live out his natural lifespan.
As for the ultimate person,
they eat according to their appetite,
clothe according to their form,
wander where they can dwell,
act according to their emotions.
They leave the world's surplus without coveting it,
relinquish all things without seeking profit.
They reside in vast, open spaces,
roam in boundless wilderness,
ascend the supreme sovereign,
rely on the Great Unity,
play with heaven and earth in the palm of their hand.
How could they be concerned with poverty, wealth, plumpness, or thinness!
Thus, the Rúists cannot make people have no desires;
they merely stop them when they desire.
They cannot make people have no joys;
they merely prohibit them when they rejoice.
Making the world fear punishment and dare not steal
is not as good as eliminating the very thought of stealing!
The Yuè people obtain the rán snake
and consider it a delicacy,
while the central states acquire it and discard it as useless.
Thus, knowing its uselessness,
even the greedy can decline it;
not knowing its uselessness,
even the honest cannot yield it.
The reason rulers destroy and lose their states,
abandon their altars of land and grain,
die at others' hands,
and become laughingstocks of the world,
is often due to such desires.
Chóuyóu coveted the bribe of a large bell and lost his state;
the lord of Yú coveted the jade of Chuíjí and was captured;
Duke Xiàn admired the beauty of Lí Jī and brought chaos for four generations;
Duke Huán relished Yì Yá's cooking and was not buried timely;
the Hú king indulged in the pleasures of female musicians and lost his territory.
Had these five rulers
followed their emotions, renounced excess,
taken themselves as the measure,
and not been swayed by external things,
would they have suffered such great calamities?
Therefore, in archery,
it is not that the arrow misses the target,
but the learner does not focus on the arrow;
in charioteering, it is not that the reins fail to guide,
but the learner does not concentrate on the reins.
Knowing that a winter fan
or a summer fur coat are useless to oneself,
then all changes in things become like dust.
Thus, trying to stop boiling with hot water
only makes it boil more;
truly understanding the root cause,
one simply removes the fire.
In the governance of the Great Purity,
harmony and tranquility prevailed in serene stillness,
genuineness and simplicity were pure and unadorned,
leisure and calm reigned without agitation,
changes occurred without forced causes,
inwardly, it aligned with the Dào,
outwardly, it harmonized with righteousness,
actions unfolded with cultural refinement,
deeds were swift and beneficial to all things,
words were concise and followed reason,
conduct was straightforward and in tune with emotions,
hearts were joyful and free from deceit,
affairs were plain and unembellished,
thus, there was no need to choose auspicious days,
no divination with tortoise shells or stalks,
no plotting of beginnings,
no debating of ends,
in peace, they rested;
when stirred, they acted,
their bodies united with heaven and earth,
their essence merged with yīn and yáng,
in harmony with the four seasons,
illuminated by the sun and moon,
they vied with the Creator as equals.
Hence, heaven bestowed virtue,
earth bore joy,
the four seasons never lost their order,
wind and rain brought no calamity,
the sun and moon shone pure and radiant,
the five planets followed their orbits without straying.
At that time,
the mysterious and primal essence flourished and shone everywhere,
phoenixes and qílín arrived,
divination stalks and tortoise shells gave omens,
sweet dew descended,
bamboo seeds abounded,
sulfur emerged,
and vermilion grass sprouted,
mechanical tricks and deceitful falsehoods
found no place in people's hearts.
But when it came to the decadent age,
they carved mountain rocks,
extracted gold and jade,
pried open clams and shells,
smelted copper and iron,
and all things ceased to thrive.
Wombs were ripped open, the young killed,
qílín no longer roamed,
nests overturned, eggs destroyed,
phoenixes no longer soared,
fire was drilled from wood,
trees were felled to build towers,
forests burned for farming,
marshes drained for fishing,
so turtles and dragons departed,
human tools fell short,
hoarded stores overflowed,
and among the myriad things, those sprouting, budding, or in egg and womb that failed to mature
accounted for more than half.
Mounds of soil piled into hills,
fields fertilized for grain,
wells dug for water,
rivers dredged for gain,
walls raised for defense,
beasts captured for domestication,
then yīn and yáng clashed in discord,
the four seasons lost their sequence;
thunderbolts shattered and destroyed,
hail and sleet fell fiercely,
mists, fog, snow, and frost did not clear,
and all things withered and died young,
disasters ran rampant through thickets,
boundaries crowded the fields,
wild growths were cut down,
seedlings flourished briefly,
plants with tender shoots,
bearing blossoms,
or laden with fruit that perished
were too numerous to count.
Even when grand palaces with interconnected rooms were built,
linked by continuous pillars,
with rafters and eaves adorned,
carved and engraved intricately,
tall branches and elegant curves,
lotus and water lilies,
five colors vying in brilliance,
flowing and dazzling in splendor,
with winding extensions and curved joints,
soaring and layered in complexity,
lush and tangled in profusion,
all intertwined and supporting each other,
even Gōngshū
and Wáng Ěr would have no place to apply their chisels, planes, or saws,
yet it still could not satisfy the ruler's desires.
Thus, pines, cypresses, and fungi withered in summer,
the Jiāng, Hé,
and other great rivers ceased to flow,
strange sheep roamed the pastures,
swarms of locusts filled the fields,
heaven sent drought, the earth cracked,
phoenixes did not descend,
and beasts with hooked claws,
protruding fangs,
horns on their heads,
and spurs emerged to prey fiercely.
The people, confined in hovels and thatched huts,
had nowhere to turn,
and those dead from cold, hunger, and starvation lay piled upon one another.
When it came to dividing mountains, streams, and valleys with borders,
tallying populations to assign quotas,
building walls and digging moats,
setting up machines and barriers for defense,
adorning official duties,
establishing dress codes,
distinguishing noble from base,
grading the worthy and the un- (
worthy),
regulating praise and blame,
implementing rewards and punishments,
then weapons arose and conflicts were born,
and among the people, suppression and premature death,
cruel killings of the innocent and punishment of the guiltless,
thus came into being.
The harmony between Heaven and Earth,
the molding and transformation of all things by yīn and yáng,
all ride on a single breath.
Therefore, when those above and below are of divided hearts,
the breath rises and steams upward;
when ruler and minister are not in harmony,
the five grains do not grow.
Forty-six days before the winter solstice,
Heaven holds harmony but has not yet sent it down,
Earth embraces the breath but has not yet raised it.
Yīn and yáng linger,
breathing and soaking deeply,
enveloping customs,
weighing the myriad differences,
extending broadly to suit the multitude,
mutually nurturing and fermenting,
thus giving birth and nourishing all living beings.
Hence, the austerity of spring and the flourishing of autumn,
winter thunder and summer frost,
all are born of thieving breaths.
From this we observe that
Heaven, Earth, and the cosmos,
are like one person's body;
within the six directions,
are the pattern of one person.
Therefore, one who understands nature
cannot be threatened by Heaven and Earth;
one who discerns correspondences
cannot be deluded by strange phenomena.
Thus, the sage,
knowing the distant from the near,
unites the myriad differences into one.
The people of old
shared the same breath with Heaven and Earth,
and wandered at ease with the whole age.
At that time,
there were no benefits of rewards,
no威慑 of punishments,
no establishment of ritual, righteousness, integrity, or shame,
no setting up of slander, praise, benevolence, or baseness,
yet the myriad people did not invade, deceive, tyrannize, or oppress each other,
as if still in a state of混沌 darkness.
When it came to the decadent age,
people were numerous but wealth scarce,
labor was toilsome but sustenance insufficient,
whereupon resentment and strife arose,
and thus benevolence was valued.
Benevolence and baseness were not uniform,
cliques and factions formed,
deceit and schemes were set up,
hearts harbored machinations and cunning artifices,
and innate nature was lost,
thus righteousness was valued.
The passions of yīn and yáng,
all have the stirrings of blood and breath,
men and women lived together in groups without distinction,
thus ritual was valued.
The passions of innate nature and life,
became excessive and mutually oppressive,
and being compelled,
there was no harmony,
thus music was valued.
Therefore, benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music
are means to rescue from decline,
not the ultimate way of comprehensive governance.
Now, benevolence
is to save from strife;
righteousness
is to save from loss;
ritual
is to save from excess;
music
is to save from sorrow.
When divine clarity is settled under Heaven, the heart returns to its origin;
when the heart returns to its origin, the people's nature is good;
when the people's nature is good, Heaven, Earth, yīn, and yáng follow and embrace them,
then wealth is sufficient,
wealth is sufficient and people are well-provided,
greed, baseness, resentment, and strife do not arise.
From this we observe that
then benevolence and righteousness are not needed.
When the Dào and virtue are settled under Heaven and the people are pure and simple,
then their eyes do not crave for colors,
their ears do not indulge in sounds,
they sit and sing folksongs,
wear their hair loose and wander freely.
Even if there were the beauty of Máo Qiáng,
Xī Shī,
they would not know delight;
even the "Plume Dance",
"Wǔ Xiàng" music, they would not know pleasure.
Licentiousness and lack of distinction
do not arise.
From this we observe that
then ritual and music are not needed.
Therefore, when virtue declines, then benevolence arises;
when conduct fails, then righteousness is established;
when harmony is lost, then music is tuned;
when ritual becomes excessive, then appearance is adorned.
Hence, knowing divine clarity, one then knows that Dào and virtue are not to be contrived;
knowing Dào and virtue, one then knows that benevolence and righteousness are not to be practiced;
knowing benevolence and righteousness, one then knows that ritual and music are not to be cultivated.
Now, turning away from the root and seeking it in the branches,
abandoning the essential and searching for it in the details,
one cannot be spoken to about the ultimate.
The vastness of Heaven and Earth
can be measured with compass and gauge;
the movements of stars and moon
can be obtained by calendrical calculation;
the sound of thunder
can be reproduced with drums and bells;
the changes of wind and rain
can be known through musical pitches.
Therefore, what is large and visible
can be measured;
what is bright and observable
can be covered;
sounds that can be heard
can be tuned;
colors that can be discerned
can be distinguished.
Now, the utmost large
cannot be contained by Heaven and Earth;
the utmost minute
cannot be grasped by divine intelligence.
When it comes to establishing pitch standards and calendars,
distinguishing the five colors,
differentiating the clear and turbid,
tasting the sweet and bitter,
then the uncarved block is broken up to make vessels.
Establishing benevolence and righteousness,
cultivating ritual and music,
then virtue is displaced and becomes artifice.
When artifice arises,
intelligence is adorned to startle the ignorant,
deceit is set up to cleverly deceive superiors.
Under Heaven, there may be those who can sustain it,
but none who can truly govern it.
In ancient times, when Cāng Jié created writing, Heaven rained grain,
and ghosts wept at night;
when Bó Yì invented wells,
dragons ascended to the dark clouds,
and spirits perched on Kūnlún;
the more wisdom and ability increased, the more virtue diminished.
Therefore, the Zhōu tripod depicted Chuí
making him bite his finger,
to show that great cleverness is not to be practiced.
Thus, in the governance of the ultimate person,
the heart dwells with the spirit,
the form is harmonized with nature,
in stillness embodying virtue,
in movement comprehending principles,
following the nature of spontaneity and complying with inevitable transformations,
profoundly non-active, yet the world naturally harmonizes;
tranquilly without desires, yet the people naturally become simple;
without prayers for good omens, yet the people do not die young;
without resentment and strife, yet sustenance is sufficient;
embracing all within the seas,
blessings extending to later generations,
yet no one knows who does it.
Therefore, in life there is no title,
in death no posthumous name,
wealth is not accumulated and fame not established,
the giver does not consider it virtuous,
the receiver does not decline,
virtue intermingles and returns, yet none feel filled or dissatisfied.
Thus, where virtue gathers,
the Dào cannot harm it;
what wisdom does not know,
argument cannot explain.
The argument without words,
the Dào that is not spoken,
if one somehow penetrates it,
it is called the celestial storehouse.
Take from it without depletion,
draw from it without exhaustion,
none know where it comes from,
this is called the Shining Pearl.
The Shining Pearl
provides for and nourishes the myriad things.
Relieving the impoverished and destitute,
supplementing what is lacking,
then reputation arises;
promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
quelling disorder and prohibiting tyranny,
then achievements are accomplished.
When the world is free from disasters and calamities,
even deities have no means to施展 their virtue;
when superiors and inferiors are harmonious and united,
even the worthy have no grounds to establish their merits.
In the time of Róngchéngshì,
geese formed rows on the roads and dwelled in places,
infants were left in nests atop trees,
surplus grain was placed at field boundaries,
tigers and leopards could be followed by the tail,
venomous snakes could be trodden upon,
yet no one knew how this came to be so.
When it reached the time of Yáo,
ten suns appeared simultaneously,
scorching the grains and crops,
killing the grasses and trees,
and the people had nothing to eat.
Yàyǔ,
Jiǔyīng,
Dàfēng,
Fēngxī,
Záochǐ,
Xiūshé
all became scourges to the people.
Yáo then sent Yì to execute Záochǐ at the marsh of Chóuhuá,
slay Jiǔyīng upon the Xiōng River,
shoot down Dàfēng in the wilds of Qīngqiū,
shoot down the ten suns from above and kill Yàyǔ below,
cut down Xiūshé at Dòngtíng,
and capture Fēngxī in Sānglín.
The myriad people were all joyful,
and established Yáo as the Son of Heaven.
Thereupon, the breadth, narrowness, peril, ease, distance, and proximity of the world began to have measured pathways.
In the time of Shùn,
Gònggōng stirred up and deluged with floodwaters,
reaching to Kōngsāng,
when Lóngmén had not yet opened,
Lǚliáng had not yet burst forth,
the Jiāng and Huái rivers flowed connected,
the four seas were a vast expanse,
the people all ascended hills and mounds,
and sought refuge in trees.
Shùn then sent Yǔ to dredge the three rivers and five lakes,
cleave open Yīquē,
channel the Chán
and Jiàn rivers, level and open ditches and land,
flowing eastward into the sea.
The great waters receded,
the nine provinces dried,
and the myriad people all settled into their nature.
Therefore, Yáo and
Shùn are praised as sages.
In later ages,
there were emperors Jié and
Zhòu; Jié built palaces of fine jade,
terraces of precious stone,
corridors of ivory,
and beds of jade;
Zhòu made enclosures of meat,
pools of wine,
burning and consuming the wealth of the world,
exhausting and tormenting the strength of the myriad people.
He disemboweled remonstrators,
ripped open pregnant women,
plundered the world,
and tyrannized the common people.
Thereupon, Tāng led three hundred war chariots to attack Jié at Náncháo,
banishing him to Xiàtái;
King Wǔ with three thousand armored soldiers defeated Zhòu at Mùyě,
killing him in Xuānshì.
The world was pacified and stabilized,
the common people harmonized and gathered,
therefore Tāng and
Wǔ are praised for their worthiness.
From this perspective,
those who have the reputation of worthiness and sageliness
must encounter the calamities of chaotic times.
Now, the ultimate person living in a chaotic age,
embodying virtue and embracing the Way,
holding boundless wisdom,
gags his mouth and stills his speech,
thus dying without speaking is common,
yet the world does not know to value their silence.
Thus, the Way that can be spoken of
is not the eternal Way;
the name that can be named
is not the eternal name.
What is recorded on bamboo and silk,
engraved on metal and stone,
and can be transmitted to others
is its coarse aspect.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings
differed in affairs but shared the same intent;
took different paths but reached the same destination.
Later scholars,
not knowing the oneness of the Way's embodiment,
nor the essence of virtue's totality,
take the traces of accomplished deeds,
sit solemnly together and discourse on them,
beating drums, singing, and dancing to them,
thus, though broad in learning and rich in knowledge,
they cannot avoid confusion.
The Book of Songs says:
"I dare not tackle a tiger with bare hands,
nor cross a river without a boat.
People know one thing,
but do not know the other."
This expresses it.
The Thearch embodies the Great One,
the King models himself on Yin and Yang,
the Hegemon follows the four seasons,
the Ruler employs the six pitch-standards.
The Great One
encompasses heaven and earth,
subdues mountains and rivers,
inhales and exhales Yin and Yang,
extends and pulls the four seasons,
disciplines the eight extremities,
weaves the warp and woof of the six directions,
covers, dewes, illuminates, and guides,
universal and impartial,
from flying insects to wriggling creatures,
none do not look up to its virtue and live.
Yin and Yang
receive the harmony of heaven and earth,
form the bodies of the myriad differences,
contain pneuma and transform things,
to complete all categories,
waxing and waning, coiling and stretching,
sinking into the immeasurable,
ending and beginning, empty and full,
turning in the originless.
The four seasons
bring forth in spring and grow in summer,
harvest in autumn and store in winter,
taking and giving have their moderation,
exiting and entering have their measure,
opening and closing, expanding and contracting,
not losing their sequence,
joy and anger, firm and gentle,
not departing from their principle.
The six pitch-standards
are about life and death,
reward and punishment,
giving and taking away,
without these there is no Way,
thus being careful with scales and measures, standards and lines,
examining lightness and heaviness,
is sufficient to govern within their borders.
Therefore, one who embodies the Supreme Unity
understands the nature of heaven and earth,
comprehends the principles of the Way and its virtue,
has a brilliance that shines like the sun and moon,
a spirit that connects with all things,
movements and stillness harmonized with yin and yang,
joy and anger attuned to the four seasons,
virtue and grace extended beyond the borders,
and reputation passed down to later generations.
Those who model themselves on yin and yang
have virtue that matches heaven and earth,
brightness that parallels the sun and moon,
essence that unites with ghosts and spirits;
they bear the round (heaven) and tread the square (earth),
embrace standards and hold the measuring line,
internally able to govern themselves,
externally able to win people's hearts,
issue commands and decrees,
and none under heaven fail to follow like the wind.
As for those who follow the four seasons,
they are pliable but not brittle,
firm but not broken,
broad but not unrestrained,
solemn but not perverse,
gentle and accommodating,
nurturing all kinds of beings,
their virtue embraces the foolish and tolerates the unworthy,
without any private affections.
Those who employ the six pitch-pipes
suppress disorder and prohibit violence,
promote the worthy and depose the unworthy,
support the fallen to make them upright,
break down dangers to create peace,
straighten the crooked to make them straight,
understand the principles of prohibition, release, opening, and closing,
seizing the moment and adapting to circumstances to subdue people's hearts.
An emperor who embodies yin and yang will be encroached upon;
a king who models on the four seasons will be diminished;
a hegemon who regulates with the six pitch-pipes will be disgraced;
a ruler who loses the standard will be overthrown.
Thus, if small acts as large,
it becomes vast and distant, and no one feels close;
if large acts as small,
it becomes narrow and confined, and cannot accommodate.
When noble and humble do not lose their proper form,
then the world is well-governed.
Heaven cherishes its essence,
earth cherishes its balance,
humans cherish their emotions.
The essence of heaven
is the sun, moon, stars, thunder, lightning, wind, and rain;
the balance of earth
is water, fire, metal, wood, and earth;
the emotions of humans
are thought, consideration, intelligence, joy, and anger.
Therefore, close the four passes,
stop the five excesses,
and you will merge with the Way.
Thus, the divine spirit hides in formlessness,
the vital energy returns to utmost purity,
then the eyes are bright but not used for seeing,
the ears are sharp but not used for hearing,
the mouth is appropriate but not used for speaking,
the heart is clear and unobstructed but not used for thinking,
yielding and not acting,
harmonious and not arrogant,
the true nature of life and emotions,
and cunning and artifice cannot mix in.
If essence is emitted through the eyes, then vision is clear;
if it resides in the ears, then hearing is sharp;
if it stays in the mouth, then speech is appropriate;
if it gathers in the heart, then thoughts are penetrating.
Therefore, close the four passes and you will be free from trouble for life,
all joints will not wither,
neither dying nor being born,
neither empty nor full,
this is called the True Person.
Generally, the causes of disorder
all lie in excessive indulgences.
The excessive indulgences arise from five sources:
constructing great frameworks,
building palaces and halls,
extended towers and plank roads,
chicken perches and well railings,
pillars, beams, and brackets,
supporting each other,
ornate wooden decorations,
coiled and intricately carved,
exquisite carvings and engravings,
bizarre patterns and swirling waves,
flowing and rippling designs,
diamond shapes and twisted embraces,
sharp, intricate, chaotic gloss,
clever artifices tangled together,
mutually crushing and interlocking,
this is indulgence in wood.
Digging deep ponds,
extending to distant banks and cliffs,
drawing streams from valleys,
adorning winding shores,
piling layered stones,
to pure and long embankments,
suppressing rushing rapids,
to raise surging waves,
winding and turning back,
imitating the Yú
and Wú rivers, planting more lotuses and water chestnuts,
to feed turtles and fish,
swans and ducks,
with abundant rice and millet,
dragon boats with pheasant heads,
floating and playing music for amusement,
this is indulgence in water.
Building high city walls,
setting up dangerous barriers,
elevating the grandeur of towers and pavilions,
enlarging the expanse of parks and gardens,
to exhaust the finest views,
the height of the lofty gate towers,
reaching up to the blue clouds,
multi-storied great halls,
rivaling Kūnlún,
building long walls,
connected by covered passages,
leveling heights and raising lows,
accumulating earth into mountains,
connecting paths over long distances,
straight roads through flat and dangerous terrain,
galloping all day,
without tripping or falling,
this is indulgence in earth.
Large bells and tripods,
beautiful precious vessels,
decorated with flowery patterns and openwork,
intertwined and twisted,
reclining rhinoceroses and crouching tigers,
coiled dragons and linked designs,
dazzling and confusing brilliance,
shining and radiant,
towering and intricate,
curved into patterns,
carved and polished ornaments,
forged tin with patterned surfaces,
now dim, now bright,
suppressing flaws and eliminating blemishes,
frost-like patterns deeply set,
like bamboo mats and reeds,
intertwined brocade and intricate threads,
seemingly dense yet sparse,
this is indulgence in metal.
Boiling, frying, burning, and roasting,
adjusting flavors to perfection,
exhausting the variations of sweet and sour from Jīng
and Wú,
burning forests to hunt,
setting large trees ablaze,
blowing bellows and pipes,
to melt copper and iron,
grinding and forging tirelessly,
never satisfied day after day,
mountains stripped of tall trees,
forests without zhè and nài trees,
burning wood for charcoal,
scorching grass for ash,
the plains bare and white,
not in their proper season,
above obscuring the sky's light,
below exhausting the earth's resources,
this is indulgence in fire.
Any one of these five
is enough to cause the loss of the world.
Therefore, in ancient times, the design of the Bright Hall
was such that the dampness below could not reach it,
the fog and dew above could not enter,
the winds from all four directions could not assail it,
earthen structures were unadorned,
wooden work was unhewn,
metal vessels were unengraved,
clothing had no angled cuts,
caps had no carved ridges,
the hall was large enough for movement and orderly patterns,
quiet and clean enough to offer sacrifices to the Supreme Deity,
and to honor ghosts and spirits,
thus showing the people the knowledge of frugality and moderation.
The allure of sounds and flavors,
exotic treasures from distant lands,
rare and peculiar objects,
are enough to alter one's heart and will,
unsettle the spirit,
and stir the vital energy—
such things are beyond count.
Now, the wealth produced by Heaven and Earth
fundamentally does not exceed the five elements.
When the sage regulates the five phases,
then governance does not fall into disarray.
As for human nature,
when the heart is content and desires fulfilled, there is joy;
with joy comes movement;
with movement comes stepping;
with stepping comes swaying;
with swaying comes singing;
with singing comes dancing.
If singing and dancing lack restraint,
and without restraint,
then one leaps about like beasts.
In human nature,
when the heart bears sorrow or loss, there is grief;
grief leads to mourning;
mourning leads to indignation;
indignation leads to anger;
anger leads to agitation;
agitation results in restless hands and feet.
In human nature,
when faced with infringement, there is anger;
anger causes blood to surge;
blood surging stirs the qi;
qi stirred leads to outbursts of rage;
outbursts of rage allow for the release of resentment.
Thus, bells, drums, pipes, and flutes,
shields, axes, feathers, and banners,
are used to adorn joy.
Mourning garments and staffs,
weeping and leaping with restraint,
are used to adorn sorrow.
Weapons, armor, feathers, and banners,
gongs, drums, axes, and battle-axes,
are used to adorn anger.
There must be the substance,
before the form is applied.
In ancient times, when sage kings ruled above,
governance and education were equitable,
benevolence and love permeated all,
high and low were of one heart,
rulers and ministers harmonious,
clothing and food were abundant,
households were provided for and people satisfied,
fathers were kind and sons filial,
elder brothers good and younger brothers obedient,
the living bore no resentment,
the dead had no regrets,
the world was harmonious and united,
and each person attained their desires.
When people rejoice together,
with no means to express it,
the sage kings thus created rituals and music to harmonize and moderate it.
In the governance of decadent ages,
farming and fishing are heavily taxed,
tolls and markets impose urgent levies,
marshes and weirs are entirely restricted,
nets have nowhere to be spread,
plows and hoes have no place to be used,
the people's strength is exhausted by corvée labor,
resources are depleted by taxes and tributes,
those at home have no food,
travelers have no provisions,
the elderly are not cared for,
the dead are not buried,
wives are pawned and children sold,
to meet the demands from above,
yet still unable to suffice,
even foolish men and simple women harbor hearts of wandering,
and spirits of sorrow,
and only then do they strike great bells,
beat resounding drums,
blow panpipes and sheng,
pluck qin and se,
thus losing the root of music.
In ancient times, the demands from above were light and the people's needs were met,
the ruler bestowed his virtue,
ministers exhausted their loyalty,
fathers exercised their kindness,
sons devoted their filial piety,
each giving their love without regret or resentment among them.
The three-year mourning period
is not forced upon them;
they find no joy in listening to music,
no sweetness in eating delicacies,
for the heart of longing and remembrance has not yet ceased.
In later ages, customs deteriorate and morals decay,
desires abound,
rituals and righteousness are abandoned,
rulers and ministers deceive each other,
fathers and sons distrust one another,
resentment fills their breasts,
thoughts of love are entirely lost;
clad in mourning garments and wearing hempen bands,
they jest and laugh within,
even if observing it for three years,
they lose the essence of mourning.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had one capital region,
the feudal lords each had one domain,
each guarding their own portion,
not permitted to encroach upon one another.
If any failed to uphold the kingly way,
oppressed the myriad people,
fought over land and invaded territories,
disrupted governance and violated prohibitions,
did not come when summoned,
did not act when ordered,
did not stop when prohibited,
did not change when admonished,
then armies were raised to attack them,
their rulers were executed,
their factions replaced,
their tombs sealed,
their altars transformed,
and their descendants divined for replacement.
In later ages, efforts focused on expanding territory and invading lands,
annexing without cease,
raising unrighteous armies to attack innocent states,
killing guiltless people and cutting off the lineage of ancient sages;
large states launched attacks,
small states fortified their defenses,
driving away others' oxen and horses,
capturing others' sons and daughters,
destroying others' ancestral temples,
seizing others' precious treasures,
shedding blood for a thousand miles,
leaving exposed bones filling the wilds,
to satisfy the desires of greedy rulers—
this is not the purpose for which arms are meant.
Therefore, arms
are for punishing tyranny,
not for committing tyranny.
Music
is for achieving harmony,
not for indulgence.
Mourning
is for expressing grief fully,
not for pretense.
Thus, in serving parents, there is a way,
and love is the essential task;
in the court, there is decorum,
and respect is paramount;
in observing mourning, there are rituals,
and grief is the main focus;
in employing arms, there is strategy,
and righteousness is the foundation.
When the foundation is established, the way is practiced;
when the foundation is harmed, the way is abandoned.
The method of the ruler
is to engage in effortless action,
and to teach without words,
remaining serene and unmoving,
adhering to one standard unwaveringly,
following tradition and entrusting subordinates,
holding them accountable without toil.
Thus, though the mind knows the plan, the mentors expound the way;
though the mouth can speak, the envoys articulate the words;
though the feet can walk, the guides lead the way;
though the ears can hear, the upright officials offer advice.
Therefore, deliberations leave no strategy amiss,
actions involve no missteps,
words become literary works,
and conduct sets an example for the world,
advancing and retreating in accordance with the times,
moving and resting in accord with principle,
not swayed by beauty or ugliness, love or hate,
not driven by rewards or punishments, anger or joy,
names each having their own name,
categories each their own kind,
affairs as if spontaneous,
with nothing originating from oneself.
Thus, the ancient kings
wore crowns with hanging beads in front,
to obscure their vision;
had yellow silk plugging their ears,
to dampen their hearing;
the Son of Heaven had an outer screen,
to shield himself.
Therefore, what is governed from afar
is managed from nearby,
what is administered on a large scale
is guarded with small means.
For the eyes, if they look recklessly, lead to licentiousness;
the ears, if they listen recklessly, lead to confusion;
the mouth, if it speaks recklessly, leads to disorder.
These three gates,
must be guarded with utmost care.
If you wish to regulate it,
you will instead estrange it;
if you wish to adorn it,
you will instead harm it.
The qi of heaven is the hún,
the qi of earth is the pò;
return them to the mysterious chamber,
each residing in its abode.
Guard them without loss,
and above connect with Tàiyī.
The essence of Tàiyī,
communicates and merges with heaven.
The way of heaven is mysteriously silent,
without form or rule,
heaven cannot be reached,
its depth cannot be fathomed,
yet it transforms with humans,
knowledge cannot grasp it.
In ancient times, when Shénnóng governed the world,
his spirit did not race within his breast,
his wisdom did not extend beyond the four realms,
embracing his benevolent and sincere heart,
timely rains fell,
the five grains flourished,
spring gave birth, summer nurtured,
autumn harvested, winter stored.
Monthly inspections and seasonal evaluations,
at year's end achievements were presented,
tasting the grains in season,
sacrificing in the Míngtáng,
the structure of the Míngtáng,
had a roof but no four walls,
wind and rain could not assail it,
cold and heat could not harm it.
Leisurely entering it,
he nurtured the people with impartiality.
His people were simple, earnest, upright, and sincere,
without contentious strife yet wealth sufficed,
without toiling yet achievements were made.
Relying on the resources of heaven and earth, and harmonizing with them,
thus authority was stern but not exercised,
punishments were set aside and not used,
laws were sparing and not burdensome,
hence his transformation was divine.
His territory reached south to Jiāozhǐ,
north to Yōudū,
east to Yánggǔ,
west to Sānwēi,
all followed his rule.
At that time,
laws were lenient, punishments relaxed,
prisons were empty,
and the world shared one custom,
none harbored treacherous hearts.
The governance of decadent times is not so,
those above love to take without measure,
those below are greedy and wolfish without yielding,
the people are impoverished and contentious,
efforts are laborious yet fruitless,
cunning and deceit sprout and thrive,
thieves and robbers multiply and flourish,
above and below resent each other,
commands are not obeyed.
The ruling officials do not strive to return to the Way,
distorting and violating the root, while attending to the branches,
diminishing their virtue,
piling up their punishments,
and wishing to govern thereby,
is no different from holding a slingshot to attract birds,
or brandishing a stick to tame dogs—
chaos only worsens.
When water is turbid, fish gasp;
when governance is harsh, the people rebel.
Thus, those who raise tigers, leopards, rhinos, and elephants
build enclosures for them,
supply their desires,
satisfy their hunger and fullness,
vent their anger and rage,
yet they cannot live out their natural lifespan,
because coercion is inherent in confinement.
Hence, when those above have many schemes, those below have many deceptions;
when those above have many affairs, those below have many skills;
when those above are vexatious, those below are unsettled;
when those above have many demands, those below contend with each other.
Not addressing the root directly,
but attending to the branches,
is like stirring up dust to settle it,
or carrying firewood to save a fire.
Therefore, the sage's affairs are few and easily managed,
his demands are scant and easily met,
he is benevolent without bestowing,
trustworthy without speaking,
he obtains without seeking,
achieves without acting,
solidly preserving authenticity,
embracing virtue and extending sincerity,
the world follows him,
as an echo responds to sound,
as a shadow resembles a form,
for he cultivates the root.
Punishments are insufficient to change customs,
killings are insufficient to prohibit evil,
only spiritual transformation is valued.
The utmost essence is spirit.
A loud shout can be heard only a hundred paces,
but where the will is directed,
it reaches a thousand miles;
the winter sun's warmth,
the summer shade's coolness,
all things return to them, yet none makes it so.
Thus, the image of the utmost essence,
comes without being summoned,
goes without being waved away,
profound and obscure,
none know who makes it so,
yet achievement comes naturally.
The wise cannot recite it,
the eloquent cannot describe it.
In the past, Sūn Shū'áo lay peacefully,
and the people of Yǐng had no use for their weapons;
Shìnán Yíliáo juggled balls,
and the conflict between two families could not involve his words.
Leather armor and iron mail,
glaring eyes and gripping wrists,
how distant they are from warding off weapons!
Contracts and bundles of silk,
punishments and axes of execution,
how feeble they are in resolving difficulties!
Relying on eyes to see clearly,
relying on words to issue commands,
how difficult it is to govern thereby!
When Qú Bóyù was prime minister,
Zǐgòng went to observe him,
and asked:
"How do you govern the state?"
He replied:
"By governing without governing."
Jiǎn Zǐ wished to attack Wèi,
and sent Shǐ Àn to spy.
Returning, he reported:
"Qú Bóyù is prime minister,
we cannot attack."
Solid fortresses and perilous barriers—
how could they suffice to achieve this!
Thus, Gāo Yáo, though mute, served as chief judge,
and the world had no cruel punishments—
there is value beyond words.
Shī Kuàng, though blind, served as grand steward,
and Jìn had no chaotic governance—
there is value beyond sight.
Hence, orders without words,
vision without seeing,
this is how Fúxī and Shénnóng served as teachers.
Thus, when the people are transformed by those above,
they follow not their words, but their actions.
Thus, Duke Zhuāng of Qí loved bravery,
and though he did not encourage fighting,
the state faced many troubles,
gradually leading to the rebellion of Cuī Zhù.
King Qǐngxiāng loved beauty,
and though he did not encourage criticism,
the people were much confused and chaotic,
accumulating until the disaster of Zhāo Qí.
Therefore, the movement of the utmost essence,
is like the growth of spring qi,
or the withering of autumn qi;
even with galloping relays and urgent posts,
none can match its speed.
Thus, the ruler of men—
is he not like an archer!
A hair's breadth here,
becomes a vast distance there.
Hence, be cautious in what stirs it.
When Róng Qǐqī played once,
Confucius was joyful for three days,
moved by harmony.
When Zōu Jì struck one note,
King Wēi was sorrowful all evening,
moved by melancholy.
Stirred by zithers and lutes,
manifested in sounds and music,
they could make people sorrowful or joyful.
Hanging laws and setting rewards,
yet failing to change customs and practices—
their sincere heart is not applied.
Nìng Qì sang a merchant's song beneath a cart,
and Duke Huán sighed and awoke—
the utmost essence penetrates people deeply!
Hence it is said:
Music—listen to its tones
and you know its customs;
see its customs
and you know its transformation.
Confucius learned to play the zither from Master Xiāng,
and thus understood King Wén's aspirations,
perceiving the subtle to grasp the evident.
Jìzǐ of Yánlíng listened to the music of Lǔ
and recognized the customs of the Yīn and Xià dynasties,
discussing the near to comprehend the distant.
Created in ancient times,
applied for a thousand years,
their writings remain undiminished—
how much more could they transform people in their own era!
In the time of Tāng,
a seven-year drought occurred;
he prayed with his own body at the Sānglín sanctuary,
whereupon clouds gathered from all four seas,
and rain fell across a thousand miles.
Embracing sincerity and demonstrating devotion,
he moved heaven and earth;
divine influence reached beyond the borders,
commands were obeyed and prohibitions heeded—
how could this be considered difficult!
The ancient sage-kings embodied perfect essence within,
while discarding personal preferences outwardly;
their speech accorded with genuine feeling,
their decrees clarified their intent;
they demonstrated through rites and music,
influenced through songs and ballads,
their legacy flowing unblocked for ten thousand generations,
reaching across the four directions without exhaustion.
Even birds, beasts, and insects
were transformed along with them—
how much more those who enforce laws and issue decrees!
Thus the highest form is spiritual transformation,
the next prevents wrongdoing,
the last rewards the worthy and punishes the violent.
When weighing scales balance left and right,
impartial to heavy or light,
they can achieve fairness.
When the marking line aligns inner and outer,
impartial to curved or straight,
it can achieve correctness.
When a ruler applies laws,
impartial in likes and dislikes,
they can establish true governance.
Weighing light and heavy
without missing a gnat's head,
rectifying distortions
without losing needle-point accuracy,
straightening the crooked
without selfishly avoiding peril—
deceit cannot bend it,
slander cannot disrupt it,
no special favor is established,
no grudge remains hidden.
This is employing method while releasing human bias,
thus the wise ruler does not rely solely on intellect.
As boats float on water,
and carts roll on land,
this is nature's propensity.
When wood smashes an axle,
or rocks breach a boat,
we blame not wood or stone but clumsy craftsmanship—
for intentional fault lies not in them.
Thus when the Way possesses cunning, confusion follows;
when virtue harbors schemes, danger arises;
when the mind has eyes, dizziness ensues.
No weapon is deadlier than determined will
—Mòyé swords pale in comparison;
no invasion greater than yīn-yáng imbalance
—war drums seem trivial.
Now consider scales and compass squares:
once set, they never change,
altering not for Qín or Chǔ's prestige,
modifying not for Hú or Yuè's customs,
constant and unswerving,
square-moving yet unyielding,
once established in a day,
passed down for myriad generations,
achieved through non-action.
Thus states may have fallen rulers,
but the world never lacks the Way;
people may face destitution,
but principle remains unblocked.
From this we see:
non-action
is the source of the Way.
Who grasps the Way's source
responds to things boundlessly;
who relies solely on human talent
rarely achieves perfect governance.
Tāng and Wǔ were sage rulers,
yet couldn't sail reed boats with Yuè people on rivers;
Yī Yǐn was a worthy minister,
yet couldn't ride bay steeds with Hú people on grasslands;
Confucius and Mòzǐ were broadly learned,
yet couldn't traverse thickets and cliffs with mountain dwellers.
From this we see
human understanding of things is shallow.
To presume illuminating all within seas,
preserving every land,
without following natural principles,
but relying solely on one's ability—
such folly's end is near.
Thus intellect alone cannot govern the world.
With Jié's strength,
he could twist horns and straighten hooks,
tear iron and crush metal,
topple giant sacrificial animals,
slay giant turtles in water,
capture bears on land,
yet Tāng with three hundred war chariots
trapped him at Míngtiáo,
capturing him at Jiāomén.
From this we see:
courage alone cannot secure the world.
If intellect cannot govern,
nor courage strengthen,
then human talent alone is insufficient—
this is clear.
Yet the true ruler
never leaving temple halls
knows beyond the four seas
by using things to understand things,
using people to know people.
Thus collective strength applied
never fails to prevail;
multitude's wisdom employed
never fails to accomplish.
A sunken well lacks giant turtles
due to its narrowness;
a small garden lacks tall trees
due to its confinement.
Those lifting heavy tripods
may fail from lacking strength,
but when moving them elsewhere,
not all need be strong.
Thus a thousand-person group lacks no bridge-builders,
a ten-thousand gathering wastes no effort.
Though Huáliú and Lǜ'ěr steeds
cover a thousand miles daily,
set them to catch rabbits,
they're inferior to wolves and badgers—
skills differ.
An owl catches fleas at night,
distinguishing autumn hairs,
yet in daylight, wide-eyed
it misses hills and mountains—
natures vary.
The flying serpent rides mist to soar,
the winged dragon mounts clouds to ascend,
monkeys climb trees with agility,
fish swim waters with speed.
Thus ancient cart-makers:
painters didn't carve,
carvers didn't paint,
craftsmen mastered single skills,
scholars held singular offices,
each keeping their duty,
none interfering,
people finding proper place,
things finding stability,
thus tools never wore out,
tasks never neglected.
Light debts are easily repaid,
simple duties easily kept,
light burdens easily borne.
When superiors hold simplified standards,
subordinates perform achievable tasks,
ruler and minister endure long without resentment.
The ruler's way
resembles the star-offering representative:
dignified, silently profound,
yet receiving blessings and fortune.
Thus those attaining the Way neither fake ugliness nor ornamentation,
neither fake goodness nor extremes;
one person receiving it feels not overwhelmed,
ten thousand receiving it feel not constrained.
Therefore, neither over-indulging in kindness nor cruelty
brings governance to completion.
Those practicing excessive kindness
emphasize lavish giving.
Rewarding without merit,
ennobling without labor,
makes officials neglect duties,
and idlers rush for advancement.
Those practicing excessive cruelty
execute arbitrarily.
Killing the innocent,
punishing the upright,
discourages moral cultivation,
and emboldens rebels to defy authority.
Thus excessive kindness breeds deceit,
excessive cruelty breeds chaos.
Customs of deceit and chaos
are winds of a dying state.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler governs,
if the state has those to be punished, the ruler shows no anger;
if the court has those to be rewarded, the sovereign takes no credit.
The punished bear no grudge against the sovereign,
for the punishment fits their crimes;
the rewarded feel no gratitude toward the superior,
for the reward results from their merits.
When the people understand that punishments and rewards
all depend on their own conduct,
they devote themselves to achieving merits and cultivating their work,
without seeking undeserved favors from the sovereign.
Thus, the court may appear deserted with no traces of activity,
yet the fields are opened up and free of weeds,
so the highest ruler
is merely known to exist by those below.
Now, when a bridge pillar stands straight and unmoving,
it allows for adjustment whether looking up or down;
when the sovereign remains tranquil and unperturbed,
all officials can follow their duties.
Just as a standard-bearer in the army,
if pointing arbitrarily, would cause chaos.
Cleverness is insufficient to bring great peace,
wisdom is inadequate to secure safety;
rather than praising Yáo and condemning Jié,
it is better to conceal one's cleverness and return to cultivating the Way.
Through clarity, tranquility, and non-action,
Heaven provides the timely opportunities;
through integrity, frugality, and upholding principles,
Earth produces wealth;
by residing in simplicity and being praised for virtue,
the sage offers counsel.
Thus, the humble attracts all things to return,
the empty causes all under heaven to entrust.
When the sovereign attends to governance,
clear and bright without obscurity,
with an open mind and humble will,
then all ministers converge and advance together,
regardless of foolish or wise, worthy or unworthy,
none fails to exhaust their abilities.
Thereupon, they begin to display their rituals,
establishing them as the foundation.
This is like riding the momentum of the multitude as a chariot,
and steering the wisdom of the masses as horses;
even through dark wilderness and dangerous paths,
there is no way to be led astray.
If the sovereign dwells deep in seclusion
to avoid dampness and heat,
behind multiple gates and layers
to guard against traitors and thieves,
not knowing the conditions within the neighborhoods internally,
nor the shapes of mountains and marshes externally,
beyond the curtains,
the eyes cannot see;
beyond ten lǐ ahead,
the ears cannot hear what is outside a hundred steps.
Yet if there is nothing in the world
that one does not comprehend,
it is because those who channel information are vast,
and those who deliberate are numerous.
Thus, without leaving the door, one knows the world;
without peeping through the window, one knows the Way of Heaven.
By harnessing the wisdom of the multitude,
the world is not too much to possess.
Relying solely on one's own mind,
even one's own person cannot be preserved.
Therefore, the sovereign covers all with virtue,
does not exercise his own cleverness,
but follows what benefits the myriad people.
If lifting a heel benefits the world,
then residing above the common people
is not burdensome;
positioned before the common people
is not harmful;
elevating them does not make them haughty,
pushing them does not make them resentful.
The Way of the sovereign is round,
revolving without end,
transforming and nurturing like a spirit,
empty and non-active, following along,
always behind and not leading.
The Way of the minister is square,
discussing what is right and acting appropriately,
initiating affairs first,
maintaining clear duties,
thereby achieving success.
Thus, when sovereign and minister follow different Ways, there is order;
when they follow the same Way, there is chaos.
Each finds their proper place,
residing in their appropriate roles,
then superior and inferior have means to employ each other.
When the sovereign attends to governance,
with an open mind and humble will,
clear and bright without obscurity,
then all ministers converge and advance together,
regardless of foolish or wise, worthy or unworthy,
none fails to exhaust their abilities;
then the sovereign gains the means to control the ministers,
the ministers gain the means to serve the sovereign,
and the way to govern the state becomes clear.
King Wén was wise and fond of asking,
thus he became a sage.
King Wǔ was brave and fond of asking,
thus he achieved victory.
For by harnessing the wisdom of the multitude,
there is nothing one cannot undertake;
by using the strength of the multitude,
there is nothing one cannot overcome.
A weight of a thousand jūn
even Wū Huò cannot lift;
but if the multitude unites,
a hundred people have strength to spare.
Thus, relying on the strength of one person,
even Wū Huò is not dependable;
but by employing the control of the multitude,
the world is not too much to possess.
Yǔ dredged the rivers and channeled the streams,
bringing benefits to the world,
yet he could not make water flow westward.
Jì opened the land and cleared the grass,
enabling the people to farm,
yet he could not make grains grow in winter.
Was it because human effort fell short?
It was because the circumstances made it impossible.
To push against impossible circumstances,
without following the principles of the Way,
even a divine sage cannot accomplish his task,
let alone the sovereigns of the present age!
If the load is heavy and the horses weak,
even Zào Fù cannot travel far.
If the carriage is light and the horses excellent,
even a mediocre driver can pursue speed.
Therefore, when the sage undertakes affairs,
how can he go against the principles of the Way,
defy the nature of spontaneity,
treat the crooked as straight,
or the bent as extended?
He never fails to utilize them according to their inherent qualities.
Thus, what is lifted by accumulated strength
is never unconquered;
what is done by collective wisdom
is never unaccomplished.
The deaf can be made to chew sinews,
but cannot be made to hear;
the mute can be made to guard the borders,
but cannot be made to communicate.
Forms have their incompleteness,
and abilities have their limitations.
Therefore, each form occupies one position,
each ability serves one task.
If strength matches the responsibility,
then lifting it is not heavy;
if ability suits the task,
then performing it is not difficult.
Regardless of size or length,
each finds its proper place,
then the world becomes uniform,
with no one surpassing another.
The sage employs all inclusively,
thus there is no wasted talent.
If the sovereign values uprightness and esteems loyalty,
with the loyal and upright in high positions,
managing affairs with correctness,
then slanderers, flatterers, traitors, and evildoers have no way to advance.
It is like square and round not covering each other,
and crooked and straight not fitting together.
Birds and beasts do not flock together
because their kinds differ;
tigers and deer do not roam together
because their strengths are unequal.
Thus, when a sage achieves his ambition and resides in high position,
slanderers, flatterers, traitors, and evildoers who wish to assail the sovereign
are like sparrows seeing a harrier
or mice encountering a wildcat—
they are certain to lose their lives.
Therefore, the actions of the sovereign
must be undertaken with caution.
If the appointed are the right people,
then the state is well-governed,
superior and inferior are harmonious,
ministers are close,
and the people are attached.
If the appointed are not the right people,
then the state is in danger,
superior and inferior are at odds,
ministers are resentful,
and the people are in chaos.
Thus, one misstep in appointment
causes lifelong harm.
The path of gain and loss
hinges on the sovereign's authority.
Therefore, when the marking line is straight above,
the wood is straight below;
not by forced effort,
Therefore, if the ruler is truly upright,
then honest officials will be entrusted with duties,
and treacherous individuals will go into hiding.
If the ruler is not upright,
then wicked people will achieve their ambitions,
and the loyal will remain concealed.
Why is it that people do not strike at jade or stone but strike at gourds?
It is because they gain nothing from jade and stone, so they do not attack them.
If the ruler holds to fairness and balance,
as if following a plumb line for high and low,
then any minister who comes with wicked intentions
is like throwing an egg at a stone
or casting fire into water.
Thus, when King Líng admired slender waists,
the people starved themselves to achieve it;
when the King of Yuè valued bravery,
the people all faced danger and vied to die.
From this we see
that the handle of power and influence
can indeed shift customs.
Yáo as a commoner
could not spread benevolence through a single village;
Jié in the highest position
could enforce orders and prohibitions.
From this we see
that virtue alone is insufficient to govern,
while power can change customs—this is clear.
The "Shū" says:
"When one man has blessings,
the myriad people rely on him."
This refers to this.
The world is often dazzled by reputation,
but seldom examines the reality,
hence recluses are honored for their fame,
and wanderers become prominent for their eloquence.
Examining what they honor and make prominent
has no other reason
than that the ruler does not clarify the distinctions of merit and demerit, benefit and harm,
but approves the debates of many mouths.
A well-governed state is not like this;
those who speak on affairs must base it on the law,
and those who act must be governed by office.
The superior holds the titles
to demand the reality,
the ministers adhere to their duties
to demonstrate their achievements,
words cannot exceed the facts,
actions cannot surpass the law,
ministers gather like spokes around a hub,
none daring to monopolize the ruler.
Matters not covered by law,
yet beneficial to the state and aiding governance,
must be tested through fivefold practice
and secretly examined to observe their outcome,
listening comprehensively
to discern their influence,
not biased toward one corner,
not partial to one affair,
thus standing centered and all-encompassing, illuminating the entire realm,
ministers are just and fair,
none daring to be wicked,
all officials fulfill their duties,
striving to present their public deeds.
The ruler is astute above,
officials exert themselves below,
treachery and evil vanish,
various achievements advance daily,
thus the brave give their all in the military.
A disordered state is not like this;
those praised by the masses
are rewarded without merit,
while those upholding their duties
are punished without crime.
The ruler is dim and unenlightened,
ministers form cliques and are disloyal,
persuaders roam with clever arguments,
practitioners compete in pursuits.
When the ruler issues commands,
they criticize them with附和;
what the laws prohibit,
they violate with wickedness.
The clever strive for cunning deceit,
the brave engage in strife,
high ministers monopolize power,
lower officials hold sway,
cliques and factions circle,
deceiving their superior,
the state may seem to exist,
but the ancients called it perished.
Moreover, those who do not manage official duties, do not bear armor,
do not till the southern fields, yet have a sage's reputation
are not fit to teach the state.
Qíjì, Lù'ěr,
the swiftest horses in the world,
if driven, they do not advance,
if led, they do not stop,
even fools would not mount them.
Now the mechanism of order and disorder,
its tracks are visible,
yet rulers of the age fail to perceive it,
this is why the path of governance is blocked.
Power and influence
are the ruler's chariot;
ranks and emoluments
are the minister's reins and bit.
Thus, the ruler occupies the crucial point of power,
and holds the handle of ranks and emoluments,
examines the measure of urgency and ease,
and appropriately regulates giving and taking,
so the world exerts effort without weariness.
The relationship between minister and ruler
lacks the depth of father and son or the kinship of flesh and blood,
yet they strive to the death,
not sparing their lives—why?
Circumstances make it so.
Formerly, Yù Ràng
was a minister of Zhōngháng Wénzǐ.
Zhì Bó attacked the Zhōngháng clan,
annexing their territory,
Yù Ràng turned his back on his lord and served Zhì Bó.
When Zhì Bó fought Zhào Xiāngzǐ beneath Jìnyáng,
he was killed and disgraced,
his state divided into three.
Yù Ràng sought to take revenge on Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
lacquering his body to appear leprous,
swallowing charcoal to change his voice,
knocking out teeth to alter his appearance.
With the same heart of one man
serving two lords,
he either betrayed and left one,
or sought to sacrifice himself for the other—
was it due to differences in the depth of his commitment?
The grace of others made it so.
Zhòu unified the world,
had feudal lords pay court,
wherever human footprints reached,
wherever boats sailed,
all submitted.
Yet King Wǔ with three thousand armored soldiers
captured him at Mùyě.
Was it because the Zhōu people died for principle and the Yīn people betrayed?
It was because their ruler's virtue and righteousness were profound, and his commands were heeded.
When the wind is swift, waves rise;
when trees are lush, birds gather;
this is the energy of mutual influence.
Thus, if a minister does not get what he desires from the ruler,
the ruler also cannot get what he seeks from the minister.
What ruler and minister bestow
is a situation of mutual repayment.
Hence, the minister exhausts his effort and dies for principle to give to the ruler,
while the ruler dangles ranks to trade with the minister.
Thus, the ruler cannot reward ministers without merit,
nor can ministers die for a ruler without virtue.
If the ruler's virtue does not flow down to the people,
yet he wishes to use them,
it is like whipping a lame horse.
This is like expecting ripe crops without waiting for rain—
a certainly impossible outcome.
The way of ruling people
lies in dwelling in stillness to cultivate oneself,
and being frugal to lead those below.
In stillness, those below are not disturbed;
in frugality, the people do not resent.
If those below are disturbed, governance becomes chaotic;
if the people resent, virtue becomes shallow.
If governance is chaotic, the virtuous will not offer counsel;
if virtue is shallow, the brave will not die for it.
Therefore, if the ruler favors birds of prey and fierce beasts,
rare and exotic objects,
is crafty, restless, indulgent, and wasteful,
does not cherish the people's strength,
gallops in hunting,
comes and goes untimely,
then all officials will focus on chaos,
affairs will be laborious and resources depleted,
the myriad people will be sorrowful and bitter,
and livelihoods will not be maintained.
If the ruler favors high towers and deep pools,
carving and engraving,
embroidered patterns and designs,
fine and coarse silks, damasks and brocades,
precious toys, pearls and jades,
then taxes will be levied without limit,
and the strength of the myriad people will be exhausted.
When Yáo possessed the world,
it was not out of greed for the wealth of the myriad people
or comfort in the ruler's position,
but because the common people fought with force,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few,
so Yáo personally practiced frugal conduct,
and clarified the benevolence of mutual love,
to harmonize and unite them.
Therefore, thatch roofs were left untrimmed,
rough-hewn rafters were left uncarved,
the main roads were left unpainted,
reed mats were left unhemmed,
