the grand broth was left unseasoned,
and millet food was left unrefined.
He toured the realms to implement teachings,
toiled diligently for all under heaven,
and journeyed across the five sacred mountains.
Was it that his provisions were insufficient for enjoyment?
He believed that for the state, there should be no self-interest.
As he aged and his will weakened,
he handed over all under heaven to Shùn,
like stepping back and shedding worn sandals.
In decadent eras, it is not so;
upon gaining the wealth of all under heaven in a single day,
holding the position of a sovereign,
they exhaust the strength of the common people
to indulge their sensory desires,
focusing solely on palaces, towers, and pavilions,
ponds, gardens, and parks,
fierce beasts, bears, and brown bears,
and rare curiosities.
Thus, the poor cannot even taste chaff and bran,
while tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears gorge on fodder and grain;
the common people lack even whole coarse garments,
yet the palaces are adorned with embroidered silks.
The sovereign hastens these useless endeavors,
while the common people suffer throughout the land,
causing all under heaven to lose their innate nature.
The dwelling of a sovereign
is like the brightness of the sun and moon;
all under heaven turn their heads to look,
incline their ears to listen,
and crane their necks and rise on tiptoes to gaze.
Thus, without tranquility, one cannot illuminate virtue;
without serenity, one cannot reach far;
without breadth, one cannot cover all;
without kindness, one cannot embrace the masses;
without fairness, one cannot make decisive judgments.
Therefore, when a wise ruler employs people,
it is like a skilled craftsman working with wood:
the large pieces are used for boats, pillars, and beams,
the small pieces for joinery and tenons,
the long pieces for eaves and rafters,
the short pieces for brackets and corbels.
Regardless of size or length,
each finds its appropriate place;
squares and circles,
each has its application.
Different shapes and varied materials
can all be put to use.
Among all things under heaven,
none is more poisonous than xīdú,
yet skilled physicians collect and store it,
for it has its uses.
Thus, even the timber of wild forests
should not be discarded,
let alone people!
Now, those not recommended by the court
or praised in the countryside
are not necessarily unworthy;
it is that the positions they are given do not suit them.
When a deer ascends a mountain,
even a large stag cannot keep pace,
but when it descends,
a shepherd boy can chase it—
such is the variation in abilities.
Therefore, those with grand strategies
should not be burdened with trivial skills,
and those with petty cleverness
should not be entrusted with great tasks.
Each person has their talent,
each thing its form;
some bear one responsibility and are overwhelmed,
while others bear a hundred and still find it light.
Thus, those fixated on minute calculations
are bound to overlook the grand scheme of heaven and earth;
those who never err in small selections
may falter in major undertakings.
It is like a fox that cannot be made to fight an ox,
or a tiger that cannot be made to chase mice.
Among people today,
some wish to pacify the nine provinces,
subdue distant lands,
save endangered states,
restore extinct lineages,
aiming to uphold righteousness and correct evils,
resolve complexities and untangle chaos,
yet they are judged by the etiquette of inner chambers,
the trivialities of secluded spaces;
others, with mere cunning tricks,
flattering and pleasing speech,
conforming to local customs,
catering to the eyes and ears of the masses,
are entrusted with the authority of all under heaven,
the pivot of order and chaos—
this is like shearing hair with an axe,
or felling trees with a knife,
all misplaced in their application.
A sovereign
sees through the eyes of all under heaven,
hears through the ears of all under heaven,
ponders with the wisdom of all under heaven,
acts with the strength of all under heaven.
Thus, his commands reach far and wide,
and his ministers' sentiments are heard above;
officials communicate effectively,
and all ministers gather like spokes to a hub.
He does not reward out of personal favor,
nor punish out of personal anger.
Therefore, his authority is established and unshaken,
his insight brilliant and unobscured,
his laws clear and not harsh,
his perception penetrating and unclouded.
The truths of good and evil
are daily presented before him without opposition.
Thus, the worthy exhaust their wisdom,
the unworthy exert their strength,
his virtue and favor cover all without bias,
his ministers strive diligently without slacking,
those nearby live in peace,
those afar cherish his virtue.
Why is this so?
Because he has mastered the way of employing people,
and does not rely solely on his own talents.
Hence, one who borrows a carriage and horse
travels a thousand miles without tiring his feet;
one who rides a boat
crosses rivers and seas without needing to swim.
In the nature of a sovereign,
none do not wish to gather the wisdom of the realm,
and exhaust the strength of the multitude.
Yet, among ministers who express their will and offer loyalty,
few escape personal hardship.
If what is spoken is correct,
even if from a commoner or grass-gatherer,
it should not be discarded.
If what is spoken is wrong,
even if from a minister or sovereign,
planning in the court above,
it may not be adoptable.
The place of right and wrong
cannot be judged by nobility or baseness.
Thus, an enlightened ruler, listening to his ministers,
if their plans are usable,
feels no shame for their low rank;
if their words are practicable,
does not demand eloquence.
A benighted ruler is not so:
those he loves, is familiar with, and keeps close,
even if crooked and unjust,
he fails to see;
those distant and lowly,
even if exerting utmost loyalty,
he remains unaware.
He silences speakers with rhetoric,
punishes advisers with crimes.
To wish to illuminate the realm
and preserve all lands thus
is like plugging the ears to listen to pitch,
or covering the eyes to see colors—
far indeed from clarity and insight.
Law
is the measure of all under heaven,
and the plumb line of the sovereign.
To promulgate laws
is to rectify lawlessness;
to establish rewards
is to reward the deserving.
After laws are set,
those who meet the standard are rewarded,
those who breach the line are punished.
The noble are not lightly punished,
nor the humble heavily penalized;
lawbreakers, even if worthy, must be punished,
while those within the measure, even if unworthy, must be guiltless.
Thus, the public way is open, and private ways are blocked.
In ancient times, officials were appointed
to restrain the people,
preventing them from acting arbitrarily.
The ruler was established to govern the officials,
preventing them from acting autonomously.
Legal codes and ritual principles
serve to restrain the ruler,
preventing him from deciding arbitrarily.
When none can act arbitrarily,
the Way prevails;
when the Way prevails, principle is realized,
thus returning to non-action.
Non-action
does not mean stagnation and immobility,
but that nothing is imposed from the self.
The inch is born from the grain,
the grain from the form,
the form from the shadow,
the shadow from the sun.
This is the foundation of measurement.
Music is born from sound,
sound from pitch,
pitch from the wind,
this is the origin of tones.
Law is born from righteousness,
righteousness from collective suitability,
collective suitability aligns with human hearts,
this is the essence of governance.
Thus, those who understand the foundation
are not confused by details,
those who grasp the essentials
are not perplexed by complexities.
Law does not fall from heaven,
nor spring from earth,
it arises among humans
and in turn rectifies them.
Therefore, what one possesses oneself, one does not condemn in others;
what one lacks oneself, one does not demand of others.
What is established for the subordinates
is not abandoned by the superiors;
what is forbidden for the people
is not practiced by the ruler.
A perished state is said to be so
not because it lacks a ruler,
but because it lacks law.
To alter the law
is not to have no law,
but to have law and not use it,
which is equivalent to having no law.
Hence, when a ruler establishes laws,
he first makes himself the model and standard,
thus his commands are followed throughout the land.
Confucius said:
"If the ruler is upright,
he need not give orders, and things are done.
If he is not upright,
even with orders, he is not obeyed."
Thus, when prohibitions are upheld by the ruler himself,
then commands are followed by the people.
The rule of a sage ruler
is like Zàofǔ's driving:
he harmonizes the reins and bits,
moderates speed with the harmony of his lips,
maintains correct measures in his heart,
and controls rhythm within his grasp.
Internally, he aligns with his inner mind,
externally, he matches the horses' intent.
Thus, he can advance and retreat along the line,
turn and curve in perfect circles,
take the road to distant goals,
with energy to spare,
truly mastering the art.
Therefore, power and authority
are the ruler's chariot;
the great ministers
are the ruler's team of horses.
If the ruler's body leaves the safety of the chariot,
and his hands lose the hearts of the horses,
yet he remains unharmed,
such a thing has never occurred in past or present.
Thus, if the chariot and horses are uncoordinated,
even Wáng Liáng could not steer the way;
if ruler and ministers are disharmonious,
even Táng and Yú could not achieve good governance.
Wielding the art to驾驭 them,
then the wisdom of Guǎn and Yàn is fully utilized;
clarifying roles to show them,
then the villainy of Zhí and Qiāo ceases.
Leaning over the wellhead to peer at the bottom,
even with sharp vision, one cannot see the pupils;
but using a mirror to reflect light,
the division of an inch can be clearly observed.
Thus, the enlightened ruler's eyes and ears are not overworked,
his spirit is not exhausted.
When things arrive, he observes their changes;
when events come, he responds to their transformations.
Those nearby are not disordered,
and those afar are well governed.
Therefore, he does not rely on chance methods,
but follows the way of necessity,
so ten thousand actions leave no strategy unfulfilled.
Now, for a driver,
if the horse's body is attuned to the chariot,
and the driver's heart is in harmony with the horse,
then traversing dangers and reaching afar,
advancing, retreating, and circling around,
all is as intended.
Even with fine steeds like Qíjì and Lù'ěr,
if a Zānghuó drives them,
the horses will become unruly,
and the person cannot control them.
Thus, in governance, what is valued is not self-righteousness,
but ensuring no wrongdoing can occur.
Hence it is said:
"Do not allow desires to arise,
and do not say they need not be sought.
Do not create opportunities for contention,
and do not say there will be no strife."
In this way,
human talents are liberated and public justice prevails.
Excess is restrained by measure,
and insufficiency reaches utility,
so the world can be unified.
If one neglects duties and heeds false praise,
abandons public service and employs factions,
then those with unusual skills will leap ahead and usurp positions,
while those holding office will be blocked and not advanced.
In this case,
the people's customs will be chaotic in the state,
and meritorious officials will contend in the court.
Thus, laws, rules, and measures
are what the ruler uses to control the subordinates.
To discard and not use them
is like galloping without reins or bits;
the ministers and common people
will instead toy with their superior.
Therefore, having the art means controlling others;
lacking it means being controlled by others.
A fish large enough to swallow a boat,
if swept away and out of water,
is controlled by ants,
for it has left its abode.
A monkey losing its tree is caught by a fox,
for it is not in its place.
If the ruler abandons his responsibilities and competes with subordinates in affairs,
then officials will hold their posts by doing nothing,
and those in charge will flatter the ruler to gain favor.
Thus, ministers conceal their wisdom and do not use it,
instead shifting tasks back to their superior.
The wealthy and noble in their labors,
the insightful in their observations,
the arrogant in their respect—
their influence cannot match the ruler's.
If the ruler does not employ the capable but prefers to act himself,
his wisdom will daily be exhausted, and he will bear the blame alone.
When strategies fail below,
he cannot uphold principles;
when his conduct declines in the state,
he cannot exercise control.
His wisdom insufficient for governance,
his authority inadequate for punishment,
he has no means to interact with his subordinates.
If joy and anger show in his heart,
desires appear outwardly,
then office-holders will deviate from righteousness to flatter the superior,
officials will pervert the law to follow the trend,
rewards will not match achievements,
punishments will not fit crimes,
superiors and subordinates will be disunited,
and ruler and ministers will resent each other.
Thus, if those in power curry favor with the ruler,
and when errors occur, there is no one to blame,
and crimes go unpunished,
then the百官 will be troubled and chaotic,
and wisdom cannot resolve it;
slander and praise will sprout,
and clarity cannot illuminate it.
Not rectifying the root but instead cultivating oneself,
then the ruler labors more,
and the ministers become more idle.
This is like replacing the cook in slaughtering an animal
or acting as the great carpenter in carving.
Racing against a horse,
one's tendons snap but still cannot keep up;
mounting the chariot and taking the reins,
then the horse is tamed under the crossbar.
Thus, Bólè examines them,
Wáng Liáng drives them,
the enlightened ruler rides them—
without the toil of driving or examining, he reaches a thousand miles,
for he rides on others' abilities as his wings.
Therefore, the ruler
does nothing yet maintains his hold,
stands firm without personal preferences.
Action gives rise to slander;
preferences trigger flattery.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí loved fine food,
and Yìyá cooked his firstborn son to tempt him;
the lord of Yú treasured valuables,
and Duke Xiàn of Jìn hooked him with jade and horses;
the king of the Hú loved music,
and Duke Mù of Qín lured him with female musicians;
all were controlled by others through their desires for profit.
Thus, what is well established cannot be uprooted,
It is said that establishment lies in the formless.
Fire is hot, but water extinguishes it;
metal is hard, but fire melts it;
wood is strong, but an axe fells it;
water flows, but earth blocks it.
Only the Creator
is something no thing can overcome.
Thus, when inner desires do not emerge, it is called "barring";
when external evils do not enter, it is called "closing."
With inner barring and outer closing,
what affair cannot be regulated!
With outer closing and inner barring,
what task cannot be accomplished!
Not using it enables one to use it;
not acting enables one to act.
When the spirit toils, it scatters;
when the ears and eyes indulge, they exhaust.
Therefore, the ruler who possesses the Way
extinguishes thoughts and dismisses intentions,
maintains clarity and emptiness to await,
does not substitute words for others,
does not seize affairs from them,
follows names to demand substance,
assigns officials to manage themselves, employs without commanding,
holds responsible without instructing,
takes not knowing as the Way,
and regards "how to" as a treasure.
In this way,
the affairs of the hundred officials
each have their proper domains.
To grasp the handle of power and authority
makes transforming the people easy.
The ruler of Wèi employed Zǐlù,
for his authority was weighty;
Jǐng and Huán had ministers like Guǎn and Yàn,
for their positions were esteemed.
The timid overcome the brave, and the foolish control the wise,
because those they rely on for power prevail.
Thus, a branch cannot be greater than the trunk,
the tip cannot be stronger than the root—
this speaks of light and heavy, small
and large having means to control each other.
Like the five fingers attached to the arm:
grasping, pulling, seizing, snatching—
none fails to follow one's will,
speaking of the small belonging to the large.
Therefore, one who gains the advantage of power
holds something very small,
yet bears something very great;
guards something very simple,
yet controls something very vast.
Thus, a tree ten arm-spans around
can support a roof of a thousand jun;
a key five inches long
controls opening and closing.
Is it because its material's size is sufficient for the task?
It is because its position is crucial.
Kǒng Qiū
and Mò Dí
cultivated the methods of former sages,
mastered the theories of the six arts,
spoke their words with their mouths,
practiced their aims with their bodies,
yet those who admired their righteousness and followed their influence,
serving them, were no more than a few dozen.
Had they occupied the Son of Heaven's position,
then the whole world would have become Ruist and Mohist.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ grieved at Wén Wúwèi's death in Sòng,
raised his sleeves and rose,
with robes and caps lining the roads,
and soon formed an army at the walls of Sòng—
such is the weight of authority.
King Wén of Chǔ loved wearing the lynx cap,
and the whole state of Chǔ imitated him;
King Wǔlíng of Zhào wore a shell-adorned belt and pheasant-feather headdress at court,
and the whole state of Zhào transformed accordingly.
Were they commoners in plain clothes,
even if they wore lynx caps,
shell-adorned belts, and pheasant headdresses at court,
they would not escape being laughed at.
As for the people's fondness for goodness and delight in correctness,
without awaiting prohibitions or executions,
those who naturally adhere to the laws
are not one in ten thousand.
Issue orders that must be followed:
those who comply benefit,
those who oppose suffer misfortune.
Before the shadow moves a day,
all within the seas are aligned as if by a plumb line.
Thus, if one grasps the blade of a sword,
even Běigōngzǐ or Sīmǎ Kuǎikuì could not be made to face the enemy;
but hold its hilt,
and point its tip,
then even an ordinary person can achieve victory.
Now, if Wū Huò or Jí Fān
pull an ox by the tail from behind,
the tail may break but the ox won't follow,
because it's against its nature;
but if a mulberry twig
is used to pierce its nose,
then a child of five chi
can lead it around the four seas,
because it's with its nature.
A rudder seven chi long
controls a ship's left and right,
using water as its resource;
the Son of Heaven issues commands,
with orders obeyed and prohibitions heeded,
using the multitude as his power.
To guard against what harms the people,
and open up what benefits them—
the execution of authority
is like breaching a bank or breaking a dam.
Thus, sailing downstream
makes it easy to reach the destination;
riding with the wind
makes it easy to go far.
Duke Huán, in establishing governance,
removed beasts that ate meat,
birds that ate grain,
and set traps and nets,
and with these three acts, the hundred clans were pleased.
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān, and kin resented it;
cut the shins of morning waders, and the myriad people rebelled;
with these two acts, he lost the world.
Thus, righteousness
cannot benefit every person under heaven,
but benefiting one can make the world follow like the wind;
tyranny
cannot harm all the masses within the seas,
but harming one can make the world turn away in rebellion.
Hence, Duke Huán's three acts led to nine assemblies of feudal lords;
Zhòu's two acts left him without even a commoner's status.
Therefore, actions and measures must be carefully considered.
When the ruler collects taxes from the people,
he must first calculate the year's harvest,
estimate the people's stores,
know the numbers of plenty and famine, surplus and shortage,
and only then take from carts, clothes, and food to supply his desires.
High towers and multi-storied pavilions,
connected rooms and linked galleries—
these are not un-beautiful,
yet if the people have no dugouts or humble huts
to shelter themselves,
the enlightened ruler takes no pleasure in it.
Rich wines and sweet delicacies—
these are not un-tasty,
yet if the people have chaff, husks, beans, or grains
that do not reach their mouths,
the enlightened ruler finds no sweetness in it.
Comfortable beds and soft mats—
these are not un-peaceful,
yet if the people dwell in border towns,
face danger and hardship,
dying in marshes or exposed corpses,
the enlightened ruler feels no ease.
Thus, the rulers of old
felt deep compassion for the people:
if the state had the hungry,
they did not double flavors in their meals;
if the people suffered cold,
they did not wear furs in winter.
Only when the year was abundant and the people prosperous
did they hang bells and drums,
display shields and axes,
and ruler and ministers, high and low,
rejoiced together with one heart,
with no mourners in the state.
Therefore, in ancient times, metal and stone instruments, pipes and strings
were used to express joy;
weapons, armor, axes, and blades
were used to display anger;
cups, ladles, sacrificial vessels, and stands,
the rituals of toasting and response,
were used to manifest delight;
mourning clothes, hempen shoes,
beating the breast and jumping in grief, weeping and wailing,
were used to convey sorrow.
These all had fullness within and took form without.
But when it comes to a chaotic ruler,
he takes from the people without considering their strength,
demands from below without measuring their stores,
so that men and women cannot attend to farming and weaving
to supply the ruler's demands.
Toil is diligent, but resources are exhausted;
ruler and ministers resent each other.
Thus, the people reach lips parched and livers boiling,
having today but no stores for tomorrow,
and only then does he start to strike great bells,
beat resounding drums,
blow yu reeds and shēng pipes,
play qin and se zithers.
This is like wearing armor into the ancestral temple
or draping silk gauze to join the army—
it misses the source from which music arises.
Now, the livelihood of the people is such that
with one person tilling the plow,
they cannot farm more than ten mǔ,
and the yield from average fields,
the harvest for the entire year,
does not exceed four dàn per mǔ,
yet wives, children, and the elderly
depend on it for sustenance.
At times, there are worries of floods, droughts, and calamities,
and there are also the expenses for the ruler's taxes, chariots, horses, and military equipment to provide.
From this perspective,
the lives of people are indeed pitiable!
Considering the vastness of heaven and earth,
it is estimated that three years of farming should leave a surplus of one year's food,
so that in nine years, there should be a reserve of three years' worth,
in eighteen years, a store of six years' worth,
and in twenty-seven years, a stockpile of nine years' worth.
Even if floods, droughts, and disasters strike,
the people will not suffer destitution or become refugees.
Therefore, if a state lacks a reserve of nine years' food,
it is called insufficient;
if it lacks a store of six years' worth,
it is called distressed and urgent;
if it lacks a reserve of three years' worth,
it is called impoverished and wanting.
Thus, when there is a benevolent and enlightened ruler,
he takes from the people with moderation,
and supports himself with restraint,
then he can receive the blessings of heaven and earth,
and avoid the plight of hunger and cold.
But if there is a greedy and tyrannical ruler,
who harasses those below,
plunders his people,
to satisfy endless desires,
then the common people will have no means to enjoy the harmony of heaven and partake in the virtues of earth.
Food is the foundation of the people.
The people are the foundation of the state.
The state is the foundation of the ruler.
Therefore, the one who rules over others,
aligns with the timing of heaven above,
exhausts the resources of earth below,
and utilizes human strength in between,
so that all living things thrive and grow,
and the five grains flourish.
He teaches the people to raise the six domestic animals,
to plant according to the seasons,
to diligently cultivate the fields,
to proliferate the planting of mulberries and hemp,
whether the land is fertile or barren, high or low,
each according to its suitability.
On hills, mounds, and steep slopes where the five grains do not grow,
plant bamboos and trees,
in spring, cut the withered branches,
in summer, gather the fruits and melons,
in autumn, store the coarse grains,
in winter, cut firewood and kindling,
to serve as resources for the people.
Thus, in life, there is no lack of supplies,
and in death, no corpses left abandoned.
Therefore, according to the laws of the ancient kings,
in hunting, one should not wipe out the whole herd,
not take the fawns or young,
not drain the ponds to fish,
not set fire to the forests to hunt.
Before the jackals sacrifice their prey,
traps and nets must not be set in the wild;
before the otters sacrifice their fish,
nets must not be cast into the waters;
before the hawks and falcons have matured,
snares must not be spread in the valleys;
before the trees and grasses have shed their leaves,
axes must not enter the mountains and forests;
before the insects have hibernated,
one must not use fire to clear the fields.
Pregnant animals must not be killed,
eggs and nestlings must not be taken,
fish shorter than a chǐ must not be caught,
pigs not yet a year old must not be eaten.
Thus, the growth of plants and trees is like steam rising,
the return of birds and beasts is like flowing springs,
the return of flying birds is like clouds and mist,
all because there is a way to attract them.
Therefore, in the governance of the ancient kings,
when the clouds from the four seas arrive, they repaired the borders;
when the frogs croaked and the swallows descended,
they cleared and maintained the roads;
when the yin energy descended to the hundred springs,
they built bridges;
when the constellation Zhāng was at its zenith at dusk,
they focused on planting grains;
when the star Dàhuǒ was at its zenith,
they planted millet and beans;
when the star Xū was at its zenith,
they planted winter wheat;
when the constellation Mǎo was at its zenith,
they gathered and stored the harvest,
and cut firewood.
They reported to heaven above,
and promulgated to the people below.
This is how the ancient kings responded to the seasons and prepared accordingly,
enriching the state and benefiting the people,
filling the empty lands and attracting those from afar,
their way was complete.
It was not that they could see everything with their eyes or walk everywhere with their feet,
but that they desired to benefit others.
Since the desire to benefit others was never forgotten in their hearts,
the officials naturally made preparations.
The heart, in relation to the nine orifices and four limbs,
cannot perform a single task itself,
yet movement, rest, hearing, and sight
all regard it as the master,
because it never forgets the desire to benefit them.
Thus, Yáo did good, and all good came to him;
Jié did wrong, and all wrongs gathered around him.
Accumulating good leads to success,
accumulating wrong leads to ultimate disaster.
In general, in human conduct,
the heart should be cautious, but the aspirations should be great;
wisdom should be comprehensive, but actions should be upright;
abilities should be many, but affairs should be few.
By "the heart should be cautious," it means
to consider calamities before they arise,
prepare for disasters before they occur,
guard against faults and be prudent in small matters,
not daring to indulge one's desires.
By "aspirations should be great," it means
to encompass all states,
unify diverse customs,
and embrace all the people,
as if uniting them into one clan,
with right and wrong converging like spokes to a hub.
By "wisdom should be comprehensive," it means
to revolve and circulate,
without beginning or end,
flowing widely in all directions,
like an abundant spring that never runs dry,
so that all things flourish,
and none fail to respond.
By "actions should be upright," it means
to stand straight without bending,
remain pure and untainted,
not change principles in poverty,
nor indulge ambitions in prosperity.
By "abilities should be many," it means
to be equipped with both civil and military skills,
movement and rest conforming to propriety,
in initiating or halting actions,
adapting appropriately in every detail,
without any clashes or obstructions,
so that everything is perfectly suited.
By "affairs should be few," it means
to grasp the handle and hold the method,
obtain the essential to respond to the multitude,
hold the simple to govern the vast,
remain in stillness and maintain centrality,
operating like the pivot of the jade circlet,
uniting one with ten thousand,
as if matching tally tokens.
Thus, a cautious heart
guards against the subtle;
great aspirations
embrace everything;
comprehensive wisdom
knows all;
upright actions
refrain from certain deeds;
many abilities
can manage everything;
few affairs
simplify what is held.
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven held court,
he had the high ministers offer upright remonstrance,
the academicians recite poetry,
the blind musicians present admonitions and the masters recite,
the commoners convey messages,
the historians record his errors,
and the steward reduce his meals.
Yet this was still considered insufficient,
so Yáo set up the drum for bold remonstrance,
Shùn erected the wooden board for criticism,
Tāng had officials to correct faults,
King Wǔ established the drum of caution and vigilance,
so that even the slightest error,
was already guarded against.
As for the sages' attitude towards goodness,
no matter how small, they did not fail to promote it;
and towards faults,
no matter how minor, they did not fail to correct them.
Tāng, Yáo, Shùn, and Wǔ,
all reposed facing south and ruled the world as kings.
At that time,
they beat the great drum to eat,
played the "Yōng" music to clear the feast,
offered sacrifices at the hearth after meals,
conducted affairs without shamans,
ghosts and spirits dared not cause calamities,
mountains and rivers dared not bring disasters,
they could be called supremely noble,
yet they trembled with fear,
growing more cautious day by day.
From this perspective,
the hearts of sages are cautious.
The Book of Songs says:
"Only this King Wén,
with great care and reverence,
brightly served the Lord on High,
thus securing abundant blessings."
Is this not what it means?
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he distributed grain from Jùqiáo,
scattered coins from Lùtái,
restored Bǐgān's tomb,
honored Shāngróng's neighborhood,
paid respects at Chéngtāng's temple,
freed Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
let people dwell in their homes,
farm their fields,
regardless of old or new,
he only drew close to the worthy,
employing what was not originally his,
using people not originally his followers,
yet as peacefully as if they had long been his.
From this perspective,
the aspirations of sages are grand.
King Wén comprehensively observed gains and losses,
extensively examined rights and wrongs,
the reasons for Yáo and Shùn's prosperity,
and Jié and Zhòu's downfall,
all recorded in the Mingtáng,
thus simplifying wisdom and broadening knowledge,
to respond to the limitless.
From this perspective,
the wisdom of sages is all-encompassing.
Chéng and Kāng continued the legacy of Wén and Wǔ,
upheld the system of the Mingtáng,
observed traces of survival and demise,
witnessed changes in success and failure,
spoke only what accorded with the Way,
acted only what accorded with righteousness,
did not speak carelessly,
did not act recklessly,
choosing the good before engaging in affairs.
From this perspective,
the conduct of sages is upright.
As for Confucius's mastery,
his wisdom surpassed Cháng Hóng,
his courage subdued Mèng Bēn,
his feet could outrun hares in the suburbs,
his strength could lift a city gate,
his abilities were many.
Yet his courage and strength went unheard,
his skills unknown,
he devotedly practiced filial piety,
becoming an uncrowned king,
his deeds were few but significant.
In the 242 years of the Spring and Autumn period,
fifty-two states perished,
thirty-six rulers were assassinated,
he selected the good and eliminated the vile,
to establish the kingly way,
his discourse was vast.
Yet when besieged in Kuāng,
his complexion did not change,
he continued playing the zither and singing,
facing the brink of death,
encountering peril and hardship,
upholding righteousness and principle without fear,
his discernment was clear.
While serving as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
he judged cases with decisive rulings,
composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
without mentioning ghosts or spirits,
not daring to act arbitrarily.
The wisdom of sages,
though already abundant,
is governed by restraint,
hence their actions bring glory.
The wisdom of fools,
though already scant,
is burdened with many pursuits,
hence their actions lead to ruin.
Wú Qǐ and Zhāng Yí,
whose wisdom fell short of Confucius and Mòzǐ,
yet vied for the favor of powerful rulers,
this is why they met dismemberment.
Those who educate with correctness,
find it easy and sure to succeed;
those who deceive the world with cunning,
find it difficult and sure to fail.
Whoever seeks to establish a course in the world,
yet abandons the easy and sure path,
for the difficult and doomed one,
does so out of folly and delusion.
These six contrasts,
must not go unexamined.
To know all things but not human principles,
cannot be called wisdom.
To love all creatures but not humanity,
cannot be called benevolence.
The benevolent love their kind,
the wise are not misled.
The benevolent, even when making harsh decisions,
show their unwillingness in expression.
The wise, even in complex matters,
demonstrate their clarity in effect.
Introspecting with empathy,
what the heart does not desire,
it does not impose on others,
understanding the distant from the near,
knowing others from oneself,
this is how the wise align and act.
Minor teachings lead to great preservation,
small punishments bring vast peace,
only compassion, extended through action,
is what the wise decide uniquely.
Thus benevolence and wisdom sometimes diverge,
sometimes converge,
convergence is correctness,
divergence is adaptability,
their principle is one.
Officials uphold the law,
gentlemen determine righteousness.
Law without righteousness,
makes one merely an official,
insufficient for governance.
Farming is laborious,
weaving is taxing.
Such toilsome tasks,
yet people do not abandon them, knowing they provide food and clothing.
Human nature cannot do without food and clothing,
the way to these begins with farming and weaving,
as all people commonly see.
Matters like farming and weaving,
start with great effort but end in benefit.
Many things can be prepared for,
but fools prepare for few;
many situations allow adaptability,
but fools adapt to few;
this is why fools have many troubles.
What can be prepared for,
the wise fully prepare;
what can be adapted to,
they fully adapt;
this is why the wise have few troubles.
Thus the wise endure hardship first and gain harmony later,
while fools start with joy and end in sorrow.
Asking what brings glory today,
and righteousness tomorrow,
is easy to say.
Asking what is righteous today,
and glorious tomorrow,
is hard to know.
Ask a blind musician:
"What is white silk like?"
He says:
"Gǎo-like."
Ask:
"What about black?"
He says:
"Dàn-like."
But present him with white and black,
and he cannot distinguish them.
People see white and black with their eyes,
speak of white and black with their mouths,
the blind musician can speak of white and black,
but cannot know white and black,
so his speech on white and black is like others',
but his distinction of white and black differs.
Being filial to parents at home,
loyal to the ruler abroad,
regardless of foolish, wise, worthy, or unworthy,
all know it is righteous,
but those who can demonstrate loyalty and filial piety
and understand their origins
are few.
All people in thought,
first deem something possible before acting,
whether it turns out right or wrong,
this distinguishes the foolish from the wise.
In human nature,
nothing is more valuable than benevolence,
nothing more urgent than wisdom.
Benevolence serves as the substance,
wisdom as the means to act.
These two are the foundation,
supplemented by courage, strength, eloquence, intelligence,
swiftness, diligence, skill, acuity,
and keen perception—all are additional benefits.
If one's character is not cultivated,
yet all manner of skills are fully acquired,
lacking benevolence and wisdom as the guiding principles,
adding more virtues to this
only increases the harm.
Thus, to be courageous and resolute without benevolence
is like wielding a sharp sword while insane;
to be eloquent and quick-witted without wisdom
is like riding a fine horse yet losing one's way.
Even with talents,
if applied inappropriately,
or situated unsuitably,
they merely aid in deception and covering up wrongs.
Having many skills
is worse than having few.
Therefore, one with ambitious intentions
should not be given advantageous power;
one with a foolish nature
should not be entrusted with sharp tools.
Fish find joy in swimming where there is water,
but if the pond breaks and the water dries up,
they are eaten by ants and insects.
If someone manages to repair the embankments,
and fills the gaps and leaks,
the fish benefit from it.
A state has means to survive,
a person has means to live.
What enables a state to survive
is righteousness and benevolence;
what enables a person to live
is doing good deeds.
A state without righteousness,
no matter how large, will surely perish;
a person without good intentions,
no matter how brave, will surely be harmed.
In governing a state,
the ruler should not interfere with what is beyond his control;
being filial to parents,
respectful to elder brothers and sisters-in-law,
trustworthy to friends—
these can be done without orders from above.
To neglect what one can do
and demand what one cannot control
is perverse!
A scholar in lowly and obscure circumstances,
wishing to advance upward,
must first reflect on oneself.
There is a way to advance upward:
if reputation does not rise, one cannot advance.
There is a way to gain reputation:
if not trusted by friends, one cannot gain it.
There is a way to be trusted by friends:
if not pleasing one's parents, one cannot be trusted.
There is a way to please one's parents:
if self-cultivation is not sincere, one cannot serve them.
There is a way to be sincere in self-cultivation:
if the mind is not focused, one cannot be sincere.
The way lies in what is easy, yet people seek it in what is difficult;
the proof is near, yet they seek it far away—
hence they fail to attain it.
The Way is supremely high without a top,
deeply low without a bottom,
level as a marking line,
straight as a plumb line,
round as a compass,
square as a square,
enveloping the universe without inside or outside,
penetrating heaven and earth without obstruction.
Therefore, one who embodies the Way
neither grieves nor rejoices,
neither delights nor angers,
sits without worries,
sleeps without dreams,
names things as they come,
responds to events as they arise.
The ruler is the heart of the state.
When the heart is orderly, all parts are at peace;
when the heart is disturbed, all parts are in chaos.
Thus, when one's heart is orderly,
the limbs are forgotten;
when the state is well-governed,
rulers and ministers forget each other.
Huángdì said:
"Vast and obscure,
follow the majesty of Heaven,
united in breath with the origin."
Therefore, those of utmost virtue
share the same strategies in speech,
the same aims in action,
united in heart above and below,
with no divergent paths or side views,
blocking what is evil,
guiding toward what is good,
and the people turn toward the right direction.
Thus, the *Yì Jīng* says:
"Union with others in the wilds;
it is beneficial to cross the great river."
The Way is what guides things;
virtue is what supports nature;
benevolence is the evidence of accumulated kindness;
righteousness is what aligns with the human heart and suits the collective good.
Thus, when the Way declines, virtue is used;
when virtue decays, benevolence and righteousness arise.
Hence, in ancient times, they embodied the Way without emphasizing virtue,
in middle times, they upheld virtue without letting it decay,
and in later times, they are cautious, fearing to lose benevolence and righteousness.
A gentleman cannot live without righteousness;
losing righteousness,
he loses his means to live.
A petty person cannot survive without desires;
losing desires,
he loses his means to survive.
Thus, the gentleman fears losing righteousness,
the petty person fears losing profit.
Observing what they fear,
one knows they differ.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
"Pursuing a deer without a forester;
only entering the forest.
The gentleman, perceiving the signs, should rather let it go.
To go on brings regret."
Those who give generously receive beautiful rewards;
those who incur great enmity suffer deep calamities.
To give little and expect much,
or to harbor resentment without suffering harm—
such things have never occurred in all of history.
Therefore, the sage examines the causes of actions
to know their consequences.
The way of the sage
is like setting a wine vessel in the middle of a crossroads:
passersby serve themselves,
taking more or less,
each according to what suits them.
Thus, gaining one person
leads to gaining a hundred.
If people give to their subordinates what they wish from their superiors,
who would not support them?
If they serve their superiors with what they desire from their subordinates,
who would not be pleased?
The *Shī Jīng* says:
"Cherish this one person,
respond with careful virtue."
Careful virtue is great,
the one person is small,
but being good in small things
enables one to be good in great things.
The gentleman, seeing faults, forgets punishment, hence he can admonish;
seeing worth, forgets low status, hence he can yield;
seeing need, forgets poverty, hence he can give.
Feelings are tied within,
actions manifest without.
All actions borne of genuine feeling, even if flawed, incur no resentment;
without genuine feeling, even loyalty invites dislike.
Hòu Jì greatly benefited the world, yet never boasted;
Yǔ never abandoned his labors, never hid resources, yet viewed himself as lacking.
Full as if hollow,
substantial as if empty—
this is the epitome of perfection.
All people consider their own views wise,
and delight in what pleases them.
The world never fails to promote the worthy,
yet sometimes this brings order,
sometimes chaos—
not because they deliberately evade responsibility,
but because they seek those identical to themselves.
One may not be worthy,
yet by seeking those like oneself,
and hoping to obtain worthies,
is hardly close to achieving it!
Had Yáo measure Shùn,
it would be fitting;
had Jié measure Yáo,
it would be like using a pint to measure a bushel.
Now, to speak of "húlí" (fox and raccoon dog),
one must neither know the fox,
nor know the raccoon dog.
Not only has one never seen a fox,
one must never have seen a raccoon dog either.
Fox and raccoon dog are not different;
they are of the same kind,
yet to call them "húlí"
is to not know either.
Therefore, to call the unworthy worthy,
one must not know worthiness;
to call the worthy unworthy,
one must not know unworthiness.
When a sage is in high position,
the people rejoice in his governance;
when in low position,
the people admire his intentions.
When a petty man is in high office,
it is like sleeping on a gate bar,
or sunbaking in silk floss—
not a moment of peace can be had.
Thus the Yì Jīng says:
"The horse falters,
tears of blood flow incessantly."
This means a petty man in a position not his own
cannot last long.
There is nothing that cannot be put to use.
Tiānxióng and wūhuì,
though deadly poisons among medicines,
a good physician uses them to save lives.
Dwarfs and blind musicians,
though among the most pitiable of people,
a ruler employs them for entertainment.
Thus, the sage utilizes all materials,
leaving nothing unused.
When a brave warrior shouts once,
the entire army retreats—
such is the sincerity of his expression.
Hence, to lead without response,
to intend without support,
must mean there is something amiss within.
Thus, Shùn could rectify the world without leaving his mat,
because he sought within himself.
Therefore, if those above are full of deceit,
the people will be full of fraud.
That a crooked body could cast a straight shadow
has never been heard of.
Where words cannot reach,
appearance and demeanor can.
Where appearance and demeanor cannot reach,
subtle influence can.
Moved in the heart,
illuminated by wisdom,
it manifests into form.
The most refined essence
can connect through form and momentum,
but cannot be conveyed by mere instruction.
Horses of the Róng
and Dí tribes
can all gallop,
some near, some far,
but only Zàofǔ could exhaust their strength;
the people of the Sānmiáo
can all be made loyal and trustworthy,
some worthy, some not,
but only Táng
and Yú could unify their virtue.
There must be something that cannot be transmitted.
Zhōngháng Móubó could wrestle a tiger with his hands,
but could not keep it alive—
for though his strength was superior, his skill fell short.
Employing what a hundred people can do,
one gains the strength of a hundred;
promoting what a thousand people love,
one wins the hearts of a thousand;
just as when felling a tree by pulling its roots,
thousands of branches and leaves must follow.
A kind father's love for his son
is not for repayment,
and cannot be unraveled from his heart;
a sage king's nurturing of the people
is not for their utility,
but an inexorable nature;
like fire's innate heat,
ice's innate cold—
what need for cultivation there!
But to rely on their strength,
depend on their service,
is like a boat on fire.
Thus, the noble person sees the beginning,
and thereby knows the end.
Matchmakers may praise someone,
yet none feel grateful;
hiring laborers and forcing them to eat,
wins no affection.
Even a kind father or loving mother
adds nothing beyond this;
if done with ulterior motive,
kindness does not connect.
Thus, sending off the departed
is not for welcoming the coming;
bestowing on the dead
is not solely for the living.
If sincerity comes from within,
its influence reaches far.
Brocades and embroideries in the temple
honor refinement;
guī and zhǎng jades presented first
esteem substance.
When refinement does not surpass substance, that is the noble person.
Hence, building a cart all year,
without a three-inch linchpin,
it cannot be driven;
a craftsman carving a door,
without a one-foot bolt,
it cannot be secured.
Thus, the noble person acts with an eye on the outcome.
The essence of the heart
can transform spiritually,
but cannot guide others;
the essence of the eyes
can discern subtly,
but cannot illuminate through instruction.
In the realm of profound mystery,
it cannot be explained to others.
Therefore, Shùn governed the world without leaving his mat,
while Jié brought chaos without descending his steps—
for emotion speaks louder than shouts.
To lack in oneself
and seek in others
is unheard of in all history.
Speaking the same words and being trusted by the people
means trust precedes the words.
Issuing the same commands and transforming the people
means sincerity lies beyond the commands.
When a sage is above,
the people are influenced and transformed—
emotion leads the way.
Action from above
that finds no response below
is due to discord between emotion and command.
Thus the Yì Jīng says:
"The arrogant dragon will have cause to repent."
A three-month-old infant
knows nothing of gain or loss,
yet understands a loving mother's affection—
such is the power of emotion.
Therefore, the utility of words
is pathetically small!
The utility of wordlessness
is vastly great!
To embody the words of a noble person
is trustworthiness.
To align with the intentions of a noble person
is loyalty.
When loyalty and trustworthiness take form within,
their influence responds without.
Thus, Yǔ danced with shield and axe between the two stairways, and the Sānmiáo submitted.
When an eagle soars over a river,
fish and turtles dive deep,
birds take flight—
all flee from the threat.
A son dying for his father,
a minister dying for his lord—
there are those in the world who do this,
not to seek fame through death,
but because a sense of grace hidden within
cannot evade such hardship.
Thus, when people enjoy sweetness,
it's not specifically for the heel,
yet the heel benefits.
The noble person's grief and pain
are not feigned expressions,
but resonate in people's hearts.
They do not come from without,
but emerge from within.
Righteousness honors the ruler,
benevolence cherishes the father.
Thus, the ruler towards the ministers
can determine their life and death,
but cannot make them act deceitfully or lightly;
the father towards the son
can give him life and raise him,
but cannot prevent him from having worries and deep thoughts.
Therefore, when righteousness surpasses the ruler,
and benevolence surpasses the father,
then the ruler is honored and the ministers are loyal,
the father is kind and the son is filial.
When a sage is in power,
he transforms and nurtures like a spirit.
The highest says:
"It is my nature!"
The next says:
"Without that,
how could it be like this!"
Thus, the *Book of Songs* says:
"Holding the reins as if weaving silk,"
the *Book of Changes* says:
"Containing elegance, one can remain steadfast."
Acting in the near,
it forms patterns in the far.
To examine one's nightly conduct,
the Duke of Zhōu felt ashamed before his shadow,
hence the nobleman is cautious when alone.
Neglecting the near and seeking the far,
is obstructed.
Hearing goodness is easy,
but correcting oneself is difficult.
The master saw the three transformations of the grain,
and said profoundly:
"The fox dies facing its mound,
shall I be like the head of the grain?"
Thus, the nobleman, upon seeing goodness, reflects deeply on himself.
If one's self is rectified,
embracing the far becomes easy.
Hence, the *Book of Songs* says:
"If you do not act personally,
the common people will not trust you."
The petty man in his endeavors
seeks mere gain;
the nobleman seeks righteousness.
What they seek is the same,
but what they aspire to differs!
Striking a boat in the water,
fish sink and birds soar,
hearing the same sound but reacting differently,
their nature is one.
Xì Fùjī marked his lane with a pot of food,
Zhào Xuānmèng saved his life with a bundle of dried meat;
their rites were not elaborate, yet their virtue was abundant.
A benevolent heart, touched by gratitude, gives rise to compassion,
hence it penetrates deeply into people.
The same cry,
if from a family elder, is seen as deep kindness,
but from a debtor, it sparks conflict.
Thus it is said:
"No weapon is sharper than the will,
Mòyé is inferior;
no enemy is greater than the forces of yīn and yáng,
war drums are minor."
The sage does good
not to seek fame, yet fame follows him;
fame does not expect profit, yet profit returns to him.
Thus, people's joys and sorrows
are not for Zhí's sake,
yet Zhí's influence persists.
Hence, the ultimate cannot be contained.
So, as if blinded yet feeling his way,
as if stumbling yet finding support,
the sage governs
so indifferently that his worth is unseen,
yet in the end, he is known to be great.
Like the sun's journey,
even a swift steed cannot compete in distance.
If one seeks something at night,
he is equal to a blind guide;
when the east brightens,
it illuminates all.
Action that brings benefit
is followed by loss,
thus the *Book of Changes* says:
"When stripping cannot be completed,
it is followed by return."
Accumulating thin makes thick,
accumulating low makes high,
so the nobleman daily strives diligently to achieve brilliance,
while the petty man daily grumbles until disgrace.
Their growth and decline,
even Lí Zhū could not perceive.
King Wén of Zhōu pursued goodness as if he could not reach it,
and retained any lack of goodness as an ill omen,
not because the days were insufficient,
but because his deep concern drove him.
Hence, the *Book of Songs* says:
"Although Zhōu is an old state,
its mandate is renewed."
Embracing genuine feelings and substance,
heaven cannot destroy it,
earth cannot bury it.
Its sound spreads between heaven and earth,
matching the light of the sun and moon—
this is what is sweet and joyful.
If one inclines toward goodness,
even if he errs, there is no resentment;
if he does not incline toward goodness,
even loyalty brings disaster.
Thus, blaming others is不如 blaming oneself,
seeking from others is不如 seeking from oneself to attain.
Sound summons itself,
appearance displays itself,
name defines itself,
pattern organizes itself—
none are not of oneself.
Wielding a sharp point to stab,
holding a blade to strike—
it is one's own appearance that summons,
why blame others?
Thus, Guǎn Zhòng, though in brocade,
even if plain, ascended the temple;
Zǐ Chǎn, though dyed fine silk,
was beautiful but not honored.
Empty yet able to be full,
bland yet having flavor—
he who wears coarse cloth but holds jade within.
Thus, a divided heart cannot win one person,
a single heart can win a hundred.
A man planting orchids,
beautiful but not fragrant;
a stepson receiving food,
well-fed but not glossy—
emotion does not interact between them.
Life is what we borrow,
death is where we return.
Thus, Hóng Yǎn stood straight for benevolence and died,
Prince Lǚ opened his arms and accepted the blade—
not letting what is entrusted harm the return.
Therefore, in times of order, use righteousness to protect oneself;
in times of chaos, use oneself to protect righteousness.
The day of death
is the end of one's actions,
hence the nobleman is cautious in every application.
The cowardly
are not fearful beforehand,
but lose their resolve when difficulty arrives;
the greedy
do not desire beforehand,
but see profit and forget the harm.
The Duke of Yú saw the jade of Chuíjí,
unaware that the disaster of Guó would reach him.
Thus, the ultimate person
cannot be deterred or robbed.
When people desire glory,
they do it for themselves—
what benefit does it bring to others?
The sage's practice of righteousness,
arises from deep concern within their hearts—
how could it be for personal gain!
Thus, many have been emperors and kings,
yet only the Three Sovereigns are celebrated;
many have lived in poverty and low status,
yet only Bó Yí is singled out.
If nobility made one a sage,
then the noble would be numerous;
if lowliness made one benevolent,
then the lowly would be abundant—
why then are sages and benevolent ones so few!
The joy of singular devotion is profound,
swiftly, day by day, renewing oneself,
forgetting that old age approaches.
Starting from the lesser,
returning to the greater,
this accumulation is inevitable.
Not deceiving oneself,
thus one does not deceive others;
hence, like walking a single beam,
one remains vigilant even with no one watching.
So, it is easy to make others trust you,
but hard to clothe oneself in self-confidence.
When emotions stir first,
their movement meets no resistance;
meeting no resistance,
there is no obstruction;
only when obstructions arise does one seek relief.
Thus, the actions of Táng and Yú,
were not to pander to feelings,
but in satisfying themselves, the world was governed;
Jié and Zhòu did not intentionally harm it,
yet in pleasing themselves, all affairs were ruined;
thus, through likes and dislikes, order and chaos are distinguished.
The sage's conduct,
neither fully aligns nor
wholly diverges.
It is like a drum,
not tuned to anything,
yet harmonizes with all.
Strings, pipes, metal, and stone,
varying in size and length, have their order,
differing in sound but blending in harmony.
Ruler and minister, high and low,
each with distinct duties,
perform different tasks yet coordinate.
The weaver advances daily,
the plowman retreats step by step—
their actions oppose,
but their success is one.
Shēn Xǐ heard a beggar's song and felt sorrow,
went out to look,
and it was his mother.
At the battle of Ài Líng,
Fū Chāi said:
"The barbarian's chant is auspicious;
perhaps Gōu Wú will thrive!"
The same sound,
yet interpretations differ,
due to the emotions within.
Thus, with a sorrowful heart, singing brings no joy;
with a joyful heart, weeping holds no grief.
When Mǐn Zǐ Qiān ended his three-year mourning,
took up a lute to play,
the Master said:
"The strings are the same,
but the sound is not."
Refinement is
the means to connect with things;
emotions tied within seek expression outward.
Using refinement to suppress emotion loses emotion;
using emotion to override refinement loses refinement.
When refinement and emotion communicate,
then the phoenix and qílín appear,
speaking of ultimate virtue embracing the distant.
Shū Zǐ Yáng told his son:
"A skilled craftsman hones within the square and chisel."
Within the square and chisel,
indeed, nothing is not encompassed;
the sage king governs the people thus,
Zào Fǔ trains horses thus,
Yī Luò treats illness thus—
each draws from the same material.
When the ruler's intent is clear, the people follow;
it stems from sincerity within.
Unspoken, yet trusted;
uncalled, yet they come—
something preceded it.
Anxious about being unknown,
one lacks self-awareness.
Arrogance arises from inadequacy,
embellished falsehoods from pride.
Those sincere within,
joyful and unanxious,
like the owl's love for its call,
the bear's love for roaming—
who among them is arrogant!
Spring maidens ponder,
autumn scholars grieve,
thus knowing the transformation of things.
Crying out in weeping,
sighing in sorrow,
one knows the stirring of sound.
In demeanor and expression,
in bending and stretching, postures curved or straight,
one discerns true and false feelings.
Thus, the sage trembles with awe within,
reaching the utmost heights.
Achievement of merit and fame
is of heaven;
following principle and accepting order
is of humans.
Tài Gōng Wàng
and Zhōu Gōng Dàn—
heaven did not create them for King Wǔ;
Chóng Hóu
and È Lái—
heaven did not birth them for Zhòu;
there was their era,
and there were their people.
Teaching originates from the noble,
and the common people receive its benefit;
profit stems from the common people,
and the noble enjoy its fruits.
In the time of Dōng Hù Jì Zǐ,
lost items were not picked up on roads,
plows and leftover grain were left in the fields overnight,
allowing both noble and common to find their proper place.
Thus, when one person has cause for celebration,
the multitude relies on it.
In general, the high value the left,
so the lower to the higher say "left,"
as a subject's expression.
The low value the right,
so the higher to the lower say "right,"
as a ruler's concession.
Thus, if the ruler moves left, they lose respect;
if the subject turns right, they lose honor.
Small pleasures harm the Way,
slight deviations damage propriety.
Zǐ Chǎn excelled in rhetoric,
lawsuits were frequent but not wicked;
losing touch with emotion
blocks expression.
The way to build a state:
artisans avoid deceitful work,
farmers exert full effort,
scholars conceal no conduct,
officials uphold the law without fail.
It is like setting a net:
pull its main cord, and all meshes open.
Shùn and Yǔ did not receive the mandate twice;
Yáo and Shùn passed on greatness,
first manifest in small ways.
Applied to one's wife,
extended to brothers,
then abdicated to the state,
and the world followed like the wind.
Thus, in warfare, the large knows the small;
in humanity, the small knows the large.
The way of the noble:
near, yet unattainable;
low, yet unclimbable;
bearing nothing, yet overcoming all;
with time, it shines;
with distance, it flourishes.
Understanding this way,
one cannot seek it in others—
it must be found within oneself.
Abandoning self to seek in others
leads far astray.
The noble person
finds contentment within but lacks renown,
while the petty person lacks contentment but has renown in excess.
Observing the distance between excess and deficiency,
the distinction becomes clearly evident.
To harbor without expressing,
to keep emotions without sprouting—
such a thing has never been heard of.
The noble person thinks of righteousness and does not consider gain,
while the petty person covets gain and disregards righteousness.
The Master said:
"In the same act of crying,
one says:
'Oh, what can I do? How do you treat me!'
The sorrow is the same,
but the reasons for the sorrow differ."
Thus, sorrow and joy penetrate human emotions deeply.
Digging land and filling ponds
are not inherently meant to toil the people;
disorder arises when each follows their own path.
The underlying sentiment is the same,
but its application to people differs.
Hence, Táng
and Yú diligently strove daily to achieve kingship,
while Jié and Zhòu daily indulged in pleasure leading to their demise,
unaware of later generations' criticism.
In general human emotion,
relief from suffering brings joy,
and loss of joy brings sorrow;
thus, one who knows the joy of life
must know the sorrow of death.
The righteous cannot be deceived with profit,
the brave cannot be coerced with fear,
just as the hungry and thirsty cannot be fooled with empty vessels.
Excessive desires harm righteousness,
excessive worries impair wisdom,
excessive fears damage courage.
Rudeness arises from petty persons,
even barbarians are capable of it;
goodness arises from noble persons,
shining brilliantly to rival the sun and moon,
and the world cannot suppress or seize it.
Thus, a well-governed state delights in what preserves it,
while a perishing state also delights in what causes its downfall.
If metal and tin do not melt, they cannot be cast;
if rulers' concerns are not sincere, they cannot govern the people.
If concerns are not for the people,
then the bond with the people is severed;
when the ruler returns to fundamentals,
the people's bond is secured.
With supreme virtue, small details are complete,
and major principles are upheld.
Duke Huán of Qí upheld principles but lacked thoroughness,
while Duke Wén of Jìn was thorough but failed to uphold principles.
Duke Wén of Jìn succeeded within the women's quarters,
but failed beyond the borders;
Duke Huán of Qí failed within the women's quarters,
but succeeded in his court.
Water flows downward and becomes vast,
the ruler humbles himself to ministers and becomes enlightened.
When the ruler does not compete with ministers for merit,
the way of governance is unobstructed.
Guǎn Yíwú
and Bǎilǐ Xī devised plans and accomplished them,
while Duke Huán of Qí
and Duke Mù of Qín received and followed them.
The confused perceive east as west,
which is delusion,
but upon seeing the sun, they awaken.
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi said to his ministers:
"Young men, do not think me old and feeble,
and must report any faults I have."
Thus, Marquis Wǔ, by not accepting feebleness, surely avoided it,
so in old age he did not abandon his duties,
understanding the discourse on survival and perishation.
Humans cannot create,
but can act;
they can act,
but cannot ensure success.
Human action
is completed by Heaven.
Lifelong goodness
cannot be achieved without Heaven;
lifelong evil
cannot perish without Heaven.
Thus, good and bad
depend on me;
fortune and misfortune
do not depend on me.
Hence, the noble person only ensures what is within their control.
Nature
is received from Heaven;
destiny
is encountered through timing.
To have talent
but not meet the right era
is Heaven's doing.
What fault had Tàigōng,
what crime had Bǐgān?
Following their nature and direction,
some were harmed, some benefited.
Seeking follows the Way,
but attainment lies in destiny;
thus, the noble person can do good
but cannot guarantee fortune;
they cannot bear to do wrong
but cannot certainly avoid misfortune.
The ruler
and ministers are like branches and leaves.
If the root is not good,
yet the branches and leaves flourish—
such a thing has never been heard of.
In an era with the Way,
one gives people to the state;
in an era without the Way,
one gives the state to people.
Yáo ruled the world and his worries did not cease,
but upon handing it to Shùn, his worries dissolved.
Worried, he guarded it,
yet joyfully yielded to the worthy,
never privatizing the benefits.
All things have their application;
nothing is too small to be useful.
If left unused,
even jade becomes dirt.
Human nature
seeks the lesser evil in harm,
and the greater benefit in advantage.
Thus, among same flavors, those who prefer rich cuts
must find them sweet;
among same teachers, those who excel beyond the group
must find it enjoyable.
Without finding it sweet or enjoyable,
yet able to become exemplary—
such a thing has never been heard of.
The noble person advances with the times,
gaining through righteousness—
what fortune is this!
When times are unfavorable, they withdraw,
yielding through righteousness—
what misfortune is this!
Thus, Bóyí starved to death at the foot of Shǒu Mountain,
yet never regretted it,
abandoning what he despised
to gain what he valued.
Fortune sprouts subtly,
while calamity arises abruptly.
Fortune and calamity begin imperceptibly,
so people are heedless;
only the sage sees the beginning and knows the end.
Hence, the tradition says:
"When Lǔ's wine was thin, Hándān was besieged;
when mutton soup was not served, the Sòng state was endangered."
The enlightened ruler's rewards and punishments
are not for themselves,
but for the state.
Those pleasing to oneself but useless to the state
receive no reward;
those opposing oneself but beneficial to the state
receive no punishment.
Thus, King Zhuāng of Chǔ said to Gòng Yōng:
"The virtuous receive my ranks and emoluments,
the meritorious receive my fields and homes.
Of these two,
you have neither,
so I have nothing to give you."
Could this not be called not transgressing principle?
His dismissal of him
was still not a denial.
Zhōu's governance reached perfection,
Yīn's governance was good,
Xià's governance was implemented.
Implemented governance is not necessarily good,
good governance is not necessarily perfect.
The perfectly perfected person
does not admire implementation,
does not feel ashamed of goodness,
embodies virtue and treads the Way,
and上下 delights together,
not knowing how it comes to be.
There have been many rulers of states,
yet only Duke Huán of Qí and
Duke Wén of Jìn are uniquely renowned;
on Mount Tài there were seventy altars,
yet only the Three Sovereigns are uniquely spoken of.
The ruler does not seek from his ministers,
the ministers do not borrow from their ruler,
cultivating the near and extending to the far,
and later generations praise their greatness.
Without surpassing their neighbors, they accomplished illustrious deeds,
yet none can reach such heights.
Thus, the rites of Xiàojǐ could be practiced,
but none could wrest away his fame,
for it necessarily did not capture what he cherished.
Righteousness carried in appropriateness is called the noble person,
appropriateness abandoned by righteousness is called the petty person.
The thoroughly wise attain without toil,
the next toil without distress,
the lowest are distressed yet do not toil.
The ancients savored without greed,
modern people are greedy without savoring.
Singing refines its sound,
sound that falls short of its beauty.
Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo,
aided and played together,
still are not enough to reach the ultimate.
If a person can honor the Way and practice righteousness,
their joy, anger, taking, and giving
will be like grass following the wind.
Duke Shào relaxed imprisonments and released detainees during silkworm mulberry and plowing seasons,
enabling all common people to return to their trades and duties;
King Wén declined a thousand-li territory,
and requested the abolition of the roasting-pillar punishment.
Thus, when sages initiate actions,
their advances and retreats do not miss the timing,
like wearing thin silk in summer,
or being handed the carriage strap when boarding.
Lǎozi studied with Shāng Róng,
saw the tongue and understood preserving softness;
Lièzǐ studied with Húzǐ,
observed the shadow post and understood holding back.
Hence, the sage does not precede things,
but constantly controls them,
akin to piling firewood,
where the latter comes on top.
People love through righteousness,
form groups through factions,
and grow strong through groups.
Therefore, where virtue is applied broadly,
there authority extends far;
where righteousness is applied shallowly,
there military control is small.
The Wú bell destroys itself with its sound,
the grease candle consumes itself with its light,
tigers and leopards are shot for their patterns,
gibbons are targeted for their agility,
thus Zǐlù died due to courage,
Cháng Hóng was trapped due to wisdom.
One can use wisdom to be wise,
but not use wisdom to be unwise.
Thus, those traversing cliffs cannot walk a straight line,
those exiting forests cannot take a direct path,
night travelers feel ahead with their hands in darkness,
for situations have their limits,
and clarity has its intolerances.
If one can penetrate the obscure and enter the bright,
they may be spoken with about the ultimate.
Magpie nests know the wind's origin,
otter burrows know the water's level,
the shining sun foretells the evening,
the dark magpie foretells rain.
To say human wisdom is inferior to birds and beasts
is not so.
Thus, mastering one skill,
understanding one phrase,
allows for specialized discourse,
but not broad response.
Nìng Qī beat the ox horn and sang,
Duke Huán appointed him as Minister of Agriculture;
Yōngménzǐ met Lord Mèngcháng by weeping,
tears streaming to his cap strings.
Singing and weeping,
are what many can do;
yet one utterance,
entering ears,
moving hearts,
is the pinnacle of essence.
Thus, the laws of Táng and
Yú can be emulated,
but their understanding of human hearts is unmatched.
Duke Jiǎn was killed for his weakness,
Zǐyáng was overthrown for his harshness,
both failing to grasp the proper way.
Hence, singing not matching the pitch,
its clarity and muddiness are the same;
outside the plumb line or inside it,
both miss straightness.
King Zhòu used ivory chopsticks, and Jīzǐ lamented;
Lǔ buried with figurines, and Confucius sighed,
seeing the beginning, they knew the end.
Thus, water emerges from mountains,
and enters the sea;
crops grow in fields,
and are stored in granaries;
the sage sees their origin and knows their destination.
Murky water makes fish gasp,
harsh orders make people rebel,
steep walls will collapse,
precipitous banks will crumble,
so Shāng Yāng established laws and was torn apart,
Wú Qǐ enforced severity and was drawn by chariots.
Governing a state is like tuning a se zither,
if the large string is too tight,
the small string will snap.
Thus, tight reins and frequent whipping
are not the driving for a thousand lǐ.
The sound that has sound
does not exceed a hundred lǐ;
the sound without sound
extends throughout the four seas.
Therefore, emolument exceeding merit brings loss,
fame exceeding reality brings obscurity.
When conduct matches and reputation corresponds,
fortune and misfortune do not come in vain.
Having ominous dreams in person,
cannot overcome upright conduct;
having evil omens in the state,
cannot overcome good governance.
Thus, ahead there are rewards of carriages and crowns,
which cannot be taken without merit;
behind there are prohibitions of axes and blades,
which cannot be suffered without crime.
Those who cultivate purity and correctness
do not stray from the Way.
The noble person does not deem small goodness insufficient and abandon it,
for small goodness accumulates into great goodness;
nor does they do small misdeeds thinking them harmless,
for small misdeeds accumulate into great misdeeds.
Thus, accumulated feathers sink a boat,
numerous light things break an axle,
so the noble person prohibits the subtle.
One pleasure does not suffice to form goodness,
accumulated pleasures become virtue;
one regret does not suffice to form fault,
accumulated regrets become evil.
Hence, the goodness of the Three Dynasties
is the accumulated praise of a thousand years;
the evil of Jié and Zhòu
is the accumulated condemnation of a thousand years.
Heaven has four seasons,
humans have four uses.
What are the four uses?
Seeing and forming shapes, none are brighter than the eyes;
hearing and refining, none are keener than the ears;
weighing and closing, none are firmer than the mouth;
containing and storing, none are deeper than the heart.
Eyes see the form,
ears hear the sound,
mouth speaks the sincerity,
and heart conveys the essence,
then the transformations of all things all have their limits.
Land expands through virtue,
ruler is honored through virtue,
is the highest;
land expands through righteousness,
ruler is honored through righteousness,
is the next;
land expands through strength,
ruler is honored through strength,
is the lowest.
Thus, the pure become kings,
the mixed become hegemons,
those with neither perish.
In the past, the Two Sovereigns had phoenixes in their courts,
the Three Dynasties had them at their gates,
the Zhōu house had them at their marshes.
The cruder the virtue,
the farther they arrive;
the finer the virtue,
the closer they arrive.
The noble man is truly benevolent,
whether he acts benevolently or not,
he remains benevolent.
The petty man is truly not benevolent,
whether he acts or not,
he remains not benevolent.
Goodness originating from oneself,
rather than from others,
is like the flourishing of benevolent virtue.
Thus when nature overcomes desire, there is prosperity;
when desire overcomes nature, there is ruin.
To understand the way of heaven,
observe its patterns;
to understand the way of earth,
examine its vegetation;
to understand the way of humans,
follow their desires.
Do not startle or alarm,
and all things will order themselves;
do not disturb or interfere,
and all things will become clear.
One who examines only a single aspect
cannot be spoken with about transformation;
one who scrutinizes only a single moment
cannot be spoken with about greatness.
The day does not know the night,
the moon does not know the day,
the sun and moon are bright but cannot combine,
only heaven and earth can contain them.
What can encompass heaven and earth
is said to be the formless.
An arrogant and excessive ruler has no loyal ministers,
a glib-tongued person has no necessary trustworthiness.
Intertwined trees have no branches to grasp,
ordinary ditches have no fish that swallow boats.
Shallow roots mean short ends,
a wounded trunk means withered branches.
Happiness arises from non-action,
trouble arises from excessive desires.
Harm arises from lack of preparation,
weeds arise from lack of weeding.
The sage does good as if fearing to fall short,
prepares for calamity as if fearing unavoidable.
To want no dust in the eyes while in a dust storm,
to want not to get wet while crossing water,
is impossible.
Therefore, one who knows himself does not blame others,
one who knows fate does not blame heaven.
Happiness arises from oneself,
calamity arises from oneself.
The sage does not seek praise,
does not avoid slander,
corrects himself and acts uprightly,
and all evils naturally cease.
Now to abandon correctness and pursue crookedness,
to turn away from right and follow the crowd,
is to run with the vulgar,
with no inner standard of conduct,
thus the sage turns to himself and does not follow them.
The Way having chapters, forms, and boundaries
is not the ultimate;
tasting it has no flavor,
looking at it has no form,
it cannot be transmitted to others.
Large spurge removes water,
pepperweed cures distension,
used without moderation,
they instead cause illness.
Many things appear similar but are not,
only the sage knows their subtleties.
A good charioteer does not forget his horses,
a good archer does not forget his crossbow,
a good leader does not forget his subordinates.
Truly able to love and benefit them,
the world can be followed.
Without love or benefit,
even a child will rebel against its father.
In the world, there is the highest nobility, but it is not power or position;
there is the greatest wealth, but it is not gold or jade;
there is the longest life, but it is not a thousand years;
returning to one's original heart and nature is nobility;
satisfying one's disposition and knowing contentment is wealth;
understanding the distinction between life and death is longevity.
One whose words are never right,
whose actions are never appropriate,
is a petty man.
One who examines one matter,
masters one skill,
is a middling man.
One who covers all and possesses everything,
with skills and the judgment to employ them,
is a sage.
Following one's nature in action is called the Way;
attaining one's innate nature is called virtue.
When nature is lost, then humanity is valued;
when the Way is lost, then righteousness is valued.
Thus with the establishment of humanity and righteousness, morality declines;
with the adornment of rites and music, simplicity scatters;
with the formation of right and wrong, the people are confused;
with the honoring of pearls and jade, the world contends.
All these four
are creations of a declining age,
used in a decadent era.
Rites are to distinguish noble and humble,
differentiate high and low;
righteousness is to harmonize the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, and friends.
Those who practice rites today
are reverent but envious;
those who practice righteousness
give alms and expect virtue;
ruler and minister blame each other,
flesh and bone generate resentment,
thus losing the root of rites and righteousness,
so they conflict and incur much blame.
Where water accumulates, fish that eat each other appear;
where earth accumulates, beasts that harm themselves appear;
where rites and righteousness are adorned, hypocritical and deceitful scholars appear.
To want no dust in the eyes while blowing ashes,
to want not to get wet while crossing water,
is impossible.
In ancient times, people were ignorant and knew not east from west,
their appearance did not exceed their feelings,
and their words did not exceed their actions.
Their clothes were warm but plain,
their weapons blunt and edgeless,
their songs joyful without variation,
their cries mournful without sound.
They dug wells to drink,
plowed fields to eat.
They had no means to display beauty,
nor did they seek gain.
Relatives did not slander or praise each other,
friends did not resent or virtue each other.
When rites and righteousness arose,
and goods and wealth were valued,
then deception and hypocrisy sprouted,
blame and praise intermingled,
resentment and virtue proceeded together,
then there appeared the goodness of Zēng Shēn and Xiàojǐ,
and the evil of Dào Zhí and Zhuāng Qiāo arose.
Thus with grand carriages and dragon banners,
feathered canopies and hanging tassels,
teams of four horses and connected riders,
there must be burglars picking locks, tomb robbers breaking in;
with exquisite patterns and elaborate embroidery,
fine silks and thin gauzes,
there must be those wearing straw sandals,
in short, ragged hemp clothes.
Thus the high and low leaning on each other,
the short and long comparing with each other,
is also clear.
The tadpole becomes a quail,
the water beetle becomes a dragonfly,
all born not of their kind,
only the sage knows their transformation.
The Hú people see hemp,
not knowing it can be made into cloth;
the Yuè people see fine hair,
not knowing it can be made into felt.
