Thus one who does not understand things
is hard to speak with about transformation.
Once Tàigōng Wàng and Zhōu Gōng Dàn received their fiefs and met,
Tàigōng Wàng asked Zhōu Gōng:
"How will you govern Lǔ?"
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Honor the honorable, cherish the kin."
Tàigōng said:
"Lǔ will weaken from this!"
Zhōu Gōng asked Tàigōng:
"How will you govern Qí?"
Tàigōng said:
"Promote the worthy and exalt achievement."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Later there will surely be a ruler who is robbed and killed!"
Afterward, Qí daily grew greater,
achieving hegemony,
but in twenty-four generations, the Tián clan replaced it;
Lǔ daily diminished,
until in thirty-two generations it perished.
Thus the Yì Jīng says:
"Treading on frost, solid ice arrives."
The sage's perception of
beginning and end is subtle!
Thus the hill of dregs arises from the ivory chopsticks,
the roasting rack arises from the hot branding iron.
Zǐlù rescued a drowning person and accepted a cow as gratitude,
Confucius said:
"The state of Lǔ will surely be fond of saving people from distress."
Zǐgòng ransomed a person
but did not accept money from the treasury,
Confucius said:
"The state of Lǔ will no longer ransom people."
Zǐlù's acceptance encouraged virtue,
Zǐgòng's refusal stopped goodness.
Confucius' wisdom,
understanding the great from the small,
knowing the distant from the near,
made him proficient in argumentation.
From this we see,
integrity has its place,
but cannot be publicly practiced universally.
Thus conduct aligned with customs,
can be followed;
affairs matching abilities,
are easily accomplished.
Affecting false purity to confuse the world,
assuming haughty conduct to oppose the masses,
the sage does not consider this popular custom.
Spacious houses and broad rooms,
interconnected doors and communicating chambers,
are where humans feel at ease,
yet birds entering become anxious.
High mountains and dangerous barriers,
deep forests and thick undergrowth,
are where tigers and leopards delight,
yet humans entering become fearful.
River valleys connecting to plains,
accumulated waters and layered springs,
are where giant turtles and alligators thrive,
yet humans entering die.
"Xiánchí", "Chéngyún", "Jiǔsháo", "Liùyīng",
are what humans enjoy,
yet birds and beasts hearing them startle.
Deep gorges and steep banks,
tall trees with long branches,
are where gibbons and monkeys delight,
yet humans climbing them tremble.
Forms differ and natures vary,
what brings joy to some
brings sorrow to others,
what provides security for some
presents danger to others.
Even heaven and earth's coverage,
the sun and moon's illumination,
enable each to suit its nature,
settle in its dwelling,
occupy its appropriate place,
exercise its capabilities.
Thus the foolish have their strengths,
the wise have their shortcomings;
a pillar cannot pick teeth,
a small bamboo cannot support a house;
horses cannot bear heavy loads,
oxen cannot chase speed,
lead cannot make knives,
copper cannot make crossbows,
iron cannot make boats,
wood cannot make cauldrons.
Each used where appropriate,
applied where suitable,
then all things become equal,
with no reason to surpass each other.
A bright mirror suits reflecting form,
but for holding food
it比不上 bamboo utensils;
a sacrificial ox with pure hair,
fits temple offerings,
but for bringing rain,
it比不上 black dragons.
From this we see,
things have no inherent nobility or baseness.
Value them for their valued aspects,
and nothing lacks value;
disparage them for their disparaged aspects,
and nothing escapes disparagement.
Uncut jade isn't嫌厚,
horn tips aren't嫌薄;
lacquer isn't嫌黑,
powder isn't嫌白.
These four are opposites,
but equally essential
makes their utility identical.
Now fur coats and straw raincoats, which is more essential?
When rain comes, fur coats aren't used,
when entering halls, raincoats aren't worn,
this shows alternation according to needs.
Like boats, carriages, shields, sleds, and tents,
each certainly has its appropriate use.
Thus Lǎozǐ said
"not exalting worthies",
meaning don't put fish in trees,
or sink birds in abysses.
Thus Yáo's governance of the world,
had Shùn as Minister of Education,
Xiè as Minister of War,
Yǔ as Minister of Works,
Hòujì as Minister of Agriculture,
Xīzhòng as Chief Artisan.
In guiding the myriad people,
those near water fished,
those in mountains gathered,
those in valleys herded,
those on plains farmed.
Land suited their occupations,
occupations suited their tools,
tools suited their uses,
uses suited their people.
Marshes produced nets,
hillsides grew crops,
enabling exchange of what they had for what they lacked,
skilled work for unskilled,
thus few rebelled,
and many obeyed.
Like scattering chess pieces on ground,
round ones roll to marshes,
square ones stay on heights,
each following where it settles,
how can there be superiority or inferiority!
Like wind passing through panpipes,
suddenly stirring them,
each responds with clear or turbid notes.
Gibbons obtaining lush trees,
don't abandon them for caves;
badgers finding dams,
don't leave them for edges;
creatures never avoid their benefits
for their harms.
Therefore neighboring states visible to each other,
chicken and dog sounds audible between them,
yet footsteps never cross feudal borders,
chariot tracks never extend beyond thousand miles,
all because each attains its settled peace.
Thus chaotic states appear full,
ordered states appear empty,
dying states appear insufficient,
surviving states appear abundant.
Emptiness
doesn't mean no people,
but all keeping their duties;
fullness
doesn't mean more people,
but all chasing trivialities;
abundance
doesn't mean more wealth,
but desires restrained and affairs few;
insufficiency
doesn't mean no goods,
but people restless and expenditures many.
Thus ancient kings' legal records,
weren't created arbitrarily,
but followed existing patterns.
Their prohibitions and punishments,
weren't enacted arbitrarily,
but maintained existing order.
Generally governing things not with things,
but with harmony;
governing harmony not with harmony,
but with people;
governing people not with people,
but with rulers;
governing rulers not with rulers,
but with desires;
governing desires not with desires,
but with nature;
governing nature not with nature,
but with virtue;
governing virtue not with virtue,
but with Dào.
Examining human nature,
its turbidity and lack of clarity
comes from external contamination.
Qiāng, Dī, Bó, Dí peoples,
babies born all sound alike,
but when grown,
even with repeated translations,
cannot understand each other's speech,
due to different teachings and customs.
If three-month-old babies
were moved to another country at birth,
they wouldn't know their original customs.
From this we see,
clothing and ritual customs
aren't inherent to human nature,
The nature of bamboo is to float,
but when cut into strips,
bound together and thrown into water, it sinks,
having lost its original form.
The nature of metal is to sink,
yet placed on a boat it floats,
for it finds support in circumstance.
Plain silk is inherently white,
dyed with black ink it turns dark;
fine silk is naturally yellow,
stained with cinnabar it becomes red.
Human nature is without evil,
but long immersed in customs, it changes.
Changed, one forgets one's roots,
merging with what seems innate.
Thus, the sun and moon desire brightness,
yet floating clouds obscure them;
river waters wish to be clear,
but sand and silt muddy them;
human nature seeks balance,
yet cravings and desires harm it.
Only the sage can discard external things and return to oneself.
One who is confused while sailing a boat,
not knowing east from west,
upon seeing the Big Dipper and Pole Star, awakens.
Nature is also humanity's Polaris.
Having self-awareness,
one does not lose the essence of things;
lacking self-awareness,
one acts in confusion and turmoil.
It is like traveling in Lǒngxī,
the more frantic one is, the deeper one sinks.
Confucius said to Yán Huí:
"I forget myself in serving you,
and you forget yourself in serving me.
Even so,
though you may forget me,
something unforgettable remains."
Confucius understood the fundamental.
Those who indulge desires and lose their nature,
their actions are never upright.
Governing the self with this leads to peril,
governing a state with this brings chaos,
leading an army with this results in defeat.
Therefore, those who do not comprehend the Dào
cannot return to their nature.
Thus, the ancient sage kings,
able to attain it within themselves,
could enforce orders and prohibitions,
their names passed down to later ages,
their virtue spread across the four seas.
Hence, in all undertakings,
one must first calm the mind.
With spirit clear and mind tranquil,
things can then be rectified.
Like a seal pressed into clay,
it imparts straightness where it is straight,
and tilt where it is tilted.
Thus, when Yáo promoted Shùn,
he decided based on sight;
when Duke Huán selected Nìng Qī,
he judged by hearing alone.
To therefore abandon method and rely solely on ears and eyes,
chaos is certain to worsen.
That ears and eyes can make judgments
is due to reflecting one's innate nature;
if hearing is misled by slander or praise,
and eyes are dazzled by colors,
then desiring to rectify affairs
becomes difficult.
One bearing grief hears singing and weeps,
one carrying joy sees weeping and laughs.
Grief that brings joy,
laughter that brings sorrow—
it is what one carries that causes it.
Thus, emptiness is valued.
So, water agitated gives rise to waves,
qi disordered clouds the intellect.
Clouded intellect cannot govern,
wavy water cannot be level.
Therefore, the sage king holds to the One and does not lose it,
the nature of all things is fathomed,
the four barbarians and nine provinces submit.
The One is supremely precious,
unmatched under heaven.
The sage relies on what is unmatched,
thus the people's lives are secured.
Those practicing benevolence must discuss it through grief and joy,
those upholding righteousness must clarify it through giving and taking.
Human eyes cannot see beyond ten lǐ,
yet wanting to illuminate all people within the seas,
grief and joy are insufficient.
Without the wealth of the world at disposal,
yet wanting to provide for all the myriad people,
material benefits cannot suffice.
Moreover, joy, anger, grief, and pleasure
arise from stimulation and are spontaneous.
Thus, crying issues from the mouth,
tears flow from the eyes,
these are all pent-up inside and manifest outwardly.
Like water flowing downstream,
smoke rising upward—
who is there to push them?
Thus, forced weeping
may be pained but not sorrowful,
forced affection
may smile but not harmonize.
When emotion springs from within
and sound responds without,
thus Lí Fùjī's pot of meal
surpassed Duke Xiàn of Jìn's Chuíjí jade;
Zhào Xuānmèng's bundle of dried meat
was worthier than Zhì Bó's great bell.
Hence, lavish rites are insufficient to prove love,
but sincere heart can embrace the distant.
Thus, Gōngxī Huá in supporting his parents
was as if with friends;
Zēng Shēn in supporting his parents
was as if serving a stern ruler or fierce lord;
in their support, it was the same.
So, the Hú people notch bones,
the Yuè people cut arms,
the central states smear blood—
their methods differ,
but in trustworthiness, they are one.
The Sānmiáo tie hair atop the head,
the Qiāng people collar their necks,
the central states use caps and hairpins,
the Yuè people cut their hair short—
in their attire, it is the same.
Under Emperor Zhuānxū's law,
if a woman did not avoid men on the road,
she was exorcised at the crossroads.
In modern capitals,
men and women rub shoulders,
bumping in the streets—
in their customs, it is the same.
Thus, the rites of the four barbarians differ,
yet all honor their ruler and love their kin,
respect their elders;
the Xiǎnyǔn's customs are opposite,
yet all cherish their children and revere their superiors.
Birds fly in formation,
beasts dwell in groups—
who teaches them?
Thus, the state of Lǔ adopted the rites of the Ru,
practiced the methods of Confucius,
yet its territory shrunk and reputation fell,
unable to draw the near or attract the far.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè
cut his hair and tattooed his body,
without the attire of leather caps and inserted tablets,
or the demeanor of restraint and bows,
yet he defeated Fūchāi on Lake Wǔ,
faced south and hegemonized the world,
the twelve lords of Sìshàng
all led the Jiǔyí to pay homage.
States of the Hú, Mò, and Xiōngnú,
with loose bodies and unbound hair,
squatting arrogantly and speaking contrarily, yet their states do not perish—
it is not necessarily that they lack rites.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ in wide-sleeved robes,
had his orders obeyed across the world,
thus hegemonizing the lords.
Lord Wén of Jìn in coarse cloth,
a sheepskin coat,
leather sword belt,
established awe within the seas.
Must it be that only the rites of Zōu and Lǔ are called rites?
Therefore, entering a state, follow its customs;
entering a home, avoid its taboos;
do not intrude violating prohibitions,
do not advance opposing resistance—
even if going to barbarian, naked lands,
charting courses beyond the distant,
one will encounter no hardship.
Rites are the patterning of substance;
benevolence is the manifestation of kindness.
Thus, rites are crafted according to human feelings to regulate and adorn,
and benevolence bursts forth from sincerity to show compassion.
Rites should not exceed substance,
benevolence should not overflow kindness—
this is the way to govern an age.
The three-year mourning period
forces what people cannot endure,
using artifice to supplement emotion.
The three-month mourning attire
cuts off grief and strains innate nature.
The Ru and Mò do not trace the beginnings and ends of human feelings,
but insist on implementing contrary regulations.
The five mourning garments.
Grief is held within the emotions,
burial corresponds to the means of support,
not forcing people to do what they cannot,
not preventing people from what they cannot cease,
measures not losing appropriateness,
slander and praise have no cause to arise.
In ancient times, it was not that they did not know the elaborate rituals of ascending and descending, circling and turning,
or the postures of "Cǎi Qí" and "Sì Xià",
but they considered them time-consuming and troubling to the people with no practical use,
thus establishing rituals sufficient only to assist reality and convey meaning.
In ancient times, it was not that they could not display bells and drums, flourish pipes and flutes, brandish shields and axes, wave feather banners,
but they considered it a waste of resources and disruptive to governance,
thus establishing music sufficient only to harmonize joy and express intent,
without excess in sound for pleasure.
It was not that they could not exhaust the state and burden the people,
empty treasuries and deplete wealth,
adorn with pearls and scale-like decorations,
bind with silk ribbons and knots,
in pursuit of lavish funerals,
but they considered it impoverishing the people and ruining livelihoods, with no benefit to dry bones and decaying flesh,
thus burial was sufficient only for gathering and concealing the remains.
In the past, when Shùn was buried at Cāngwú,
the market did not change its shops;
when Yǔ was buried at Kuàijī Mountain,
farmers did not alter their fields;
this shows understanding of the distinction between life and death,
and mastery of the appropriateness of extravagance and frugality.
A disordered state is not so,
words and actions contradict each other,
inner feelings and outer appearances oppose,
rituals become overly intricate,
music becomes excessively chaotic,
honoring the dead harms the living,
prolonged mourning invites hypocrisy,
thus customs become corrupt in the world,
and slander and praise sprout in the court,
which is why the sage abolishes and does not use them.
Righteousness is acting appropriately according to principle,
ritual is embodying emotions and establishing form.
(Ritual is
embodiment).
In the past, the Yǒuhù clan perished for righteousness,
knowing righteousness but not appropriateness;
Lǔ practiced ritual but was weakened,
knowing ritual but not embodiment.
The rituals of the Yǒuyú clan,
their altar used earth,
worshipped the central eaves,
buried in formed fields,
their music was "Xián Chí", "Chéng Yún", "Jiǔ Sháo",
their attire favored yellow.
The rituals of the Xiàhòu clan, their altar used pine,
worshipped the household,
buried with wall screens and feather fans,
their music was "Xià Yuè", "Jiǔ Chéng", "Liù Yì", "Liù Liè", "Liù Yīng",
their attire favored blue.
The rituals of the Yīn people,
their altar used stone,
worshipped the door,
buried with planted pines,
their music was "Dà Hù", "Chén Lù",
their attire favored white.
The rituals of the Zhōu people,
their altar used chestnut,
worshipped the stove,
buried with planted cypress,
their music was "Dà Wǔ", "Sān Xiàng", "Jí Xià",
their attire favored red.
Rituals and music differed,
attire and systems contrasted,
yet all maintained the affections between close and distant, the order between superior and inferior.
Now, holding to one ruler's legal codes,
to criticize the customs of transmitted eras,
is like gluing the pegs to tune a se.
Thus, the enlightened ruler establishes ritual and righteousness as clothing,
divides conduct and restraint as a belt.
Clothing should cover the form,
follow the classics,
allow flexibility,
comfort the body,
suit movement,
not strive for bizarre beauty,
or sharp tailoring.
The belt should fasten ties and gather the lapel,
bind securely and connect firmly,
not rush to create patterned, sparse, or short shoes.
Thus, establishing ritual and righteousness,
practicing utmost virtue,
without being constrained by Ruists or Mohists.
What is called clarity,
is not about seeing others,
but seeing oneself.
What is called acuity,
is not about hearing others,
but hearing oneself.
What is called penetration,
is not about knowing others,
but knowing oneself.
Therefore, the body is where the Dào resides,
if the body is virtuous, the Dào is attained.
With the attainment of the Dào,
in sight, one is clear;
in hearing, one is acute;
in speech, one is fair;
in action, one is followed.
Thus, when the sage manages and regulates things,
it is like a craftsman carving and fitting tenons,
or a butcher cutting and separating,
skillfully achieving appropriateness without breakage,
while clumsy workers do not,
large parts jam and won't enter,
small parts are loose and incomplete,
agitated in mind,
awkward in hand, and increasingly unsightly.
When the sage carves and shapes things,
he splits and divides them,
separates and disperses them;
after excess and loss,
he restores them to unity;
once the root is exposed,
he returns it to the gate;
after carving and polishing,
he reverts to simplicity.
Combined, it becomes the Dào and Dé;
separated, it becomes models and standards.
Its turning enters the mysterious and obscure,
its scattering responds to the formless.
How can ritual, righteousness, restraint, and conduct
exhaust the root of ultimate order?
Those in the world who understand affairs
often deviate from the root of the Dào and Dé,
saying
ritual and righteousness are sufficient to govern the world,
this cannot be discussed as method.
What is called ritual and righteousness
are the legal codes and customs of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
the traces of one era.
Like straw dogs and clay dragons when first made,
adorned with blue and yellow,
wrapped in fine embroidery,
bound with red silk,
the priest in solemn attire,
the officials in formal caps
escort them.
After they are used,
they are just earth and grass cuttings,
who then values them!
Thus, in Shùn's time,
the Yǒumiáo did not submit,
so Shùn improved governance and ceased warfare,
holding shield and axe to dance.
In Yǔ's time,
the world had great floods,
Yǔ ordered the people to gather soil and pile firewood,
choosing hills to dwell on.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he carried the ancestral tablet and marched,
the realm was unsettled,
hence the three-year mourning.
Yǔ had the disaster of vast floods,
the tasks of dams and ponds,
so burial occurred by evening after morning death.
These are how sages responded to the times and adapted to change,
observing circumstances and applying appropriateness.
Now, those who know to practice with shield and axe laugh at hoe and spade,
who know the three-year
and criticize the one-day [mourning],
this is like approving ox and disapproving horse,
or using zheng to laugh at yu.
To respond to change thus,
is no different from playing one string to accompany "Jí Xià".
To use the changes of one era
to match transformation and respond to the times,
is like wearing linen in winter and fur in summer.
One sight cannot suit a hundred shots,
one garment cannot last the year.
The sight must correspond to elevation,
the garment must suit cold and heat.
Thus, as eras differ, affairs change;
as times shift, customs alter.
Therefore, the sage assesses the era to establish laws,
acts according to the time.
The ancient kings,
fēnged at Tài Shān,
shàned at Liángfù,
over seventy sages,
their laws and measures differed,
not intending to oppose,
but because times and worlds varied.
Thus, do not emulate the laws they established,
but emulate how they established laws.
How they established laws
is to move with transformation.
Those who can move with transformation hold the utmost nobility therein.
Thus, the song of Hú Liáng
can be followed,
but the means by which he sang
cannot be replicated;
the laws of the sages
can be observed,
but the reasons for their legislation
cannot be traced;
the words of debaters can be heard,
but the intent behind their words cannot be shaped.
The Chúnjūn sword may be cherished,
but the skill of Ōuyě cannot be prized.
Now, Wáng Qiáo and Chìsòngzǐ,
by breathing and exhaling,
expelling the old and taking in the new,
shedding form and abandoning intellect,
embracing simplicity and returning to truth,
roam in the profound and subtle,
ascending to connect with the cloudy heavens.
Now, to learn their way,
without grasping their nurturing of vital energy and dwelling in spirit,
and merely imitating their every exhale and inhale,
their occasional bending and stretching,
it is clear they cannot ride the clouds and ascend.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings,
held the world lightly,
minimized all things,
equated life and death,
unified transformations,
embraced the heart of great sages,
to reflect the nature of all things,
above, befriending the divine spirits,
below, acting in harmony with creation.
Now, to learn their way,
without attaining their clarity and sagely insight,
and merely adhering to their legal codes and decrees,
it is clear they cannot bring about order.
Hence it is said:
"Obtaining ten sharp swords,
is not as good as gaining Ōuyě's skill;
obtaining a hundred swift horses,
is not as good as acquiring Bólè's method."
The utmost simplicity has no form,
the most subtle Way has no measure,
thus heaven's roundness does not conform to compasses,
earth's squareness does not fit squares.
From past to present is called time,
the four directions and up-down are called space,
the Way lies within them, yet none know its location.
Thus, those whose sight does not reach far,
cannot be spoken to of greatness;
those whose wisdom is not broad,
cannot be discussed with about the ultimate.
In the past, Féng Yí attained the Way,
and dived into great rivers;
Qīnfù attained the Way,
and dwelled on Kūnlún.
Biǎn Què used it to heal illnesses,
Zào Fǔ to handle horses,
Yì to shoot,
Chuí to carve,
their actions differed,
but the Way they followed was one.
Those endowed with the Way to comprehend things,
have no reason to oppose each other.
Like irrigating fields from the same pond,
they receive water equally.
Now, butchering an ox and cooking its meat,
some use sour,
some use sweet,
simmering, frying, roasting, grilling,
harmonizing in myriad ways,
yet the source is one ox's body.
Felling pián, nán, yùzhāng trees and splitting them,
some become coffins,
some become pillars or beams,
cutting, breaking, shaping,
used in myriad ways,
yet all from one tree's simplicity.
Thus, the words of the hundred schools,
their points and presentations oppose,
but their alignment with the Way is one.
Like the gathering of silk, bamboo, metal, and stone instruments, the music is the same,
though the melodies differ by family
without losing the essence.
Bólè, Hán Fēng, Qín Yá, Guǎn Qīng,
each judged differently,
but their understanding of horses was one.
Thus, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
their legal codes varied in method,
but their winning of the people's hearts was equal.
Thus, Tāng entered Xià and used their laws,
King Wǔ entered Yīn and practiced their rites,
what caused Jié and Zhòu's downfall,
was what enabled Tāng and Wǔ to bring order.
Thus, with chisels, knives, saws laid out,
without a skilled craftsman, wood cannot be shaped;
with furnace, bellows, pipes set up,
without a clever smith, metal cannot be worked.
Butcher Tǎn once dismembered nine oxen in a morning,
and his blade could still shave hair;
Cook Dīng used his knife for nineteen years,
and its edge was as if newly ground.
Why?
He moved within the spaces between.
As for compasses, squares, hooks, and lines,
these are tools of skill,
not the means to skill itself.
Thus, a se without strings,
even Master Wén could not make music;
with only strings, it cannot evoke sorrow.
Thus, strings are the means to sorrow,
not the cause of sorrow.
As for craftsmen creating
interlinked mechanisms, moving parts,
hidden closures, intricate fittings,
entering into the profound subtlety,
the peak of spiritual harmony,
moving between mind and hand,
with no boundary to things,
a father cannot teach this to his son.
A blind musician's intuitive sensing of things,
expressing spirit through dance,
manifesting in the strings,
a brother cannot convey to his brother.
Now, what makes level is the water level,
what makes straight is the plumb line.
But what can achieve level and straight
without relying on these tools,
this is an unshared technique.
Thus, strike the gōng note and gōng responds,
pluck the jué note and jué vibrates,
this is the resonance of the same tone.
When it has no match among the five tones,
yet all twenty-five strings respond,
this is the untransmitted Way.
Thus, emptiness and stillness
are the masters of form;
and silence and solitude
are the lords of sound.
In the world, right and wrong are not fixed,
each age affirms its own right
and denies its own wrong,
what is called right and what is called wrong differ,
all consider themselves right and others wrong.
From this perspective,
what agrees with oneself,
may not necessarily be right;
what opposes one's heart,
may not necessarily be wrong.
Thus, those seeking right,
are not seeking truth,
but what agrees with themselves;
those rejecting wrong,
are not opposing falsehood,
but removing what opposes their heart.
What opposes me,
may not disagree with others;
what agrees with me,
may not be unquestioned by custom.
The ultimate right has no wrong,
the ultimate wrong has no right,
this is true right and wrong.
If something is right here and wrong there,
wrong here and right there,
this is called one right and one wrong.
This one right and wrong,
is a corner's perspective;
that one right and wrong,
is the universe's view.
Now, if I wish to choose right to abide by,
and choose wrong to discard,
I do not know the world's so-called right and wrong,
which is truly right or wrong.
Lǎozi said:
"Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish."
The lenient say
do not stir it often,
the strict say
just ensure the salt and sour are right.
Jìn Pínggōng spoke inappropriately,
Shī Kuáng raised his qín and struck him,
causing him to stumble over his robe against the palace wall.
Attendants wanted to repair it,
but Pínggōng said:
"Leave it!
Let this remind me of my fault."
Confucius heard of it and said:
"Pínggōng was not unfeeling of his body,
but wished to encourage remonstrance."
Hánzǐ heard of it and said:
"Ministers acting disrespectfully and not punished,
this is indulging error.
No wonder, Pínggōng did not achieve hegemony!"
Thus, a guest introduced someone to Mìzǐ.
When the guest left,
Mìzǐ said:
"The person you introduced has three faults:
he looked at me and smiled—that is frivolity;
he spoke without mentioning his teacher—that is rebellion;
he spoke intimately despite our shallow acquaintance—that is disorder."
The guest replied:
"Smiling upon seeing you is openness;
speaking without mentioning one's teacher demonstrates adaptability;
speaking intimately despite shallow acquaintance shows loyalty."
Thus, the guest's demeanor
remained the same,
yet some considered him a noble person,
others a petty person—
this depends on the viewer's perspective.
Hence, when interests align,
loyal words deepen closeness;
when estranged,
even apt advice is met with suspicion.
A birth mother treating her son's head sore
until blood flows to his ears
is seen as utmost love;
if a stepmother did this,
onlookers would deem it jealousy.
The act is identical,
but the observer's standpoint differs.
From a city wall, oxen appear as sheep,
sheep as pigs—
due to the elevated position.
Gazing into a pan of water shows a round reflection,
into a cup, an oval one.
The face's shape remains unchanged,
yet it appears round or oval—
due to the vessel used for reflection.
Now, though I seek to rectify myself and interact with others,
how can I know how the world views me?
If I change and compete with the world,
it's like fleeing rain—
nowhere avoids getting drenched.
Constantly striving for emptiness
prevents true emptiness;
but not forcing emptiness yet naturally being empty—
this is the aspiration that achieves all.
Thus, one who comprehends the Dào is like a cart axle:
it does not move itself,
yet with the hub, it travels千里,
revolving from an endless source.
One ignorant of the Dào is like a lost person:
told directions east, west, south, north,
they seem clear where they stand,
but one turn astray,
and suddenly they're lost again.
Thus, they remain subordinates forever,
like a swan in the wind, never settled for a moment.
Therefore, the sage embodies the Dào and returns to nature,
unchanging to await change,
thus nearing avoidance of trouble.
In a well-governed era, offices are easy to maintain,
tasks easy to perform,
rituals easy to practice,
duties easy to fulfill.
Hence, people do not hold multiple posts,
officials do not handle diverse affairs;
scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants
are distinct by region and state.
Thus, farmers discuss strength with farmers,
scholars discuss conduct with scholars,
artisans discuss skill with artisans,
merchants discuss numbers with merchants.
So scholars have no neglected actions,
farmers no wasted efforts,
artisans no harsh tasks,
merchants no lost goods;
each content in their nature,
not interfering with others.
Thus, when Yīyǐn initiated construction,
he had the long-legged tread plows,
the strong-backed carry soil,
the one-eyed check levels,
the hunchbacked apply plaster—
each suited to their role,
and human nature was harmonized.
The Hú people are adept with horses,
the Yuè people with boats;
different forms and kinds,
changing tasks causes confusion,
losing position brings low status,
gaining influence brings honor.
The sage unites and employs them,
the principle is one.
Foresight and distant vision,
seeing clearly for千里,
are heights of human talent,
yet a well-governed era does not demand this from the people.
Vast knowledge and strong memory,
eloquent and quick-witted speech,
are beauties of human wisdom,
yet an enlightened ruler does not seek this from subordinates.
Defying the world and轻视 objects, untainted by custom,
are scholars' lofty actions,
yet a well-governed era does not use this to transform the people.
Divine mechanisms and hidden closures,
carving without trace,
are wonders of human skill,
yet a well-governed era does not make this the people's trade.
Thus, Chánghóng and Shīkuàng,
foreseeing fortune and disaster,
their words never failing,
cannot share offices with the masses;
Gōngsūn Lóng, with his sharp debates and opposing arguments,
distinguishing similarity and difference,
separating hardness and whiteness,
cannot walk the same path as the masses;
Běirén Wúzé, who criticized Shùn and threw himself into the Qīnglíng Abyss,
cannot be a model for the world;
Lǔbān and Mòzǐ,
who made wooden kites that flew
for three days without landing,
cannot be employed as ordinary artisans.
Thus, what is too high to reach
cannot be the people's standard;
conduct too hard to match
cannot be the state's custom.
Holding weights without missing a zhū or liǎng,
the sage does not use such people,
but relies on scales;
judging heights without error by a cùn or shì,
the enlightened ruler does not appoint such,
but seeks the water level.
Why?
Because human talent cannot be exclusively relied upon,
but measures can be passed down through generations.
Thus, a well-governed state can be maintained even with simplicity,
and military strategies can be applied with flexibility.
If one waits for Yǎoniǎo and Fēitù to draw a chariot,
then no one in the world would ride;
if one waits for Xīshī and Luòmù to marry,
then one would remain unmarried for life.
Yet without awaiting ancient heroes, people are self-sufficient—
by utilizing what they already have.
A Qíjì can travel千里
in one day;
a nag horse with ten rests
reaches it in ten days.
From this we see,
human talent cannot be solely relied upon,
but the Dào and methods can be universally applied.
The laws of a chaotic era
set high standards and punish those who fall short,
impose heavy burdens and penalize those who cannot bear them,
create dangers and execute those who dare not face them.
When people are oppressed by these three demands,
they feign wisdom and deceive superiors,
commit evils and seek escape.
Thus, even with steep laws and harsh punishments,
their deceit cannot be stopped.
Why?
Because strength is insufficient.
Hence the proverb says:
"Birds peck when cornered,
beasts charge when desperate,
people deceive when impoverished."
This refers to this.
Discussions on Dào and Dé
are like the sun and moon:
south or north of the river,
their essence cannot be altered;
galloping for千里,
their position cannot be changed.
Customs of choice and avoidance
are like dwelling in a house:
the east family calls it west,
the west family calls it east;
even with Gāoyáo judging,
he could not fix its position.
Thus, with identical choices,
praise or blame depends on custom;
with equal conduct,
failure or success depends on timing.
The accumulated good deeds of Tāng and Wǔ
can be matched;
their encounter with the eras of Jié and Zhòu
was bestowed by heaven.
Now, having the intent of Tāng and Wǔ
but lacking the era of Jié and Zhòu,
and wanting to achieve霸主之业,
is nearly impossible.
In the past, King Wǔ wielded spear and axe to conquer Yīn,
then held tablet and staff to preside over court.
After King Wǔ's death,
the people of Yīn rebelled,
so the Duke of Zhōu ascended the eastern palace,
stepped upon the mounting stone,
assumed the Son of Heaven's position,
stood with his back to the screen to receive feudal lords,
exiled his uncle Cài,
executed his uncle Guǎn,
subdued Yīn and ended Shāng,
sacrificed to King Wén in the Bright Hall,
and after seven years returned governance to King Chéng.
King Wǔ emphasized military might before civil virtue,
not because he intended change,
but to respond to the times.
The Duke of Zhōu exiled one brother and executed another,
not because he was unkind,
but to quell disorder.
Thus when affairs accord with the age, success is achieved;
when efforts match the times, reputation is established.
Previously, Duke Huán of Qí assembled feudal lords with chariots,
then governed his state with executions;
Duke Wén of Jìn assembled feudal lords with armored chariots,
then governed his state with ritual and righteousness.
Duke Huán was gentle first and stern later,
Duke Wén stern first and gentle later,
yet their orders were obeyed throughout the realm,
and their authority over feudal lords was equal
because they understood changes in circumstances.
When Yán Hé of Lǔ was offered the prime ministership,
and gifts were sent to him first,
he breached a wall to escape,
becoming renowned throughout the land.
Had he encountered Shāng Yāng or Shēn Bùhài,
punishment would have extended to three clans,
let alone himself!
Many praise ancient people and exalt their conduct,
yet when contemporaries share similar qualities
they don't value them,
not because of inferior talent,
but because the times are unsuitable.
Thus six thoroughbreds or four swift steeds
to cross rivers
are less convenient than a hollow log
due to situational requirements.
Therefore those who achieve merit
simplify their actions and carefully consider timing.
Contemporary common people
consider success as worthy,
overcoming troubles as wise,
suffering misfortune as foolish,
and dying for principles as stupid,
but I believe each reaches their ultimate purpose.
Prince Bǐgān
was not unaware that feigning madness could save his life,
yet he preferred upright conduct and loyal death,
thus he didn't do otherwise.
Bóyí and Shūqí
were not incapable of accepting office
to achieve merit,
yet they preferred reclusion and extraordinary conduct,
thus they didn't pursue it.
Xǔ Yóu and Shànjuǎn
were not unable to pacify the world
and benefit people with virtue,
yet they felt ashamed to disturb harmony with material things,
thus they didn't accept.
Yù Ràng and Yāolí
were not unaware of enjoying family life
and living comfortably,
yet they preferred sincerity and commitment,
dying for their lords,
thus they didn't remain.
Viewing Bǐgān from Jīzǐ's perspective,
he seems foolish;
viewing Jīzǐ from Bǐgān's perspective,
he seems base;
viewing Bóyí from Guǎn and Yàn's perspective,
he seems stupid;
viewing Guǎn and Yàn from Bóyí's perspective,
they seem greedy.
Choices mutually criticize,
desires oppose each other,
yet each delights in their pursuits
—who shall arbitrate?
Master Zēng said:
"When boats are struck in water,
birds hear and soar high,
fish hear and hide deep."
Thus though pursuits differ,
all find what suits them.
When Huìzǐ passed Mèngzhū with hundred chariots,
Zhuāngzǐ saw him
and discarded his leftover fish.
Pelicans drink gallons yet remain unsatisfied,
while eels die from dew-like sips.
Zhì Bó possessed three Jìn territories yet remained unsatiated,
while Lín Lěi and Róng Qǐqī
wore ragged clothes yet felt content.
From this we see
that inclinations differ
—why mutually condemn?
Those who value life don't endanger themselves for gain,
those who establish integrity don't avoid difficulties,
the avaricious disregard safety for profit,
the fame-seeking won't take unjust gains.
Comparing these
is like ice and charcoal, hook and line
—when would they unite?
If sages mediate,
they encompass and embrace all
without taking sides.
Birds belong to nests,
foxes to dens.
Nest-builders
complete nests and perch there,
burrowers
finish dens and dwell there.
Choices and righteous acts
are humanity's nests and dens;
each enjoys their peace,
attains their goals,
thus becoming complete persons.
Therefore those who discuss the Way
unify and equalize all.
The way to govern a state:
rulers issue no harsh decrees,
officials no troublesome administration,
scholars no hypocritical conduct,
artisans no extravagant crafts.
Affairs are orderly and undisturbed,
implements complete and unadorned.
Chaotic ages differ:
actors compete in ostentation,
ritualists boast with hypocrisy,
carriages reach extreme ornamentation,
utensils hasten to elaborate carving.
Traders fight for rare goods as treasures,
scribes thrive on complexity as wisdom,
competing in sophistry,
protracting unresolved,
benefitting no governance.
Artisans craft curios
taking years to complete,
useless for practical purposes.
Thus Shénnóng's code stated:
"If strong men don't plow,
some will starve;
if women don't weave,
some will freeze."
So he plowed personally,
his wife wove herself,
leading the world by example.
Guiding the people,
he didn't value rare goods,
nor treasure useless objects.
Thus those who didn't plow vigorously
couldn't sustain life;
those who didn't weave diligently
couldn't cover their bodies;
surplus and deficiency
rested on each individual.
With ample food and clothing,
wickedness didn't arise,
peace prevailed
and the world was harmonious,
so even Confucius and Zēng Shēn
had no need to display goodness,
Mèng Bēn and Chéng Jīng
no occasion to demonstrate power.
Decadent age customs:
using clever deception,
adorning useless things,
valuing distant goods,
treasuring rare wealth,
neglecting life-sustaining tools.
They diluted the world's purity,
shattered its simplicity,
corralled horses and oxen as livestock.
Confusing the masses,
they called clear turbid,
scattering human nature into chaos.
Integrity dissolved,
people lost true disposition.
Then appeared kingfisher feathers, rhinoceros horns, ivory,
embroidered patterns to dazzle eyes;
fine meats, millets,
fragrant wines
to glut mouths;
bells, drums, pipes, flutes,
strings, bamboos, metals, stones
to debauch ears;
choices, conduct,
etiquette, slander
to confuse minds.
Thus, the common people were in turmoil and chaos,
chasing profit day and night,
entangled in trivialities and superficialities,
where law and righteousness contradicted each other,
and conduct and benefit were at odds.
Even with ten Guǎn Zhòngs,
it would be impossible to govern.
Moreover, the wealthy ride in carriages and wear embroidered silk,
their horses adorned with tassels and ivory,
with curtains, cushions, and mats,
decorated with intricate patterns and silk ribbons,
blending blue and yellow hues,
so splendid it defies description;
while the poor in summer wear coarse cloth and rope belts,
munching beans and drinking water to fill their bellies,
merely enduring the summer heat,
and in winter, don tattered sheepskin,
their short robes failing to cover their bodies,
huddling by the stove for warmth;
thus, though they are all registered commoners,
the gap between rich and poor is
like that between a ruler and a slave,
beyond comparison.
Those who employ cunning skills and deceitful practices
can satisfy themselves for a lifetime;
while those who uphold integrity and follow principles,
refusing unjust gains,
cannot escape the plight of hunger and cold;
to expect people to abandon frivolity and return to fundamentals
is like digging a spring and then blocking its flow.
Furthermore, elaborate carvings and engravings
harm agricultural work;
fine embroidery and silk weaving
injure women's labor.
When farming is neglected,
and women's work is impaired,
it becomes the root of hunger and the source of cold.
When hunger and cold strike together,
those who can avoid breaking laws and facing punishment
are unheard of in all history.
Thus, benevolence or baseness depends on the times
not on conduct,
benefit or harm lies in fate
not in wisdom.
In a defeated army,
even the brave flee,
and commanders cannot stop them;
in a victorious formation,
the timid fight to the death,
too frightened to run.
So when a river bursts its banks, a whole village's
fathers, sons, and brothers
abandon each other and flee,
scrambling up hills and slopes,
climbing high mounds,
the swift-footed leading,
unable to care for one another;
in a peaceful and content world,
seeing a neighbor drown,
one still feels compassion,
how much more for one's own kin!
Thus, when secure, one's kindness extends to neighbors,
and ambitions diminish;
when in danger, one forgets even relatives,
and benevolence cannot save them.
A swimmer cannot rescue the drowning,
for his hands and feet are preoccupied;
a burned person cannot put out a fire,
for his body is in pain.
When people have surplus, they yield;
when lacking, they contend.
Yielding gives rise to ritual and righteousness,
contention sparks violence and chaos.
Knocking on a door for water or fire,
none will refuse,
for these are abundant;
in the forest, no one sells firewood,
on the lake, no one vends fish,
for these are plentiful.
Thus, with abundant goods, desires lessen,
and when needs are met, strife ceases.
In the time of the Qín emperor,
some people salted their children,
due to insufficient benefit;
under the Liú family's rule,
lonely men took in orphans,
for wealth was ample.
So in orderly times, petty men uphold integrity,
and profit cannot tempt them;
in chaotic times, noble men turn corrupt,
and laws cannot restrain them.
Tài Qīng asked Wú Qióng:
"Do you know the Dào?"
Wú Qióng said:
"I do not know."
He then asked Wú Wéi:
"Do you know the Dào?"
Wú Wéi said:
"I know the Dào."
Tài Qīng said:
"Does your knowing the Dào have specifics?"
Wú Wéi said:
"I know the Dào has specifics."
Tài Qīng said:
"What are these specifics?"
Wú Wéi said:
"I know the Dào can make weak,
can make strong;
can make soft,
can make hard;
can make dark,
can make light;
can make obscure,
can make clear;
can envelop heaven and earth,
can respond to the limitless.
This is how I know the specifics of the Dào."
Tài Qīng then asked Wú Shǐ:
"Earlier,
I asked Wú Qióng about the Dào,
Wú Qióng said:
'I do not know.'
I asked Wú Wéi,
Wú Wéi said:
'I know the Dào.'
I said:
'Your knowing the Dào,
does it have specifics?'
Wú Wéi said:
'I know the Dào has specifics.'
I said:
'What are these specifics?'
Wú Wéi said:
'I know the Dào can make weak,
can make strong;
can make soft,
can make hard;
can make dark,
can make light;
can make obscure,
can make clear;
can envelop heaven and earth,
can respond to the limitless.
This is how I know the specifics of the Dào.'
If so,
then between Wú Wéi's knowing and Wú Qióng's not knowing,
which is right and which is wrong?"
Wú Shǐ said:
"Not knowing is profound,
while knowing is shallow.
Not knowing is internal,
while knowing is external.
Not knowing is refined,
while knowing is crude."
Tài Qīng looked up to the sky and sighed:
"Then is not knowing actually knowing?
And knowing actually not knowing?
Who understands that knowing is not knowing?
And not knowing is knowing?"
Wú Shǐ said:
"The Dào cannot be heard,
for what is heard is not it.
The Dào cannot be seen,
for what is seen is not it.
The Dào cannot be spoken,
for what is spoken is not it.
Who understands that which gives form to formless forms!"
Thus, Lǎo Zǐ said:
"When all under heaven know beauty as beauty,
there is already ugliness."
Hence,
"those who know do not speak,
those who speak do not know"
indeed.
Báigōng asked Confucius, saying:
"Can one engage in subtle discourse with others?"
Confucius did not respond.
Báigōng said:
"If one throws a stone into water,
what would happen?"
He replied:
"The skilled divers of Wú and Yuè could retrieve it."
Báigōng said:
"If one pours water into water,
what would happen?"
Confucius said:
"When the waters of Zī and Shéng merge,
Yìyá could taste and distinguish them."
Báigōng said:
"Then, after all, one cannot engage in subtle discourse with others?"
Confucius said:
"How can you say that!
Only with those who understand what words mean!
Those who understand what words mean
do not use words to speak.
Those struggling for fish get wet,
those chasing beasts run fast -
not because they enjoy it.
Thus, the ultimate discourse discards words,
the ultimate action is non-action.
What the shallow-minded contend over
is trivial indeed!"
Báigōng failed to grasp this,
and thus died in the bath chamber.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Words should have their ancestor,
affairs should have their lord.
It is precisely because of ignorance
that I am not understood."
This refers to Báigōng.
When Huìzǐ drafted state laws for King Huì,
and presented them to the people upon completion,
the people all praised them.
Submitted to King Huì,
the king was greatly pleased,
and showed them to Zhái Jiān,
who said:
"Excellent!"
King Huì said:
"Excellent,
can they be implemented?"
Zhái Jiān said:
"They cannot."
King Huì said:
"Excellent yet unimplementable,
why is that?"
Zhái Jiān replied:
"Consider those lifting heavy logs -
the front calls 'yéhǔ',
the rear responds likewise,
these are songs encouraging strength in heavy lifting.
Are there no passionate melodies of Zhèng and Wèi?
Yet they are not used
because they are not as suitable.
Governing a state lies in ritual,
not in eloquent debate."
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"The more laws are promulgated,
the more thieves and robbers abound."
This refers to that.
Tián Pián expounded the Way and its methods to the King of Qí,
who responded:
"What I possess
is the state of Qí.
The Way and its methods can hardly eliminate troubles -
I wish to hear about governing Qí."
Tián Pián replied:
"My words concern no governance,
yet can serve as governance.
This is like a forest having no timber,
yet can yield timber.
I hope Your Majesty will consider what I mean,
and draw from it for governing Qí.
Though I cannot eliminate its troubles myself,
between heaven and earth,
within the six directions,
all can be molded and transformed.
The governance of Qí
is hardly worth asking about!
This is what Lǎodān called
'the form of the formless,
the image of the imageless'.
What Your Majesty asks about
is Qí,
what Tián Pián discusses
is timber.
Timber does not reach the forest,
the forest does not reach rain,
rain does not reach yīn and yáng,
yīn and yáng do not reach harmony,
harmony does not reach the Way."
When Báigōng Shèng obtained the state of Jīng,
he could not share its treasury with others.
After seven days,
Shí Qǐ entered and said:
"Gained through unrighteousness,
yet unable to distribute it,
disaster is sure to come.
If you cannot give to others,
better burn it,
lest others harm us for it."
Báigōng would not listen.
After nine days,
Shègōng entered,
distributed the goods from the great treasury to the masses,
issued weapons from the high armory to the people,
then attacked him accordingly,
capturing Báigōng in nineteen days.
To desire possession of
a state not rightfully one's own
may be called ultimate greed.
Unable to benefit others,
and having no way to preserve oneself,
may be called ultimate folly.
Báigōng's stinginess
differs little from an owl's love for its young.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"To hold and fill it
is not as good as stopping in time.
To hone and sharpen it
cannot long be maintained."
When Zhào Jiǎnzǐ designated Xiāngzǐ as his successor,
Dǒng Yùyú said:
"Wúxù is lowly,
why make him successor
now?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"This man's character
enables him to endure shame for the state."
Another day,
when Zhì Bó drank with Xiāngzǐ and struck his head,
the ministers requested to kill him,
but Xiāngzǐ said:
"When our former lord established me,
he said I could endure shame for the state -
did he say I could stab others?"
After ten months,
when Zhì Bó besieged Xiāngzǐ at Jìnyáng,
Xiāngzǐ deployed troops and attacked him,
crushing Zhì Bó,
and made his skull into a drinking vessel.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Knowing the masculine,
yet keeping to the feminine,
one becomes a ravine for the world."
When Nièquē asked Bèiyī about the Way,
Bèiyī said:
"Straighten your form,
unify your vision,
and heavenly harmony will arrive.
Gather your knowledge,
rectify your measure,
and spirit will come to dwell.
Virtue will adorn you,
and the Way will reside with you.
Be ignorant like a newborn calf,
seeking no causes."
Before he finished speaking,
Nièquē fell asleep,
then entered trance.
Bèiyī walked away singing:
"Form like dry bones,
heart like dead ashes.
Truly knowing reality,
not clinging to causes.
Vast and boundless,
no mind to consult with.
What kind of man is this!"
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Understanding everything clearly,
can you be without knowledge!"
Lord Xiāng of Zhào launched an attack against the Dí and triumphed,
capturing Zuǒrén
and Zhōngrén.
When the messenger came to report the victory,
Lord Xiāng was about to eat but wore a worried expression.
His attendants said:
"In one morning, two cities have fallen,
which is a reason for joy.
Now you have a worried look,
why is that?"
Lord Xiāng replied:
"The greatness of the Jiāng
and Hé rivers
lasts no more than three days.
Fierce winds and torrential rains
do not last even until midday.
Now the virtue and conduct of the Zhào clan have not accumulated sufficiently,
yet in one morning two cities have fallen.
Will our downfall not soon reach us?"
Confucius heard of this and said:
"The Zhào clan will surely prosper!"
For worry
is the means to prosperity,
while joy
is the means to downfall.
Victory is not what is difficult;
maintaining it
is what is difficult.
Worthy rulers use this to maintain victory,
so their blessings extend to later generations.
Qí, Chǔ,
Wú, and Yuè all once achieved victory,
yet ultimately met their downfall,
because they did not understand how to maintain victory.
Only a ruler who possesses the Dào can maintain victory.
Confucius had the strength to lift the bar of a city gate,
yet he refused to be known for his physical power.
Mòzǐ, in defense and attack,
made Gōngshū Bān yield,
yet he refused to be known for his military prowess.
Those who are skilled at maintaining victory
use strength as if it were weakness.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"The Dào is empty,
yet in using it, it is never filled."
Huì Mèng visited King Kāng of Sòng,
and King Kāng, stamping his feet and clearing his throat,
said sharply:
"What I, the ruler, delight in
is courage and strength;
I do not delight in those who practice rén and yì.
What will you, my guest, teach me?"
Huì Mèng replied:
"I have a Dào here
that makes even the most courageous
unable to stab into one;
even the strongest
unable to strike a hit.
Does Your Majesty alone have no interest in this?"
The King of Sòng said:
"Excellent!
This is what I wish to hear."
Huì Mèng said:
"Being stabbed but not penetrated,
struck but not hit,
this is still a humiliation.
I have a Dào here
that makes even the courageous dare not stab,
even the strong dare not strike.
Not daring to stab,
not daring to strike,
does not mean they lack the intent.
I have a Dào here
that makes people fundamentally lack such intent.
Lacking the intent
still means they have no heart for love and benefit.
I have a Dào here
that makes all men and women under heaven joyfully possess a heart of love and benefit.
This surpasses courage and strength,
being the highest of the four levels.
Does Your Majesty alone have no interest in this?"
The King of Sòng said:
"This is what I desire to obtain."
Huì Mèng replied:
"It is embodied by Confucianism
and Mohism.
Confucius
and Mò Dí,
without land, became rulers;
without office, became leaders.
All men and women under heaven crane their necks and rise on tiptoe, wishing to bring them peace and benefit.
Now you, Great King,
are the lord of ten thousand chariots.
If you truly have such a will,
then all within the four borders will receive its benefits.
This would make you far more worthy than Confucius
and Mò Dí!"
The King of Sòng had no reply.
Huì Mèng left,
and the King of Sòng said to his attendants:
"How persuasive he was!
This guest has used his words to overcome me!"
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Courage in daring leads to death;
courage in not daring leads to life."
From this perspective,
great courage actually appears as not being courageous.
In the past, Yáo had nine assistants,
Shùn had seven,
and King Wǔ had five.
Yáo, Shùn,
and King Wǔ, with their nine,
seven, and five assistants,
could not handle a single task themselves,
yet they received success with folded hands,
skillfully riding on the resources of others.
Thus, if a man races with a fine horse, he cannot surpass the horse,
but if he rides in a carriage, the horse cannot surpass him.
In the north, there is a beast
named Jué,
with front legs like a mouse's and hind legs like a rabbit's.
When it scurries, it stumbles;
when it runs, it topples.
It often gathers sweet grass for the Qióngqióng Jùxū,
and when Jué is in danger or trouble,
the Qióngqióng Jùxū always carry it on their back and flee.
This is using what one is capable of
to rely on what one is not capable of.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"He who replaces the great carpenter in chopping
rarely avoids injuring his hand."
Bó Yí advised Lord Sì of Wèi on the art of kingship,
and Lord Sì responded to him, saying:
"What I possess
is a state of a thousand chariots,
and I wish to receive your teaching for it."
Bó Yí replied:
"If Wū Huò can lift a thousand jūn,
how much more just one jīn!"
Dù Hè advised Lord Zhāowén of Zhōu on how to bring peace to the world,
and Lord Zhāowén said to Dù Hè:
"I wish to learn how to secure Zhōu."
Dù Hè replied:
"If what I say cannot be done,
then it cannot secure Zhōu.
If what I say can be done,
then Zhōu will be secure on its own.
This is what is called achieving security without actively securing it."
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"The greatest cutting does not sever;
thus, striving for numerous parts loses the whole."
According to the law of the state of Lǔ,
if a person from Lǔ became a servant or concubine in another state,
anyone who could ransom them
would receive gold from the treasury.
Zǐ Gòng ransomed a person from Lǔ from another state,
but upon returning, he declined to accept the gold.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Cì (Zǐ Gòng) is mistaken in this!
When a sage undertakes an action,
it can transform customs and practices,
and his teachings of obedience can be passed to later generations;
it is not merely for personal conduct.
Now in Lǔ, the wealthy are few and the poor are many.
If one ransoms a person and accepts gold,
it is considered lacking integrity;
if one does not accept the gold,
then no one will ransom people again.
From now on,
people of Lǔ will no longer ransom others from other states."
Confucius can indeed be said to understand transformation.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Perceiving the small is called clarity."
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi asked Lǐ Kè:
"Why was it that Wú perished?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Because it repeatedly fought battles and repeatedly won."
Marquis Wǔ said:
"Repeatedly fighting and winning
is a blessing for a state.
Yet it perished solely because of this;
what is the reason?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Frequent warfare exhausts the people,
and constant victories make the ruler arrogant.
With an arrogant ruler employing exhausted people,
for a state not to perish
is rare indeed in the world.
Arrogance leads to recklessness,
recklessness leads to exhausting resources;
exhaustion breeds resentment,
resentment leads to extreme anxieties.
When both high and low reach their limits,
Wú's demise was actually late!
This is why Fūchāi took his own life at Gānsuì."
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"When merit is achieved and fame is secured,
withdraw from your position
—this is the Way of Heaven."
Nìng Yuè wanted to seek service with Duke Huán of Qí,
but being impoverished had no means to advance himself.
So he became a traveling merchant,
driving a freight cart
to trade in Qí,
and at dusk lodged outside the outer city gate.
Duke Huán was welcoming guests at the outskirts,
opened the city gates at night,
cleared the freight carts,
with torches burning brightly
and a large retinue following.
Nìng Yuè was feeding his ox beneath the cart,
saw Duke Huán and felt sorrow,
so he struck the ox's horn and urgently sang a merchant's song.
Duke Huán heard it,
tapped his attendant's hand and said:
"How extraordinary!
The singer is no ordinary man!"
He ordered him to be carried in a following carriage.
When Duke Huán returned,
his followers requested instructions,
and Duke Huán granted him robes and headgear before receiving him.
Nìng Yuè appeared,
and persuaded him about ruling the world.
Duke Huán was greatly pleased,
and was about to appoint him,
when his ministers contended:
"This visitor
is from Wèi.
Wèi is not far from Qí;
you should send someone to inquire about him.
If he is indeed worthy,
it wouldn't be too late to employ him then."
Duke Huán said:
"Not so.
To inquire
is to worry about his minor faults.
To forget a man's great merits because of his minor faults
is how rulers lose the talents of the world."
Whenever we listen, we must verify,
but having heard once, we need not question repeatedly,
for we have grasped the essence.
Moreover, men are inherently difficult to be perfect;
we should weigh and use their strengths, that is all."
In this appointment,
Duke Huán got it right.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Heaven is great,
Earth is great,
the Dào is great,
and the King is also great.
Within the realm there are four greats,
and the King occupies one of them."
This means he is able to encompass them.
Great King Dànfù dwelt in Bīn,
and the Dí people attacked him.
He served them with furs, silks, pearls and jade, but they wouldn't accept,
saying:
"What the Dí people seek
is land, not material goods."
Great King Dànfù said:
"To live alongside people's elder brothers and then kill their younger brothers,
to dwell with people's fathers and then kill their sons—
I cannot bear to do this.
All of you, strive to remain here!
To be my subjects
—how is it different from being subjects of the Dí people?
Moreover, I have heard it said:
'Do not use what sustains life to harm life itself.'"
Taking his staff, he left them,
and the people linked together and followed him,
eventually establishing a state below Qí Mountain.
Great King Dànfù may be said to have known how to preserve life.
Though wealthy and noble,
he did not injure his body for the sake of sustenance;
though poor and humble,
he did to burden his form for the sake of profit.
Now those who inherit their ancestors' ranks and emoluments
inevitably fear losing them gravely.
Yet life itself has existed for a long time,
and they lightly lose it—
is this not delusion?"
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"One who values his body as much as the world
can be entrusted with the world.
One who loves his body as much as the world
can be given the world."
Prince Móu of Zhōngshān said to Zhānzǐ:
"Though dwelling by the rivers and seas,
my heart remains beneath the Wèi palace gates.
What should I do about this?"
Zhānzǐ said:
"Value life.
Valuing life, you will轻视 profit."
Prince Móu of Zhōngshān said:
"Though I know this,
I still cannot master myself."
Zhānzǐ said:
"If you cannot master yourself, then follow it."
"Following it,
wouldn't the spirit resent it?"
"If you cannot master yourself yet forcibly refrain from following it,
this is called double injury.
Those doubly injured
will not live long!"
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Knowing harmony is called constancy,
knowing constancy is called clarity,
enhancing life is called auspicious,
the mind forcing the vital breath is called forceful."
Hence
"use its light,
but return to its clarity."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ asked Zhān Hé:
"How should one govern a state?"
Zhān Hé replied:
"Why do you understand governing the self,
but not understand governing the state?"
The King of Chǔ said:
"I have received the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain,
and wish to learn how to preserve them."
Zhān Hé replied:
"I have never heard of one who governs himself well yet the state falls into chaos,
nor have I heard of one who is disordered himself yet the state is well-governed.
Therefore the root lies in the self;
I dare not respond with branches."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Good."
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Cultivate it in your self,
and your virtue will be genuine."
Duke Huán was reading in his hall,
while Wheelwright Biǎn was carving a wheel below the hall.
Putting down his mallet and chisel, he asked Duke Huán:
"What kind of book is it
that Your Majesty is reading?"
Duke Huán replied:
"The books of the sages."
Wheelwright Biǎn said:
"Where are those men now?"
Duke Huán said:
"They have died."
Wheelwright Biǎn said:
"Then this is nothing but the dregs of the sages!"
Duke Huán flushed with anger and said furiously:
"When I read books,
how can a craftsman dare to criticize them!
If you have an explanation, you may live;
if not, you shall die."
Wheelwright Biǎn said:
"Indeed,
I have an explanation.
Let me illustrate with my wheel-carving:
If I go too fast,
it becomes bitter and doesn't fit;
if I go too slow,
it becomes sweet but isn't firm.
Neither too sweet nor too bitter,
responding to the hand,
satisfying to the heart -
this is how one achieves perfection.
I cannot teach this to my son,
nor can my son learn it from me.
Therefore, at sixty years of age,
I'm still growing old carving wheels.
Similarly, what the sages spoke of
died with them,
having exhausted their substance -
only their dregs remain!"
Hence Lǎozi said:
"The Way that can be spoken of
is not the constant Way;
the name that can be named
is not the constant name."
Formerly, Sīchéng Zǐhǎn served as minister of Sòng.
He told the ruler of Sòng:
"The safety or danger of the state,
the order or chaos among the people,
depend on how you exercise rewards and punishments.
Bestowing ranks and rewards
is what the people like -
you should handle that yourself.
Executions and punishments
are what the people resent -
let me take responsibility for those."
The ruler of Sòng said:
"Excellent!
I will take the credit for good deeds,
while you receive the resentment -
this way I know the feudal lords won't laugh at me."
So the ruler of Sòng handled rewards while Zǐhǎn administered punishments.
The people all knew that the power over life and death
rested solely with Zǐhǎn.
The ministers drew close to him,
the common people feared him.
Before a year had passed,
Zǐhǎn seized the ruler of Sòng and monopolized the government.
Hence Lǎozi said:
"Fish should not be taken out of the deep;
the sharp instruments of the state should not be shown to others."
Wáng Shòu was carrying books on his back when traveling,
and met Xú Féng in Zhōu.
Xú Féng said:
"Actions
should respond to circumstances;
changes arise according to the times,
so those who understand timing have no fixed ways.
Books
are where words come from,
words come from knowledge,
and those who know don't hoard books."
Thereupon Wáng Shòu burned his books and danced.
Hence Lǎozi said:
"Much talk often leads to exhaustion -
better to hold fast to the center."
Minister Zǐ Pèi invited King Zhuāng to drink,
and King Zhuāng agreed.
Zǐ Pèi prepared everything at Jīngtái,
but King Zhuāng didn't go.
The next day,
Zǐ Pèi stood barefoot with hands clasped,
facing north below the hall,
saying:
"Yesterday you promised to come,
but didn't actually go.
I wonder,
have I committed some offense?"
King Zhuāng said:
"I heard you prepared this at Qiángtái.
Qiángtái
looks south to Liàoshān,
faces north to Fānghuáng,
with the river on the left and Huái on the right -
its pleasures make one forget death.
Someone of my shallow virtue
cannot withstand such pleasures.
I feared I might linger and not return."
Hence Lǎozi said:
"Not seeing what is desirable
keeps the mind from confusion."
When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn was exiled,
he passed through Cáo,
where the ruler of Cáo treated him disrespectfully.
Xī Fùjī's wife told Xī Fùjī:
"Our lord has been discourteous to the prince of Jìn.
I observe his followers
are all worthy men.
If they assist him to return to Jìn,
he will surely attack Cáo.
Why not show him kindness first?"
So Xī Fùjī sent him a pot of food with a jade disc.
Chóng'ěr accepted the food but returned the jade.
When he returned to his state,
he raised an army and attacked Cáo,
conquering it,
but ordered the troops not to enter Xī Fùjī's neighborhood.
Hence Lǎozi said:
"To yield is to be preserved whole,
to be bent is to become straight."
When King Gōujiàn of Yuè fought with Wú and was defeated,
his state was destroyed and his life endangered,
trapped at Kuàijī.
With furious heart and bold courage,
his spirit surging like a fountain,
he selected and trained soldiers
who would rush into fire to extinguish it.
Yet he offered himself as a servant
and his wife as a concubine,
personally carrying weapons
and serving as the Wú king's vanguard,
until finally he captured him at Gānsuì.
Hence Lǎozi said:
"The soft overcoming the hard,
and the weak overcoming the strong -
there is no one in the world who doesn't know this,
but no one can put it into practice."
The King of Yuè personally practiced it,
thus he dominated the Central States.
When Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào died,
before he was buried,
Zhōngmóu defected to Qí.
Five days after the burial,
Xiāngzǐ raised troops to attack it.
Before the encirclement was complete,
a hundred feet of the city wall collapsed by itself.
Xiāngzǐ sounded the gongs to retreat.
His officers remonstrated:
"You were punishing Zhōngmóu's crime,
and the city wall collapsed by itself -
this is Heaven helping us.
Why withdraw?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"I heard from Shū Xiàng:
'The noble man doesn't take advantage of others' gains,
nor press others in danger.'
Let them repair their walls,
then we'll attack after they're repaired."
When Zhōngmóu heard of his righteousness,
they surrendered.
Hence Lǎozi said:
"It is precisely because he does not contend
that no one in the world can contend with him."
Duke Mù of Qín said to Bó Lè:
"You have grown old in years.
Is there anyone among your disciples who can be sent to seek out horses?"
He replied:
"For a fine horse,
one can judge by its shape, sinews, and bones.
But for a horse of unparalleled quality under heaven,
it seems to vanish, to be lost,
as if missing its very essence.
Such a horse,
raises no dust and leaves no tracks.
My sons
are all of mediocre talent;
they can be told how to recognize fine horses,
but cannot be instructed about the horse of unparalleled quality.
I have a companion who gathers firewood with me named Jiǔfāng Yīn,
and in judging horses,
he is not inferior to me.
I request you grant him an audience."
Duke Mù met with him,
and sent him to seek a horse.
After three months he returned,
reporting:
"I have found a horse.
It is at Shāqiū."
Duke Mù asked:
"What kind of horse is it?"
He replied:
"A yellow mare."
When someone was sent to fetch it,
it was a black stallion.
Duke Mù was displeased,
summoned Bó Lè and asked him:
"A failure indeed!
The one you sent to seek a horse
cannot even tell its color,
or distinguish male from female,
how could he possibly know anything about horses!"
Bó Lè sighed deeply and said:[40"Has it come to this!
This is precisely why he is countless times better than I.
What Yīn observes
is the heavenly mechanism.
He grasps the essence and forgets the coarseness,
dwells on the inner qualities and ignores the outer appearance,
he sees what he should see and overlooks what he need not see,
looks at what he should look at and disregards what he should not.
What he judges
is something more valuable than the horse itself."
When the horse arrived, it indeed turned out to be a thousand-lǐ steed.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"Great straightness seems bent,
great skill seems clumsy."
Wú Qǐ became the Prime Minister of Chǔ,
went to Wèi,
and asked Qū Yíjiù:
"The king, unaware of my lack of talent,
has made me Prime Minister.
I ask you, sir, to observe how I will govern."
Qūzǐ said:
"What do you intend to do?"
Wú Qǐ said:
"I plan to reduce the ranks of Chǔ's nobility and standardize their emoluments,
curtail the surplus and relieve the deficiencies,
sharpen the weapons and armor,
to contend for advantage in the world at the right time."
Qūzǐ said:
"I have heard it said
that those who were good at governing states in the past
did not alter their old ways,
nor change their constant practices.
Now you intend to reduce the ranks of Chǔ's nobility and standardize their emoluments,
curtail the surplus and relieve the deficiencies;
this is to alter their old ways,
and change their constant practices.
Those who implement this will not prosper!
I have heard it said:
'Anger
is contrary to virtue,
weapons
are instruments of calamity,
strife
is what people shun.'
Now you secretly plan contrary to virtue,
fondly use instruments of calamity,
and practice what people shun;
this is the height of perversity.
Moreover, when you used Lǔ's troops,
you should not have succeeded against Qí,
yet you did.
When you used Wèi's troops,
you should not have succeeded against Qín,
yet you did.
I have heard it said,
'Unless one brings calamity upon others,
one cannot create disaster.'
I have long been perplexed that our king has repeatedly defied the heavenly way,
violated human principles,
yet has encountered no disaster until now;
it must be awaiting you, sir."
Wú Qǐ, alarmed, said:
"Can it still be changed?"
Qūzǐ said:
"One who has formed the punishment
cannot change it.
You would do better to deepen your benevolence and sincerely practice it."
Lǎozǐ said:
"Blunt the sharpness,
untangle the knots,
soften the glare,
merge with the dust."
Jìn attacked Chǔ,
advancing ninety lǐ without halt.
The ministers requested to counterattack,
but King Zhuāng said:
"In the time of my predecessor,
Jìn did not attack Chǔ.
Now that Jìn attacks Chǔ during my reign,
this is my fault.
How can I let the ministers suffer disgrace?"
The ministers said:
"In the time of your former servants,
Jìn did not attack Chǔ.
Now that Jìn attacks Chǔ during our service,
this is our crime.
We beg the king to counterattack."
King Zhuāng bowed his head, tears soaking his lapel,
rose and bowed to his ministers.
When the people of Jìn heard of this, they said:
"The ruler and ministers vie to take the blame upon themselves,
and the ruler humbly defers to his ministers;
this state cannot be attacked."
That night they withdrew their army and returned.
Therefore Lǎozǐ said:
"He who can bear the disgrace of the state
is called the master of the altars of soil and grain."
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
Mars was in the constellation Heart,
and the duke became fearful.
He summoned Zǐ Wéi and inquired of him,
saying:
"Mars is in Heart;
what does this mean?"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"Mars
signifies Heaven's punishment;
Heart
is the celestial division corresponding to Sòng,
so the calamity will befall you, my lord.
Nevertheless,
it can be transferred to the prime minister."
The duke said:
"The prime minister
is the one appointed to govern the state;
to transfer death to him
would be inauspicious.
I beg to bear it myself."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the people."
The duke said:
"If the people die,
for whom would I be lord?
I would rather die alone!"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the harvest."
The duke said:
"The harvest
is the people's livelihood.
If the harvest fails,
the people will surely die.
For a ruler to seek to kill his people to preserve his own life—
who would then take me as their lord?
It seems my fate has reached its end;
say no more!"
Zǐ Wéi turned and stepped back,
facing north and bowing twice, saying:
"I dare to congratulate you, my lord!
Heaven, though lofty, hears what is below.
You have spoken three times as a true ruler should,
so Heaven will surely reward you three times.
This very night the star will shift three lunar mansions,
and you will gain twenty-one years of life."
The duke said:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"Because you have spoken three times as a true ruler should,
there will be three rewards.
The star must shift three mansions;
each mansion covers seven stars,
and each shift of a star equals one year—
three times seven makes twenty-one,
so I say you will gain twenty-one years of life.
I ask to remain at the foot of the steps to observe this.
If the star does not shift,
I beg to die for it."
The duke said:
"So be it."
That night,
the star indeed shifted three mansions.
Therefore, Lǎozi said:
"He who can bear the state's misfortunes
is called the king of the world."
Long ago,
when Gōngsūn Lǒng was in Zhào,
he said to his disciples:
"If a person has no ability,
I, Lǒng, cannot associate with them."
A visitor dressed in coarse cloth with a rope belt came to see him and said:
"I can shout."
Gōngsūn Lǒng turned to his disciples and asked:
"Has there ever been anyone among you who could shout?"
They replied:
"No one."
Gōngsūn Lǒng said:
"Enroll him as a disciple."
Several days later,
they went to persuade the King of Yān,
and when they reached the river,
the ferry was on the other side.
They had the skilled shouter call out,
and with one shout the ferry came.
Thus, when sages dwell in the world,
they do not reject those with skills.
Therefore, Lǎozi said:
"No person is abandoned,
no thing is abandoned;
this is called embracing the light."
Zǐ Fā attacked Cài
and overran it.
King Xuān welcomed him in the suburbs,
granting him a hundred qǐng of farmland and the title of Zhíguī.
Zǐ Fā declined and did not accept,
saying:
"Governing the state and establishing order,
so that the feudal lords come as guests—
this is due to the virtue of the ruler.
Issuing commands and giving orders,
so that the enemy flees before the armies engage—
this is due to the might of the general.
Deploying troops and defeating the enemy in battle—
this is due to the strength of the common people.
To take credit for the people's efforts and claim rank and emolument for it
is not the way of benevolence and righteousness."
Thus, he declined and did not accept.
Therefore, Lǎozi said:
"Achieve success but do not claim merit.
Precisely because one does not claim merit,
it never leaves."
When Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Yuán,
he set a deadline of three days with his ministers.
After three days, Yuán had not surrendered,
so Duke Wén ordered the troops to withdraw.
A military officer said:
"Yuán will probably surrender within a day or two."
The ruler said:
"I did not know that Yuán could not be taken in three days when I
set the deadline with my ministers.
To persist beyond the deadline without withdrawing,
gaining Yuán but losing trust—
I will not do that."
When the people of Yuán heard this, they said:
"With a ruler like this,
how can we not surrender?"
So they surrendered.
When the people of Wēn heard of it,
they also requested to surrender.
Therefore, Lǎozi said:
"Profound and dark,
yet within it there is essence.
This essence is very real;
within it there is trustworthiness."
Hence,
"Fine words can win respect,
fine deeds can elevate others."
Gōngyí Xiū served as prime minister of Lǔ
and was fond of fish.
When someone from the state offered him fish,
Gōngyí Xiū did not accept it.
His disciple asked him:
"You are fond of fish, Master,
yet you refuse it;
why is that?"
He replied:
"It is precisely because I am fond of fish
that I do not accept it.
If I accept fish and am dismissed from the premiership,
though fond of fish,
I would not be able to provide myself with fish.
If I do not accept fish and remain in the premiership,
then I can always provide myself with fish."
This shows understanding of both serving others and preserving oneself.
Therefore, Lǎozi said:
"He puts himself last, yet ends up in front;
he disregards his own life, yet his life is preserved.
Is it not because he is selfless
that he can accomplish his private ends?"
Another version says:
"He who knows contentment avoids disgrace."
The old man of Húqiū said to Sūnshū Áo:
"There are three things people resent;
do you know them?"
Sūnshū Áo said:
"What are they?"
He replied:
"Those with high rank—
scholars envy them;
those with great office—
the ruler dislikes them;
those with ample emolument—
resentment gathers around them."
Sūnshū Áo said:
"The higher my rank,
the humbler my aims;
the greater my office,
the more cautious my heart;
the more ample my emolument,
the broader my generosity.
By these means, may I avoid the three resentments?"
Therefore, Lǎozi said:
"Thus, the noble must take the humble as root,
the high must take the low as foundation."
The Grand Marshal's hook-maker, at eighty years of age,
still never missed the fine point of a hook.
The Grand Marshal asked him:
"Are you skillful,
or is there a Way to it?"
He replied:
"I have something I hold to.
At twenty, I took delight in making hooks,
and looked at nothing else;
I observed nothing but hooks."
Thus, the use of one's abilities
must rely on what is not used,
thereby long maintaining their usefulness.
How much more so for holding to non-action?
What thing would not be accomplished by it!
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
