"Those who devote themselves to the Dào
are identical with the Dào."
King Wén cultivated virtue and improved governance,
and after three years, two-thirds of the empire inclined toward him.
King Zhòu heard of it and grew troubled, saying:
"If I rise early and retire late,
striving to compete with him,
it will torment my heart and weary my body.
But if I let him be and do nothing,
I fear he will overthrow me."
Chóng Hóuhǔ said:
"The Earl of Zhōu, Chāng, is benevolent and righteous, skilled in strategy;
his heir, Fā, is brave and resolute;
his second son, Dàn, is respectful, frugal, and knows the times.
If you follow their lead,
you cannot bear the calamity;
if you release and pardon them,
your person is certain to be endangered and lost.
Though a crown may be worn out,
it must still be placed on the head.
Before they have fully formed,
I beg you to plan against them!"
Then Qū Shāng confined King Wén in Yǒulǐ.
Thereupon, Sàn Yíshēng used a thousand pieces of gold to seek out rare treasures under heaven,
obtaining a zōuyú,
jīsī steeds,
a hundred measures of dark jade,
a hundred strings of great cowries,
black leopards,
yellow bears,
blue àn,
a thousand sets of white tiger patterned furs,
and presented them to Zhòu,
gaining access through Fèi Zhòng.
Zhòu saw them and was pleased,
then released him,
slaughtered an ox, and bestowed it upon him.
King Wén returned,
built a gate of jade,
constructed a spiritual terrace,
selected female attendants,
struck bells and drums,
and waited for Zhòu's failings.
Zhòu heard of this,
and said:
"The Earl of Zhōu, Chāng, has changed his ways and altered his conduct;
I have no more worries!"
Thereupon, he made the roasting grill,
cut open Bǐgān,
ripped open pregnant women,
and killed remonstrators.
Thus, King Wén achieved his scheme.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Know the honorable,
but keep to the disgraced,
and be the valley of the world."
King Chéng asked Yǐn Yì about governance, saying:
"What virtue must I practice
for the people to be devoted to their superiors?"
He replied:
"Employ them according to the seasons,
and respect and comply with them."
The King said:
"To what extent should this reach?"
He said:
"As if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice."
The King said:
"So fearful?
A king of men!"
Yǐn Yì replied:
"Between heaven and earth,
within the four seas,
if you treat them well, they are our charge;
if not, they become our enemies.
In the past, the ministers of Xià and Shāng
turned against Jié
and Zhòu to serve Tāng
and Wǔ; the people of Sùshā all attacked their own lord and returned to Shénnóng.
This is clearly known in the world.
How can one be without fear?"
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"What others fear,
one must also fear."
A follower of Zhí asked Zhí, saying:
"Does even a robber have a Dào?"
Zhí said:
"How could it be that he lacks a Dào!
To intuit what is hidden in storage—that is sageliness;
to enter first—that is courage;
to exit last—that is duty;
to divide equally—that is benevolence;
to know what is feasible—that is wisdom.
Without these five,
none in the world
can become a great robber."
From this perspective,
the mind of a thief must rely on the Dào of the sages to be effective.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Cut off sageliness, discard wisdom,
and the people will benefit a hundredfold."
The Chǔ general Zǐfā enjoyed seeking out men of skill and Dào.
A skilled thief from Chǔ went to see him, saying:
"I heard you seek men of skill and Dào.
I am a market thief from Chǔ,
wishing to offer my skill as one of your troops."
Zǐfā heard this,
did not wait to fasten his belt,
nor straighten his cap,
went out to meet him, and treated him with courtesy.
His attendants remonstrated:
"A thief
is a robber of the world.
Why treat him with courtesy?"
The lord said:
"This is not something my attendants can intervene in."
Not long after,
Qí raised troops to attack Chǔ.
Zǐfā led his army to face them,
but his troops were thrice repelled.
The worthy officials of Chǔ exhausted their strategies and devoted their sincerity,
yet the Qí army grew stronger.
Thereupon, the market thief came forward and requested:
"I have a minor skill,
and wish to perform it for you."
Zǐfā said:
"Agreed."
Without questioning further, he sent him off.
The thief went out at night, untied the Qí general's tent curtain, and presented it.
Zǐfā then had someone return it,
saying:
"A soldier gathering firewood
found the general's curtain
and returns it to your attendants."
The next night, he went again and took his pillow,
and Zǐfā again had it returned.
The next night, he went again and took his hairpin,
and Zǐfā again had it returned.
The Qí army heard of this,
was greatly alarmed,
and the general discussed with his officers:
"If we do not leave today,
the Chǔ army will likely take our heads."
Thus, they withdrew their army and left.
Therefore, no skill is too trivial, and no one too lowly,
it rests with the ruler how he uses them.
Hence, Lǎozǐ said:
"The unskillful man
is the resource for the skillful man."
Yán Huí said to Zhòngní:
"I have improved."
Zhòngní said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"I have forgotten rituals and music."
Zhòngní said:
"That is good,
but still not enough."
Another day, he saw him again,
and said:
"I have improved."
Zhòngní said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"I have forgotten benevolence and righteousness."
Zhòngní said:
"That is good,
but still not enough."
Another day, he saw him again,
and said:
"I can sit and forget."
Zhòngní, startled, said:
"What is sitting and forgetting?"
Yán Huí said:
"I cast aside my limbs,
dismiss my intelligence,
detach from form and abandon knowledge,
and become one with the transforming and penetrating [Way],
this is called sitting and forgetting."
Zhòngní said:
"Being one means without preference,
transforming means without constancy.
Since you, my master, recommend the worthy,
I, Qiū, ask to follow behind you."
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Can you keep the soul and embrace the One,
without departing from it?
Can you concentrate your breath and achieve softness,
like an infant?"
Duke Mù of Qín raised an army,
intending to launch a surprise attack on Zhèng.
Jiǎn Shū said:
"It cannot be done.
I have heard that in surprising a state,
with chariots, one should not exceed a hundred lǐ,
with men, not more than thirty lǐ,
because before plans can be leaked,
before armor and weapons can become dull or damaged,
before provisions can be exhausted,
and before the people can become weary and sick,
all rely on the height of their morale and the peak of their strength to reach,
thus they can intimidate the enemy when they strike.
Now we are marching several thousand lǐ,
and crossing the territories of many feudal lords,
to surprise a state;
I do not see how it can succeed.
May Your Lordship reconsider carefully!"
Duke Mù did not listen.
Jiǎn Shū saw the army off,
weeping in mourning clothes.
The army then set out,
passed through Zhōu and headed east.
A Zhèng merchant, Xián Gāo, pretending under the order of the Earl of Zhèng,
presented twelve oxen to feast the Qín army and hosted them as guests.
The three commanders, fearful, then plotted, saying:
"We have marched several thousand lǐ to surprise others,
yet before arriving, they already know of it;
their preparations must be complete beforehand,
making a surprise attack impossible."
They turned the army around and left.
At that time,
Duke Wén of Jìn had just died,
and was not yet buried.
Xiān Zhěn said to Duke Xiāng:
"In the past, our late lord had dealings with Duke Mù,
known throughout the land,
and no feudal lord was unaware.
Now our lord has died and is not yet buried,
yet they do not mourn our loss,
nor do they request passage;
this is to treat our late lord as dead and weaken our orphaned state.
I request to attack them!"
Duke Xiāng agreed.
Xiān Zhěn raised troops and encountered the Qín army at Yáo,
where he heavily defeated them,
capturing their three armies and returning.
When Duke Mù heard of this,
he donned plain clothes and faced the ancestral temple,
to explain himself to the multitude.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"To know yet think one does not know is best.
Not to know yet think one knows is sickness."
The queen of the King of Qí died,
and the king wished to appoint a new queen but had not decided,
so he had his ministers deliberate.
Lord Xuē wanted to align with the king's intention,
so he presented ten earrings, praising one pair as especially beautiful.
The next day,
he inquired where the beautiful earrings had gone,
and thus advised establishing that consort as queen.
The King of Qí was greatly pleased,
and hence valued Lord Xuē highly.
Thus, when a ruler's intentions are revealed outwardly,
they become controlled by their ministers.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Block the openings,
shut the doors,
and to the end of life, there will be no toil."
Lú Áo traveled to the Northern Sea,
passed through the Great Yin,
entered the Dark Gate,
and reached the heights of Méng Gǔ.
There he saw a scholar,
with deep-set eyes and dark temples,
a long neck and hawk-like shoulders,
broad above and narrow below,
standing tall and dancing in the wind.
Catching sight of Lú Áo,
he slowly lowered his arms,
and fled beneath a stone tablet.
Lú Áo approached to look at him,
and saw him leaning on a turtle shell, eating clams.
Lú Áo spoke to him, saying:
"Only I, Áo, have turned my back on the crowd and left my companions,
to exhaustively observe beyond the six directions—
is it not I, Áo, alone?
I, Áo, loved to wander from youth,
and have not slackened into adulthood.
I have traversed the four extremes,
only the northern darkness remained unseen.
Now I have finally met you here, sir;
might you befriend me, Áo?"
The scholar,
baring his teeth, laughed and said:
"Ha!
You, a man of the central states,
how could you have come so far?
This place still has the light of the sun and moon and carries the arrayed stars,
where yīn and yáng move,
and the four seasons are born.
Compared to the nameless lands,
it is like a corner room.
As for me, I have traveled south to the wilds of Wǎng Lǎng,
rested north in the land of Chén Mò,
exhausted the west in the regions of Yǎo Míng,
and passed through the east to the light of Hóng Méng.
There, below is no earth, above no heaven;
listening, one hears nothing;
looking, one becomes dazzled.
Beyond that,
there are still the boundless shores of Tài Wò.
With one leap, I cover thousands and thousands of lǐ,
yet I have not been able to reach its end.
Now you have just begun to travel here,
and yet speak of exhaustive observation—
is it not too far-fetched?
But you may stay here!
I have an appointment with Hàn Màn atop the nine heavens,
and cannot linger long."
The scholar raised his arms and straightened his body,
then entered the clouds.
Lú Áo looked up to watch him,
but saw nothing.
He then halted his carriage,
his heart in turmoil,
dismayed as if having suffered a loss.
He said:
"I compared to that gentleman,
am like a yellow swan and a grub.
All day I travel,
never leaving a foot's space,
yet I thought myself far-reaching—
is it not lamentable!"
Therefore, Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The short-lived cannot understand the long-lived,
the small-minded cannot comprehend the great-minded;
the morning mushroom knows not the cycle of the moon,
the summer cicada knows not the passing of spring and autumn."
This speaks to what is unseen by the perceptive.
Mìzǐ governed Dǎnfù for three years,
when Wūmǎqī, wearing a mourning garment and coarse short robe,
altered his appearance,
and went to observe the transformation.
He saw a night fisherman,
who would release any fish he caught,
and Wūmǎqī asked him:
"The purpose of fishing
is to catch fish.
Now you catch them and release them;
why is that?"
The fisherman replied:
"Mìzǐ does not wish people to take small fish.
What I caught were small fish,
hence I released them."
Wūmǎqī returned and reported to Confucius, saying:
"Mìzǐ's virtue has reached its peak!
He makes people act in the dark
as if under the threat of severe punishment.
How has Mìzǐ achieved this?"
Confucius said:
"I once asked him about governance,
and he said:
'Sincerity in this leads to punishment in that.'
Mìzǐ must be practicing this method."
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Discard that and take this."
Wǎngliǎng asked the shadow:
"Is that which is shining brightly
the divine light?"
The shadow said:
"No."
Wǎngliǎng said:
"How do you know?"
The shadow said:
"When Fúsāng receives the day's end,
the sun shines on the universe,
its brilliant light
illuminates the four seas.
But close the doors and shut the windows,
and it cannot enter.
As for the divine light,
it flows everywhere simultaneously,
reaching all extremes,
touching the sky above,
and spreading over the earth below,
nurturing all things without form,
and in the blink of an eye, it embraces beyond the four seas.
How can the term 'shining brightly' name it!"
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"The softest things in the world
overcome the hardest things in the world."
Guāngyào asked Wúyǒu:
"Do you truly exist?
Or do you truly not exist?"
Wúyǒu did not respond.
Unable to get an answer,
Guāngyào looked closely at his appearance:
dark and sudden,
looking, one cannot see its form,
listening, one cannot hear its sound,
grasping, one cannot obtain it,
gazing, one cannot reach its limit.
Guāngyào said:
"How noble!
Who can reach such a state?
I can achieve 'non-being',
but I cannot achieve the 'non-being of non-being'.
Even when I reach the 'non-being of non-being',
how could I ever attain this!"
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"That which is without substance enters into that which has no crevices.
I thereby know the benefit of taking no action."
Báigōng Shèng was plotting a rebellion,
and after court, he stood still,
leaning on an inverted cane,
its tip piercing his chin,
blood flowing to the ground without his knowledge.
A person from Zhèng heard of this and said:
"If he forgets his own chin,
what would he not forget?"
This illustrates that when the spirit ventures outward,
and thoughts are agitated within,
one cannot properly manage one's body.
Thus, when the spirit is used for distant matters,
what is near is neglected.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Without going out the door, one knows the world;
without peeping through the window, one sees the Way of Heaven.
The farther one goes,
the less one knows."
This refers to that.
When the Qín emperor gained the world,
fearing he could not hold it,
he sent troops to guard the borders,
built the Great Wall,
repaired passes and bridges,
set up barriers and fortifications,
prepared relay carriages,
and stationed border officials.
Yet the Liú family took it from him,
as easily as turning a doorknob.
In the past, King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
defeating him at Mùyě,
then sealed Bǐgān's tomb,
honored Shāngróng's neighborhood,
barricaded Jīzǐ's door,
paid respects at Chéngtāng's temple,
distributed grain from Jùqiáo,
scattered money from Lùtái,
broke drums and snapped drumsticks,
unstrung bows and cut strings,
abandoned houses and slept in the open to show simplicity,
removed swords and girdles to show no enmity.
Thereupon, the world sang and rejoiced,
feudal lords brought gifts and paid homage,
and it lasted thirty-four generations without being taken away.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Those who are good at closing
need no bolt, yet it cannot be opened.
Those who are good at tying
need no cord, yet it cannot be undone."
Yīn Xū learned charioteering,
but after three years had gained nothing,
suffering privately,
often thinking of it in his sleep.
In the middle of the night, he dreamed of receiving the 'autumn drive' from his master.
The next day,
he went to court.
His master saw him and said:
"I am not withholding the way from you,
but feared you were not ready to receive it.
Today, I will teach you the autumn drive."
Yīn Xū stepped back,
bowed facing north twice, and said:
"I am blessed by heaven,
for I dreamed of receiving it just last night."
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Attain the utmost emptiness;
maintain steadfast tranquility.
All things arise together,
and I observe their return."
In the past, Sūnshū Áo three times became prime minister
without showing joy;
three times he lost the position
without showing worry.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ
was desired by the people of Wú to be king but refused;
Xǔ Yóu
declined the empire and would not accept it;
Yànzǐ, making a covenant with Cuī Zhù,
faced death without changing his demeanor;
these all had far-reaching understanding.
When the spirit understands life and death,
what thing can confuse it?
In Jīng, there was a man named Cìfēi,
who obtained a precious sword in Gānduì.
Returning and crossing the river,
in the middle of the stream,
the waves of Yánghóu
and two jiāo dragons surrounded his boat.
Cìfēi asked the boatman:
"Have you ever seen anyone survive such a situation?"
The reply was:
"Never seen it."
Thereupon, Cìfēi, enraged, glared, bared his arms, and drew his sword,
saying:
"A warrior can be persuaded with rites of benevolence and righteousness,
but cannot be coerced or robbed.
These are but rotten flesh and decaying bones in the river.
To abandon my sword to save myself—
what attachment would I have to it?"
He leaped into the river and stabbed the jiāo,
cutting off their heads.
Everyone in the boat survived,
the wind and waves completely subsided,
and the King of Jīng ennobled him as Zhíguī.
Confucius heard of it and said:
"How admirable!
Not to abandon his sword for rotten flesh and decaying bones—
that describes Cìfēi!"
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Only those who do not value life
are wiser than those who cherish it."
A man from Qí named Chúnyú Kūn used the strategy of vertical alliance to persuade the King of Wèi,
and the King of Wèi found him eloquent.
He prepared ten carriages,
intending to send him to Jīng,
and Chúnyú Kūn took his leave and set off.
Yet, feeling that the vertical alliance was insufficient,
he again used the horizontal alliance to persuade the King of Wèi,
his words seeming plausible.
The King of Wèi then halted his journey and distanced himself from him.
Losing the essence of the vertical alliance,
and unable to accomplish the matters of the horizontal alliance,
this is why he became isolated.
For words have their source,
and affairs have their foundation.
Losing that source and foundation,
even if one has many skills,
it is worse than having few.
Thus, on the Zhōu tripod, Chuí was depicted,
but with his finger bitten off,
showing that the ancient kings saw that great cleverness should not be pursued.
Hence, Shènzǐ said:
"A craftsman knows how to make a door,
and can use a door,
but does not truly understand the door,
so it must be closed before it can function as a door."
Among the Mohists, there was one named Tián Jiū,
who wished to see King Huì of Qín,
prepared carriages and readied the shafts,
but stayed in Qín for
three years without gaining an audience.
A visitor spoke of him to the King of Chǔ,
and he went to see the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ was very pleased with him,
gave him a credentials,
and sent him as an envoy to Qín.
Upon arrival, he thus met King Huì,
and persuaded him.
After leaving his lodging,
he sighed deeply and
told his attendants:
"I stayed in Qín for three years without an audience,
unaware that the path could be reached through Chǔ."
Things inherently may seem near yet be far,
or far yet near.
Therefore, the actions of great men
are not constrained by rigid rules,
but proceed to their ultimate goal.
This is what the "Guǎnzǐ" calls
"birds fly, yet there is a plumb line."
The Fēng River is a thousand fathoms deep,
and does not accept dust or dirt,
but if gold or iron is thrown in,
their forms appear on the surface.
Not that it isn't deep and clear,
but fish, turtles, dragons, and snakes refuse to dwell there.
Thus, on stone, the five grains do not grow,
and on barren mountains, elk and deer do not roam,
for there is no shelter.
Once, Zhào Wénzǐ asked Shū Xiàng:
"Of the six generals of Jìn,
who will fall first?"
He replied:
"Likely the Zhōngháng
and Zhì clans."
Wénzǐ said:
"Why?"
He answered:
"In their governance,
they mistake harshness for discernment,
severity for clarity,
oppressing subordinates for loyalty,
and numerous schemes for merit.
It is like stretching leather:
stretch it,
and it may become large,
but that is the way to tear it."
Hence, Lǎozǐ said:
"When governance is obscure,
the people are pure.
When governance is scrutinizing,
the people are cunning."
Duke Jǐng said to the Grand Diviner:
"What can your art do?"
He replied:
"I can make the earth shake."
Yànzǐ went to see the duke,
and the duke said:
"I asked the Grand Diviner,
'What can your art do?'
He replied,
'I can make the earth shake.'
Can the earth really shake?"
Yànzǐ remained silent and did not answer.
Upon leaving, he saw the Grand Diviner and said:
"Previously, I saw the Hooked Star between the constellations Jū and Xīn,
could the earth have shaken?"
The Grand Diviner said:
"Yes."
Yànzǐ left,
and the Grand Diviner hurried to see the duke, saying:
"It is not that I can make the earth shake,
but the earth was going to shake anyway."
Tián Zǐyáng heard of this and said:
"Yànzǐ remained silent and did not answer
because he did not want the Grand Diviner to die.
He went to see the Grand Diviner
for fear the duke would be deceived.
Yànzǐ can be said to be loyal to his superior and kind to his subordinates."
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Square, but does not cut;
sharp, but does not pierce."
Marquis Wén of Wèi hosted a feast for his officials at Qǔyáng.
As the drinking reached its peak,
Marquis Wén sighed deeply and said:
"Alas, I have no Yù Ràng as my minister!"
Jiǎn Zhòng raised his cup and approached,
saying:
"I propose a toast to you!"
The marquis said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"I have heard that
parents with obedient children do not know filial sons,
and rulers with wise governance do not know loyal ministers.
As for Yù Ràng's lord,
what was he like?"
Marquis Wén accepted the cup and drank it,
draining it without offering a toast in return,
saying:
"Without Guǎn Zhòng
and Bào Shū as ministers,
I thus have the achievement of Yù Ràng."
Hence, Lǎozǐ said:
"When the state is in chaos,
there are loyal ministers."
Confucius visited Duke Huán's temple,
where there was a vessel
called the Yòuzhī.
Confucius said:
"How excellent!
To have seen this vessel."
Turning, he said:
"Disciples, fetch water!"
When water was brought,
he poured it in;
when half-full, it stood upright,
when full, it tipped over.
Confucius suddenly changed his expression and said:
"Excellent,
this illustrates holding fullness!"
Zǐgòng, standing by his side, asked:
"May I ask about holding fullness?"
He said:
"Reduce it by restraining."
Zǐgòng asked:
"What does it mean to reduce by restraining?"
He replied:
"All things flourish and then decline,
joy reaches its peak and turns to sorrow,
the sun reaches its zenith and then moves,
the moon becomes full and then wanes.
Therefore, with intelligence and wisdom,
guard it with simplicity;
with extensive knowledge and broad debate,
guard it with restraint;
with martial prowess and courage,
guard it with caution;
with wealth, honor, and vast possessions,
guard it with frugality;
with virtue that benefits all under heaven,
guard it with humility.
These five principles
are how the ancient kings held the world without losing it.
Opposing these five,
none have not faced peril."
Thus, Lǎozǐ said:
"Those who follow this Way do not desire fullness.
Only by not being full
can they endure without seeking renewal."
King Wǔ asked Tài Gōng:
"I am about to attack Zhòu,
which in the world is a subject killing his lord and inferiors attacking their superior.
I fear that future generations will engage in endless warfare,
with ceaseless conflict.
What should be done about this?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Excellent,
Your Majesty's question!
When one has not yet captured the game,
one only fears the wound is too small;
once it is captured,
one fears only that too much flesh is damaged.
If the king wishes to maintain it long,
then block the people's senses,
guide them entirely toward useless activities,
and bothersome teachings.
Let them all enjoy their occupations,
be at ease in their sentiments,
make the clear obscure and guide them into darkness,
then remove their helmets and load them with books,
untie their swords and gird them with court tablets.
Institute three years of mourning,
to reduce population growth.
Use lofty words and humble deference,
to make the people not contend.
Use wine and meat to connect with them,
yú and sè to entertain them,
ghosts and spirits to awe them.
Elaborate patterns and proliferating rites,
to cover up their substance.
Generous burials and prolonged mourning,
to empty their households.
Pearls in the mouth,
scale-decorated burial suits,
silk ribbons,
to impoverish their wealth.
Deep digging and high mounds,
to exhaust their strength.
With households poor and clans small,
there will be few who plan troubles.
Using this to transform customs,
one can hold the world without losing it."
Therefore Lǎo Zǐ said:
"When transformation gives rise to desires arising,
I will stabilize them with the simplicity of the nameless."
In ancient times, there were those who wore helmets and rolled collars yet ruled the world,
whose virtue gave life without killing,
gave without taking,
the world did not criticize their attire,
all embraced their virtue.
At that time,
yīn and yáng were harmonious,
wind and rain were timely,
all things multiplied and grew,
nests of magpies could be reached down and explored,
birds and beasts could be tethered and followed,
must it necessarily be wide-sleeved robes and broad sashes,
curved lapels and elaborate caps!
In ancient times, people lived in marshes and nested in caves,
in winter they could not endure frost, snow, fog, and dew,
in summer they could not bear the heat and mosquitoes.
The sages therefore acted, building with earth and framing wood,
to make houses,
with beams above and eaves below,
to shelter from wind and rain,
to avoid cold and heat,
and the common people were content.
When Bó Yú first made clothing,
he twisted hemp into threads,
passing by hand and hanging by finger,
the result was like a net.
Later generations made looms with heddles and treadles for ease of use,
and the people could cover their bodies and ward off cold.
In ancient times, they sharpened plows to farm,
polished clamshells to weed,
used wooden hooks to gather firewood,
carried earthen jars to draw water,
the people labored hard with little benefit.
Later generations made léi sì, yōu, and chú,
axes for gathering firewood,
well-sweeps for drawing water,
the people rested more and benefited greatly.
In ancient times, great rivers and famous valleys,
cut off roads,
blocking passage back and forth,
so they hollowed logs and made planks,
to make boats,
thus whether the terrain had or lacked,
they could transport goods.
To tread over a thousand miles in straw sandals,
the toil of carrying loads on shoulders,
they therefore made bending wheels and building carts,
harnessing horses and yoking oxen,
the people reached far without fatigue.
Because fierce birds and beasts harmed people with no means to stop them,
they smelted metal and forged iron,
to make weapons,
so fierce beasts could not harm.
Thus when people faced difficulties, they sought convenience,
when troubled by calamities, they created preparations,
each using their knowledge,
to remove what harmed them,
and pursue what benefited them.
Constant ways cannot be followed blindly,
tools and implements cannot be fixed,
thus the laws and measures of former kings have changed.
Ancient practices:
weddings did not name the host,
Shùn married without informing his parents,
which was against rites.
Establishing the heir by primogeniture,
yet King Wén passed over Bó Yì Kǎo and used King Wǔ,
which was against rule.
Rites say marry at thirty,
yet King Wǔ was born when King Wén was fifteen,
which was against law.
The Xià Hòu clan laid the coffin at the eastern steps,
the Yīn people between the two pillars,
the Zhōu people at the western steps,
these are differences in rites.
The Yǒu Yú clan used earthen coffins,
the Xià Hòu clan used plastered enclosures,
the Yīn people used outer coffins,
the Zhōu people set up feather screens,
these are differences in burial.
The Xià Hòu clan sacrificed at night,
the Yīn people at day,
the Zhōu people at sunrise in the morning,
these are differences in sacrifice.
Yáo had the "Great Manifestation",
Shùn the "Nine Successions",
Yǔ the "Great Xià",
Tāng the "Great Huò",
Zhōu the "Martial Elephant",
these are differences in music.
Thus the Five Emperors had different ways yet their virtue covered the world,
the Three Kings had different deeds yet their names extended to later ages,
all these adapted rites and music according to the times.
Just as Shī Kuáng adjusted the zither's pegs,
moving them up and down without inch or foot measure,
yet none failed to hit the note.
Thus one who comprehends the essence of rites and music can create them,
speaking from an inner foundation,
and thereby knowing the compass of the measuring square.
Lord Zhāo of Lǔ had a nurturing mother whom he loved,
when she died he wore the plain cap for her,
thus arose the mourning for a nurturing mother.
Yáng Hóu killed Liǎo Hóu and stole his wife,
thus the grand feast abolished the rite for wives.
The systems of former kings,
if unsuitable, were abolished;
matters of declining ages,
if good, were established;
thus rites and music have never been constant.
Therefore the sages create rites and music,
but are not bound by rites and music.
Governing a state has constants,
yet benefiting the people is fundamental.
Administration and teaching have norms,
yet effective implementation is paramount.
If it benefits the people,
it need not imitate antiquity.
If it suits the affairs,
it need not follow the old.
The decline of the Xià and Shāng,
came from not changing laws, and they perished.
The rise of the Three Dynasties,
came from not copying each other, and they ruled.
Thus the sages adapt laws to the times,
rites to customs,
clothing and tools each for their utility,
laws, measures, and decrees each according to their appropriateness.
Therefore changing antiquity should not be faulted,
and following customs is not necessarily praiseworthy.
All rivers differ in source yet all return to the sea;
all schools of thought differ in practice yet all aim at governance.
When the Kingly Way declined, the *Book of Songs* was composed;
when the Zhōu court fell into decay and ritual righteousness crumbled,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* were written.
The *Book of Songs* and *Spring and Autumn Annals* represent the beauty of learning,
yet both were creations of an age of decline.
Confucians follow them to instruct the world,
but how can this compare to the flourishing of the Three Dynasties!
To value the *Book of Songs* and *Spring and Autumn Annals* as the Way of antiquity,
yet there was a time before these works were composed.
To speak of the Way in its deficiency
is not as good as speaking of it in its completeness.
Reciting the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents* of the former kings
is not as good as hearing their words;
hearing their words
is not as good as grasping why they spoke.
Those who grasp why they spoke
understand what words cannot express.
Thus, the Way that can be spoken of
is not the constant Way.
When the Duke of Zhōu served King Wén,
his actions were not self-willed,
his affairs were not self-determined,
his body seemed too frail to bear clothing,
his words seemed too hesitant to leave his mouth,
yet in serving King Wén,
he was reverent and attentive,
as if fearing incapability,
anxious lest he fail,
truly exemplifying filial devotion.
When King Wǔ passed away,
and King Chéng was young,
the Duke of Zhōu continued King Wén's legacy,
assumed the Son of Heaven's registry,
administered the governance of the realm,
quelled the rebellions of the Yí and Dí tribes,
punished the crimes of Guǎn and Cài,
stood with his back to the screen to receive feudal lords in audience,
meting out punishments and rewards with decisive authority,
without seeking counsel,
his might shook heaven and earth,
his prestige awed all within the seas,
truly exemplifying martial prowess.
When King Chéng came of age,
the Duke of Zhōu returned the registry and handed over governance,
turning north to present himself as a subject and serve him,
acting only upon request,
proceeding only after receiving approval,
without any intention of arbitrariness,
without any sign of boastful pride,
truly exemplifying ministerial loyalty.
Thus, one person underwent three transformations
to respond to the times.
How much more so when a state sees multiple changes of era,
and a country sees multiple changes of ruler,
with people using their positions
to indulge their likes and dislikes,
employing their authority to satisfy their desires,
yet attempting to use a single code of conduct
and a fixed set of laws
to adapt to changing circumstances—
their inability to hit the mark of flexibility
is evident.
Thus, what the sage follows is called the Way;
what the sage does is called affairs.
The Way is like bells and chimes,
tuned once and never changed;
affairs are like lutes and zithers,
retuned after each piece.
Therefore, laws, institutions, rituals, and righteousness
are tools of governance,
but not the means of governance itself.
Thus, taking benevolence as the warp
and righteousness as the woof
is what remains unchanged for ten thousand generations.
As for assessing people's talents
and examining their utility according to the times,
even daily changes are permissible.
How can there be a constant law for all under heaven!
Aligning with worldly affairs,
understanding human principles,
complying with heaven and earth,
and securing blessings from spirits,
then governance can be rectified.
In ancient times, the people were pure, the craftsmen sincere,
the merchants simple, the women chaste,
hence governance and education were easily transformative,
and customs easily shifted.
In the present age, virtue has further declined,
folk customs have further weakened,
and attempting to govern a corrupt populace
with simple and chaste methods
is like driving a fierce horse without bit, bridle, or whip.
In the past,
Shénnóng had no decrees, yet the people obeyed;
Táng and Yú had decrees but no punishments;
the Xiàhòu clan did not break their word;
the Yīn people made oaths;
the Zhōu people made covenants.
Reaching the present age,
people endure shame and take insult lightly,
greedily seek gain with little sense of shame,
and attempting to govern them with the ways of Shénnóng
would surely lead to chaos.
Bóchéng Zǐgāo declined being a feudal lord to farm,
and all under heaven esteemed him.
People of the present time
who resign from office to live in seclusion
become the lowest in their villages and towns—
how can they be compared!
Ancient weapons
were merely bows and swords;
spear shafts had no sharp points,
long halberds had no blades.
Weapons of later ages
used high siege towers for attack,
protective screens for defense,
repeating crossbows for shooting,
and chariots for combat.
In ancient attacks on states,
they did not kill the young,
nor capture the elderly.
What was righteous in ancient times
is laughed at today.
What was honorable in the past
is considered disgraceful now.
What brought order in antiquity
causes disorder today.
Shénnóng and Fúxī imposed no rewards or punishments, yet the people did no wrong;
however, those who establish governance cannot discard laws to rule the people.
Shùn wielded shield and axe to subdue the Yǒumiáo,
yet those who wage war cannot lay aside arms to control the violent.
From this perspective,
laws and measures
are means to assess folk customs and regulate urgency;
tools and instruments
should be suited to the times and adapted appropriately.
When sages create laws, all things are regulated;
when worthies establish rituals, the unworthy are constrained.
Those who are bound by laws
cannot be entrusted with far-reaching endeavors;
those constrained by rituals
cannot be made to adapt to change.
Those whose ears cannot distinguish clear and turbid sounds
should not be tasked with tuning music;
those whose minds do not grasp the roots of order and chaos
should not be allowed to establish laws.
One must have the ear that hears the unique,
the vision that sees the unseen,
then one can master the Way and act.
Yīn changed Xià,
Zhōu changed Yīn,
the Spring and Autumn period changed Zhōu—
the rituals of the Three Dynasties differed;
which antiquity should be followed!
The great ones create, and the disciples follow.
Knowing the origin of laws and governance,
one adapts with the times;
not knowing the source of laws and governance,
even if following antiquity,
one ends in chaos.
The legal records of the present age change with the times,
ritual and righteousness shift with customs,
yet scholars follow and inherit traditions,
clinging to records and preserving the old,
believing that without this, there is no governance—
this is like fitting a square peg into a round hole;
wanting to achieve proper fit and stability
becomes difficult indeed.
Now, Confucians and Mohists praise the Three Dynasties, King Wén, and King Wǔ
but do not practice their ways;
this is advocating what they do not practice.
They criticize the present age but do not reform it;
this is practicing what they criticize.
Praising what they approve,
practicing what they disapprove,
thus they exhaust themselves daily in thought without benefiting governance,
toil in body and drain their wisdom without aiding their lord.
Consider painters who prefer drawing ghosts and spirits
and dislike depicting dogs and horses—
why is that?
Ghosts and spirits never appear in the world,
while dogs and horses are seen daily.
Preserving the endangered and governing the chaotic
cannot be done without wisdom;
yet praising the Way of antiquity,
even a fool can do in excess.
Therefore, unused laws
the sage king does not implement;
unverified words
the sage king does not heed.
The energy of Heaven and Earth,
nothing is greater than harmony.
Harmony means
the balancing of yīn and yáng,
the division of day and night,
which gives birth to things.
At the spring equinox, they are born;
at the autumn equinox, they mature.
Birth and maturation
must obtain the essence of harmony.
Therefore, the way of the sage
is lenient yet firm,
strict yet gentle,
soft yet upright,
fierce yet benevolent.
If too rigid, it breaks;
if too soft, it curls.
The sage positions himself between rigidity and softness,
thus grasping the root of the Way.
Accumulated yīn sinks,
accumulated yáng soars;
only when yīn and yáng connect
can harmony be achieved.
The marking line as a measure
can be coiled and tucked away,
pulled and stretched out,
it can be straight and serve as a guide.
Thus, the sage embodies it.
It is pliable but not wayward,
short but not exhausted,
straight but not rigid,
enduring but not forgotten—
is it not only the line that possesses these qualities?
Hence, kindness extended leads to weakness,
weakness then lacks authority;
strictness extended leads to harshness,
harshness then lacks harmony;
affection extended leads to indulgence,
indulgence then lacks order;
punishment extended leads to cruelty,
cruelty then lacks closeness.
In the past,
Duke Jiǎn of Qí relinquished the reins of his state,
and solely entrusted them to his high ministers.
The generals and ministers seized power and controlled authority,
formed cliques for private gain,
and public justice did not prevail.
Thus, they enabled Chéng Chéngcháng and Chīyí Zǐpí to accomplish their coup.
That the Lǚ lineage lost its sacrifices and the Chén clan took the state
was born of such softness and weakness.
Zǐyáng of Zhèng was resolute and fond of penalties;
in meting out punishment,
he was firm and unforgiving.
A retainer who broke a bow,
fearing the crime and dreading execution,
took advantage of the panic caused by a mad dog to kill Zǐyáng.
This was the result of such rigidity and fierceness.
Now those who do not understand the Way,
seeing the meek and weak being encroached upon,
then pride themselves on being resolute;
seeing the resolute perish,
then pride themselves on being meek and weak.
This is to have no fundamental master within,
while perceptions and hearsay clash externally,
so they never settle on a definite course throughout life.
It is like the singing of one who knows nothing of music:
if the notes are low, it is stifled and inflexible;
if high, it is shrill and discordant.
But when it comes to the songs of Hán É, Qín Qīng, and Xuē Tán,
the melodies of Hóu Tóng and the prolonged tunes,
with passion in the will,
accumulated within,
overflowing and expressed in sound,
then none fail to match the scales and harmonize with human hearts.
Why is that?
Because there is a fundamental master within that determines the high and low,
not accepting from outside but setting its own standard.
Now when a blind man walks on the road,
if people say left, he goes left;
if they say right, he goes right.
If he meets a gentleman, he is guided to an easy path;
if he meets a petty person, he falls into a ditch.
Why is that?
Because his eyes have no means to perceive objects.
Thus, Wèi employed both Lóu Zhái and Wú Qǐ and lost the Héxī region,
King Mǐn relied solely on Nào Chǐ and died in the eastern temple,
because they had no method to control them.
King Wén employed both Lǚ Wàng and Shào Gōng Shì and became king,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ solely appointed Sūn Shū Áo and achieved hegemony,
because they had a method to control them.
Using stringed music, songs, drumming, and dancing for enjoyment,
circling and bowing in courtesy to cultivate ritual,
thick burials and prolonged mourning to send off the dead—
these were established by Confucius,
yet Mòzǐ opposed them.
Universal love and exalting the worthy,
honoring ghosts and opposing fate—
these were established by Mòzǐ,
yet Yángzǐ opposed them.
Preserving nature and safeguarding genuineness,
not burdening the form with material things—
these were established by Yángzǐ,
yet Mèngzǐ opposed them.
Choices and rejections differ among people,
each has an understanding heart.
Thus, right and wrong have their place;
if one grasps their place, nothing is wrong;
if one loses their place, nothing is right.
The peoples of Dānxué, Tàiméng, Fǎnzhǒng, Kōngtóng, Dàxià, Běihù, Jīgōng, and Xiūgǔ
each have different rights and wrongs,
customs that are contrary,
yet ruler and minister, high and low,
husband and wife, father and son,
have means to direct each other.
What is right here
is not right there;
what is wrong here
is not wrong there.
It is like how the axe, hatchet, hammer, and chisel each have their own application.
In the time of Yǔ,
he governed by listening through the five tones,
suspended bells, drums, chimes, and hand-bells,
and set up a small drum,
to await scholars from all directions,
issuing the call:
"Those who would teach me the Way, strike the drum;
those who would instruct me in righteousness, strike the bell;
those who would inform me of affairs, shake the hand-bell;
those who would speak to me of worries, strike the chime;
those with legal disputes, shake the small drum."
At that time,
he would rise ten times during a single meal,
and interrupt his bath three times to grasp his hair,
laboring for the people of the world.
If one in such circumstances could not achieve goodness and demonstrate loyalty,
then their talent was insufficient.
In the time of Qín,
they built high towers and pavilions,
vast parks and enclosures,
distant imperial highways,
cast bronze statues,
dispatched exiles for garrison duty,
collected fodder and straw,
levied head taxes and basket tributes,
delivering them to the Shàofǔ.
Able-bodied men
reached west to Líntáo and Dídào,
east to Kuàijī and Fúshí,
south to Yùzhāng and Guìlín,
north to Fēihú and Yángyuán,
with corpses on the roads measured by ditches.
At that time,
those who offered loyal advice were deemed inauspicious,
and those who spoke of benevolence and righteousness were called mad.
When it came to Emperor Gāo,
he preserved the perishing and continued the severed lines,
raised the great righteousness of the world,
personally rolled up his sleeves and took up arms,
to plead for the people's lives before the August Heaven.
At that time,
the heroes and brave of the world were exposed in wilderness and marshes,
facing arrows and stones ahead,
and falling into streams and ravines behind,
emerging from a hundred deaths with one chance of life,
to contend for the power of the world,
rousing military spirit and sharpening sincerity,
to decide their fate in a single day.
At that time,
those in rich robes and broad belts who spoke of Confucianism and Mohism
were considered unworthy.
When violence and chaos had been overcome,
and the land was greatly settled,
continuing the civil enterprise,
establishing military achievements,
treading the register of the Son of Heaven,
creating the Liú clan's cap,
gathering the Confucians and Mohists of Zōu and Lǔ,
penetrating the legacy teachings of former sages,
bearing the flags of the Son of Heaven,
riding the great carriage,
setting up the nine streamers,
striking the great bell,
beating the sounding drum,
performing the Xiánchí,
and brandishing shield and axe.
At that time,
those who stood for military might were suspected.
Within a single generation,
civil and military alternated as dominant,
each used according to the time.
Nowadays, those who practice martial arts reject the civil,
and those who practice civil arts reject the martial,
civil and military mutually disparage,
unaware of the utility of timing and circumstances.
This is like seeing one corner of a room,
and not knowing the vastness of the eight extremes.
Thus, facing east to look,
one cannot see the western wall;
facing south to gaze,
one cannot behold the north;
only by having no fixed direction
can one be unobstructed everywhere.
What preserves a state
is the Way and its virtue;
what destroys a family
is the blockage of principle.
Yáo had no city of a hundred households,
Shùn not even land to plant an awl,
yet they possessed the world.
Yǔ had no following of ten men,
Tāng no fief of seven lǐ,
yet they ruled as kings over the feudal lords.
King Wén dwelt in the area of Qízhōu,
his territory no more than a hundred lǐ square,
yet he was established as Son of Heaven,
because he had the Way of the True King.
At the height of Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu,
wherever human footprints reached,
wherever boats and carriages traveled,
all was made into commanderies and counties,
yet they died by others' hands,
laughed at by the world,
because they had the form of ruin.
Thus the sage observes transformation to see its signs.
When virtue waxes or wanes,
the wind signals it first.
Therefore, those who attain the Kingly Way,
though small, will surely become great;
those who have the form of ruin,
though established, will surely fail.
When the Xià was about to perish,
the Grand Historian Zhōng Gǔ first fled to Shāng,
and after three years Jié then perished.
When the Yīn was about to fall,
the Grand Historian Xiàng Yì first submitted to King Wén,
and after one year Zhòu then perished.
Thus when the sage perceives the traces of survival and ruin,
the moment of success and failure,
it is not merely at the wilderness of Míngtiáo,
or the day of Jiǎzǐ.
Now if we say the strong win by measuring land and counting people,
the rich profit by weighing grain and assessing gold,
if so,
then no ruler of ten thousand chariots would fail to become hegemon or king,
and no state of a thousand chariots would ever be destroyed.
If the traces of survival and ruin
were so easily known,
even foolish men and simple women could discuss them.
Lord Xiāng of Zhào became hegemon with the city of Jìnyáng,
while Zhì Bó was captured with the lands of the three Jìn;
King Mǐn perished with the great Qí,
while Tián Dān achieved merit with Jímò.
Thus a state facing ruin,
though large, is not to be relied on;
the Way being practiced,
though small, cannot be轻视.
From this we see
that survival lies in attaining the Way, not in size;
ruin lies in losing the Way, not in smallness.
The Book of Songs says:
"Then He turned His gaze westward,
this is where He would dwell."
This speaks of leaving Yīn and moving to Zhōu.
Thus the rulers of chaotic states
strive to expand their territory but not to practice benevolence and righteousness,
seek to elevate their position but not to cultivate the Way and virtue.
This is to discard what makes for survival,
and create what makes for ruin.
Thus Jié, imprisoned at Jiāomén,
could not fault his own conduct,
but regretted not killing Tāng at Xiàtái;
Zhòu, confined in the Xuānshì,
did not reflect on his faults,
but regretted not executing King Wén at Yǒulǐ.
Had these two rulers, in their position of strength and greatness,
cultivated the way of benevolence and righteousness,
Tāng and Wǔ would have been too busy saving themselves from punishment
to dare contemplate any plans!
If above they disordered the brightness of the three luminaries,
and below lost the hearts of the myriad people,
even without Tāng and Wǔ,
who would have been unable to seize power?
Now if one does not examine what lies with oneself,
but instead prepares against others,
the world does not have only one Tāng or Wǔ—
kill one person,
and there will surely be successors.
Moreover, the reason Tāng and Wǔ, though small and weak, were able to become kings,
was because they had the Way;
the reason Jié and Zhòu, though strong and great, were ultimately overthrown,
was because they were without the Way.
Now if one does not practice what enabled others to become kings,
but instead increases what causes oneself to be overthrown,
this is to hasten down the path to ruin.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he wanted to build a palace on Mount Wǔxíng.
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"It cannot be!
Mount Wǔxíng
is a place of solid barriers and dangerous obstacles.
If our virtue can cover it,
then those of the world presenting tribute will have to detour.
If we have violent and chaotic conduct,
then the world's attack on us will be difficult."
This is why they lasted thirty-six generations without being overthrown.
The Duke of Zhōu can be said to have known how to maintain fullness.
In ancient times,
the "Zhōu Shū" stated:
"Words from superiors
are for inferiors to implement;
words from inferiors
are for superiors to utilize.
Words from superiors
represent constancy;
words from inferiors
represent expediency."
This is the method of preserving or destroying states.
Only the sage is capable of understanding expediency.
Speaking with absolute honesty,
and keeping promises without fail,
are considered noble conduct in the world.
When Zhígōng's father stole a sheep, the son testified against him;
Wěi Shēng died waiting for a woman he had promised to meet.
Though straightforward in testifying against his father,
and faithful in dying for a woman,
despite their honesty and faithfulness,
who would value them!
To forge commands in the army
is a grave offense.
When Duke Mù of Qín raised troops to attack Zhèng,
he passed through Zhōu territory heading east.
A Zhèng merchant Xián Gāo, heading west to trade cattle,
encountered the Qín army between Zhōu and Zhèng,
forged the order of the Earl of Zhèng,
presented twelve cattle as provisions,
entertained the Qín army and made them retreat,
thus preserving the State of Zhèng.
Therefore, in certain situations,
honesty can become a fault,
while deception can become an achievement.
What does it mean to breach etiquette yet achieve great merit?
When King Gōng of Chǔ battled Jìn's Lì at Yīnlíng,
Lǚ Qí shot at King Gōng,
hit his eye and captured him,
Pān Wāng, Yǎng Yóujī, Huáng Cuīwēi, and Gōngsūn Bǐng together rescued him.
King Gōng, terrified, lost composure,
Huáng Cuīwēi lifted his foot and kicked the king's body,
whereupon King Gōng regained awareness.
Angered by this disrespect,
he vigorously rose up,
and the four ministers carried him away.
When Cāngwú Rǎo married a beautiful wife,
he yielded her to his elder brother,
this is what is called loyal affection that cannot be practiced.
Therefore, the sage judges the right and wrong of matters,
bending or stretching with them,
without fixed norms,
sometimes yielding, sometimes advancing.
Soft and pliant like rushes,
it is not out of fear or coercion;
firm, strong, fierce, and resolute,
with aspirations reaching the blue clouds,
it is not for boasting or arrogance;
it is to act according to the time and adapt to changes.
In the interaction between ruler and minister,
kneeling and bowing humbly
are to show mutual respect;
but when pressed by crisis,
kicking the ruler's body
is something no one in the world can condemn.
Thus, where loyalty lies,
etiquette cannot hinder it.
A filial son serving his parents
with a gentle expression and humble posture,
offering the belt and arranging the shoes;
but when they are drowning,
he grabs their hair to save them,
not daring to be arrogant or disrespectful,
but to rescue them from death.
So, when drowning, he grabs his father;
when praying, he names his ruler;
circumstances make it inevitable.
This is why expediency is established.
Thus, Confucius said:
"Some you can study with,
but not pursue the Way together.
Some you can pursue the Way with,
but not stand firm together.
Some you can stand firm with,
but not exercise expediency together."
Expediency
is the unique insight of the sage.
Therefore, to oppose first and then harmonize
is called knowing expediency;
to harmonize first and then err
is called not knowing expediency.
Those who do not know expediency
turn good into ugliness.
Thus, ritual
is the flower of reality and the pattern of artifice;
in moments of urgent crisis,
it becomes useless.
Therefore, the sage interacts with the world through culture,
but acts according to reality as appropriate,
not confined to a single path,
stagnant and unchanging,
thus failures are few and successes many,
decrees are executed throughout the world without opposition.
The orangutan knows the past but not the future;
the magpie knows the future but not the past;
this is the distinction between long and short.
Cháng Hóng was an expert in calculations for the Zhōu court,
understanding the energies of heaven and earth,
the movements of the sun and moon,
the changes of wind and rain,
the numbers of pitch-pipes and calendars,
there was nothing he did not comprehend,
yet he could not foresee his own death
by being torn apart.
Sū Qín
was a commoner of humble origins,
worn shoes and thin covers,
yet he managed the lords of ten thousand chariots,
subdued the various feudal lords,
but could not avoid the calamity of being torn apart by chariots.
King Yǎn of Xú clothed himself in kindness and benevolence,
practiced righteousness personally,
had thirty-two states paying homage on land,
yet he died and his state perished,
with no descendants left.
Minister Wén Zhǒng assisted King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
avenged his grievances and wiped out his shame,
captured Fūchāi himself,
expanded territory by thousands of miles,
yet he died by the sword of his own lord.
These all understood the pivot of order and chaos,
but did not know the means to preserve their lives.
Thus, Cháng Hóng knew the way of heaven but not human affairs;
Sū Qín knew expedient schemes but not fortune and misfortune;
King Yǎn of Xú knew benevolence and righteousness but not timing;
Wén Zhǒng knew loyalty but not strategy.
The sage is not like this;
he assesses the times to undertake affairs,
weighs affairs to devise plans,
thus extending across the world without being excessive,
confining within narrow limits without being obstructed.
If the world falls into chaos and disorder,
ritual and righteousness cease,
laws and order collapse,
the strong and weak exploit each other,
force contends and seizes,
no distinction between ruler and minister,
no order between noble and base,
armor breeds lice,
swallows and sparrows nest in tents,
warfare never ceases,
and only then begins the appearance of subservience,
the ritual of reverence and frugality,
it will surely be suppressed and unable to rise.
When the world is peaceful and stable,
governance and education harmonious,
the people respectful and amicable,
superiors and inferiors affectionate,
and only then begins asserting imposing airs,
displaying bravery and strength,
it will inevitably incur the law of the authorities.
Therefore, the sage
can be yin or yang,
weak or strong,
acting or resting according to the time,
achieving merit based on resources,
knowing the reversal when things move,
observing the change when affairs sprout,
transforming and creating images accordingly,
responding as situations evolve,
thus walking through life without encountering hardship.
There are deeds that can be done but not spoken of,
words that can be spoken but not acted upon,
tasks easy to attempt but difficult to accomplish,
and endeavors hard to achieve yet easy to ruin.
What is meant by "deeds that can be done but not spoken of"
refers to strategic choices;
"words that can be spoken but not acted upon"
denotes hypocrisy and deceit;
"tasks easy to attempt but difficult to accomplish"
concern affairs of state;
"endeavors hard to achieve yet easy to ruin"
pertain to governance.
These four strategies
are uniquely perceived and carefully considered by the sage.
To bend an inch in order to stretch a foot,
the sage does it;
to be crooked in small matters but upright in great ones,
the noble person practices it.
The Duke of Zhōu bore the stigma of having his brother killed,
Duke Huán of Qí had the reputation of contending for the state,
yet the Duke of Zhōu used righteousness to amend his flaws,
and Duke Huán used achievements to erase his disgrace,
and both are regarded as worthy.
If we now use minor faults to obscure great virtues,
then there would be no sage kings or worthy ministers in the world.
Thus, if there is a flaw in the eye,
but it does not impair vision,
one should not cauterize it;
if there is an ailment in the throat,
but it does not hinder breathing,
one should not drill into it.
The burial mounds on the riverbank
are too numerous to count,
yet the terrain is still considered level.
Water stirred gives rise to waves,
high and low facing each other,
differing by a few feet,
yet it is still regarded as calm.
In the past, Cáo Zǐ led troops for Lǔ,
fought three battles without victory,
and lost a thousand lǐ of territory.
Had Cáo Zǐ made plans without considering the future,
without turning his heels,
and cut his throat on the battlefield,
he would have been forever known as a defeated general.
Yet Cáo Zǐ was not ashamed of his defeat,
but ashamed to die without merit.
At the covenant of Kē,
brandishing a three-foot blade,
he confronted Duke Huán's chest,
and the losses from three battles
were recovered in a single day,
his courage renowned throughout the world,
and his merit established in Lǔ.
Guǎn Zhòng assisted Prince Jiǔ but could not see it through,
which cannot be called wise;
fleeing and running away,
not dying in the crisis,
cannot be called brave;
bound in fetters,
not avoiding the shame,
cannot be called steadfast.
With these three behaviors,
commoners would not befriend him,
rulers would not employ him.
Yet Guǎn Zhòng, freed from his bonds,
established the governance of Qí,
assembled the feudal lords nine times,
and unified the world.
Had Guǎn Zhòng sacrificed his life,
without regard for future plans,
how could he have achieved such hegemon's merit?
Now, when rulers judge their ministers,
not considering their great achievements,
but summarizing their general conduct,
and seeking minor virtues,
this is the way to lose the worthy.
Therefore, if a person has substantial virtue,
do not inquire into minor details;
if they have great reputation,
do not fault minor flaws.
A puddle from a cow's hoof cannot breed sturgeon,
and a bee's hive cannot hold a swan's egg,
for small forms cannot contain large entities.
In human nature,
none are without shortcomings.
If their overall character is sound,
even with minor faults,
they should not be burdened by them.
If their overall character is flawed,
even with the conduct of a village,
it is not enough for great tasks.
Yán Zhuōjù,
a great robber from Liángfù,
became a loyal minister of Qí.
Duàngān Mù,
a great broker of Jìn,
became a teacher to Marquis Wén.
Mèng Mǎo married his sister-in-law,
and had five children with her,
yet he served as minister of Wèi,
pacified its dangers,
and resolved its crises.
Jǐng Yáng indulged in drink,
disheveled his hair and served among women,
yet he awed the feudal lords into submission.
These four men
all had their shortcomings,
yet their achievements and fame remain undiminished,
because their overall character was sound.
Jì Āi and Chén Zhòngzǐ upheld integrity and resisted compromise,
not entering the courts of corrupt rulers,
not eating the food of chaotic times,
and thus starved to death.
Why could they not preserve the perishing and continue the severed?
Because minor principles were upheld while major strategies were abandoned.
Thus, those overly cautious in small matters achieve no success,
those who criticize others are not tolerated by the crowd,
large bodies have sparse joints,
and those with long strides cover great distances.
From ancient times to the present,
the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
none have had flawless conduct.
Therefore, the Yì Jīng says:
"Minor faults,
bring success, benefit, and steadfastness."
This means that all have faults,
but one should not desire them to be great.
Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ were the pinnacle of worldly rulers;
Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn
were the heroes among the Five Hegemons.
Yet Yáo had a reputation for lack of kindness,
Shùn was slandered for disrespecting his father,
Tāng and Wǔ had deeds of exile and regicide,
and the Five Hegemons had schemes of violence and chaos.
Therefore, the noble person does not demand perfection from anyone,
is upright but not cutting,
incorruptible but not harsh,
broadly knowledgeable but not critical,
civil and martial but not demanding.
When seeking from others, employ their abilities;
when cultivating oneself, use morality.
Demanding human effort from others
is easy to repay;
cultivating oneself with morality
is hard to achieve.
Being hard to achieve makes one's conduct lofty;
being easy to repay makes one's demands met.
The jade of the Xiàhòu clan cannot be without flaws,
the bright moon pearl cannot be without blemishes,
yet the world treasures them—
why?
Because their minor flaws do not hinder their great beauty.
If we focus on people's shortcomings
and forget their cultivation,
and yet seek to find the worthy under heaven,
then it is difficult.
Bǎilǐ Xī herding cows,
Yī Yǐn carrying the cauldron,
Tàigōng wielding the knife,
Nìng Qì singing merchant songs—
their virtue existed within them.
The crowd saw their lowly status,
their demeaning tasks, and did not understand their overall character,
considering them unworthy.
Only when they became the Three Dukes of the Son of Heaven,
and were established as worthy ministers of feudal lords,
did people begin to believe in their uniqueness.
Those who rise from among cauldrons and cutting boards,
emerge from butcher shops and taverns,
are freed from bonds and fetters,
ascend from under the cow's chin,
cleansed with hot water,
purified with torch fire,
stand in the court above,
lean on the position of the Three Dukes,
inwardly without shame to the state,
outwardly without disgrace to the feudal lords,
have an inner harmony with circumstances.
Thus, to know one's worthiness without achievements—
such was Yáo's knowledge of Shùn;
to know one's worthiness after achievements are made—
such is the market crowd's knowledge of Shùn.
To abandon measures and seek them in markets and wilderness,
is surely to miss many people.
Why?
Because one can imitate the search,
but not understand the means of selecting people.
Things that resemble each other
often confuse the rulers of the world;
deceptive similarities and appearances
dazzle the common people.
Thus, the stubborn may appear wise but are not truly wise,
the foolish may seem benevolent but are not truly benevolent,
the reckless may look courageous but are not truly courageous.
If the differences between people
were like jade versus stone,
or mallows versus amaranth,
then judging people would be easy.
But those who confuse others
are like ginseng and angelica,
or wild carrot and wild celery,
which are hard to distinguish. Thus, sword-makers are perplexed by swords resembling Moyé,
but only Ōuyě can identify their kind;
jade-workers are dazzled by jade resembling bìlú,
but only Yīdùn can discern the true nature;
foolish rulers are misled by treacherous ministers who cast doubt on gentlemen,
but only sages can perceive the subtle and understand the obvious.
So, when a snake raises its head a foot,
its length can be estimated;
when an elephant shows its tusk,
its size can be judged.
Xuē Zhú and Yōngzǐ, upon seeing a fox's claw mark on a sword, could discern its sharpness or dullness;
Yú'ér and Yìyá, when the waters of Zī and Shéng were mixed,
tasted one sip and knew their sweetness or bitterness.
Therefore, when sages evaluate the worthy,
observing one action is enough to distinguish worthiness from unworthiness.
Confucius declined the offer of Lǐnqiū,
proving he would never steal even a knife or hook;
Xǔ Yóu yielded the throne of the Son of Heaven,
showing he had no interest in feudal titles.
Thus, one who has never been burned dares not grasp fire,
having seen it burn;
one who has never been cut dares not hold a blade,
having seen it harm.
From this perspective,
observers can discuss what has not yet occurred,
and examining small details suffices to understand the whole.
Therefore, the way to judge people
is: when noble, observe whom they recommend;
when wealthy, observe whom they aid;
when destitute, observe what they refuse;
when humble, observe what they avoid;
when poor, observe what they do not take.
Watch them face difficulties,
to know their courage;
observe them in joy and pleasure,
to see their integrity;
entrust them with wealth,
to assess their benevolence;
test them with fear,
to discern their integrity;
then human nature is fully revealed.
In ancient times, those skilled in rewarding
spent little but encouraged many;
those skilled in punishing
used few penalties but stopped wrongdoing;
those skilled in giving
employed frugality yet earned gratitude;
those skilled in taking
gained much without resentment.
When Zhào Xiāngzǐ was besieged in Jìnyáng,
after lifting the siege, he rewarded five meritorious men,
with Gāo Hè as the first honored.
His attendants asked:
"During the crisis at Jìnyáng,
Hè had no great merit,
yet now he is the first rewarded,
why?"
Xiāngzǐ replied:
"During the siege of Jìnyáng,
my altars of state were in peril,
the nation faced disaster,
and all my ministers harbored arrogant disdain,
but only Hè never wavered in the rites between ruler and subject."
Thus, by rewarding one man,
all subjects under heaven
became loyal to their rulers.
This is rewarding few but encouraging many.
King Wēi of Qí set a large cauldron in his court
and reprimanded the magistrate of Wúyán:
"Your praises,
I hear daily.
But inspecting your governance,
the fields lie barren,
the granaries empty,
the prisons full.
You have deceived me with treachery."
Then he had him boiled.
Thereafter, for thirty-two years, no one picked up lost items on the roads of Qí.
This is using few penalties but stopping wrongdoing.
Duke Mù of Qín once traveled and his chariot broke down,
losing a right-side horse,
which some villagers found.
Duke Mù pursued them to the south of Qíshān Mountain,
where he saw the villagers slaughtering and eating the horse.
Duke Mù said:
"Eating the meat of a fine horse
without drinking wine afterward
harms the body.
I fear it may harm you all."
So he gave them all wine before leaving.
A year later,
in the battle of Hán against Duke Huì of Jìn,
the Jìn army surrounded Duke Mù's chariot,
and Liáng Yóumǐ seized the reins of his team,
about to capture him.
But over three hundred men who had eaten the horse meat
all fought to the death for Duke Mù beneath his chariot,
thus defeating Jìn,
and capturing Duke Huì to bring him back.
This is employing frugality yet earning gratitude.
Duke Huán of Qí, planning to launch a campaign,
found his armor and weapons insufficient,
so he ordered those with heavy crimes to contribute a rhinoceros-hide armor and a halberd,
those with minor offenses to redeem themselves with a sum of metal,
and those who lost lawsuits to provide a bundle of arrows.
The people were all pleased,
straightening arrows into shafts,
casting metal into blades,
and they marched against injustice and unprincipled states,
thus making him hegemon of the world.
This is gaining much without resentment.
Therefore, sages encourage goodness by following what the people delight in,
and stop wrongdoing by leveraging what the people detest,
so rewarding one person makes all under heaven praise it,
punishing one person makes all under heaven fear it.
Thus, the ultimate reward is not wasteful,
the ultimate punishment is not excessive.
Confucius executed Shàozhèng Mǎo, and the evil in Lǔ was blocked;
Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī, and the wrongdoing in Zhèng was stopped;
judging the distant by the near,
knowing the great by the small.
So when sames adhere to frugality yet govern broadly,
this is what is meant.
Nothing in the world is easier than doing good,
and nothing harder than doing evil.
What is called doing good
is being tranquil and non-interfering;
what is called doing evil
is being restless and full of desires.
Suiting one's disposition, renouncing excess,
free from temptation or deception,
following one's nature, preserving genuineness,
unchanged within oneself,
thus it is said doing good is easy.
Scaling city walls,
crossing dangerous passes,
forging tallies and seals,
stealing official insignia,
usurping, assassinating, falsifying, and slandering,
these are not human nature,
thus it is said doing evil is hard.
Now, the reason people commit crimes leading to imprisonment
and fall into the misery of punishment and execution
is that their cravings and desires are insatiable,
and they do not follow measures and limits.
How do we know this is so?
The laws of the world's officials state:
"Those who rob graves will be executed,
thieves will be punished."
This is what the authorities enforce.
The laws net the wicked,
tracking them down relentlessly,
and no fool or simpleton
fails to know that evildoers cannot escape,
and offenders cannot avoid punishment.
Yet the unworthy cannot overcome their desires,
incurring the guilt of death,
and suffering the shame of execution.
After the beginning of autumn,
the officers of justice crowd the gates,
and the blood of the executed flows in the streets.
Why is this?
They are deluded by the gain of wealth and profit,
and blinded to the peril of death.
Now, when troops are arrayed and arms are set,
two armies facing each other,
the general issues the order:
"Those who behead enemies will be ennobled,
those who retreat will be beheaded."
Yet the soldiers in the ranks cannot advance to achieve the merit of beheading,
but later suffer the penalty of beheading,
this is avoiding the fear of death only to meet certain death.
Therefore, the reversal of advantage and harm,
the connection of misfortune and blessing,
must be carefully considered.
There are affairs one desires to pursue,
yet precisely by doing so, one ends up losing them;
or things one seeks to avoid,
yet precisely by avoiding them, one ends up encountering them.
There was a man from Chǔ who, while riding a boat, encountered a great wind;
as the waves surged, he panicked,
and threw himself into the water.
It was not that he did not cherish life or fear death,
but rather that he was so bewildered by the fear of death that he forgot about preserving life.
Thus, human desires and cravings
are also like this.
There was a man from Qí who stole gold;
at the bustling time of the market,
he snatched it and ran.
When seized and asked for the reason, he said:
"You stole gold in the middle of the market—
why?"
He replied:
"I did not see the people,
I only saw the gold!"
When fixated on what one desires,
one forgets the consequences of the action.
Therefore, the sage carefully examines the changes in movement and stillness,
and appropriately regulates the measures of giving and receiving,
manages the emotions of likes and dislikes,
and harmonizes the moderation of joy and anger.
If movement and stillness are well-matched,
then calamity will not be encountered;
if giving and receiving are appropriate,
then guilt will not accumulate;
if likes and dislikes are managed,
then worry will not draw near;
if joy and anger are moderated,
then resentment will not be provoked.
Thus, those who have attained the Dào
do not seek gains improperly,
nor do they seize blessings;
what they possess, they do not abandon,
what is not theirs, they do not demand;
they are always full but not overflowing,
eternally empty and thus easily satisfied.
Now, dripping water is enough to fill a pot or jug,
yet the Yangtze and Yellow River cannot fill a leaky cup;
so it is with the human heart.
One should naturally use the Dào and methods to measure,
eating to satisfy hunger,
clothing to ward off cold,
and that is sufficient to nourish the seven-foot body.
If one lacks the Dào and methods to measure and instead practices frugality and restraint,
then even the power of ten thousand chariots is not enough to bring honor,
and the wealth of the world is not enough to bring joy.
Sūn Shū'áo was dismissed three times from the position of Lìngyǐn without a worried expression,
because rank and salary could not burden him;
Jīng Cìfēi, with two flood dragons coiling around his boat, remained unshaken in resolve,
because monstrous creatures could not startle him.
The sage's heart is calm and his will steady,
his spirit guarded within,
so that nothing is sufficient to confuse him.
As for a drunkard,
he bends down to enter the city gate,
thinking it a seven-foot doorway;
he leaps across the Yangtze and Huái River, thinking them ordinary ditches;
it is the wine that muddles his spirit.
A coward,
seeing a standing marker at night,
takes it for a ghost;
seeing a recumbent stone,
takes it for a tiger;
it is fear that suppresses his vital energy.
How much more so with the monstrous things of heaven and earth!
When male and female mate,
yīn and yáng interact,
the feathered become chicks and fledglings,
the furred become foals and calves,
the soft become skin and flesh,
the hard become teeth and horns,
people do not find it strange;
water produces clams and oysters,
mountains produce metal and jade,
people do not find it strange;
an old locust tree produces fire,
long-accumulated blood becomes will-o'-the-wisp,
people do not find it strange.
But if mountains produce Xiāoyáng,
waters produce Wǎngxiàng,
trees produce Bìfāng,
wells produce Fényáng,
people find them strange,
because their experience is limited and their knowledge of things shallow.
The monstrous things of the world
are uniquely seen by the sage;
the reversals of benefit and harm
are uniquely understood by the wise.
Matters of similarity and difference, suspicion and doubt,
are what confuse the common world.
What cannot be displayed throughout the land,
what cannot be made clear to the common people,
therefore, through ghosts, spirits, omens, and portents, prohibitions are established,
and by generalizing forms and inferring categories, symbolic transformations are created.
How do we know this is so?
Common sayings go:
"In sacrificing to the great heights, the pig is the foremost offering;
in burying the dead, fur garments cannot be interred;
those who play with blades, the great ancestor will seize their elbows;
those who sleep pillowed against the door lintel, ghosts and spirits will tread on their heads."
These are not written in laws and decrees,
nor are they orally transmitted by the sage.
As for sacrificing to the great heights with the pig as the foremost offering,
it is not that the pig is superior to wild beasts like deer and elk,
yet the spirits alone enjoy it—
why?
It is believed that the pig
is an animal commonly raised by households and easily obtained,
so it is honored for its convenience.
That fur garments cannot be interred with the dead—
not because they cannot provide the warmth of silk, gauze, or fine cloth to the body—
but the world considers fur garments
to be rare and expensive items,
which can be passed down to later generations;
they offer no benefit to the deceased,
yet can sufficiently support the living,
so they are restricted based on their value.
That those who play with blades have the great ancestor seize their elbows—
for playing with blades
is bound to lead to fault,
fault leads to mutual injury,
and the calamity will surely be great;
without blood-feud or enmity, in contentious fighting,
over trivial matters, one brings upon oneself punishment and execution—
a folly the unwise do not guard against,
so the great ancestor is invoked to weigh on their hearts.
That those who sleep pillowed against the door lintel have ghosts and spirits tread on their heads—
if ghosts and spirits could transform mysteriously,
they would not need doors or windows to move,
but would follow emptiness to come and go,
and then could not tread either;
for doors and windows
are where wind and air pass through,
and wind and air
are the coarse aspects of yīn and yáng;
those exposed to them will surely fall ill,
so ghosts and spirits are invoked to issue a warning.
All such matters
cannot be fully recorded in books, bamboo slips, or silk and stored in government offices,
so they are clarified through omens and portents.
To make the unwise aware of the harm,
the authority of ghosts and spirits is borrowed to proclaim the teachings—
this practice has existed for a long time.
The unwise take it as omens and portents,
the stubborn consider it false,
only those with the Dào can comprehend its intent.
Nowadays, offerings to wells, stoves,
doors, windows,
brooms,
mortars and pestles—
it is not that their spirits are believed to enjoy them,
but rather out of reliance on their virtue,
and the unending toil and hardship they endure.
Therefore, by honoring them in due season,
their contributions are not forgotten.
That which breaks through rocks to emerge,
gathers from tiny spaces,
and within a single morning rains all over the world—
is only Tài Shān;
that which, even after three years of drought, does not cease to flow,
whose moisture reaches a hundred lǐ and nourishes plants and trees—
is only the Yangtze and Yellow River;
thus, the son of heaven offers libations and sacrifices to them.
Hence, if a horse saves a person from danger,
upon its death, it is buried,
with a curtain used as a shroud;
if an ox has shown virtue to people,
upon its death, it is buried,
with a large cart's box used as a mat.
If oxen and horses, having rendered service,
are still not to be forgotten,
how much more so for humans!
This is why the sage values benevolence and accumulates kindness.
Thus, Yán Dì, who created fire,
after death became the stove spirit;
Yǔ, who labored for the world,
after death became the earth god;
Hòu Jì, who initiated farming,
after death became the grain spirit;
Yì, who eliminated the world's harms,
after death became Zōngbù.
This is how ghosts and spirits are established.
In Northern Chǔ there was a man devoted to knight-errantry,
whose children and grandchildren repeatedly admonished him to stop,
but he would not listen.
When bandits appeared in the county,
thoroughly searching his home,
the matter was indeed discovered,
and he fled in nightly alarm,
pursued until overtaken on the road.
Yet all those upon whom he had bestowed kindness fought for him,
enabling his escape and safe return.
