He then told his son:
"You repeatedly tried to stop me from being a knight-errant.
Now when faced with calamity,
I indeed relied on this to save my life.
Your admonitions to me
were of no use."
He knew how to escape from calamity,
but did not know how to avoid it altogether.
To reason about matters in this way—
is it not misguided?
A man of Sòng was marrying off his daughter
and told her:
"Marriage may not last.
If you are sent away,
you must secretly store things away.
If you secretly store and become wealthy,
it will be easier for you to remarry."
The daughter followed her father's plan,
stealing and hoarding possessions.
When her husband's family discovered her theft,
they drove her away.
Her father did not see his own fault,
but instead considered his plan successful.
He knew to store wealth in case of divorce,
but did not realize that storing wealth would cause the divorce.
To reason in this manner—
is it not perverse?
Consider those who hire carts for transport:
to save a cart's load
and exhaust an ox's strength,
when an axle is about to break,
they add extra poles and axles thinking it preparation,
not realizing that additional poles hasten the axle's breaking.
When the King of Chǔ wore a jade pendant while chasing hares,
and broke it while running,
he then wore two pendants in preparation.
But the two pendants struck each other,
breaking even more quickly.
The governance of a disordered state
resembles this.
The owl's eyes are large yet its sight is inferior to a rat's;
the millipede has many legs yet runs slower than a snake.
Thus among creatures, some large are inferior to small,
and numerous inferior to few.
As for strengthening the weak,
weakening the strong,
securing the endangered,
and preserving the perishing—
if not a sage,
who can perceive this?
Size and rank
are insufficient for judgment;
only where the Dào resides is truly valuable.
How to illustrate this?
When the Son of Heaven stays at a suburban pavilion,
the nine ministers hasten there,
high officials run,
those seated prostrate themselves,
and those leaning straighten up.
At such times,
in the bright hall and ancestral temple,
hats hang and swords are removed,
belts loosened for rest.
Not that the suburban pavilion is large and the temple small,
but because the supreme resides there.
The nobility of Heaven's Dào
is not solely due to the Son of Heaven's尊贵;
wherever it resides, all look up to it.
Hibernating insects and magpie nests
all face the celestial unity,
for ultimate harmony resides there.
If the emperor truly can embrace the Dào
and unite with ultimate harmony,
then birds, beasts, plants, and trees all receive his beneficence,
let alone the millions of people!
Permeating heaven and earth,
chaotic and pristine,
creating things without deliberate action—
this is called the Great Unity.
All emerge from this one source,
yet their manifestations differ:
some as birds, some fish, some beasts—
these are called differentiated beings.
Types are distinguished by categories,
things divided into groups,
with natures and destinies varying,
all taking physical form.
Separated and disconnected,
divided into countless varieties,
none can return to the origin.
Thus in activity they are born,
and in death they are exhausted.
All become mere things,
not the non-thing that creates things.
The thing-creator is lost among the myriad things.
Examining antiquity's great beginning,
humans were born from non-being,
taking form in existence,
and having form, are constrained by things.
Those who can return to their origin,
as if without form,
are called true persons.
The true person
has never been separated from the Great Unity.
The sage does not serve as a vessel for fame,
a storehouse for schemes,
a bearer of affairs,
nor a master of wisdom.
Concealed without form,
moving without traces,
wandering without signs.
Not initiating blessings,
not starting misfortunes.
Preserving emptiness and non-being,
acting only when compelled.
Those seeking blessing may encounter misfortune;
those seeking benefit may meet harm.
Thus those attaining peace through non-action—
losing what brings peace, they face danger;
those governing through non-interference—
losing what brings order, they face chaos.
Stars arrayed in heaven shine,
thus people point to them;
righteousness arrayed in virtue appears,
thus people observe it.
Where people point,
movement shows patterns;
what people observe,
action leaves traces.
Movement with patterns invites criticism;
action with traces invites discussion.
Therefore the sage conceals brilliance in formlessness,
hides traces in non-action.
Wángzǐ Qìngjì died by the sword,
Yì died by the peach club,
Zǐlù was minced in Wèi,
Sū Qín died by his tongue.
All people value what they cultivate
and disdain their shortcomings,
yet all drown in what they value
and exhaust themselves in what they disdain.
What they value has form;
what they disdain lacks manifestation.
Thus the strength of tigers and leopards attracts arrows;
the agility of apes and weasels attracts snares.
If one can value what they disdain
and disdain what they value,
they may be spoken to about ultimate truths.
The self-confident cannot be moved by slander or praise;
the contented cannot be tempted by power or profit.
Thus those understanding nature's essence
do not strive for what nature cannot achieve;
those understanding destiny's essence
do not worry about what destiny cannot change;
those connected with the Dào
find nothing sufficient to disturb their harmony.
Zhān Hé said:
"I have never heard of one who cultivates himself yet the state falls into chaos.
Nor have I heard of one who neglects himself yet the state becomes orderly."
If the square is not true,
it cannot make right angles;
if the compass is not true,
it cannot make circles;
the self
is the compass and square of affairs.
I have never heard of one who is crooked himself yet can straighten others.
Trace back to the heavenly mandate,
cultivate the mind's disposition,
regulate likes and dislikes,
and harmonize one's inherent nature—
then the way of governance becomes clear.
Tracing back to the heavenly mandate prevents confusion about fortune and misfortune;
cultivating the mind's disposition avoids reckless joy and anger;
regulating likes and dislikes eliminates greed for the useless;
harmonizing one's inherent nature ensures desires do not exceed moderation.
Without confusion about fortune and misfortune, actions follow principle;
without reckless joy and anger, rewards and punishments are impartial;
without greed for the useless, desires do not harm one's nature;
with desires not exceeding moderation, one nurtures nature and knows contentment.
All these four aspects
are not sought externally,
nor borrowed from others,
but attained by turning inward.
The world cannot be governed by cleverness alone,
nor comprehended through mere wisdom,
nor ordered by force of events,
nor secured by benevolence alone,
nor conquered by strength.
These five—
all are human talents,
but without abundant virtue,
none can be fully realized.
When virtue is established, the five are not endangered;
when the five are prominent, virtue has no place.
Thus, with the Way, even the foolish have surplus;
without the Way, even the wise fall short.
Cross water without swimming skills,
and even the strong will sink;
with swimming skills,
even the weak will succeed;
how much more so when relying on boats and vessels!
The root of governance
lies in pacifying the people.
The root of pacifying the people
lies in sufficiency of resources.
The root of sufficiency
lies in not disrupting the seasons.
The root of not disrupting the seasons
lies in reducing affairs.
The root of reducing affairs
lies in restraining desires.
The root of restraining desires
lies in returning to one's nature.
The root of returning to one's nature
lies in removing burdens.
Removing burdens leads to emptiness,
emptiness leads to balance.
Balance
is the essence of the Way;
emptiness
is the abode of the Way.
Those who can possess the world will not lose their states;
those who can possess their states will not ruin their families;
those who can govern their families will not neglect themselves;
those who cultivate themselves will not forget their hearts;
those who trace back to their hearts will not impair their nature;
those who preserve their nature will not be confused about the Way.
Thus, Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
"Guard carefully within,
close off completely without.
Much knowledge brings ruin—
do not look, do not listen.
Embrace spirit in stillness,
and the form will align itself.
One who cannot attain this in oneself yet claims to know others—
such a thing has never existed."
Hence, the Yìjīng states:
"Tie the sack—
no blame, no praise."
Those who achieve hegemony or kingship
are necessarily victors;
those who defeat enemies
are necessarily strong;
those who are strong
necessarily employ others' strength;
those who employ others' strength
necessarily win people's hearts;
those who win people's hearts
necessarily possess self-attainment;
those who possess self-attainment
are necessarily gentle and weak.
Strength overcomes those inferior to oneself,
but meets resistance when facing equals;
gentleness overcomes those superior to oneself,
its power immeasurable.
Thus, to turn many defeats into great victory—
only the sage can achieve this.
A skilled swimmer
need not learn to pole a boat to use it adeptly;
one with strong sinews
need not learn horsemanship to ride comfortably.
Those who take the world lightly
are not burdened by external things,
hence they can dwell in it.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù dwelled in Bīn,
the Dí people attacked him,
he offered furs, coins, pearls, and jade to no avail,
so he bid farewell to the elders and moved to Qízhōu,
the people, carrying children and supporting the aged, followed him,
and thus a state was formed.
Extending this principle,
his lineage held the world for four generations—
was this not fitting?
Those who do not cling to the world
are precisely those who can govern it.
Frost, snow, rain, and dew
give life and death to all things—
Heaven acts without action,
yet it is honored.
To enforce laws and regulations,
governing officials and managing the people—
this is the task of functionaries;
the ruler remains without affairs,
yet is revered.
To open land and cultivate wilderness—
this was Hòujì's work;
to channel rivers and dredge streams—
this was Yǔ's work;
to judge cases and maintain fairness—
this was Gāoyáo's work;
yet the one with the sage's fame
was Yáo.
Thus, one who attains the Way to rule,
though personally incapable,
will surely have the capable serve them.
Without the Way,
even with many skills,
there is no benefit.
When a boat crosses the river,
an empty vessel approaches from another direction,
collides and capsizes it—
even if one is resentful,
there will be no angry countenance.
But if someone is aboard that vessel,
one shouts to steer left,
another to steer right,
repeated calls go unanswered—
surely curses will follow.
Why no anger before, but anger now?
Because before it was empty, now it is occupied.
If one can empty oneself to wander the world,
who can blame them?
Abandoning the Way to rely on cleverness brings peril;
discarding principle to employ talent brings hardship.
Some perish due to excessive desires,
but none are endangered by lacking desire;
some bring chaos by trying to govern with desire,
but none err by upholding constancy.
Thus, cleverness cannot avert calamity,
nor does folly necessarily lead to loss of peace.
Keep to your lot,
follow principle,
neither grieve loss
nor rejoice in gain,
for success is not forced,
nor attainment sought.
What enters is received, not taken;
what departs is given, not withheld.
Life comes with spring,
death with autumn—
no gratitude for what is born,
no resentment for what dies—
this approaches the Way.
The sage does not engage in actions that could be criticized,
nor does he resent others for criticizing him;
he cultivates virtues worthy of praise,
yet does not seek others' acclaim.
He cannot prevent misfortune from coming,
but trusts that he does not invite it;
he cannot ensure blessings will arrive,
but trusts that he does not repel them.
When misfortune arrives,
it is not born from his seeking,
so he remains unperturbed in hardship;
when blessings come,
they are not achieved through his pursuit,
so he remains humble in success.
Knowing that the control of fortune and misfortune
does not lie within himself,
he dwells in contentment at leisure,
governing through non-action.
The sage preserves what he already possesses,
without seeking what he has not obtained.
Seeking what is not yet obtained
leads to losing what one has;
cultivating what one already possesses
brings what is desired.
Thus, in employing military force,
one first makes oneself invincible,
then awaits the enemy's vulnerability;
in governing a state,
one first makes it unassailable,
then awaits the enemy's susceptibility.
Shùn cultivated himself at Lìshān and the world followed his transformation,
King Wén cultivated himself at Qízhōu and all under heaven changed their customs.
Had Shùn chased after worldly benefits
and forgotten the path of self-cultivation,
he could not have preserved himself,
let alone possessed an inch of land!
Thus, governance not firmly rooted in order
yet forced through action
will surely end in peril;
conduct not firmly grounded in blamelessness
yet hastily seeking fame
will surely meet with failure.
No blessing greater than being free from misfortune,
no benefit finer than avoiding loss.
Action, as a phenomenon,
either diminishes or enhances,
either succeeds or fails,
either benefits or harms,
all being perilous,
and those who pursue it risk danger.
Thus Qín triumphed over the Róng but was defeated at Xiáo,
Chǔ conquered the central states but was defeated at Bójǔ.
Therefore, the Way cannot encourage those chasing profit,
but can pacify those avoiding harm.
Thus, often be free from misfortune,
rather than constantly seeking blessings;
often be free from fault,
rather than constantly pursuing merit.
The sage has no anxious thoughts,
no contrived reserves,
welcoming not what comes,
chasing not what goes.
Though people move east, west, south, and north,
he stands alone at the center.
Thus amid numerous distortions,
he does not lose his uprightness;
while all under heaven flows,
he alone does not leave his domain.
Thus he neither pursues beauty
nor avoids ugliness,
following the Way of Heaven;
he neither initiates
nor insists on his own views,
abiding by Heaven's principles.
He does not plan ahead,
nor neglects the timing,
aligning with Heaven's schedule;
he does not seek gains,
nor refuses blessings,
obeying Heaven's rules.
Not seeking what he lacks,
not losing what he has gained,
within there are no strange calamities,
without there are no strange fortunes.
When fortune and misfortune do not arise,
how can there be harm from others!
Doing good attracts observation,
doing wrong invites criticism;
observation leads to blame,
criticism breeds trouble.
Thus the path of Dao cannot be advanced for fame,
but can be retreated for self-cultivation;
it cannot be used for profit,
but can help avoid harm.
Therefore, the sage does not seek fame through action,
nor praise through wisdom.
He follows nature's laws,
with no personal interference.
Anxiety cannot overcome destiny,
action cannot surpass virtue,
affairs cannot exceed the Dao.
Those who act may not succeed,
those who seek may not obtain.
Humans have limitations,
while the Dao is all-penetrating,
and contending with the Dao brings disaster.
Thus the Book of Songs says:
"Without conscious knowledge,
follow the rules of God."
Having wisdom yet not acting,
shares the same path as having no wisdom;
having ability yet not intervening,
shares the same virtue as having no ability.
His wisdom
is revealed only when advisors come,
then his movements are perceived;
his ability
is shown only when tasks are assigned,
then his actions are noticed.
Having wisdom as if without,
having ability as if without,
this is the correctness of the Dao's principle.
Thus his achievements cover the world,
yet he displays no excellence;
his grace extends to later generations,
yet he claims no fame;
for when the Dao's principle prevails, human effort vanishes.
Fame and the Dao cannot both shine,
when people love fame, the Dao is not used,
when the Dao prevails over people, fame ceases.
The Dao and humans compete for prominence.
Those who glorify humans
extinguish the Dao.
When humans are glorified and the Dao extinguished,
danger is not far away.
Thus when the world has sage-like fame,
flattery arrives daily.
Those who seek posthumous fame must do good,
those who want to do good must create affairs,
creating affairs means abandoning public good for private gain,
turning from destiny to self-will.
Wishing to be praised for doing good,
and establishing fame for being virtuous,
then governance does not follow tradition,
and affairs do not accord with timing.
Governance not following tradition
brings much blame;
affairs not according with timing
yield no achievement.
With much blame and little achievement,
having no means to remedy it,
they act recklessly seeking success,
and intervene arbitrarily aiming for results.
Even if successful,
it cannot offset the blame;
if failed,
it is enough to ruin themselves.
Therefore, regarding doing good as seriously as doing wrong,
one approaches the Dao.
The world is not without honest men,
yet when dividing wealth, they must draw lots to decide shares,
believing that those with intentions cannot be as fair
as those without.
The world is not without incorruptible men,
yet those guarding treasures must lock doors and seal completely,
believing that those with desires cannot be as honest
as those without.
When people point out his flaws, he resents them;
when a mirror reveals his ugliness, he praises the mirror.
If one can interact with things without self-involvement,
then one avoids burdens.
Gōngsūn Lóng dazzled with words and traded fame,
Dèng Xī used clever arguments to confuse laws,
Sū Qín excelled in persuasion and lost his life.
Following the Dao, goodness shows no ostentation;
abiding by its principles, cleverness bears no fame.
Thus those who use cleverness in combat
begin with openness,
but often end in secrecy;
those who govern with cunning
start with order,
but often end in chaos.
Making water flow downward
anyone can manage;
forcing it upward
requires cleverness.
Thus when ornament prevails, substance is obscured;
when crafty evil prevails, uprightness is blocked.
Virtue can be cultivated in oneself,
but cannot make others violent;
the Way can bring order to oneself,
but cannot make others chaotic.
Even with the treasure of sagehood,
if one does not encounter an age of violence and chaos,
one can preserve one's life,
but cannot become a hegemon or king.
Tāng and Wǔ became kings
because they encountered Jié's
and Zhòu's tyranny.
Jié and Zhòu did not become tyrannical because of Tāng's
and Wǔ's worthiness;
rather, Tāng and Wǔ encountered Jié's
and Zhòu's tyranny and thus became kings.
Therefore, even a worthy king
must await the right encounter.
Encounter means
being able to meet with the times and thereby attain it—
it is not something that knowledge and ability can seek and achieve.
The gentleman cultivates his conduct yet makes goodness nameless,
practices generosity yet makes benevolence unmanifest;
thus, scholars practice goodness without knowing whence it comes,
the people enjoy benefits without knowing whence they arise,
and so there is non-action yet self-order.
If goodness is manifest, scholars contend for fame;
if benefits have a clear source, the people contend for merit;
once these two contentions arise,
even if there are worthy ones,
they cannot bring order.
Therefore, the sage conceals traces in doing good
and stills fame in practicing benevolence.
Forming external alliances for support,
serving great powers for safety—
this is not as good as governing internally and awaiting the time.
In all cases of serving others,
if not with precious goods and silks,
then necessarily with humble words.
Serving with jades and silks—
then goods are exhausted yet desires remain unsatisfied;
bowing low with flattering words—
then persuasion occurs yet alliances are not secured;
making pacts and swearing oaths—
then agreements are fixed yet betrayal comes unexpectedly;
even if ceding tiny portions of the state to serve others,
without a way of self-reliance,
it is insufficient for preservation.
If one truly abandons the strategy of external alliances
and diligently cultivates affairs within one's borders,
exhausts the land's productivity to increase its stores,
encourages the people to die hard to strengthen its walls,
with ruler and subjects of one mind,
sovereign and ministers sharing purpose,
uniting to guard the altars of soil and grain,
dying in instruction yet the people not deserting—
then those seeking fame will not attack the guiltless,
and those seeking profit will not assault the hard to conquer;
this is the way that surely preserves.
The people have a Way that all follow together,
have laws that all abide by together;
because righteousness cannot make them firmly united,
and authority cannot make them necessarily committed,
therefore a ruler is established to unify the people.
The ruler holding to oneness brings order;
lacking constancy brings chaos.
The way of rulership
is not that by which one acts,
but that by which one does not act.
What is called non-action?
The wise not using their position to engage in affairs,
the brave not using their position to commit violence,
the benevolent not using their position to bestow favors—
this may be called non-action.
Now non-action means attaining oneness.
Oneness
is the root of the myriad things,
the way of having no rivals.
As for human nature generally,
in youth there is wild exuberance,
in prime there is violent strength,
in old age there is fondness for profit.
In one person's lifetime there are already several changes;
how much more so when rulers frequently change laws,
and states frequently change rulers!
People use their positions to pursue their likes and dislikes;
the bypaths below become impossible to fully manage;
thus when the ruler loses oneness, chaos ensues,
worse than when there is no ruler.
Therefore the *Shī* says:
"Not erring, not forgetting,
follow the old statutes."
This refers to this.
If the ruler favors wisdom,
then he turns against the times and relies on himself,
abandoning method and employing scheming.
The things of the world are vast, yet wisdom is shallow;
using the shallow to cover the vast—
none have been capable of this.
Relying solely on one's wisdom,
loss is sure to be great.
Thus favoring wisdom
is a way to exhaust techniques;
favoring courage,
then one underestimates enemies and neglects preparations,
relying on oneself and refusing assistance.
The strength of one person
to fend off strong enemies,
not relying on the multitude but solely using personal ability—
is surely unbearable.
Thus favoring courage
is a dangerous technique.
Favoring giving,
then there is no fixed portion.
If the portions above are not fixed,
then the expectations below have no end.
If increasing taxes and levies,
filling treasuries and storehouses,
then one becomes an enemy to the people.
Taking little and giving much—
such a method has never existed.
Thus favoring giving
is a way that invites resentment.
Benevolence, wisdom, courage, strength—
these are fine talents in people,
yet none suffice to govern the world.
From this perspective,
worthiness and ability are insufficient to rely on,
and the Way and its techniques are what can be followed—this is clear.
The sage overcomes the heart-mind;
the multitude overcomes desires.
The gentleman practices upright *qì*;
the petty person practices corrupt *qì*.
What is inwardly harmonious with one's nature,
outwardly conforms to righteousness,
acts according to principle,
and is not bound by external things—
this is upright *qì*.
What craves flavors,
indulges in sounds and sights,
arises from joy and anger,
and disregards future troubles—
this is corrupt *qì*.
The corrupt and the upright injure each other;
desires and nature harm each other;
they cannot stand together.
One is established, the other abandoned;
therefore the sage reduces desires and follows nature.
The eyes love beauty,
the ears love sounds,
the mouth loves flavors;
contact with them brings pleasure.
Not knowing benefit and harm—
this is desire.
Eating what does not calm the body,
hearing what does not accord with the Way,
viewing what is not harmonious with nature—
when these three gates contend,
what uses righteousness as control
is the heart-mind.
Cutting off a boil is not without pain;
drinking bitter medicine is not without suffering;
yet one does it
for the benefit of the body.
Drinking when thirsty is not without pleasure;
eating heavily when hungry is not without satisfaction;
yet one refrains
because it harms nature.
These four things—
the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth do not know what to take or leave;
the heart-mind controls them,
so each gets its proper place.
From this perspective,
desires cannot be given free rein—
this is clear.
In all governing the self and nurturing nature,
regulating rest and activity,
moderating drink and food,
harmonizing joy and anger,
easing movement and stillness—
if what lies in oneself is attained,
then corrupt *qì* naturally does not arise.
How could this be like worrying about the rise of ailments and
the eruption of boils and preparing for them in advance!
A cauldron that holds an ox, when boiling, dares not admit flies and gnats;
jade from Kūnlún Mountain, when pure, cannot be defiled by dust and dirt.
The sage, without a mind that rejects, has a mind without ugliness;
without seizing beauty, yet beauty is not lost.
Thus in sacrificing and thinking of ancestors, one does not seek blessings;
in feasting guests and cultivating respect, one does not think of virtue;
only by not seeking can one possess it.
Those in exalted positions are esteemed
because they uphold public principles without private biases,
hence they are called honorable,
not virtuous.
Those who possess vast lands are deemed equitable
because they follow constant methods without cunning schemes,
hence they are called just,
not wise.
Internally, they avoid violent acts that would alienate the common people,
externally, they refrain from conspicuous virtues that would provoke jealousy among the feudal lords.
The rituals between superior and inferior
are inherited and never abandoned,
yet commentators remain indifferent, seeing nothing to observe—
this is what is called concealing the formless.
If not for concealing the formless,
how could anything take form?
The way of the Three Dynasties
lay in following natural conditions.
Thus, Yǔ channeled the rivers,
by following the water's flow;
Hòujì sowed seeds and cultivated grains,
by adapting to the land;
Tāng and Wǔ quelled violence and chaos,
by seizing the opportune moment.
Therefore, the world can be attained but not seized;
hegemony can be accepted but not sought.
Relying on wisdom leads to disputes with others;
relying on strength leads to struggles with others.
There is no way to make people devoid of wisdom,
but there is a way to prevent them from using their wisdom against oneself;
there is no way to make people devoid of strength,
but there is a way to prevent them from exerting their strength against oneself.
These two principles endure and become evident over time.
Thus, if a ruler's virtue remains unseen,
the feudal lords will not take precautions;
if his incompetence remains hidden,
the common people will not resent him.
Without the people's resentment, their resources can be utilized;
without the feudal lords' precautions,
the opportunities of the world can be embraced.
Affairs are accomplished through shared efforts with the multitude,
achievements are realized through alignment with the times—
the sage has no personal involvement.
Hence, Lǎozǐ said:
"The tiger finds no place to use its claws,
the rhinoceros finds no place to use its horns."
This aptly describes it.
A drum does not store sound within itself,
thus it can produce sound;
a mirror does not preset forms,
thus it can reflect shapes.
Metal and stone have the potential for sound,
but without striking, they do not ring;
pipes and flutes have the capacity for music,
but without blowing, they produce no tones.
The sage stores inwardly,
not initiating actions for external things,
controlling events as they arise,
responding to objects as they appear.
Adorning the exterior harms the interior;
forcing emotions injures the spirit;
displaying embellishments obscures the substance.
One who never forgets their virtue even for a moment
will inevitably be constrained by their nature;
one who never forgets their appearance even within a hundred paces
will inevitably burden their form.
Thus, beautiful feathers and wings harm the bones;
lush branches and leaves harm the roots.
To achieve both beauties
is impossible under heaven.
Heaven has light,
yet does not worry about the people's darkness;
the people bore doors and carve windows
to obtain illumination themselves.
Earth has wealth,
yet does not worry about the people's poverty;
the people cut trees and clear grass
to attain prosperity themselves.
Those of utmost virtue and way are like hills and mountains,
towering and unmoving,
yet travelers take them as guides.
Straightening oneself and sufficing things,
not acting as a benefactor to others,
those who utilize this do not receive their grace,
hence there is tranquility and endurance.
Heaven and earth give nothing,
thus they take nothing away;
the sun and moon bestow no favor,
thus they incur no resentment.
Those who delight in gaining will have much resentment;
those who delight in giving will be skilled at taking.
Only by erasing traces through non-action and following heaven and earth's spontaneity
can one master principle and avoid clinging to fame.
When fame arises, the way does not prevail;
when the way prevails, people hold no positions.
Thus, praise begets slander;
goodness seen begets evil followed.
Benefit is the beginning of harm;
fortune is the precursor to misfortune.
Only those who do not seek benefit avoid harm;
only those who do not seek fortune avoid misfortune.
A feudal lord who seeks hegemony will lose his lordship;
a hegemon who seeks kingship will forfeit his hegemony.
Thus, a state considers preservation as its constant;
hegemony and kingship are but temporary lodgings;
the body considers life as its constant;
wealth and honor are but temporary lodgings.
One who can avoid harming the state for the sake of the world,
and avoid harming the self for the sake of the state,
may be entrusted with the world.
Those who do not know the way
abandon what they already have
and seek what they have not obtained.
They toil in anxiety and worry,
engaging in crooked schemes.
When fortune comes, they rejoice;
when misfortune comes, they fear.
Their spirit is wearied by plotting,
their wisdom hastened by affairs.
As misfortunes and fortunes sprout,
they never repent throughout life,
and what they themselves produce
instead brings sorrow to others.
Without joy, there is worry;
their inner selves never attain peace.
Holding to nothing with no mirror to reflect,
they are called madmen.
If a ruler favors benevolence,
the无功 will be rewarded,
and the guilty will be released;
if he favors punishment,
the meritorious will be dismissed,
and the innocent will be executed.
But one without preferences
executes without incurring resentment,
bestows without claiming virtue,
following the plumb line and straightedge,
with no personal involvement in affairs,
like heaven and earth—
why would they not cover and carry all?
Thus, to unite and harmonize—
that is the ruler's role;
to regulate and punish—
that is the law's role.
When the people have been punished,
they have no resentment or regret—
this is called the way.
When the way prevails,
people have no affairs to trouble them.
The sage has no bizarre clothing,
no extraordinary conduct.
His attire draws no stares,
his actions draw no gazes,
his words invite no debate.
Successful yet not flashy,
destitute yet not fearful,
honored yet not conspicuous,
hidden yet not obscure,
different yet not strange,
his appearance shared with the multitude—
it cannot be named,
this is called great penetration.
Bowing and yielding in ascent and descent,
hastening and hovering in circumspection,
are done out of necessity,
not innate to one's nature.
Emotions lack external validation,
yet one acts compelled by necessity,
without unraveling the structure—
how could it be deliberately added?
Thus, one who sings out of necessity
does not strive for sorrow;
one who dances out of necessity
does not boast of beauty.
Singing and dancing without striving for sorrow or beauty
lack a rooted heart.
A skilled gambler does not crave excessive gains,
nor fears losing,
maintaining a calm and composed mind,
placing bets with precision,
acting in accordance with reason,
and though not guaranteed victory,
will surely accumulate many chips.
Why is this?
Success lies in method,
not in desire.
A skilled charioteer does not greedily seek the lead,
nor dreads lagging behind alone,
adjusting speed with ease in hand,
harmonizing the heart with the horse's pace,
and though not assured to be first,
the horse's strength is fully utilized.
Why is this?
Leading stems from technique,
not from desire.
Thus, eliminating desire ensures victory through method,
and abandoning cunning establishes the Way.
A merchant with too many ventures becomes poor,
a craftsman with too many skills becomes destitute,
due to a lack of focus.
So, a large tree harms its branches,
and vast waters harm their depth.
Having wisdom without strategy,
even drilling through won't reach the goal;
possessing numerous skills without a unified Way,
even if attained, cannot be maintained.
Hence, the "Book of Songs" says:
"The virtuous gentleman,
his demeanor is unified.
His demeanor unified,
his heart is tied firm."
A gentleman ties his heart to oneness!
Shùn played the five-stringed qín,
singing the poem of the "South Wind,"
to govern the world.
Zhōu Gōng did not clear away the meat dishes before him,
nor took down the bells and drums from their hangings,
yet assisted King Chéng in bringing peace to the land.
A commoner guarding a hundred acres,
has no leisure to rest,
with nowhere to shift his duties.
For one person to oversee the entire world,
finding the day long and governance insufficient,
it is by delegating to others.
Those in high positions are like the ceremonial corpse,
officials are like the priests.
The corpse does not skin dogs or roast pigs,
even if capable, it does not do so,
and not doing so causes no harm;
the arrangement of sacrificial vessels,
the order of millet and grains,
though knowing,
it does not instruct,
and not instructing,
does no harm.
One who cannot perform rituals,
should not be a priest,
but it doesn't hinder being the corpse;
one who cannot drive,
should not be a coachman,
but it doesn't hinder being an assistant.
Thus, the higher the position, the more leisurely the person,
the greater the office, the fewer the tasks.
Like tuning a qín,
though the small strings are tight,
the large strings must be loose.
Non-action is the substance of the Way;
holding back is the appearance of the Way.
Non-action controls action,
through method;
holding back controls leading,
through technique.
Relying on method brings strength,
understanding technique brings peace.
Offering someone the Biànshì's jade,
if not accepted,
is due to haste;
seeking and obtaining it,
even if resented, not refused,
is due to patience.
Three people sharing a room,
two arguing,
each believing themselves right,
unable to listen,
the third, though foolish,
will decide from the sidelines,
not by wisdom,
but by non-contention.
Two people fighting,
a weakling nearby,
helping one leads to victory,
rescuing one prevents harm,
the fighters, though strong,
are controlled by the weakling,
not by courage,
but by non-fighting.
From this, it is seen that
patience controls haste,
calm overcomes agitation,
through technique.
Abandoning the Way and technique,
seeking chance encounters,
altering constants and changing traditions,
using clever obstructions,
blaming oneself for mistakes,
taking success as opportunity,
acting secretly and changing erroneously,
never awakening in a lifetime,
this is called madness.
Bowing to misfortune,
swelling with fortune,
regretting errors,
boasting of achievements,
never turning back,
this is called madness.
Round conforms to the compass,
square to the square,
moving like beasts,
stopping in patterns,
can lead few,
but not many.
Vegetables in neat rows,
jars and pots with bases,
measuring grain to pound,
counting rice to cook,
can manage a household,
but not a state.
Washing cups to eat,
cleaning vessels to drink,
rinsing before serving,
can support family elders,
but not feast an army.
Without simplicity, one cannot govern greatly;
without conciseness, one cannot unite the masses.
Great music must be simple,
great rites must be concise.
Simplicity enables heaven,
conciseness enables earth.
Great music holds no resentment,
great rites make no demands,
within the four seas,
all are unified,
thus enabling imperial rule.
One with a troubled heart,
cannot find peace even on a fine bed with mats,
cannot enjoy delicacies like wild rice and fattened ox,
cannot delight in the sounds of qín, sè, and yú.
When worries are resolved and anxieties removed,
then one eats sweetly, sleeps peacefully,
lives securely, and enjoys freely.
From this, it is seen that
nature has its joys,
and death its sorrows.
Now, striving to increase what nature cannot enjoy,
while harming what brings natural joy,
thus even if possessing the world's wealth,
honored as the Son of Heaven,
one cannot avoid being a sorrowful person.
Human nature, in general,
delights in tranquility and hates anxiety,
enjoys leisure and detests toil.
A heart often free of desires,
can be called tranquil;
a body often free of tasks,
can be called leisurely.
Wandering the heart in tranquility,
resting the body in leisure,
awaiting heaven's decree,
finding inner joy,
without external pressures,
even the vastness of the world
cannot shift one's steadfastness,
the sun and moon wane without affecting one's will,
thus even if lowly, one feels noble,
even if poor, one feels rich.
The great Way has no form,
great benevolence has no favorites,
great debate has no sound,
great integrity does not boast.
Great courage does not boast,
these five un abandoned,
and one nearly approaches the right path.
An army with too many orders becomes chaotic,
wine with too many restrictions leads to disputes.
Chaos results in defeat and surrender,
disputes lead to mutual harm.
Thus, what begins with grandeur often ends in baseness,
what begins with joy often ends in sorrow,
and what starts simply
must end in harmony.
Now, with fine wine and delicacies to entertain guests,
humble postures and gentle words to receive them,
one intends to foster joy,
yet competing to fill cups
instead gives rise to fights,
fighting leads to mutual injury,
three clans bear grudges,
reverting to what they detest,
this is the harm caused by wine.
The fault of the Shī is bias,
the fault of music is criticism,
the fault of rites is blame.
The Zhǐ note is not without the Yǔ sound,
nor is the Yǔ note without the Zhǐ sound,
all five notes have their sounds,
yet they are named by Zhǐ and Yǔ
because of their dominance.
Thus, benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and courage
are all possessed by the sage,
yet each is given a single name
to denote its greatness.
Yáng energy arises in the northeast
and ends in the southwest;
yīn energy arises in the southwest
and ends in the northeast.
At the beginning of yīn and yáng,
they are balanced and similar,
but as each grows in its kind,
they encroach and drift apart,
some becoming so hot as to scorch sand,
some so cold as to freeze water,
hence the sage is cautious about what accumulates.
Water emerges from mountains and enters the sea,
grain grows in fields and is stored in barns,
the sage, seeing the beginning, knows the end.
On the mat,
coarse rushes come first;
in the wine vessel,
plain water comes first;
on the stand,
raw fish comes first;
in the bowl,
simple broth comes first.
These are not pleasing to the ears and eyes,
nor satisfying to the mouth and belly,
yet the ancient kings valued them,
prioritizing the root over the branch.
The sage interacts with things,
amid countless changes and turns,
there must be an unchanging core that responds to change.
Cold and warmth are opposites,
in extreme cold, the ground cracks and water freezes,
yet fire does not diminish its heat;
in extreme heat, stones melt and metal flows,
yet fire does not increase its intensity.
The changes of cold and heat
do not diminish or enhance it,
for its nature is fixed.
The sage always follows rather than leads,
responds rather than initiates;
not advancing to seek,
not retreating to yield;
waiting for three years with the times,
the times may leave me behind;
leaving the times for three years,
the times may be behind me;
neither departing nor approaching,
standing firm in one's place.
The Way of Heaven has no favorites,
it only sides with virtue.
Those who possess the Way
do not miss opportunities with others;
those without the Way
lose opportunities and seek to take from others.
Rectify oneself and await destiny,
for when the time comes, it cannot be welcomed and reversed;
blocking and forcing a meeting,
when the time has passed, it cannot be pursued and retrieved.
Thus, do not say, "I have no means, so the world stays away,"
nor say, "I do not desire it, so the world does not come."
The ancients who preserved themselves
delighted in virtue and forgot their lowliness,
thus fame did not stir their will;
delighted in the Way and forgot their poverty,
thus profit did not move their hearts.
Though fame and profit fill the world,
they are not enough to sway one's will,
thus one can embrace all and remain joyful,
tranquil and serene.
Therefore, those who govern themselves well
can be spoken to about the Way.
From oneself upward to the vast wilderness,
it is indeed far;
from death to the endlessness of heaven and earth,
it is indeed immense.
With a life of limited years,
to worry about the chaos under heaven
is like worrying that the river has too little water
and weeping to increase it.
The tortoise lives three thousand years,
the ephemeral fly but three days;
for the ephemeral to worry about the tortoise's means of nurturing life
would surely make people laugh.
Thus, those who do not worry about the chaos under heaven
but delight in governing themselves
can be spoken to about the Way.
The noble person doing good cannot ensure blessings will come,
nor can avoiding wrongdoing prevent calamities from arriving.
When blessings arrive,
they are not sought,
thus one does not boast of merit;
when calamities come,
they are not caused by one,
thus one does not regret one's actions.
When utmost inner cultivation meets with unexpected disaster,
it is all due to Heaven,
not to man,
thus the heart remains constantly peaceful and detached,
unburdened in virtue;
barking dogs do not startle,
for one trusts in one's true nature.
Therefore, those who know the Way are not perplexed,
those who know fate do not worry.
When a ruler of ten thousand chariots dies,
his bones are buried in the wild plains,
his spirit is honored in the bright hall,
for the spirit is more valued than the form.
Thus, when the spirit governs, the form follows;
when the form dominates, the spirit is impoverished.
Though intelligence and perception are used,
they must return to the spirit,
this is called the Great Balance.
In ancient times, the use of arms
was not for the benefit of expanding territory or coveting treasures,
but to preserve the perishing and continue the severed,
quell the chaos under heaven,
and rid the myriad people of harm.
All creatures with blood and breath,
bearing fangs and horns,
with claws in front and spurs behind,
those with horns butt,
those with teeth bite,
those with venom sting,
those with hooves kick,
in joy, they play together,
in anger, they harm each other,
such is their innate nature.
Humans have needs for clothing and food,
yet things cannot suffice,
thus they live together in mixed groups,
if distribution is unequal,
and demands unmet,
then contention arises.
Contention leads to the strong coercing the weak and the brave invading the timid.
Humans lack strong sinews and bones,
or sharp claws and teeth,
so they cut leather to make armor,
and smelt iron to make blades.
Greedy and gluttonous individuals
ravage the world,
causing the myriad people to turmoil,
unable to find peace in what they have.
The sage rises with fervor,
to punish the violent,
pacify the chaotic age,
smooth dangers and remove filth,
turning turbidity into clarity,
and peril into peace,
so humanity may not be cut off.
The origins of warfare are indeed distant!
Huángdì once battled Yándì,
Zhuānxù once contended with Gònggōng.
Thus, Huángdì fought on the plains of Zhuōlù,
Yáo battled by the shores of Dānshuǐ,
Shùn attacked the Yǒumiáo,
Qǐ assaulted the Yǒuhù.
Since the time of the Five Emperors, it could not be ceased,
how much less in an age of decline!
Military forces are instruments
for suppressing violence and quelling rebellion.
When Yándì caused fire disasters,
Huángdì thus captured him;
when Gònggōng created flood damage,
Zhuānxū thus executed him.
When instructing them with principles
and guiding them with virtue fails to secure compliance,
then awe them with martial might.
When aweing them with martial might fails to secure obedience,
then control them with weapons and armor.
Thus, when a sage employs military force,
it is like combing hair or weeding seedlings:
what is removed is minor,
while the benefits gained are substantial.
Killing innocent people
to sustain an unrighteous ruler
brings the gravest harm;
exhausting the wealth of the world
to satisfy one man's desires
invites the deepest calamity.
If Xià Jié
and Yīn Zhòu had faced immediate consequences for harming the people,
they would not have resorted to creating the roasting pillar;
if Jìn Lì
and Sòng Kāng had met their end upon committing a single unrighteous act,
they would not have escalated to invasion and tyranny.
These four rulers
all had minor faults that went unpunished,
thus leading to plundering the world,
harming the common people,
indulging one man's wickedness,
and perpetuating disasters across the land,
which the principles of Heaven do not condone.
The purpose of establishing a ruler
is to suppress violence and quell rebellion.
Yet if one harnesses the strength of the masses
only to become a cruel oppressor,
it is like adding wings to a tiger—
why not eliminate him!
Just as those who stock ponds with fish must remove otters,
and those who raise fowl and beasts must eliminate wolves,
how much more so in governing people!
Therefore, the military of a true king or hegemon
is planned with deliberation,
strategized with schemes,
and supported with righteousness,
not to destroy what exists,
but to preserve what is perishing.
Thus, upon hearing that a hostile ruler is brutalizing his people,
they dispatch troops to his borders,
condemning his unrighteousness,
and criticizing his transgressions.
When the army reaches his outskirts,
the commander orders:
"Do not cut down trees!
Do not disturb graves!
Do not burn crops!
Do not destroy stockpiles!
Do not capture civilians!
Do not seize livestock!"
Then a proclamation is issued:
"The ruler of this state,
arrogant toward Heaven and disrespectful to spirits,
unjust in trials, killing the innocent,
slaughtering the guiltless,
is one whom Heaven condemns
and the people despise.
Our army's arrival
aims to depose the unrighteous and restore the virtuous.
Those who defy Heaven's way
and lead the people astray
shall perish, clan and all!
Those whose families comply
shall be rewarded with family estates.
Those whose villages comply
shall be rewarded with village honors.
Those whose townships comply
shall be enfeoffed with townships.
Those whose counties comply
shall be made marquises of counties."
Conquering a state without harming its people,
deposing its ruler and reforming its governance,
honoring its scholars and promoting its worthies,
aiding its orphans and widows,
relieving its poor,
freeing prisoners from jail,
and rewarding the meritorious.
The people open their gates to welcome them,
prepare rice and store it,
fearing only that they might not come.
This is how Tāng
and Wǔ achieved kingship,
and how Qí Huán
and Jìn Wén established hegemony.
Thus, when a ruler is unprincipled,
the people yearn for troops
as in drought they long for rain,
or thirst they crave drink—
who would then take up arms against them?
Therefore, when righteous troops arrive,
they halt without battle.
In later ages, armies
face rulers who, though unprincipled,
all dig moats,
fortify walls and defend,
while attackers seek not to suppress violence or remove harm,
but to invade lands and expand territories.
Hence, it comes to corpses fallen and bloodshed,
protracted over days,
with the achievements of kings and hegemon's rarely emerging,
due to their self-serving motives.
Those who fight for territory cannot become kings,
those who fight for themselves cannot establish merit.
Those who act for others gain many supporters,
those who act for themselves are abandoned by the masses.
With popular support,
even the weak become strong;
abandoned by the masses,
even the great must perish.
Armies lose strength when they stray from the Way,
and gain strength when they follow it;
generals become inept when they stray from the Way,
and skillful when they follow it;
states survive when they uphold the Way,
and perish when they lose it.
What is called the Way
embodies roundness and models squareness,
turns its back to darkness and embraces light,
is soft on the left and firm on the right,
treads in obscurity and wears brightness,
changes without constancy,
holds the origin of unity,
and responds boundlessly,
which is called divine intelligence.
Roundness
represents Heaven,
squareness
represents Earth.
Heaven is round and endless,
so its form cannot be seen;
Earth is square and boundless,
so its gates cannot be peered into.
Heaven transforms and nurtures without form,
Earth grows and produces beyond measure,
vast and boundless,
who can fathom its depths!
All things have signs,
only the Way has none.
The reason it has no signs
is that it lacks constant form or state.
It revolves without end,
mirroring the movement of sun and moon,
as spring and autumn alternate,
as day and night cycle,
ending only to begin anew,
brightening only to dim again,
with none able to grasp its order.
Instituting punishment yet having no punishment,
thus achievements can be made;
mastering things without being a thing,
thus victory is inexhaustible.
Punishment and warfare reach their zenith
when they arrive at no punishment,
which may be called the zenith of zeniths.
Therefore, the greatest military leaves no wounds,
communing with spirits and gods,
the five weapons need not be sharpened,
and none under Heaven dare oppose it.
War drums need not leave their storage,
yet all rulers tremble in fear wherever they are.
Thus, those who win in the temple become emperors,
those who transform spiritually become kings.
What is called winning in the temple
means modeling Heaven's Way,
and spiritual transformation
means emulating the four seasons.
Cultivating governance within one's borders draws distant admiration for one's virtue,
securing victory before battle makes other states submit to one's might,
all due to internal order.
Those who attained the Way in ancient times
remained still and emulated heaven and earth,
moved in accordance with the sun and moon,
their joy and anger aligned with the four seasons,
their shouts comparable to thunder,
their tones and breath not contrary to the eight winds,
their bending and stretching not violating the five measures.
From the lowly creatures with scales and shells
to the lofty ones with fur and feathers,
like branches following the trunk and leaves threaded together,
the myriad things and hundred clans,
from root to tip,
all have their order.
Therefore, they enter small spaces without feeling cramped,
dwell in large ones without feeling empty,
soak into metal and stone,
moisten plants and trees;
within the cosmos and the six directions,
down to the tip of a fine hair,
all follow in harmony.
The Way's pervasive influence,
subtle and delicate,
is present everywhere,
hence its power to prevail is great.
In archery,
if the posture and measure are not correct,
the target cannot be hit;
a steed, if one part is not used properly,
cannot cover a thousand lǐ.
Those who fight but do not win
fail not on the day the drums beat,
but because their usual conduct lacked discipline long before.
Thus, an army that has attained the Way
does not need to set chariot wheels in motion,
saddles are not placed on horses,
drums do not stir the dust,
banners remain furled,
armor avoids arrows,
blades do not taste blood,
the court does not change positions,
merchants do not leave their shops,
farmers do not abandon their fields.
By summoning righteousness and holding others accountable,
large states will surely pay homage,
small towns will surely surrender.
Acting upon the people's desires
and utilizing their strength,
to eliminate cruelty and remove villains,
thus, shared benefit leads to mutual sacrifice,
shared feelings lead to mutual accomplishment,
shared desires lead to mutual pursuit,
shared aversions lead to mutual assistance.
Moving in accord with the Way,
the world becomes its guide;
considering the people's interests,
the world fights for it.
Hunters chasing game,
with chariots speeding and people running,
each exerting their full effort,
without the threat of punishment,
yet they coordinate to drive and block,
because they share the same benefit.
Crossing a river in the same boat,
suddenly encountering wind and waves,
sons of a hundred clans,
quickly grabbing oars and steering the boat,
like left and right hands,
not because they are close,
but because their worry is the same.
Therefore, when a wise king employs his army,
it is to rid the world of harm,
and to share the benefits with all the people.
The people's willingness to serve
is like a son serving his father,
a younger brother serving his elder;
the force applied
is like a collapsing mountain or a bursting dam,
what enemy dares to withstand it!
Thus, those skilled in using troops
utilize them for their own purposes;
those unskilled in using troops
use them for their own personal gain.
Using them for their own purposes,
then all under heaven can be utilized;
using them for personal gain,
then what is gained is meager.
There are three levels of military strategy:
governing the state,
managing the territory,
practicing benevolence and righteousness,
spreading virtue and kindness,
establishing just laws,
blocking evil paths,
ministers drawing close and adhering,
the common people harmonious and united,
sovereign and subjects of one mind,
ruler and ministers combining strength,
feudal lords submitting to its might and all quarters embracing its virtue,
cultivating governance in the court yet repelling enemies a thousand lǐ away,
with a mere gesture or pointing, the world responds—
this is the highest form of using troops.
Vast territory and numerous people,
wise ruler and loyal generals,
prosperous state and strong army,
strict discipline and trust,
clear commands,
when two armies face each other,
with drums and bells in sight,
before weapons clash, the enemy flees and scatters—
this is the middle form of using troops.
Knowing the suitability of the land,
familiar with the advantages of strategic passes,
understanding the changes of orthodox and unorthodox tactics,
observing the methods of formation and dispersal,
gripping the drumstick and beating the drum,
when naked blades meet,
flying arrows exchange,
wading through blood and treading on intestines,
carrying the dead and aiding the wounded,
blood flowing for a thousand lǐ,
exposed bones filling the fields,
only then achieving victory—
this is the lowest form of using troops.
Now, all under heaven know to manage the trivial,
but none know to cultivate the root,
abandoning the root and tending to the branches.
The means by which the military assists victory are many,
but the means that ensure victory are few.
Sturdy armor and sharp weapons,
solid chariots and fine horses,
ample supplies and provisions,
numerous and well-equipped soldiers—
these are great assets to the army,
yet victory does not lie in them.
Understanding the movements of stars, sun, and moon,
the patterns of punishments, virtues, and extraordinary changes,
the advantages of positioning and direction—
these aid in battle,
yet complete victory does not lie in them.
What ensures a good general's victory
often involves unfathomable wisdom
and indescribable ways,
difficult to share with the masses.
Discussing appointments carefully,
timing movements appropriately,
clarifying roles of officers and soldiers,
managing weapons and armor,
organizing the five-man squads,
linking the hundred-man units,
clarifying drums and banners—
this is the duty of the Grand Commandant.
Managing military camps,
allocating land fairly,
positioning troops correctly—
this is the duty of the Marshal.
Knowing the dangers and ease ahead and behind,
assessing the enemy's difficulty and ease,
sending scouts without omission—
this is the duty of the Scout.
Maintaining roads swiftly,
managing moving supplies,
ensuring fair measurements,
settling troops orderly,
providing wells and stoves—
this is the duty of the Minister of Works.
Managing supplies in the rear,
moving camps without loss,
no excessive carts,
no left-behind equipment—
this is the duty of the Supply Officer.
All these five officers, to the general,
are like limbs and hands to the body;
one must select the right persons,
assess their talents,
so that each office is胜任 by its holder,
and each person can perform their duties.
Instruct them with governance,
clarify them with orders,
so that they become like tigers and leopards with claws and teeth,
or flying birds with six wings—
none will fail to be utilized.
Yet all these are tools that assist victory,
not what ensures victory.
The success or failure of the military
fundamentally lies in governance.
If governance prevails over the people,
and subordinates adhere to their superiors,
then the military is strong.
If the people prevail over governance,
and subordinates rebel against their superiors,
then the military is weak.
Therefore, virtue and righteousness sufficient to win the hearts of the world's people,
achievements sufficient to meet the world's urgent needs,
selections sufficient to gain the hearts of worthy scholars,
planning sufficient to understand the balance of strength and weakness—
these are the roots of certain victory.
Vast territory and numerous people
are not enough to constitute strength;
solid armor and sharp weapons
are not enough to guarantee victory;
high walls and deep moats
are not enough to ensure security;
harsh commands and numerous punishments
are not enough to establish authority.
Those who implement policies for preservation,
though small, will surely survive;
those who implement policies for ruin,
though large, will surely perish.
In the past, the territory of the Chǔ people
stretched south to Yuán
and Xiāng, north around Yǐng
and Sì, west encompassing Bā
and Shǔ, east wrapping around Tán
and Pī, with Yǐng
and Rǔ as ditches,
the Jiāng and Hàn as moats,
fortified by Dènglín,
and encircled by Fāngchéng.
The mountains reached the clouds,
the valleys were too deep for sunlight;
the terrain was advantageous and easily defensible,
the soldiers and people were brave,
with alligator hides, rhinoceros, and wild oxen
used for armor and helmets,
long spears and short lances
aligned in the front ranks,
crossbows massed in the rear,
chariots deployed on the flanks,
swift as arrows,
united as thunder and lightning,
dispersing like wind and rain.
Yet their army was defeated at Chuíshā,
and their forces shattered at Bójǔ.
Despite the strength of the Chǔ state,
measuring its land and counting its people,
it could have divided the world in half.
However, King Huái feared Mèngcháng Jūn to the north,
abandoned the defense of his altars of land and grain, and submitted to powerful Qín,
leading to military defeat and territorial loss,
dying abroad without returning.
The Second Emperor, holding the position of Son of Heaven,
possessed all under heaven,
wherever human footprints reached,
where boats and oars could travel,
all were made into commanderies and counties.
Yet he indulged his sensory desires,
exhausted extravagant variations,
heedless of the people's hunger, cold, poverty, and destitution.
He raised carriages for ten thousand chariots and built the Ēpáng Palace,
conscripted the poor from the left side of the villages,
collected more than half of the harvest as taxes,
the people subjected to immediate punishment and execution,
those who pulled carts and died on the road
numbered tens of thousands in a single day.
The world was scorched as if by burning heat,
tormented as if by bitter suffering,
superiors and inferiors found no peace,
officials and people had no mutual trust.
The conscript Chén Shèng rose up in Dàzé,
baring his arm and shoulder,
proclaiming the Great Chǔ,
and the world responded.
At that time,
he had no solid armor or sharp weapons,
no strong crossbows or powerful rams.
They cut jujube trees for spear shafts,
used awls and chisels as blades,
sharpened bamboo sticks,
wielded carrying poles and hoes,
to face long halberds and strong crossbows,
yet in attacking cities and seizing land,
none failed to surrender.
The world became like boiling porridge and swarming ants,
cleared like clouds and rolled up like a mat,
across thousands of li.
His status was the lowest,
and his equipment highly inadequate,
yet when one man sang, the whole world joined in,
because resentment had accumulated among the people.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
facing east, he encountered Jupiter,
at Fàn he encountered floods,
at Gòngtóu he encountered landslides,
a comet appeared, seeming to hand its handle to the Yīn people.
At the time of battle,
ten suns were disordered in the sky,
wind and rain struck in the midst,
yet there were no rewards for braving difficulties ahead,
nor punishments for retreating behind,
before the white blades were fully drawn, the world was already won.
Therefore, those skilled in defense need no one to resist them,
and those skilled in attack need no one to fight them.
They understand the principles of prohibition and allowance, opening and blocking,
ride the momentum of the time,
and follow the people's desires to take the world.
Thus, those skilled in governance accumulate virtue,
those skilled in using troops store up wrath.
Virtue accumulated makes the people usable,
wrath stored makes authority establishable.
Therefore, if the civil influence applied is shallow,
then the authority that compels is small;
if the virtue extended is broad,
then the authority that controls is wide.
When the authority that controls is wide,
then we are strong and the enemy weak.
Therefore, those skilled in using troops
first weaken the enemy and then engage in battle,
thus expending less than half the effort yet achieving double the results.
Tāng's territory was only seventy li, yet he became king,
because he cultivated virtue;
Zhì Bó had a thousand li of land but perished,
because he exhausted warfare.
Thus, a state of a thousand chariots that practices civil virtue will become king,
a state of ten thousand chariots that loves using troops will perish.
Therefore, a complete army first ensures victory and then seeks battle,
a defeated army first battles and then seeks victory.
If virtue is equal,
the numerous will overcome the few;
if strength is matched,
the wise will overcome the foolish;
if wisdom is equal,
then the strategic will capture the unstrategic.
In all military operations,
one must first wage war in the temple:
Which ruler is wiser?
Which general is more capable?
Which people are more attached?
Which state is better governed?
Which has more accumulated reserves?
Which has more refined soldiers?
Which has sharper armor and weapons?
Which has more ready equipment?
Thus, by planning in the temple hall,
one can determine victory a thousand li away.
Those with tangible forms,
the world disputes and sees them;
those with written records,
people transmit and study them;
these are all things that prevail through form,
but those skilled in form do not emulate them.
What is valued in the Way,
is its formlessness.
Being formless,
it cannot be coerced or pressured,
cannot be measured,
cannot be tricked or deceived,
cannot be planned or considered.
Where wisdom is visible, people devise strategies against it;
where form is visible, people achieve results against it;
where the multitude is visible, people submit to it;
where weapons are visible, people prepare against them.
Actions and movements,
bending and stretching,
that can be tricked or deceived,
are all not good.
The movements of the skilled,
emerge like spirits and proceed like ghosts,
shine like stars and move mysteriously;
advancing, retreating, bending, stretching,
without revealing any trace;
rising like a luán bird, vibrating like a lín,
flying like a phoenix, soaring like a dragon;
erupting like a whirlwind,
swift like startling lightning.
Striking the dead with life,
riding the declining with vigor,
overwhelming the slow with speed,
controlling the hungry with fullness.
Like using water to extinguish fire,
like pouring boiling water on snow,
where can it not succeed?
Where can it not reach?
Internally, empty the spirit,
externally, indifferent to will,
operate without form,
emerge unexpectedly.
Going with the drifting,
coming with the fleeting,
none know where it goes.
Emerging with the gaps,
entering with the intervals,
none know where it gathers.
Suddenly like thunder,
swift like wind and rain,
as if emerging from the earth,
as if descending from the sky,
alone in going out, alone in coming in,
none can resist or contain it.
Swift like an arrow,
how can it be matched?
One dark, one bright,
who knows its beginning or end?
Before seeing it launch,
it has already arrived.
Thus, those skilled in using troops,
seeing the enemy's weakness,
exploit it without hesitation,
pursue without letting go,
press without retreating.
Strike when they hesitate,
overwhelm when they are unsettled,
swift thunder leaves no time to cover ears,
sudden lightning allows no moment to shield eyes.
Those skilled in using troops,
are like sound and its echo,
like the drum and its beat,
no time to blink,
no time to breathe.
At this moment,
looking up, one cannot see the sky,
looking down, one cannot see the ground,
hands do not wave spears,
weapons are not fully drawn,
striking like thunder,
pressing like wind,
burning like fire,
overwhelming like waves.
The enemy, when still, does not know what to defend,
when moving, does not know what to do.
Thus, when drums sound and flags wave,
those in the way cannot but collapse and crumble,
who in the world dares to assert authority and resist, standing in their front!
Therefore, those who take the initiative win,
those who wait are defeated,
those who are targeted perish.
Troops, when calm, are firm;
when unified, they are powerful;
when decisive, they are brave;
when doubtful, they flee;
when divided, they are weak.
Thus, if you can divide the enemy's troops,
and doubt their hearts,
then even a little is more than enough;
if you cannot divide the enemy's troops,
nor doubt their hearts,
then even several times more is insufficient.
Thus, Zhòu's troops numbered a million,
but had a million different hearts;
King Wǔ's troops were three thousand,
all focused and united as one.
Therefore, a thousand people with one heart gain the strength of a thousand;
ten thousand people with different hearts have not the use of one.
Generals, soldiers, officials, and people,
moving and still like one body,
only then can they respond to the enemy and engage in battle.
Thus, decide the plan and then act,
be decisive and then move,
the general without doubtful plans,
the soldiers without divided hearts,
movements without slackness,
words without emptiness,
affairs without experimentation,
responding to the enemy must be swift,
launching attacks must be urgent.
Therefore, the general takes the people as his body,
and the people take the general as their heart.
If the heart is sincere, the limbs are intimate and firm;
if the heart is doubtful, the limbs waver and flee.
If the heart is not unified,
the body does not move in coordination;
if the general is not sincere and resolute,
the soldiers will not be brave.
Thus, the troops of a good general,
are like the tiger's teeth,
like the rhinoceros's horn,
like the bird's feathers,
like the millipede's legs,
can march,
can rise,
can bite,
can gore,
strong without harming each other,
numerous without injuring one another,
all driven by one heart.
Therefore, if the people truly follow orders,
even if few, there is no fear;
if the people do not follow orders,
even if many, they are few.
Thus, if subordinates do not亲近 their superiors,
their hearts are not used;
if soldiers do not fear their general,
their formation does not fight.
Defense must be firm,
and attack must be victorious,
without awaiting crossed weapons or clashing blades,
the mechanism of survival or destruction is already evident.
There are three forms of military momentum,
and two types of strategic advantage.
There is the momentum of morale,
the momentum of terrain,
and the momentum of opportunity.
When the commander is fully courageous and underestimates the enemy,
the soldiers are resolute and delight in battle,
the entire army,
even a force of a million,
has aspirations reaching the blue clouds,
spirit like a whirlwind,
voices like thunder,
with accumulated sincerity surpassing and imposing awe upon the enemy,
this is called the momentum of morale.
Gorge paths and ferry passes,
great mountains and famous fortresses,
where dragons and serpents coil,
bamboo hats dwell,
narrow winding paths,
fish-trap gates,
where one person guards the defile,
and a thousand dare not pass,
this is called the momentum of terrain.
Taking advantage of their fatigue and weariness, laxity and disorder,
hunger, thirst, freezing, and heatstroke,
pushing them when they are tottering,
pressing them when they are exposed,
this is called the momentum of opportunity.
Skillfully using spies,
carefully devising plans and considerations,
setting up ambushes and hidden troops,
concealing one's form,
striking unexpectedly,
so that the enemy's troops
have nowhere to properly prepare,
this is called knowing strategic advantage.
Formations of soldiers are orderly,
the front lines selected,
advancing and retreating together,
squads and platoons cohesive,
front and rear not interfering,
left and right not obstructing,
few receiving wounds,
many injuring the enemy,
this is called tactical advantage.
When authority and momentum take form,
officers and soldiers are focused and sharp,
selecting the good and employing talent,
officials are the right people,
plans are set and strategies decided,
clear about life and death,
actions taken at the right time,
none are not shaken and alarmed.
Thus, an attack does not require siege towers or cloud ladders to capture a city,
battle does not require crossing weapons or clashing blades to defeat the enemy,
this is understanding the certainty of victory.
Therefore, if troops are not certain to win,
they do not carelessly engage in combat;
if an attack is not certain to succeed,
it is not launched recklessly.
Thus, victory is assured before battle,
the balance is weighed before action.
Hence, the masses gather without scattering in vain,
troops set out without returning empty-handed.
Only when there is no movement,
and when moving, it shakes heaven and earth,
resists Tài Shān,
sweeps across the four seas,
ghosts and spirits relocate,
birds and beasts are startled.
In this way,
then there are no contending troops in the fields,
and no defending cities in the state.
Tranquility to counter agitation,
order to await chaos,
formlessness to control form,
non-action to respond to change,
even if unable to defeat the enemy,
it is the way the enemy cannot achieve victory.
If the enemy moves before me,
then their form is revealed;
if they are agitated and I am calm,
then their strength is exhausted.
When their form is seen, victory can be controlled;
when their strength is spent, authority can be established.
Observe what they do,
and adapt accordingly;
watch their deviations and uprightness,
to control their fate;
bait them with what they desire,
to exhaust their steps.
If they show an opening,
quickly fill the gap,
exploit their changes and restrain them,
use up their energy and strike them.
If the enemy returns to stillness,
use unexpected tactics against them,
if they do not respond to us,
fully employ harmony alone.
If they move in response,
and their actions are visible,
they hold to a rear position,
adapt and shift with them.
Where they have accumulation,
there must be depletion,
if their essence turns left,
attack their right flank.
When the enemy collapses and flees,
the rear can certainly be shifted.
If the enemy is pressured but does not move,
it is called sluggishness;
strike them like thunder,
cut them down like grass and trees,
dazzle them like fire and lightning,
desiring speed and swiftness,
so that men have no time to step or run,
chariots no time to turn their wheels,
soldiers like planted trees,
crossbows like goat horns,
even if the enemy is numerous,
none dare resist the momentum.
All that have semblance,
can be overcome;
all that have form,
can be responded to;
therefore, the sage hides form in nothingness,
and lets the mind wander in emptiness.
Wind and rain can be blocked,
but cold and heat cannot be shut out,
because they are formless.
To be able to penetrate the subtle and minute,
pierce metal and stone,
reach the farthest extremes,
extend above the nine heavens,
coil below the yellow reeds,
only the formless can do so.
Those skilled in using troops
should strike when there is chaos,
not attack when there is order,
not assault a majestic enemy,
not strike a steady flag.
Before the enemy's appearance is visible,
hold them with strategy.
When they show signs of defeat,
then control them accordingly.
If the enemy holds to strategy,
move to exploit their weaknesses.
Using emptiness to respond to substance,
they will surely be captured.
If tigers and leopards do not move,
they do not fall into traps;
if deer do not move,
they do not encounter nets;
if birds do not move,
they do not get caught in snares;
if fish and turtles do not move,
they do not bite on hooks.
Nothing is not controlled by movement.
Therefore, the sage values stillness,
for stillness can respond to agitation,
later can respond to earlier,
density can overcome sparseness,
fullness can capture gaps.
Thus, when a skilled general employs his troops,
he unifies their hearts,
consolidates their strength,
so the brave cannot advance alone,
nor the timid retreat alone.
Halting, they stand like mountains;
striking, they move like wind and rain.
Where they assault is certain to crumble,
nothing remains unbroken or unharmed.
Moving as one body,
none can withstand them.
Hence, many are the enemies wounded,
but few are our own who engage in hand-to-hand combat.
For the alternating flick of five fingers
is not as effective as a clenched fist's single thump;
the successive advance of ten thousand men
is not as potent as the simultaneous arrival of a hundred.
Now, tigers and leopards are agile,
bears and brown bears are powerful,
yet humans eat their flesh and use their hides as mats
because these beasts cannot communicate their intelligence and unify their strength.
Water's nature overcomes fire,
yet if the Zhānghuá Tower is ablaze,
and you try to extinguish it with dippers and ladles,
even if you drain wells and exhaust ponds,
it will be of no avail.
But if you douse it with pots, jars, basins, and urns,
the fire can be put out in no time.
Now, between people and people,
there is no inherent advantage like water over fire,
yet attempting to match many with few
fails to achieve success,
which is also clear.
Some military strategists say:
"The few can match the many."
This refers to command,
not to combat.
Some lead many but use them sparsely,
due to lack of cohesion;
others lead few but use them fully,
through harmonious application of strength.
As for achieving victory with few over many
by exhausting everyone's talents
and utilizing all their strength,
from ancient times to the present,
it has never been heard of.
No spirit is more revered than heaven,
no advantage more convenient than earth,
no action more urgent than timing,
no resource more beneficial than people.
All these four
are the trunk and branches of military affairs,
yet they must await the Dao to be put into action,
to be used as one.
Now, earth's advantage surpasses heaven's timing,
skillful action surpasses earth's advantage,
and momentum surpasses manpower.
Thus, those relying solely on heaven can be bewildered,
those relying solely on earth can be constrained,
those relying solely on timing can be pressured,
and those relying solely on people can be deceived.
Benevolence, courage, trustworthiness, and integrity
are fine qualities in people,
yet the brave can be lured,
the benevolent can be deprived,
the trustworthy can be easily cheated,
and the upright can be easily plotted against.
A general leading many,
if he has but one such flaw,
will be captured by others.
From this perspective,
it is clear that victory in war is determined by strategic principles,
not by the worth of individual talents.
Thus, it is self-evident.
Therefore, for deer, traps can be set;
for fish and turtles, nets can be used;
for swans and wild geese, arrows with strings can be applied;
only the formless cannot be dealt with.
Hence, the sage hides in the boundless,
so his true state cannot be observed;
he operates without form,
so his formations cannot be traversed.
Without fixed laws or rituals,
he responds appropriately to what comes;
without name or shape,
he transforms into whatever image is needed.
Profound and subtle,
vast and remote,
through winter and summer,
spring and autumn,
reaching to the highest ends above,
plumbing the deepest depths below,
changing and transforming without cease,
unhindered and unblocked,
he establishes his mind in the obscure wilderness,
and conceals his will in the swirling abyss.
Even with the sharpest eyes,
who can perceive his true state?
What military strategy deliberates in secret is the way of heaven;
what it plans and charts is the terrain;
what it speaks of openly is human affairs;
what it uses to decide victory is strategic advantage.
Thus, when a superior general employs his troops,
he comprehends the way of heaven above,
utilizes the advantages of earth below,
and wins the hearts of people in between.
Then he acts with opportunity,
and strikes with momentum,
so that his army is never defeated.
As for the average general,
he does not understand heaven's way above,
nor earth's advantages below,
but relies solely on men and momentum.
Though not necessarily flawless,
his victories are still many.
When an inferior general employs troops,
he is well-informed but self-confusing,
knowledgeable but self-doubting,
fearful when stationary,
hesitant when acting,
