so his movements lead to capture by others.
Now, suppose two men cross blades,
their skill equal,
yet the courageous one is sure to win.
Why?
Because his action is sincere.
Using a giant axe to strike a paulownia branch,
one need not wait for an auspicious day to break it.
But if a giant axe is placed on the branch
without human force applied,
even aligned with the constellations,
and considering cosmic influences,
it cannot break it,
due to lack of momentum.
Thus, water when agitated becomes fierce;
arrows when propelled fly far.
Even with the finest arrows from Qí and Jùnlù,
tipped with silver and tin,
and facing the thinnest silk curtains
or rotten lotus shields,
they alone cannot penetrate.
But if aided by the power of sinew and horn,
and the force of bow and crossbow,
they can pierce rhinoceros armor and pass through leather shields.
The swiftness of wind
can tear off roofs and break trees;
under empty ascent to great heights,
from atop high hills,
it is because there is something propelling it.
Therefore, those skilled in using troops
build momentum like breaching a dam holding accumulated water a thousand ren high,
or rolling round rocks down a ten-thousand-zhàng gorge.
When the world sees our troops' inevitable use,
who would dare to fight us?
Thus, a hundred men resolved to die
are superior to ten thousand destined to flee,
let alone a full army's multitude
charging into fire and water without turning back!
Even if challenged to cross blades with all under heaven,
who would dare claim superiority?
What is called the celestial configuration
is the Green Dragon on the left,
the White Tiger on the right,
the Vermilion Bird in front,
and the Black Tortoise behind.
What is called terrestrial advantage
is life behind and death in front,
male on the left and female on the right.
What is called human affairs
is faithful rewards and certain punishments,
timely movements and halts,
swift actions and decisions.
These are passed down as models and standards,
for they are adaptable,
yet they are not the source of creation.
Models and standards
change with the times.
Thus, standing in the shade of a hall, one knows the sequence of sun and moon;
seeing ice in a bottle, one understands the cold and heat of the world.
The subtleties of how things manifest themselves are profound,
and only the sage comprehends their ultimate essence.
Thus, the drum does not partake in the five notes but governs them;
water does not partake in the five flavors but harmonizes them;
the general does not partake in the affairs of the five officials but supervises them.
Therefore, one who can harmonize the five notes
does not partake in them;
one who can blend the five flavors
does not partake in them;
one who can govern the affairs of the five officials
cannot be measured by ordinary means.
Hence, the mind of the general
is abundant like spring,
expansive like summer,
serene like autumn,
and steadfast like winter,
adapting and transforming with circumstances,
shifting and changing with the times.
Shadows do not straighten for crooked objects;
echoes do not become turbid for clear sounds.
Observe the origins of things,
and respond each with what overcomes them.
Thus, act upholding righteousness,
proceed following reason,
cut decisively when the moment requires,
and achieve success by leveraging resources,
so that others know our point of departure but not our destination,
know our actions but not our gathering forces.
At first, be like a fox,
so the enemy underestimates and advances lightly;
then unite like a rhinoceros or tiger,
so the foe flees in panic.
The swooping bird lowers its head,
the pouncing beast hides its claws,
tigers and leopards do not bare their fangs,
and biting dogs do not show their teeth.
Thus, the way of using troops
is to show softness yet meet with firmness,
display weakness yet strike with strength,
contract as if yielding then expand in response,
intend to go west but show east,
first oppose then unite,
begin in obscurity and end in clarity,
like a ghost leaving no trace,
like water causing no wound.
Thus, the direction shown is not the true course,
what is seen is not the real plan;
every move and stillness,
none can decipher,
like a thunder strike,
impossible to prepare for.
Tactics are never repeated,
hence victory can be assured a hundredfold.
Communicating with the profound and bright,
none know its gateway,
this is called ultimate divinity.
The reason troops are strong
is their willingness to die;
the reason the people are willing to die
is righteousness;
the reason righteousness can be upheld
is authority.
Thus, unite them with culture,
discipline them with martial rigor,
this is called certain victory;
authority and righteousness applied together,
this is called ultimate strength.
What people delight in
is life,
and what they detest
is death;
yet against high walls and deep moats,
arrows and stones falling like rain,
on open plains and vast marshes,
amidst clashing blades,
soldiers still vie to charge forward,
not because they scorn death or relish injury,
but because rewards are trustworthy and punishments clear.
Thus, if the superior regards subordinates as sons,
subordinates will regard the superior as a father;
if the superior regards subordinates as younger brothers,
subordinates will regard the superior as an elder brother.
If the superior regards subordinates as sons,
he is sure to rule the four seas;
if subordinates regard the superior as a father,
they are sure to rectify the world.
If the superior treats subordinates as younger brothers,
they will not hesitate to die for him;
if subordinates serve the superior as an elder brother,
they will not hesitate to perish for him.
Thus, enemies bound as father, son, or brothers
cannot be fought against,
for accumulated kindness has been bestowed first.
Hence, if the four horses are not in harmony,
even Zàofǔ cannot travel far;
if the bow and arrow are not tuned,
even Yì cannot surely hit the mark;
if ruler and minister are at odds,
even Sūnzǐ cannot respond to the enemy.
Therefore, cultivate internal governance to accumulate virtue,
block external disgrace to assert authority,
observe toil and rest to understand satiety and hunger;
thus, when the day of battle comes,
they will look upon death as returning home.
Hence, the general must share sweetness and bitterness with the troops,
endure hunger and cold alike,
so their willingness to die can be fully realized.
Thus, the skilled generals of old
always led by personal example:
in heat, not raising a canopy,
in cold, not wearing furs,
to endure heat and cold with them;
on steep paths, not riding,
on hills, dismounting,
to share toil and rest equally;
eating only after the army's food is cooked,
drinking only after the army's well is dug,
to share hunger and thirst;
in battle, standing where arrows and stones reach,
to share safety and danger.
Thus, when a fine general employs troops,
he often uses accumulated virtue to strike accumulated resentment,
uses accumulated love to strike accumulated hatred—
how could he not prevail!
The ruler demands two things from the people:
that they toil for him,
and that they die for him.
The people hope for three things from the ruler:
that the hungry be fed,
the weary be rested,
and the meritorious be rewarded.
If the people fulfill their two duties,
yet the ruler fails their three hopes,
even if the state is large,
the population numerous,
the military will still be weak.
If the suffering find joy,
the toiling gain benefits,
achievements in battle are fully recognized,
and families of the fallen are surely rewarded,
once these four are trusted by the people,
even if the ruler shoots birds in the clouds,
fishes in deep abysses,
plays the qín and sè,
sounds bells and yú pipes,
enjoys liùbó games,
tosses arrows into tall pots,
the military will still be strong,
and orders will still be obeyed.
Thus, if the superior is worthy of respect,
the subordinates can be used;
if virtue is worthy of admiration,
authority can be established.
A commander must possess three penetrations,
four righteousnesses,
five conducts,
and ten preservations.
The so-called three penetrations are:
understanding the way of heaven above,
learning the terrain below,
and observing human affairs in between.
The so-called four righteousnesses are:
benefiting the state without exhausting the troops,
serving the ruler without regard for one's own life,
facing difficulties without fearing death,
and resolving doubts without avoiding blame.
The so-called five conducts are:
being pliable yet unrollable,
firm yet unbreakable,
benevolent yet unoffendable,
trustworthy yet undeceiveable,
and courageous yet unbullyable.
The so-called ten preservations are:
having a clear spirit that cannot be muddied,
far-reaching plans that cannot be coveted,
firm principles that cannot be changed,
bright wisdom that cannot be obscured,
not greedy for goods,
not excessive with things,
not addicted to arguments,
not confined to methods,
not easily pleased,
and not easily angered.
This is called the ultimate banner,
profound and mysterious,
who can understand its essence!
Actions must hit the target,
words must accord with principles,
movements must follow the timing,
and solutions must strike the key;
mastering the mechanism of movement and stillness,
clarifying the rhythm of opening and closing,
examining the gains and losses of actions,
as if matching tally and token;
swift as a drawn crossbow,
forceful as a released arrow,
now a dragon, now a snake,
moving without constant form,
none see where it strikes,
none know its limits,
when attacking, it cannot be defended against,
when defending, it cannot be attacked.
It is heard that those skilled in using troops
must first cultivate themselves,
and then seek from others;
first make themselves invincible,
and then seek victory.
Cultivating oneself among people,
seeking victory over enemies,
if one cannot govern oneself,
yet attacks the chaos of others,
it is like using fire to save fire,
using water to respond to water,
how can it be controlled!
If a potter were to transform into clay,
they could not form pots and bowls;
if a weaver were to transform into silk,
they could not weave patterned brocade.
Sameness is insufficient for mutual governance,
thus difference is used for surprise,
when two sparrows fight each other,
none die;
when a sparrowhawk arrives,
they disperse,
because it is of a different kind.
Thus stillness is the surprise to agitation,
order to chaos,
satiety to hunger,
and ease to labor.
The interaction of surprise and normality,
is like water, fire, metal, and wood taking turns as male and female.
Those skilled in using troops,
wield the five killings to respond,
thus able to secure complete victory.
The unskilled dwell in five deaths due to greed,
thus moving and being captured by others.
In warfare, value lies in plans being unfathomable,
forms being concealed,
emerging unexpectedly,
leaving no chance for preparation.
If plans are seen, they are exhausted,
if forms are seen, they are controlled.
Thus those skilled in using troops,
conceal above in heaven,
conceal below in earth,
conceal in between among people.
Concealing in heaven,
there is nothing not controlled.
What is concealing in heaven?
Extreme cold and severe heat,
fierce winds and torrential rain,
heavy fog and deep darkness,
using these to create changes.
What is concealing in earth?
Mountains, hills, and mounds,
forests, thickets, and dangerous obstacles,
where one can hide without showing form.
What is concealing among people?
Shielding in front,
watching behind,
executing surprise moves within the battle array,
striking like thunder,
swift as wind and rain,
waving great flags,
halting drum beats,
and moving in and out without form,
none knowing the beginning or end.
Thus front and rear aligned properly,
all directions like a plumb line,
movements in and out relaxed,
without overriding each other,
wings light and edges sharp,
sometimes forward, sometimes backward,
separating, joining, scattering, gathering,
without losing formation,
this is skill in cultivating battle arrays.
Understanding surprise and normality,
yin and yang,
punishment and virtue,
the five phases,
observing energies,
watching stars,
tortoise shells and stalks,
and omens,
this is skill in the way of heaven.
Setting plans and considerations,
laying ambushes,
using water and fire,
producing rare wonders,
drumming and shouting in the army,
these are to confuse their ears;
dragging branches, spreading firewood,
raising dust, stirring up ashes,
these are to confuse their eyes,
this is skill in deception and feints.
Helmets and axes secure and heavy,
firmly planted and hard to intimidate,
power and profit cannot lure,
death and danger cannot move,
this is skill in solidifying the core.
Swift and agile, light and fierce,
brave and daring, underestimating the enemy,
fast as vanishing,
this is skill in using light troops for surprise.
Surveying the terrain,
positioning encampments,
building fortifications,
examining smoke and scouts,
occupying high grounds,
stationing at exits,
this is skill in terrain.
Exploiting their hunger, thirst, cold, and heat,
fatigue, weariness, slackness, and chaos,
fear, panic, and constrained steps,
attacking with selected troops,
striking in the night,
this is skill in adapting to timing and changing circumstances.
On easy ground, use chariots,
on difficult ground, use cavalry,
crossing water,多用 bows,
in narrow passes, use crossbows,
by day,多用 banners,
by night,多用 fires,
in darkness,多用 drums,
this is skill in deploying equipment.
All these eight,
none can be lacking,
yet they are not the ultimate value in warfare.
A commander must possess unique insight and knowledge.
Unique insight means seeing what others do not see;
unique knowledge means knowing what others do not know.
Seeing what others do not see is called clarity;
knowing what others do not know is called divinity.
Clarity and divinity lead to victory beforehand.
Those who win beforehand defend in a way that cannot be attacked,
fight in a way that cannot be defeated,
and attack in a way that cannot be defended—this is the interplay of emptiness and solidity.
When there are rifts between superiors and subordinates,
when generals and officials are at odds,
when their actions are unjust,
and when the troops harbor discontent, this is called emptiness.
When the ruler is wise and the general capable,
when superiors and subordinates are united in heart,
and when morale and will are both high, this is called solidity.
Like water poured on fire,
where it strikes, it breaks through;
where it presses, it shifts;
when firmness and flexibility do not connect, and victory arises unexpectedly, this is the concept of emptiness and solidity.
Thus, those skilled in warfare do not rely on few numbers,
nor do those skilled in defense rely on small forces.
Victory lies in gaining authority;
defeat lies in losing morale.
When solid, engage in battle;
when empty, retreat.
When strong, be firm;
when weak, flee.
King Fūchāi of Wú had a territory of two thousand lǐ,
armored troops numbering seven hundred thousand,
fought Yuè in the south,
and cornered them at Kuàijī;
fought Qí in the north,
defeating them at Àilíng;
confronted the Duke of Jìn in the west,
capturing him at Huángchí.
This was the use of solid popular morale.
Later, he became arrogant and indulgent,
rejected advice and favored flattery,
grew increasingly reckless and persisted in error,
beyond correction.
Ministers resented him,
the common people did not support him,
and the King of Yuè selected three thousand troops,
capturing him at Gānsuì—
this was exploiting his emptiness.
The morale of an army has emptiness and solidity,
just as brightness must give way to darkness.
Thus, victorious armies are not always solid,
and defeated armies are not always empty.
The skilled can solidify their people's morale
to await the enemy's emptiness;
the unskilled empty their people's morale
and face the enemy's solidity.
Therefore, the interplay of emptiness and solidity in morale
is crucial in warfare.
When a state faces crisis,
the ruler summons the general from the palace and commands him:
"The fate of the state rests on you, General.
Now the state is in peril;
I ask you to lead and respond."
The general accepts the order,
then orders the invokers and grand diviners to fast for three days,
proceed to the ancestral temple,
drill the sacred turtle shell,
and divine an auspicious day
to receive the drums and banners.
The ruler enters the temple gate
and stands facing west;
the general enters the temple gate
and hastens to the hall's base,
standing facing north.
The ruler personally grasps the yuè axe,
holding the head,
and hands the handle to the general, saying:
"From here up to the heavens,
you, General, shall command."
Then he takes the axe,
holds the head,
and hands the handle to the general, saying:
"From here down to the depths,
you, General, shall command."
After receiving the axe and yuè,
the general replies:
"The state cannot be governed from without;
the army cannot be controlled from within the court.
A divided heart cannot serve the ruler;
a doubtful will cannot face the enemy.
Since I have already received authority before you,
with the power of the drums, banners, axe, and yuè,
I will not seek permission again.
I ask that you not impose a single word of command upon me.
If you do not grant this,
I dare not lead.
If you grant it,
I take my leave and depart."
Then he trims his nails and hair,
dons the ritual garment,
and exits through the gate of ill omen.
He rides the general's chariot,
bearing the banners, axe, and yuè,
burdened as if unable to bear the weight.
In facing the enemy and decisive battle,
he shows no regard, resolved to die,
with no divided loyalty.
Thus, he has no heaven above,
no earth below,
no enemy ahead,
no ruler behind.
Advancing, he does not seek fame;
retreating, he does not avoid blame.
His sole aim is to protect the people,
benefiting the ruler—
such a one is the treasure of the state,
the way of a superior general.
In this way,
the wise plan for him,
the brave fight for him,
morale soaring to the blue clouds,
swift as galloping steeds.
Thus, before armies even engage, the enemy is filled with fear.
If victorious and the enemy flees,
all receive rewards for their merits;
officials are promoted,
ranks and emoluments increased,
land is divided to make peace,
decisions are made beyond the borders,
and affairs are settled within the army.
Upon returning to the state,
he lays down the banners and returns the axe and yuè,
reporting to the ruler:
"The army requires no further governance."
Then, dressed in plain white, he vacates his quarters
and asks for punishment from the ruler.
The ruler says:
"You are pardoned!"
He retires to fast and change attire.
After a great victory, he returns home in three years;
after a medium victory, in two years;
after a minor victory, in one year.
The lands targeted by the army
must be states without virtue.
Thus, victory in battle brings no retaliation,
captured territory is not returned,
the people suffer no plagues,
the general does not die prematurely,
the five grains flourish,
wind and rain come in season.
Victory abroad
brings blessings at home.
Therefore, fame is assured, and no further harm remains!
16.1 Pò asked Hún, saying:
"What does the Dào take as its substance?"
Hún replied:
"It takes non-being as its substance."
Pò said:
"Does non-being have form?"
Hún said:
"It does not."
Pò said:
"If it is non-being,
how can it be perceived?"
Hún said:
"I merely encounter it directly!
Look at it - it has no form;
listen to it - it has no sound;
this is called the obscure and dark.
The obscure and dark
serves to illustrate the Dào,
but is not the Dào itself."
Pò said:
"I have attained it!
It is to look inward and return to oneself."
Hún said:
"All who attain the Dào
cannot be seen in form,
cannot be praised by name.
Now you already have form and name,
how can you possibly attain the Dào!"
Pò said:
"Speaking,
what purpose does it serve?
I shall return to my origin."
Pò turned to look back,
and Hún suddenly disappeared;
turning back to preserve himself,
he too sank into formlessness.
16.2 If one does not have small awakenings,
one will not have great confusion;
if one does not have small wisdom,
one will not have great folly.
16.3 People do not use flowing puddles as mirrors,
but use still water as mirrors,
because it is calm and undisturbed.
16.4 In Zhān Gōng's fishing,
he caught a thousand-year-old carp;
when Zēngzǐ held onto the hearse,
those pulling it stopped for him;
when an old mother sang as she walked, she moved Shēn Xǐ -
this is the ultimate refinement of essence.
When Hùbā played the sè,
even the fish came up to listen;
when Bóyá played the qín,
horses lifted their heads from feeding;
when Jièzǐ sang of dragons and snakes,
Lord Wén shed tears.
Thus, where jade exists in the mountains, the plants and trees are lush;
where pearls grow in the deep, the banks do not wither.
The earthworm has neither strong sinews and bones,
nor sharp claws and teeth,
yet it eats the dry soil above,
and drinks from the yellow springs below,
because it concentrates its mind single-mindedly.
16.5 When clear, it becomes bright -
in a cup of water one can see the pupil of an eye;
when turbid, it becomes dark -
in river water one cannot see Tài Shān.
16.6 Those who stare at the sun become dazzled;
those who listen to thunder become deafened.
When humans practice non-action, there is order;
when they take action, there is harm.
Those who achieve order through non-action carry non-being within.
Those who take action
cannot possess being;
those who cannot practice non-action
cannot truly take action.
When humans are silent, they have spirit;
when they speak, there is harm.
Those who have spirit through silence carry non-being,
while speaking harms their spirit.
That which is spiritual
is what the nose uses to breathe,
what the ears use to hear -
ultimately, it uses what seems useless for its function.
All things invariably use what they have to employ what they lack.
If you doubt this,
observe the panpipes and the yú reed.
16.7 Those with anxious thoughts cannot sleep;
if they stop their anxious thoughts,
then they become trapped by what they stopped.
When both are forgotten,
then the ultimate virtue becomes pure.
16.8 The sage speaks of governance throughout his life,
but what he uses is not his words.
He uses that which enables him to speak.
A singer has poems,
but what makes people appreciate them
is not the poems themselves.
A parrot can speak,
but cannot be made to speak meaningfully.
Why is this?
It obtains the words,
but not that which produces the words.
Thus, those who follow tracks
are not capable of creating tracks.
16.9 A spiritual snake can break and reconnect itself,
but cannot prevent people from breaking it.
A spiritual turtle can appear in King Yuán's dream,
but cannot escape the fisherman's trap by itself.
16.10 All four directions are doors, windows, and orientations of the Dào,
depending on where one peers from.
Thus, fishing can teach riding,
riding can teach charioteering,
charioteering can teach boating.
16.11 When people from Yuè learn long-range archery,
they shoot toward the sky,
but the arrow lands within five steps,
yet they don't change their method.
The world has changed,
yet they cling to old ways -
this is like the archery of the Yuè people.
16.12 When the moon is full,
the sun robs it of its light -
the yīn cannot override the yáng.
When the sun rises, the stars disappear -
they cannot compete with its light.
Thus, the branch cannot be stronger than the root,
the finger cannot be larger than the arm.
When the bottom is light and the top heavy,
it will certainly overturn easily.
One deep pool cannot contain two sharks,
one roost cannot hold two males -
with one, there is stability;
with two, there is conflict.
When water is still, it becomes clear and balanced;
when disturbed, it loses its equilibrium.
Therefore, only by not moving
can one achieve moving everywhere.
16.13 The reason the Jiāng
and Hé rivers can be longer than all valleys
is that they can flow downward.
Only because they can flow downward
can they rise upward.
16.14 Nothing in the world hates each other more than glue and lacquer,
yet nothing loves each other more than ice and charcoal.
Glue and lacquer destroy each other,
while ice and charcoal sustain each other.
16.15 When a wall collapses,
it is better than when it stands;
when ice melts,
it is better than when it freezes -
because they return to their origin.
16.16 The appearance of Tài Shān
is majestically high,
yet from a thousand lǐ away,
not even a mound is visible -
due to the distance.
16.17 The tip of an autumn hair
sinks into the immeasurable.
Therefore, what cannot be considered small enough to be internal
cannot be considered large enough to be external.
16.18 The orchid growing in a secluded palace
does not cease being fragrant because no one wears it.
A boat in the river or sea
does not cease floating because no one rides it.
The noble person practicing righteousness
does not stop because no one knows of it.
16.19 Jade is moist, lustrous, and gleaming;
its tone is expansive and resonant,
flowing as if it resembles something.
Without inside or outside,
it does not conceal flaws or blemishes;
approaching it feels moist,
gazing at it appears deep.
Looking in a mirror, one sees the pupil;
examining minutely, one perceives the autumn down;
its brightness illuminates the dark and obscure.
Thus, the jade of Hé Shì,
the pearl of Suí Hóu,
emerge as essences from mountains and abysses.
The nobleman wearing them
achieves harmony, auspiciousness, and tranquility;
the feudal lords and kings treasure them
as standards for all under heaven.
16.20 Chéng Héng's coercion of Zǐ Yuān Jié,
Zǐ Hǎn's refusal of what he did not desire,
thereby obtaining what he did desire,
Confucius' observation of the sticky-catcher,
Bái Gōng Shèng's reversed staff,
Wèi Jī's plea for forgiveness from Duke Huán,
Zēng Zǐ seeing Zǐ Xià and saying:
"Why have you grown plump?"
Duke Wén of Wèi encountering the man in reversed fur coat carrying fodder,
Ér Yuè untangling the knot for the King of Sòng—
these are all subtleties from which principles can be observed and discussed.
16.21 A person, marrying off their daughter, instructed her:
"You are leaving now;
be cautious not to do good!"
She asked:
"If I don't do good,
shall I do bad instead?"
The response was:
"If even good is not to be done,
how much more so for bad!"
This preserves one's innate nature.
16.22 Those confined in prison consider the day long,
while those facing execution in the market consider it short.
The length of a day has its measure,
yet in some situations it seems short,
in others long,
because the mind is not at peace.
Thus, taking uneven as even,
such evenness is not truly even.
16.23 Marrying a daughter to one suffering from diabetes,
if the husband dies, they say the girl was ill-fated;
later, it becomes hard to remarry.
Hence, one should not sit under a crumbling house,
nor stand beside a leaning wall.
16.24 Jailers often do not fall ill,
the condemned appear plump and glossy,
the punished often live long—
their minds are free from burdens.
A good physician
often treats illnesses before they arise,
thus remaining free of illness.
The sage
often addresses troubles before they occur,
thus remaining free of troubles.
16.25 The most skillful need no hooks or lines,
the expert closer needs no bolts or bars.
Chún Yú Kūn's report of the fire
belongs to this category.
16.26 Entering turbidity with purity leads to hardship and disgrace,
entering purity with turbidity leads to downfall and collapse.
The nobleman's approach to goodness
is like a wood-gatherer picking up a single stalk upon seeing it,
uprooting lush greens upon spotting them.
16.27 When two qi clash in heaven, a rainbow forms;
when two qi clash on earth, stores leak away;
when two qi clash in humans, illness arises.
Yin and yang cannot bring both winter and summer;
the moon knows not the day,
the sun knows not the night.
16.28 The skilled archer never misses the target,
excellent at shooting,
but not necessarily skilled in choosing what to shoot.
The skilled angler never loses a catch,
excellent at fishing,
but not necessarily skilled in choosing what to fish.
Thus, where there is excellence in one aspect,
there may be lack in another.
16.29 The bell and the chime stone:
near, the bell's sound fills the air;
far, the chime's sound becomes distinct.
Things inherently may not match up close what they do afar,
or afar what they do up close.
16.30 They say rice grows in water,
but not in rushing torrents;
purple mushrooms grow on mountains,
but not on solid rock surfaces;
lodestone can attract iron,
but with copper,
it does not work.
16.31 Vast waters breed large fish,
high mountains grow tall trees.
Expanding territory while thinning virtue
is like a potter making vessels:
kneading and shaping the clay without adding thickness
leads to faster breakage.
16.32 The sage does not act before the wind blows,
nor before the thunder strikes,
but moves only when compelled,
thus remaining unburdened.
16.33 As the moon waxes and wanes above,
shellfish and mollusks respond below,
like energies influencing each other,
regardless of distance.
16.34 Holding a pellet to beckon birds,
waving a stick to call dogs,
intending to attract them,
only makes them flee.
Thus, fish cannot be caught without bait,
nor beasts summoned with empty traps.
16.35 Flaying an ox's hide,
tanning it into a drum
to command the three armies,
yet for the ox itself,
it would rather bear the yoke.
The white fox fur robe,
worn by the Son of Heaven in the temple hall,
yet for the fox itself,
it would rather run in the marshes.
16.36 Losing a sheep but gaining an ox,
none would not consider the loss beneficial;
losing a finger to save the head,
none would not consider the act worthwhile.
Thus, human nature is such that
among benefits, they strive for the greater,
among harms, they strive for the lesser.
16.37 A general dares not ride a white horse,
a fugitive dares not carry a torch at night,
a guardian dares not keep a biting dog.
16.38 The rooster knows the coming dawn,
the crane knows the midnight hour,
yet they cannot escape the pot and chopping block.
16.39 Where mountains harbor fierce beasts,
the trees are left uncut;
where gardens host stinging insects,
the vegetables are left unharvested;
thus, when a state has worthy ministers,
they repel enemies a thousand miles away.
16.40 Being a Ruist yet squatting in the village,
being a Mohist yet playing the yu in court,
trying to hide tracks by running in snow,
saving the drowning yet hoping not to get wet—
these are acting contrary to what should be done.
16.41 Those who drink in darkness
may not always spill their drink.
If they act with natural balance,
even the foolish would not err.
Thus, achieving success without harmony
is impossible under heaven.
16.42 Seeking beauty, one may not attain it;
not seeking beauty, beauty may be found.
Seeking ugliness, one may not find ugliness;
not seeking ugliness, ugliness may appear.
Neither seeking beauty nor ugliness,
then neither beauty nor ugliness exists,
this is called mystical unity.
16.43 Shēn Tú Dí carried a stone and sank himself in the abyss,
but drowning cannot be taken as a lofty act;
Xián Gǎo's deception saved Zhèng,
yet deception cannot be made a constant practice.
Events may have a single fitting response,
but cannot be followed as a rule.
16.44 Some people are talkative,
like the sound of a hundred-tongued bird.
Some are sparing in speech,
like a door without grease.
16.45 When domestic animals have extra eyes or ears, it is inauspicious,
as recorded in prophetic texts.
16.46 A hundred people carrying a floating object
is not as efficient as one person carrying it and walking quickly.
There are things where having many is inferior to having few,
like twelve people pulling a cart being slower.
Some tasks inherently require complementary efforts to succeed,
as when two people are both drowning,
they cannot save each other,
but if one is on land, it becomes possible.
Thus, homogeneity cannot achieve governance;
it requires diversity to accomplish things. ,
16.47 Where Poria grows below,
dodder thrives above;
where a cluster of yarrow plants grows above,
a hidden turtle lies below;
the sage discerns the interior from the exterior,
perceiving the hidden through the visible.
16.48 Liking martial arts doesn't make one a Xiá,
enjoying literature doesn't make one a Rú,
knowing remedies doesn't make one a doctor,
loving horses doesn't make one a groom,
recognizing music doesn't make one a blind musician,
appreciating flavors doesn't make one a cook;
these are categories without a definitive master's name.
16.49 Wearing armor
is not for threats within ten paces,
but for arrows a hundred paces away, where depth of penetration matters:
deep enough to reach the internal organs,
or shallow, stopping at the skin.
The difference between life and death
cannot be measured in miles.
16.50 When the King of Chǔ lost his monkey,
the forest was devastated in the search;
when the Lord of Sòng lost his pearl,
the pond was drained of all its fish;
thus, when a marsh catches fire, the nearby woods worry.
16.51 If the ruler seeks timber,
his ministers will ravage the forests;
if the ruler seeks fish,
his ministers will dry up the valleys.
If the ruler asks for an oar,
those below will provide a boat;
if the ruler speaks a thread,
those below will respond with a thick cord.
The ruler has one virtue,
and those below praise it twofold;
the ruler has three faults,
and those below magnify them ninefold.
16.52 Wén Zhǒng knew how to strengthen Yuè,
but not how to preserve himself;
Cháng Hóng knew why the Zhōu dynasty survived,
but not why he himself would perish;
they understood the distant but not the near.
16.53 Fearing a horse might shy and not daring to ride,
or dreading a carriage might overturn and not daring to board,
is to reject public benefit due to imaginary calamities.
16.54 Those who are unfilial may even curse their parents,
yet one who bears a child cannot ensure it will be filial,
but still raises and nurtures it.
16.55 When the Fàn family was defeated,
a thief stole their bell and carried it away;
it clanged loudly,
and fearing others would hear,
he quickly covered his own ears.
To resent others hearing it is understandable;
but to cover one's own ears
is irrational.
16.56 A shēng cannot be larger than a dàn,
for the shēng is contained within the dàn;
a night cannot be longer than a year,
for the night is part of the year;
benevolence and righteousness cannot surpass the Dào and its virtue,
for they are encompassed by the Dào and its virtue.
16.57 First the needle then the thread
can make a curtain;
first the thread then the needle
cannot make a garment.
Needles can create a tent,
baskets can form a wall.
The success or failure of affairs
must begin with small things,
indicating a gradual process.
16.58 Dyeing first with blue then black works,
but first black then blue does not.
A craftsman applying lacquer first then cinnabar works,
but cinnabar first then lacquer does not.
All matters are like this;
the sequence of before and after, above and below,
must be carefully considered.
16.59 Murky water makes fish gasp for air,
physical toil disturbs the spirit. (
Thus, a state with a wise ruler
can deter enemies from a thousand miles away).
16.60 One marries through a matchmaker,
but not solely because of the matchmaker;
one befriends through an introduction,
but not solely because of the introducer.
16.61 With aligned actions and shared goals,
one will follow from a thousand miles away;
with mismatched interests
and divergent actions,
even facing neighbors do not communicate.
16.62 Though the sea is vast,
it does not accept rotten debris.
The sun and moon do not respond to incompatible energies,
and a noble person does not tolerate those not of their kind.
16.63 People do not cherish Chuí's hand,
but value their own fingers;
they do not treasure the pearls of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
but prize their own fishing hooks.
16.64 Mistaking a bundle of firewood for a ghost,
seeing smoke as an apparition.
Taking the firewood for a ghost,
one flees in panic;
believing the smoke to be a spirit,
one slaughters a pig and cooks a dog.
To act so preemptively
is worse than dealing with it later.
16.65 The skillful are good at measuring,
the wise are good at preparing.
16.66 When Yì died at Táobù,
he had no chance to shoot;
when Qìngjì died by the sword's edge,
he had no chance to fight.
16.67 To deny a false accusation, going door to door saying,
"I truly did not commit adultery with my sister-in-law,"
only makes the slander spread more.
Trying to stop words with words,
or halt actions with actions,
is like stirring up dust to settle it,
or carrying firewood to put out a fire.
Using rumors to cleanse a stain
is like wiping white silk with black dye.
16.68 An arrow can pierce rhinoceros hide at ten paces,
but cannot penetrate Lǔ silk at three hundred paces;
a Qíjì can travel a thousand miles in a day,
but may collapse from exhaustion upon arrival.
16.69 When a powerful family attacks a weaker one, it is called tyranny;
when a great state annexes a small one, it is called wisdom.
16.70 A small horse is of the same kind as a large horse,
but minor wisdom is not of the same kind as great wisdom.
16.71 To wear a sheepskin and hire out as labor
is fitting for the task;
but to wear a marten coat and carry a basket
is very strange indeed.
16.72 To consider purity as disgraceful
is like bathing and then cleaning a latrine,
or perfuming with incense and then carrying a pig.
16.73 Treating a boil without distinguishing good flesh from bad and cutting it all away,
or a farmer weeding without telling seedlings from weeds and uprooting everything—
is that not futile?
16.74 Breaching a pond to catch a turtle,
tearing down a house to find a cat,
digging up a room to catch a rat,
cutting the lip to treat a tooth decay—
such are the ways of Jié and Zhí,
whom noble people do not associate with.
Killing a warhorse to hunt a fox,
grabbing two turtles and losing a divine one,
breaking a right arm over a single hair,
snapping a Mòyé sword for a tiny knife—
to use wisdom in such ways,
is it worthy of esteem?
16.75 Better a hundred pricks with a needle,
than one stab with a knife;
better one heavy lift,
than long holding something light;
better a month of hunger,
than ten days of starvation.
The stumble of ten thousand
is better than one man's fall.
16.76 Someone praised another for his frugal labor:
pounding grain till dawn,
yet not meeting the required amount,
he was still reprimanded.
Upon investigation,
it turned out to be his mother.
Thus, the praise of a petty person
instead becomes detrimental.
16.77 The mother of the eastern household died,
and her son's weeping was not sorrowful.
The son of the western household saw this,
returned and said to his mother:
"Why do you begrudge a quick death?
I will surely mourn you bitterly."
He who wishes his mother dead,
even if she dies, cannot weep sorrowfully.
Those who claim to have no time for study,
even with time, will not study.
16.78 Seeing hollow wood float, they learned to make boats;
seeing tumbleweeds roll, they learned to make carts;
seeing bird tracks, they learned to write books;
thus they derived things by analogy.
16.79 To regard the unrighteous as righteous,
the improper as proper,
is like running naked to chase a madman,
stealing wealth to give to a beggar,
pilfering bamboo slips to copy laws,
or squatting to recite the Book of Songs
and Book of Documents.
16.80 If you cut and then stop,
even Mòyé cannot slice meat;
if you grasp and not let go,
a horse's hair can cut jade.
The sage neither halts nor acts without cause,
each year surpassing the last,
each day improving on yesterday.
16.81 A horse resembling a deer is worth a thousand gold,
yet there are no deer worth that much under heaven;
jade requires Luánzhū to become a vessel,
there are jade discs worth a thousand gold, but no Luánzhū worth a zī or chuí.
16.82 Receive light through a crack, it illuminates a corner;
receive light through a window, it illuminates the north wall;
receive light through a door, it illuminates the entire room without missing anything,
how much more so receiving light from the universe?
All under heaven borrows brightness from what lies before it!
From this we see,
small reception leads to shallow sight,
great reception leads to broad illumination.
16.83 The Jiāng River emerges from Mínshān,
the Hé River from Kūnlún,
the Jǐ River from Wángwū,
the Yǐng River from Shàoshì,
the Hàn River from Bōzhǒng,
their flows diverge and race apart,
yet all pour into the Eastern Sea,
their paths differ,
but their destination is one.
16.84 One versed in learning is like a chariot axle,
revolving within the hub,
not moving itself,
yet it travels a thousand lǐ with it,
ending only to begin anew,
turning from an inexhaustible source.
One unlearned is like a confused person,
told east, west, north, and south,
they listen intently where they stand,
but turn away and lose it,
failing to grasp the essential points.
16.85 Cold cannot generate cold,
heat cannot generate heat,
but what is neither cold nor heat can generate both.
Thus, form arises from formlessness,
before heaven and earth existed, they could be generated,
how profoundly subtle and vast!
16.86 Falling rain cannot soak,
only when it stops can it moisten;
a shot arrow cannot pierce,
only when it stops can it penetrate;
only stillness can stop all movement.
Build a terrace where it is high,
make a pond where it is low,
each according to its terrain,
daring not to alter it.
16.87 The sage uses objects,
as if binding a straw dog with red silk,
or making an earth dragon to seek rain.
The straw dog is relied upon to seek blessings,
the earth dragon is relied upon to obtain food.
16.88 A man from Lǔ was skilled at making hats,
his wife at weaving shoes,
they moved to Yuè and became greatly impoverished.
To practice one's skills in a land where they are useless,
is like planting lotuses on a mountain,
or keeping fire in a well.
Carrying a hook up a mountain,
or lifting an axe into the abyss,
wishing to obtain what one seeks,
is difficult.
Driving a carriage to Yuè,
or riding a raft into Hú,
hoping not to be lost,
is impossible.
16.89 The King of Chǔ had a white gibbon,
the king shot at it himself,
and it caught the arrow playfully;
he had Yǎng Yóu shoot it,
who merely adjusted his bow and arrow,
before shooting, the gibbon hugged the tree and wailed,
for it anticipated being hit.
16.90 The jade of Héshì,
the huáng of Xiàhòu,
presented with courtesy bring harmony and joy;
thrown at someone at night,
they cause resentment;
it depends on timing or its lack.
16.91 Painting Xīshī's face,
beautiful but not pleasing;
drawing Mèng Bēn's eyes,
large but not fearsome;
the spirit that governs form is absent.
16.92 There were brothers dividing property,
without measure,
yet the crowd praised their righteousness.
Precisely because it was immeasurable,
it could not be measured.
16.93 Ascending heights makes one desire to gaze afar,
facing depths makes one desire to peer down,
the environment causes this.
Archery makes one upright,
fishing makes one reverent,
the activity causes this.
16.94 They say killing a worn-out ox can redeem the death of a fine horse,
but no one does it.
Killing an ox
surely leads to its loss,
using certain loss to redeem uncertain death,
no one has ever done such a thing.
16.95 Jìsūnshì seized the ducal household,
Confucius persuaded him,
first complying with his actions before entering governance with him,
saying:
"Align with the crooked to reach the straight,
how can one not succeed?
Align with the straight to reach the crooked,
do not proceed with it."
This is what is called sharing the filth but taking different paths.
16.96 Many crooked lines tolerate no straight one,
many wicked tolerate no upright,
thus when men abound, they eat wolves,
when wolves abound, they eat men.
16.97 Those wishing to do evil must
appear clearly righteous,
those wishing to be crooked must seem straight.
If public justice is not upheld,
and private desires find accommodation,
from ancient times to the present,
it has never been heard of.
This is using good to conceal one's ugliness.
16.98 Many discussions create a forest.
Wingless, yet it flies;
three men create a market tiger,
one village can bend a hammer.
16.99 Those who swim and dive do not seek bathing,
for they are already sufficiently immersed.
Thus, grass-eating beasts do not suffer from changing marshes,
and water-dwelling creatures do not suffer from changing waters,
as minor shifts in behavior do not alter their inherent nature.
16.100 There are instances where trust is misplaced,
and rituals have their flaws:
Wěishēng died beneath a bridge pillar,
an example of misplaced trust;
the Kǒng family did not mourn a divorced mother,
an example of ritual error.
16.101 Zēngzǐ, upholding filial piety,
would not pass through the lane named Shèngmǔ;
Mòzǐ, opposing music,
would not enter the city of Cháogē;
Zēngzǐ, establishing integrity,
would not drink from the Dàoquán spring;
these are what is called nurturing one's aspirations.
16.102 When Zhòu used ivory chopsticks, Jīzǐ lamented;
when Lǔ buried with figurines, Confucius sighed;
thus, the sage sees frost and knows ice will follow.
16.103 When birds are about to arrive,
one sets a net to await them;
the part that catches a bird
is but one mesh of the net;
yet if one uses a net of only one mesh,
one will never catch a bird.
Now, those wearing armor
prepare for arrows to come;
if one could know exactly where they would strike,
one would hang just a single plate.
Some events cannot be planned for in advance,
some things cannot be anticipated;
they arrive suddenly and unprepared for,
hence the sage nurtures the Way to await the opportune moment.
16.104 A dappled plow ox,
with a yoke fitted to its hump,
a ring through its nose and tethered,
may produce an offspring fit for sacrifice;
the priest, after fasting and purification, sinks it into the river—
would the river god Hé Bó feel ashamed of its origin
and refuse to accept the offering?
16.105 Gaining the weapons of ten thousand soldiers
is not as good as hearing one apt word.
Obtaining the pearl of the Marquis of Suí
is not as good as understanding the cause of events.
Acquiring the jade disc of the Hé family
is not as good as knowing what is appropriate for the situation.
16.106 Those who train fine horses
do not do so to chase foxes and badgers,
but to hunt deer and elk.
Those who whet sharp swords
do not do so to cut thin silk,
but to sever rhinoceros hide.
Hence,
"Look up to the high mountain,
tread the virtuous path,"
for there dwell such men.
To see a pellet and crave an owl roast,
to see an egg and expect the dawn crow,
to see hemp fibers and demand finished cloth—
while logical in a way,
it is nonetheless as futile as waiting till dusk.
16.107 When an elephant sheds its tusks,
it does not resent others for taking them;
when one dies and leaves behind a burial mat,
one does not begrudge others for taking it.
If one can benefit others with what is of no loss to oneself,
then it is acceptable.
16.108 A madman runs east,
a pursuer also runs east;
their running east is the same,
but their reasons for doing so differ.
A drowning person enters the water,
a rescuer also enters the water;
their entering the water is the same,
but their reasons for doing so differ.
Thus, the sage equates life and death,
and the fool also equates life and death;
the sage's equating life and death comprehends the underlying principle,
while the fool's equating life and death ignores the stakes involved.
16.109 King Xú Yǎn lost his state through benevolence and righteousness,
but not all who lose their states do so because of benevolence and righteousness;
Bǐgān was mutilated for his loyalty,
but not all who are executed are necessarily loyal.
Thus, the cold tremble,
and the fearful also tremble;
this is the same name but different realities.
16.110 The bright moon pearl comes from the bàng shèn clam,
the Zhōu dynasty's ceremonial jade arises from grimy stones,
the great divination turtle emerges from ditches and gullies.
16.111 The ruler of ten thousand chariots
wears a crown worth zī and chuī weights,
and rides in a carriage worth a hundred pieces of gold.
A drum made of ox hide
commands the masses of the three armies.
16.112 Those who wish to learn singing
must first master the modes of zhǐ and yǔ;
those who seek to excel in harmony
begin with "Yáng'ē"
and "Cǎilíng";
these are instances of learning what one does not initially wish to learn,
in order to reach what one desires to master.
16.113 Those who catch cicadas by torchlight focus on brightening their flame;
those who fish focus on scenting their bait.
Brightening the flame
is to attract and draw them in;
scenting the bait
is to lure and benefit them.
To attract fish, one must first clear the water;
to attract birds, one must first plant trees.
Where water accumulates, fish gather;
where trees flourish, birds congregate.
Those fond of archery first prepare their line and arrow;
those fond of fishing first prepare their nets and traps;
none gain the benefit without the proper tools.
16.114 To give someone a horse but remove its bridle,
or give someone a carriage but detach its yoke—
what is given is little, but what is lost is much.
Hence, the village proverb says:
"To cook an ox without salt
ruins the endeavor."
16.115 Jié had his accomplishments,
Yáo had his oversights;
Mómǔ had her beauties,
Xīshī had her flaws.
Thus, the laws of a fallen state may have aspects worth following,
and the customs of a well-governed state may have aspects worth criticizing.
16.116 A piece of wǎnyǎn jade,
even lying in muddy filth,
will not be discarded by the upright;
a worn-out pot or cracked jar,
even placed on a felt mat,
will not be seized by the greedy.
Where there is beauty,
even if defiled and insulted,
the world cannot deem it lowly;
where there is ugliness,
even if elevated and honored,
the world cannot deem it noble.
16.117 Lending in spring and collecting in autumn pleases the people;
collecting in spring and lending in autumn angers the masses;
the gain and loss are the same,
but joy and resentment differ—
the timing is what varies.
16.118 To bestow virtue upon fish
is not to carry them into the deep;
to grant favor to monkeys
is not to carry them up trees;
simply let them follow what benefits them.
16.119 A marten coat that is mixed
is not as good as a pure fox fur;
thus, nothing is more detested in a person than inconsistent conduct.
16.120 There are those who judge horses and misjudge,
yet the good horse remains among those judged.
16.121 If someone sets a fire and it spreads,
some may carry fire to add to it,
others may fetch water to extinguish it;
though neither may succeed,
the gap between resentment and virtue is vast.
16.122 A man from Yǐng buying a roof beam
sought wood three arm-spans thick,
and someone gave him a chariot hub;
kneeling to measure it,
he found the thickness acceptable,
but the length insufficient.
16.123 Qú Bóyù transformed through virtue,
Gōngsūn Yāng enforced through punishment;
their ultimate aims were the same.
For the sick on their beds,
the doctor uses needles and stones,
the shaman uses offerings and straw;
their means of saving are equally aimed.
16.124 A fox's head cures mouse bites,
a chicken's head heals goiters,
horseflies disperse congealed blood,
and gnawing on wood relieves tooth decay—these are cases where analogies hold true.
But applying fat kills turtles,
magpie droppings strike hedgehogs,
rotting ashes breed flies,
and lacquer won't dry when crabs are present—these are cases where analogies fail.
Whether analogies hold or not,
what seems false may be true,
and what seems true may be false—who can penetrate such subtleties!
16.125 There are no purely white foxes in the world,
yet there are purely white fur coats—they are assembled from many white pieces.
A good learner is like the King of Qí eating chicken:
he must eat several dozen feet before being satisfied.
16.126 A knife is handy for shaving hair,
but for felling large trees, nothing but an axe will suffice.
Things inherently have what overcomes them, making suitability fall short.
16.127 Focusing on a square inch of an ox,
one doesn't realize it's larger than a goat;
viewing its whole body,
one then knows how far apart they are.
16.128 A pregnant woman seeing a rabbit results in her child having a harelip;
seeing a deer results in her child having four eyes.
16.129 A small horse with large eyes cannot be called a large horse;
a large horse with a blind eye can be called a blind horse.
Things inherently have cases of seeming so yet not being so.
Thus, losing a finger may lead to death,
while losing an arm may still allow survival—analogies cannot be rigidly applied.
16.130 Those who sharpen swords must use soft whetstones;
those who strike bells and chimes must use dampened wood;
a strong hub requires weak spokes.
Two hard things cannot harmonize,
two strong things cannot subdue each other.
Thus, a paulownia tree can break horns,
and horsehair can cut jade.
16.131 Matchmakers do not learn deception,
but their success breeds distrust.
Those who establish bravery do not learn fighting,
but their bravery leads to conflict.
Hence, the noble person does not enter prisons,
for it damages compassion;
does not enter markets,
for it compromises integrity—accumulated influences must be carefully considered.
16.132 Running doesn't use hands,
but binding hands impedes speed;
flying doesn't use the tail,
but bending the tail shortens the flight.
What is used must rely on what is not used.
Thus, what makes things visible is itself unseen;
what makes drums sound is itself silent.
16.133 Tasting one morsel of meat reveals the flavor of the whole pot;
hanging feathers and charcoal indicates humidity levels—using the small to understand the large.
Seeing one leaf fall knows the year is waning;
observing ice in a bottle knows the world's temperature—using the near to discuss the far.
16.134 Three people shoulder to shoulder cannot exit a door;
two people following each other can traverse the world.
16.135 Feet tread the ground to make footprints,
exposure creates shadows—this is easy yet difficult.
16.136 King Zhuāng executed the local historian,
while Sūnshū Áo mended caps and washed clothes;
Duke Wén discarded his mat,
later grew moldy and dark,
and Jiù Fǎn resigned and returned home—thus, falling leaves sadden the elderly.
16.137 A common tripod used daily isn't precious,
while a Zhōu dynasty鼎 unused isn't cheap—things inherently have value in being unused.
Level ground stops water flow,
equal weights balance the scale—extraordinary things must have triggers,
and things inherently can have great utility in non-use.
16.138 Being naked before bathing is acceptable,
but bathing to become naked is not;
sacrificing before feasting is acceptable,
but feasting before sacrificing is not—the sequence of things each has its propriety.
16.139 On sacrifice day speaking of dogs being born,
on wedding night speaking of mourning clothes,
on feast day speaking of visiting graves,
while crossing rivers speaking of Yánghóu's waves.
16.140 Some, knowing heaven may pardon, kill more people;
others, knowing heaven may pardon, spare more people.
Their hope for pardon is the same,
but their impact differs.
Thus, some blow on fire to ignite it,
others blow to extinguish it—the manner of blowing differs.
16.141 Slaughtering an ox to feast the village,
then insulting the neighbor's mother—kindness unreturned endangers oneself.
16.142 King Wén had a sunken chest,
Bào Shēn a hunched back,
yet they achieved order in Chǔ state.
Píchén knew things beyond the city walls,
thus accomplishing Zǐchǎn's deeds.
16.143 A dwarf asks a tall person about heaven's height;
the tall person says:
"I don't know."
The dwarf says:
"Though you don't know, you're closer than I am."
Hence, when asking about matters,
always consult those nearer to them.
16.144 When bandits approach,
a lame person warns a blind person,
the blind person carries him and runs—both survive by using their abilities.
Thus, making a mute speak
or a lame person run
wastes their capabilities.
16.145 A person from Yǐng sold his mother,
pleading with the buyer:
"This mother is old!
Please feed her well and don't mistreat her."
This is committing great injustice while seeking minor righteousness.
16.146 Shelled creatures move with firmness,
venomous insects move with stings,
bears move with grabs and swipes,
rhinoceroses move with charges—no creature neglects its strengths to use its weaknesses.
16.147 Governing a state is like weeding a field:
remove what harms the sprouts.
Now, bathers lose hair,
yet they don't stop—because what is lost is little,
what is gained is much.
16.148 A whetstone isn't sharp but can sharpen metal;
a straightening tool isn't straight but can straighten a bow—things inherently can be unstraight yet straighten,
unsharp yet sharpen.
16.149 Strength values swiftness,
wisdom values agility.
16.150 Achieving the same, speed is superior;
winning the same, slowness is inferior.
Mòyé sword is valued for responding swiftly to cut.
Cutting relentlessly,
an ox-cart breaks its linchpin.
16.151 To abandon the Six Arts because Confucius was stranded in Chén and Cài is deluded;
to avoid medicine because doctors can't cure their own illnesses is absurd.
17.1 Governing the world with the regulations of a single era
is like a passenger riding in a boat
who drops his sword midstream,
hastily notches the gunwale where it fell,
and searches for it at dusk when mooring—
how utterly ignorant of the nature of things!
To follow the traces of one corner
without knowing how to roam in accordance with Heaven and Earth—
no delusion is greater.
Though occasionally there may be coincidences,
they are not worthy of esteem.
Just like the earthen dragon in a drought year,
or the straw effigy during an epidemic—
they are treated as supreme only for that time.
17.2 The torn cloth of the Cáo family,
is prized by those with sores,
yet it is not the jade of the Xiàhòu clan.
17.3 There is no ancient or modern,
no beginning or end;
before Heaven and Earth existed, they were born—
how profoundly subtle and vast!
17.4 Where the foot treads is shallow,
yet it relies on where it does not tread to move forward;
what the intellect knows is limited,
yet it relies on what it does not know to become clear.
17.5 A swimmer kicks with the feet
and paddles with the hands;
without mastering the method,
the more they kick, the more they fail;
but when they can swim,
it is no longer by means of hands and feet.
17.6 Birds fly back to their homeland,
rabbits run to their burrows,
foxes die facing their mound,
and the hánjiāng glides over water—
each depends on where it was born.
17.7 Do not give a mirror to the blind,
nor shoes to the lame,
nor reward a Yuè person with a ceremonial cap—
they are of no use to them.
17.8 A hammer can secure a hundred handles,
yet it cannot peg itself;
the eyes can see a hundred paces away,
yet they cannot see their own corners.
17.9 Pigs do not choose between pots and bowls to eat,
stealing to fatten themselves only to hasten their death;
the phoenix soars high a thousand ren above,
thus none can capture it.
17.10 The moon illuminates the world,
yet is eclipsed by the toad;
the téngshé wanders through mist,
yet is endangered by the centipede;
the crow's strength surpasses the sun,
yet it is subdued by the owl—
abilities have their strengths and weaknesses.
17.11 None are as long-lived as a child who dies young,
while Péng Zǔ is considered short-lived.
17.12 A short rope cannot draw from the deep,
a small vessel cannot hold much,
for they are not up to the task.
17.13 Anger arises from non-anger,
action emerges from non-action.
17.14 Look at the formless,
and you will grasp what is seen;
listen to the soundless,
and you will grasp what is heard.
17.15 The ultimate flavor is not pleasing,
the ultimate words are not ornate,
the ultimate joy does not laugh,
the ultimate sound does not shout,
the great craftsman does not carve,
the great chef does not serve,
the great courage does not fight—
attain the Dào, and virtue follows.
It is like the Huángzhōng note matching the gōng,
or the Tàicù matching the shāng—
no need to change the tuning.
17.16 Betting with tiles leads to safety,
with gold to stumbling,
with jade to excitement—
thus, when what is valued lies externally,
the internal becomes hollowed out.
17.17 Those chasing game see not Tài Shān;
when desires are outward,
clarity is obscured.
17.18 To listen to the sound of sounds is deafness;
to listen to the sound of no-sound is acuity;
neither deaf nor acute,
one communicates with the divine.
17.19 The diviner holds the turtle shell,
the fortune-teller aligns the stalks,
to inquire of fate—
but where indeed is the inquiry made!
17.20 Dancers raise the beat,
and those seated, without planning, clap in unison—
their focus is the same.
17.21 The sun rises from Yánggǔ,
sets into Yúyuān,
none know its motion,
yet in a moment,
it can strike a person's neck.
17.22 None wish to learn to tame dragons,
but all wish to learn to tame horses;
none wish to learn to govern ghosts,
but all wish to learn to govern people—
for the urgency of utility.
17.23 Dismantling a gate for firewood,
blocking a well for a mortar—
in human endeavors,
sometimes it is similar.
17.24 Water and fire detest each other,
yet the cauldron stands between them,
harmonizing the five flavors.
Flesh and blood love each other,
but slanderers come between them,
and father and son endanger one another.
17.25 That which is meant to nurture instead harms the nurtured—
like cutting the feet to fit the shoes,
or shrinking the head to suit the hat.
17.26 The fragrant rush dispels fleas and lice but attracts qínqióng,
removing minor pests only to invite greater villains—
thus, a small pleasure can harm a great benefit.
17.27 A collapsing wall
is worse than having none,
yet better than a fallen roof.
17.28 The jade disc becomes a vessel
through the work of the whetstone;
the Mòyé sword cuts
by the power of grinding.
17.29 When the cunning hare is caught, the hound is cooked;
when the high-flying birds are gone, the strong bow is stored.
17.30 The gadfly and the steed,
cover a thousand lǐ without flying,
lacking provisions yet not hungry.
17.31 A fire breaks out and rain falls—
the fire is misfortune,
the rain is fortune,
thus within disaster lies blessing.
17.32 The coffin seller desires pestilence among the people,
the grain hoarder desires famine in the year.
17.33 Water calm becomes level,
level becomes clear,
clear reveals the forms of things,
which cannot be hidden—
thus it can serve as a standard.
17.34 Rivers dry and valleys empty,
hills flatten and abysses fill,
lips retract and teeth feel cold.
17.35 The depth of the river's water
has its soil in the mountains.
17.36 The same bolt of plain silk,
one end used for a hat,
the other for socks—
the hat is worn on the head, the socks
are trodden underfoot.
17.37 Those who know themselves cannot be tempted by things,
those clear about life and death cannot be coerced by danger,
thus skilled swimmers cannot be frightened from crossing.
17.38 Nothing is closer than flesh and blood,
with joints and sinews connecting them;
yet if the heart loses control,
it harms even itself—
how much more so those distant!
17.39 The sage's relation to the Way
is like the sunflower's to the sun:
though unable to follow it from beginning to end,
their turning toward it is sincere.
17.40 A palace pond overflows in heavy rain,
but dries up in drought;
the source of the Yangtze River,
however, no abyss can exhaust.
17.41 A roof cannot block sunlight without rafters,
nor can wheels pursue speed without spokes;
yet rafters and spokes alone are not enough to rely on.
17.42 Metal overcoming wood
does not mean one knife can destroy a forest;
earth overcoming water
does not mean one clod can dam a river.
17.43 A lame person seeing a tiger and not running
is not courage—
the circumstance is unfavorable.
17.44 What leans is easily toppled,
what inclines is easily pushed.
Moisture invites assistance,
dampness invites rain.
17.45 The trap set for mice moves by mechanism,
the float for fishing bobs on the water,
and the moving cart creaks under load.
17.46 A straw dog can stand but not walk;
snakebed resembles lovage but lacks its fragrance.
17.47 To say Xǔ Yóu lacks virtue,
or Wū Huò lacks strength,
would make any man show displeasure—
for all strive where they are deficient.
17.48 If a rabbit, running as it does,
were as large as a horse,
it could catch the sun and outrun the wind;
but when it becomes a horse,
it can no longer run so.
17.49 Though thunder may flash in winter,
frost may fall in summer,
the patterns of cold and heat do not change—
minor shifts cannot alter major seasons.
17.50 Huángdì generated yin and yang,
Shàngpián formed ears and eyes,
Sānglín shaped arms and hands—
thus Nǚwā transformed seventy times.
17.51 Speaking all day, one may touch on sagely matters;
shooting a hundred arrows, one may achieve Yì's
or Péng Méng's skill;
yet the world does not acknowledge it—
their adherence to principle is flawed.
17.52 A hoof of an ox or skull of a pig are also bones,
yet people do not scorch them for divination,
but must ask the turtle for fortune—
because it has passed through many years.
17.53 Those near the Áo Granary do not eat more,
those by the Jiāng
or Hé rivers do not drink more—
they only seek to fill their bellies.
17.54 Orchids and zhǐ flowers are fragrant
before they see frost;
the drum-maker avoids weapons,
yet his life ends by the full moon of May.
17.55 The tongue and teeth—
which is worn down first?
The spear's end and blade—
which is damaged first?
The cord and arrow—
which breaks first?
17.56 Now the eel and snake,
the silkworm and caterpillar,
look similar yet evoke different love and hate.
17.57 Jìn obtained Yú
and Guó with the Chuíjí jade, but the Líróng caused Jìn's downfall with beautiful women.
17.58 The deaf do not sing—
they have no way to enjoy music;
the blind do not look—
they have no way to perceive things.
17.59 Watching archery, one forgets his own skill;
reading books, one forgets his own preferences—
where the mind is focused,
there one neglects what he should guard.
17.60 If ancient ways could not be changed,
the wheeled vehicle would still lack rims today.
17.61 Have a novice play the yu,
and a craftsman cover the holes—
though the rhythm is correct, it is unlistenable,
for it lacks the spirit that masters the form.
17.62 Sharing the same ailment as the dead,
one cannot be a good doctor;
following the same path as a fallen state,
one cannot be a good advisor.
17.63 Preparing fine rice for guests while eating wild greens oneself—
the name exceeds the reality.
17.64 A nursing dog bites a tiger,
a brooding hen
attacks a fox—
where affection is involved,
they do not measure their strength.
17.65 What bends the shadow is the form,
what muddies the echo is the sound.
When feelings leak out,
the inner heart is easily gauged.
Flowers out of season
cannot be eaten.
17.66 Those going to Yuè
may go by boat,
or by cart—
though the paths differ,
the destination is the same.
17.67 Elegant women differ in form,
beautiful women differ in face,
yet all please the eye;
pears, oranges, dates, and chestnuts differ in taste,
yet all suit the palate.
17.68 Some become rich by theft,
but not all the rich are thieves;
some are poor yet upright,
but not all the poor are upright.
17.69 Thistledown resembles silk floss but cannot be used as such;
hemp fiber does not resemble cloth yet can be woven into it.
17.70 One leaving the forest cannot take a straight path;
one traversing peril cannot walk a tightrope.
17.71 Yì's ability to hit distant, tiny targets
lies not in his bow and arrow;
Zàofǔ's skill in chasing speed over distance
lies not in his reins and bit.
17.72 The sea contains what flows into it,
thus it becomes vast;
the wheel returns where it has passed,
thus it travels far.
17.73 Mutton does not crave ants,
but ants crave mutton—
because mutton is pungent;
vinegar does not crave gnats,
but gnats crave vinegar—
because vinegar is sour.
17.74 Tasting one morsel reveals the flavor of the whole pot;
hanging feathers and charcoal tells the humidity of the air—
seeing the large through the small,
understanding the far by the near.
17.75 A ten-qǐng pond can irrigate forty qǐng,
but a one-qǐng pond cannot irrigate four—
such is the difference in scale.
17.76 Moonlight allows seeing afar,
but not reading small script;
a foggy morning allows reading small script,
but not seeing beyond a short distance.
17.77 The painter meticulous with details may miss the overall appearance;
the archer focused on the small may neglect the large.
17.78 To eliminate rat holes yet ruin the village lanes,
to lance a small boil yet trigger a carbuncle—
like a pearl having a flaw,
jade having a blemish:
leaving it intact preserves its wholeness,
removing it causes damage.
17.79 Those nesting in thickets dwell where forests are lush,
for safety;
those burrowing in dens rely on embankments,
for convenience.
17.80 Wángzǐ Qìngjì could tread on deer
and wrestle rhinoceroses and tigers with his bare hands,
yet place him in a dark chamber,
and he cannot capture turtles—
such is the disadvantage of circumstance.
17.81 King Tāng exiled his ruler yet gained glory and fame,
while Cuī Zhǔ assassinated his lord and incurred great condemnation—
their actions were similar,
but their reasons for acting differed.
17.82 Lǚ Wàng inspired the elderly to strive,
Xiàng Tuō made infants proud—
each attracts admiration from their kind.
17.83 It is the wind that shakes the leaves to fall,
it is the fish that stir the water to muddiness.
17.84 The patterned coats of tigers and leopards draw arrows,
the agility of monkeys invites sudden traps.
17.85 Moving one chess piece does not suffice to reveal wisdom,
plucking one string does not suffice to express sorrow.
17.86 A three-inch pipe without a bottom,
the world cannot fill it;
a ten-dàn vessel with a stopper,
a hundred dǒu suffice.
17.87 To measure a river with a pole,
then use the water to measure after the pole ends—
how confused!
17.88 Fishers hurry to deep waters,
gatherers hurry to the mountains—
what they urgently seek is there.
In the morning market, they run;
passing the market at evening, they walk—
what they seek is gone.
17.89 A marten coat mixed with other furs
is not as pure as a fox fur;
a white jade with flaws
cannot be considered a treasure—
such is the difficulty of achieving utmost purity.
17.90 The ghosts of those slain in war despise shamans,
thieves and robbers detest barking dogs.
17.91 An altar without a village is easily offered millet and meat,
a harvest god without a state is easily prayed to for blessings.
A turtle has no ears, yet its eyes cannot be deceived—
refined in sight.
The blind have no eyes, yet their ears cannot be blocked—
refined in hearing.
17.92 A posthumous child does not long for his father,
for he holds no image in his heart;
he does not dream of his likeness,
for he has no form in his eyes.
17.93 A viper cannot be given feet,
a tiger or leopard cannot be made to climb trees.
17.94 Horses do not eat fat,
and the sang hù bird does not peck at grain—
not out of frugality.
Qín cleared the Xiáo pass,
so Wèi built walls.
17.95 Hungry horses in the stable,
silent and still;
toss fodder beside them,
and rivalry arises.
17.96 Drawing a bow to shoot,
without the string, the arrow cannot be loosed—
yet the string's role in shooting
is but one percent.
17.97 The Dào and virtue can be constant,
but power and tactics cannot—
thus, a breached pass cannot be restored,
a lost law cannot be reinstated.
17.98 A ring can illustrate roundness,
without needing a wheel;
a silk ribbon can serve as a cord,
without needing a braid.
17.99 The sun and moon do not rise together,
foxes do not have two males,
divine dragons have no equals,
fierce beasts do not form packs,
birds of prey do not fly in pairs.
17.100 Carving along a guideline ensures no error,
measuring with a suspended balance ensures no discrepancy,
observing with a set marker ensures no confusion.
17.101 Reducing one's age raises suspicion of being a younger brother,
increasing it arouses doubt of being an elder—
better to follow the natural order,
and let it be appropriate.
17.102 People do not see the dragon's flight,
yet when it rises high,
wind and rain support it.
17.103 Many borers cause the tree to break,
a large crack causes the wall to collapse.
17.104 Hanging objects,
may fall in time;
branching limbs,
may slacken in time.
17.105 Those who do not die in the cold
do not lose their comfort;
those who do not suffer heatstroke in the summer
do not forfeit their comfort—
never without comfort,
yet losing comfort.
17.106 When the bath is ready, lice mourn together;
when the great mansion is built, swallows and sparrows congratulate each other—
such is the distinction in sorrow and joy.
17.107 Liǔxià Huì saw malt sugar
and said it could nourish the aged;
Dào Zhí saw malt sugar
and said it could glue locks—
seeing the same object,
yet using it differently.
17.108 Silkworms eat without drinking,
transforming in thirty-two days;
cicadas drink without eating,
molting in thirty days;
mayflies neither eat nor drink,
dying in three days.
17.109 Humans eat arsenolite and die,
yet silkworms eat it and are not hungry;
fish eat croton seeds and die,
yet mice eat them and grow fat—
outcomes cannot be rigidly predicted by category.
17.110 Tile is formed by fire,
yet cannot withstand fire;
bamboo grows with water,
yet cannot endure water.
17.111 Stirring dust to try to settle it,
wearing a fur coat while fanning with a feather—
how could it compare to dressing suitably!
17.112 Dry bamboo holds fire,
but without drilling, it does not ignite;
earth contains water,
but without digging, it does not flow.
17.113 The ailment of the bàng oyster
is a treasure to humans;
but human ailments—
who would treasure them?
17.114 If for the winemaker's profit, one does not buy wine,
the supply dries up;
if for the cart driver's profit, one does not hire a cart,
one does not reach the destination.
Grasping fire to warm others,
one gets burned first.
17.115 When a neighbor's mother died,
he went to weep;
when his own wife died, he did not shed tears—
compelled to be so by circumstance.
17.116 In the western land of the Luǒ people,
birds and beasts do not avoid them,
for they are one with them.
17.117 A single piece of burning charcoal,
if touched, will scorch the fingers;
ten thousand stones heated together,
one can stand ten steps away without harm:
this is due to the difference in accumulation of the same heat.
Great courage and petty courage
are somewhat similar to this.
17.118 Now, take a mat six feet long:
lying down and rolling over it,
even a person of lesser ability finds it not difficult;
standing and leaping over it,
even a person of superior ability finds it not easy:
the circumstances of the action differ.
17.119 A hundred plums can sour a hundred people,
but one plum cannot even flavor one person.
17.120 To forbid all under heaven from eating because someone choked on food,
or to forbid all under heaven from riding because a carriage overturned,
would be absurd.
17.121 The angler stays still,
the net-dragger taps the boat;
the cover-net user presses down,
the lift-net user raises up:
their methods differ,
but catching fish is the same result.
17.122 Seeing an elephant's tusk, one knows it is larger than an ox;
seeing a tiger's tail, one knows it is larger than a wildcat:
one part seen reveals the nature of all parts.
17.123 A small state does not fight between large states;
two deer do not fight beside a crouching rhinoceros.
17.124 Those who assist in sacrifices get to taste the offerings;
those who intervene in fights get wounded.
Sheltering under an inauspicious tree,
one is struck by lightning.
17.125 Some call it a mound,
some call it a ridge;
some call it a rain hat,
some call it a bamboo hat:
the names differ but the reality is the same.
Head lice and the zither made of hollow wood,
the name is the same but the reality differs.
17.126 The sun and moon wish to shine, but floating clouds cover them;
the orchid and zhǐ wish to flourish, but the autumn wind ruins them.
17.127 A tiger has cubs;
those unable to pounce and seize,
it kills immediately,
to avoid weakening their martial prowess.
17.128 The seal with a turtle knob,
the worthy wear it as an ornament;
soil spread in the fields,
the capable consider it wealth.
Giving gold and jade to a drowning person
is not as good as an ordinary rope.
17.129 Looking at writing:
if above it mentions wine,
below there must be meat;
if above it mentions the year,
below there must be the month—
one infers by category.
17.130 Getting dust in the eye while in a dust storm
is in accordance with reason;
but to have dust blown in while not leaving the house
goes against the natural way.
17.131 The butcher drinks bean-leaf soup,
the carriage-maker walks on foot,
the potter uses a broken basin,
the carpenter lives in a narrow hut:
those who make things do not get to use them,
those who use them are unwilling to make them.
17.132 The hub stands firm,
thirty spokes each exert their force,
without harming one another.
If one spoke alone enters,
and all others are discarded,
how could it cover a thousand lǐ?
17.133 The night walker covers his eyes and stretches his hands forward;
the wader unharnesses his horse and loads it on the boat:
some actions are suitable in certain situations,
and some are not to be applied.
17.134 Oranges and pomelos have their homeland,
reeds and rushes have their thickets.
Beasts with the same feet roam together,
birds with the same wings fly together.
17.135 The puddles in the fields
flow into the sea;
words whispered close to the ear
are heard a thousand lǐ away.
17.136 Sū Qín walking was asked why he walked,
hurrying was asked why he hurried,
running was asked why he ran.
When one acts, there is criticism;
much activity inevitably invites pettiness.
17.137 If the skin is not seen,
how can one care for the fur!
Fearing the head and fearing the tail,
how much of the body is left!
17.138 Wishing to observe the lands of the nine provinces,
but without traveling a thousand lǐ;
having no understanding of governance and education,
yet wanting to be above the myriad people—
that is difficult.
17.139 The conspicuous is captured,
the prominent is shot at;
thus the greatest purity seems soiled,
the greatest virtue seems insufficient.
17.140 Without ever farming, grain fills the granary;
without ever raising silkworms, silk fills the bag—
if obtained not by the right way,
its use will surely be reckless.
17.141 The sea does not accept floating carcasses,
Tài Shān does not accommodate petty men,
the bladder does not rise to the sacrificial stand,
piebald horses are not used as sacrificial animals.
17.142 Using a fan in midsummer
feels pleasant,
but by winter one still does not know to put it away;
lifting clothes to wade water,
but upon reaching land not knowing to lower them—
such cannot respond to change.
17.143 There are mountains without forests,
valleys without wind,
stones without metal.
17.144 In a hall full of seated people,
the hooks they look at differ,
but their girdle rings are the same.
17.145 The worthiness of Duke Xiàn
was deceived by Lí Jī;
the wisdom of Shūsūn
was deceived by Shù Niú.
Thus when Zhèng Zhān entered Lǔ,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" said:
"The flatterer has come,
the flatterer has come."
17.146 The nobleman has fine wine,
