the rustic drums on an earthen jar;
though not pleasing,
it is not considered ugly.
17.147 Human nature favors wearing silk,
but when shooting arrows, one dons armor—
enduring inconvenience to achieve convenience.
17.148 The spokes entering the hub
each fit into their own mortise,
not connecting with one another,
just as officials each keep to their duties,
not interfering with each other.
17.149 One who avoided arrows by wearing armor
then wears it into water;
one who crossed water holding a gourd
then holds it through fire—
this can be called not understanding categories.
17.150 The nobleman governing the people
is like driving galloping horses with a rotten rein,
like treading on thin ice
with a dragon below,
like entering a forest and meeting a nursing tigress.
17.151 One who excels at employing people
is like the legs of a millipede,
numerous yet not harming each other;
like the lips and teeth,
hard and soft rubbing together yet not destroying each other.
17.152 The excellence of clear wine begins with the plow and spade;
the beauty of embroidered robes lies in the shuttle and loom.
17.153 New linen is not as good as ramie, but worn ramie is not as good as linen;
some things excel when new, others when old.
17.154 Dimples on the cheeks are lovely, but on the forehead they are ugly;
embroidery is suitable for skirts but questionable for crowns.
17.155 A horse's teeth are not a cow's hooves, a sandalwood root is not a catalpa branch;
thus, seeing one origin reveals the nature of all things.
17.156 Stones are born hard, orchids are born fragrant;
their essence is present in youth and grows clearer with age.
17.157 Supporting and lifting, thanking and yielding, gaining and losing,
promising and refusing—these are a thousand miles apart.
17.158 To whitewash the forehead while the nose is dirty;
to place a rotten rat in the altar and burn incense in the palace;
to enter water yet hate getting wet, to carry stench yet seek fragrance—
even the skilled cannot do this well.
17.159 Crops that regrow cannot be harvested;
flowers that bloom too early fall without waiting for their season.
17.160 Do not cry misfortune—a pot never falls into a well.
Pulling a hairpin to summon a will-o'-the-wisp, why be startled?
17.161 One can forbid crossing the river, but not midway in the river.
17.162 Seeing one stripe of a tiger, one cannot know its ferocity;
seeing one hair of a steed, one cannot know its speed.
17.163 The water beetle becomes a pupa, the wiggler becomes a mosquito,
the nibbled plant becomes a gall—things transform unexpectedly;
the ignorant are amazed, the knowledgeable are not surprised.
17.164 Copper's essence is green, gold's essence yellow, jade's essence white;
a hemp torch is rough, an oil lamp is smooth—
from the subtle, know the obvious; from the external, know the internal.
17.165 The taste of elephant meat is not known to the mouth,
the form of ghosts and spirits is not seen by the eyes,
the theory of catching shadows does not take shape in the mind.
17.166 Winter ice can be broken, summer wood can be tied—
time is hard to gain and easy to lose.
17.167 When trees are lush, picking all day goes unnoticed;
when autumn wind brings frost, they wither in one night.
17.168 To force-feed one with fever, to give cold drinks to save from heatstroke,
to pull a rope to save from hanging, to throw a stone to rescue a drowning—
intending to help, instead one harms.
17.169 Though wishing to prevent horse loss, one does not remove the door pivot;
though wanting to prepare for wine, one does not carry a mat.
17.170 When Mèng Bēn probes a mouse hole, the mouse may bite his finger before dying,
causing him to lose his advantage.
17.171 When mountain clouds gather, the pillar base dampens;
when poria is dug up, dodder dies.
17.172 If one house catches fire, a hundred houses burn;
if slanderers plot in secret, the common people suffer exposed bones.
17.173 Grain heats with water, a steamer releases liquid with fire;
there is fire in water, water in fire.
17.174 A sudden thunderbolt splits rocks—
yin and yang clash, a natural tendency.
17.175 Bathing in the river brings little benefit;
draining floodwaters into the sea, though not adding much, is better than stopping.
17.176 A net with one mesh cannot catch birds;
a hook without bait cannot catch fish;
meeting scholars without courtesy cannot attract the worthy.
17.177 Dodder grows without roots, snakes move without feet,
fish hear without ears, cicadas sing without mouths—
such is their inherent nature.
17.178 Cranes live a thousand years, roaming to their fullest;
mayflies are born at dawn and die by dusk, yet enjoy their pleasure completely.
17.179 When Zhòu minced Méi Bó, King Wén allied with the lords against him;
when Jié tortured remonstrators, Tāng had people mourn them.
A mad horse does not crash into trees, a rabid dog does not jump into the river—
even dumb creatures avoid self-destruction, let alone humans!
17.180 To love a bear and feed it salt, to love an otter and give it wine—
though intending to nurture them, it goes against their nature.
17.181 If the heart desires it, one breaks a boat to make an oar;
if the mind wishes it, one melts a bell to cast a bell.
17.182 Guǎnzǐ turned small humiliations into great glory;
Sū Qín transformed a hundred deceptions into one sincerity.
17.183 When the target is set, arrows gather;
when the forest grows thick, axes enter—
no one summons them; it is the force of circumstances.
17.184 To wait for profit before saving a drowning person is to profit from their drowning.
17.185 A boat that may sink or float—a fool will not step aboard.
17.186 A steed that refuses to advance when driven and does not stop when led—
a ruler should not use it for travel.
17.187 Those who criticize my actions wish to befriend me;
those who disparage my goods wish to trade with me.
17.188 Water mixed with water is undrinkable;
a one-stringed zither is unlistenable.
17.189 A fine horse dies from restraint, an upright scholar is impoverished by integrity;
the worthy are excluded from court, beauties are spurned in the palace.
17.190 The traveler ponders on the road,
while the dweller dreams in bed;
a loving mother chants in Yān,
and her wandering son longs for Jīng—
their spirits commune across the distance.
17.191 Where raw meat hangs, crows and magpies gather;
where hawks and falcons swoop, flocks of birds scatter.
The dispersal and assembly of things
occur through mutual influence.
17.192 Those who eat from a vessel do not break it;
those who enjoy its fruit do not break its branches.
Block the source, and it will run dry;
turn away from the root, and it will wither.
17.193 Intertwined lines cannot stretch freely,
interlocked rings cannot be separated—
their solution lies in not solving them.
17.194 Gazing at the river and coveting fish
is not as good as going home to weave a net.
17.195 The pearl of bright moonlustre
is a bane to the oyster but a boon to me;
the tiger’s claws and elephant’s tusks
benefit the beast but harm me.
17.196 A smooth road and a fine horse
make one want to gallop;
the joy of drinking wine
makes one want to sing.
17.197 To act upon what is right
is called decisiveness;
to act upon what is wrong
is called disorder.
17.198 An arrow in flight
cannot exceed two lǐ,
but with slow, steady steps,
pausing not even after a hundred nights,
one may cover a thousand lǐ.
17.199 The sage dwells in the shade,
the multitude in the light.
The sage walks on water,
leaving no trace;
the multitude treads on frost,
marking their path.
17.200 Different tones cannot be judged by one pitch;
different forms cannot be confined to one mold.
17.201 The farmer toils so the gentleman may be nourished;
the fool speaks so the wise may choose.
17.202 To abandon lush trees for barren wood,
to shoot not at swans but at crows—
such a one is hard to partner with in plans.
17.203 If a high hill has no valleys,
its springs will not flow abundantly;
a modest stream,
however, can irrigate fields of ten qǐng.
17.204 When things are clear,
handle them as jade or stone;
when they are obscure,
one must ponder them carefully.
17.205 To entrust the vastness of the world
to the talent of one person
is like hanging a weight of a thousand jūn on a single tree branch.
17.206 Carrying a child to climb a wall
is called ill-omened,
for if one falls, two perish.
17.207 Those skilled in handling affairs
are like boarding a boat with a mournful song—
one sings, and a thousand join in.
17.208 To desire fine grains without farming,
to delight in silken robes without weaving,
to seek achievement without effort—
such is difficult indeed.
17.209 Where there is glory and bloom, there must be withering;
where there are silks and satins, there must be hempen cloth.
17.210 There is a bird that churns the waves,
and the River God avoids the tide for it,
fearing its sincerity.
Thus, when one man is ready to die,
a thousand chariots do not take him lightly.
17.211 If a viper bites a person,
applying hémǔ and jǐn heals the wound—
for among things, some that are harmful can conversely become beneficial.
17.212 The sage enduring a chaotic age
is like waiting out a summer day until dusk:
in the twilight between mulberry and elm,
it becomes easier to endure.
17.213 Water may be still,
but it will have ripples;
a scale may be balanced,
but it will have error;
measures may be even,
but they will have discrepancy.
17.214 Without compass and square, one cannot fix circles and squares;
without marking-line and plumb, one cannot straighten the crooked.
Those who use compass, square, line, and plumb
themselves follow compass, square, line, and plumb.
17.215 Only when the boat capsizes is the skilled swimmer revealed;
only when the horse gallops is the expert driver seen.
17.216 What is chewed yet tasteless cannot be swallowed;
what is seen yet formless cannot be pondered in the heart.
17.217 With a rhinoceros or tiger behind
and the Pearl of Suí Hóu in front,
one who does not grab it
prioritizes avoiding harm over seizing gain.
17.218 Those chasing deer do not glance at hares;
those deciding on treasures worth a thousand gold do not haggle over trifles.
17.219 A bow must first be adjusted, then sought for strength;
a horse must first be tamed, then sought for excellence;
a person must first be trustworthy, then sought for ability.
17.220 The potter discards the rope,
the cartwright picks it up;
the butcher discards the whetstone,
the blacksmith retrieves it—
for their needs differ in urgency.
17.221 The light of a hundred stars is not as bright as one moon;
ten open windows do not illuminate as well as one door.
17.222 An arrow can pierce rhinoceros hide at ten paces,
yet at its farthest reach,
it cannot penetrate Lǔ gauze.
17.223 Tài Shān’s great height,
if one turns away, remains unseen;
the tip of an autumn hair,
if gazed upon, can be discerned.
17.224 A mountain yielding gold
is carved away by it;
wood breeding borers
is eaten by them;
humans creating affairs
17.225 A skilled smith cannot cast wood,
a fine carpenter cannot carve metal—
such is the nature of form and substance.
17.226 White jade needs no carving,
beautiful pearls no patterning,
for their substance is already abundant.
Thus, with unceasing half-steps,
a lame turtle can journey a thousand lǐ;
with unbroken accumulation,
a hillock can be formed.
A wall is built from earth,
timber straightened by the line—
not by forced effort,
but by following what enables it.
17.227 In the way of employing people,
it is like drilling for fire with a stick:
too sparse, and you get none;
too frequent, and you miss the spot.
It lies precisely between sparse and frequent.
17.228 Viewing evening from morning shows change;
aligning straight from crooked reveals deficiency.
The sage’s engagement with things
is like viewing form in a mirror,
discerning the truth in every curve.
17.229 Yáng Zǐ wept at the crossroads,
for it could lead south or north;
Mò Zǐ shed tears over plain silk,
for it could be dyed yellow or black.
17.230 The convergence of paths,
like the harmony of metal and stone in one tune,
though separated by a thousand years,
unite in a single sound.
17.231 Birds that do not interfere with defense,
even if close, are not shot;
those blocking the path,
even if distant, are not released.
17.232 If wine bought turns sour,
or meat purchased becomes putrid,
yet buying wine and meat never strays from the brewer's and butcher's homes,
thus seeking things must be done from those nearby.
17.233 Responding to deceit with deceit,
to cunning with cunning,
is like wearing a straw raincoat to fight fire,
digging a channel to stop water—
it only makes it more abundant.
17.234 Xī Shī
and Máo Qiáng,
their appearances are not the same,
yet the world praises their beauty,
for their loveliness is equal.
Yáo, Shùn,
Yǔ, Tāng,
their laws and records differ in kind,
but winning the people's hearts is one and the same.
17.235 The sage
acts according to the times,
achieves merit based on resources,
prepares buckets for drainage during floods,
builds earthen dragons in drought.
17.236 The woman of Línzī,
weaving fine silk while thinking of a traveler,
produces tangled and perverse work.
A room with beautiful women,
causes silk fabrics to be poorly woven.
17.237 The melodies of zhǐ and yǔ notes,
do not enter the ears of vulgar people;
harmonious and fitting tunes,
are praised by the entire assembly.
17.238 Those who pass by a treasury with hands behind their back,
rarely lack thieving intent;
thus, those who insult others' ghosts,
shake its branches when passing the shrine.
17.239 Yáng Chùfǔ of Jìn attacked Chǔ to save Jiāng,
so resolving a struggle does not lie in grappling hard,
but in striking the vital points.
17.240 Large trees have widespread roots,
high mountains have broad bases,
large feet travel far,
massive bodies have spaced joints.
17.241 A madman injures people,
yet none bear him resentment;
an infant curses the elderly,
yet none grow angry;
for harmful intent is absent.
17.242 Wěi Shēng's faithfulness,
is not as good as Suí Niú's deceit,
and how much more so for one who is unfaithful!
17.243 The son worries over his father's illness,
but it is the doctor who treats it;
the invoker makes offerings,
but the cook prepares the sacrifice.
Purity, tranquility, and contentment,
are human nature;
models, standards, and rules,
are the measures of affairs.
Knowing human nature,
one's self-cultivation is not confused;
knowing the measures of affairs,
one's actions are not mistaken.
Emanating from one source,
spreading without end,
encompassing the eight extremes,
united in one conduit,
this is called the mind.
Seeing the root and knowing the branches,
observing the direction and perceiving the outcome,
holding to one to respond to ten thousand,
grasping the essential to manage the detailed,
this is called method.
Dwelling, guided by wisdom in action;
acting, guided by wisdom in direction;
handling affairs, guided by wisdom in principles;
moving, guided by wisdom in reasons,
this is called the Way.
The Way,
placed ahead does not weigh heavy,
set behind does not rise light,
contained within a small space is not obstructed,
spread across the world is not sparse.
Therefore, causing others to praise and honor oneself,
is the power of the mind;
causing others to debase and slander oneself,
is the fault of the mind.
Words spoken from the mouth cannot be stopped by others,
actions initiated nearby cannot be restrained afar.
Affairs,
are hard to succeed but easy to fail;
reputation,
is hard to establish but easy to ruin.
A thousand-lǐ dike,
leaks from the burrow of an ant;
a hundred-xún tall house,
burns from the smoke through a chimney crack.
The "Admonition of Yáo" says:
"Trembling with fear,
be cautious day by day.
Do not trip over a mountain,
but trip over an anthill."
Therefore, people who belittle small harms,
trivialize minor matters,
often come to regret.
Worrying only after disaster strikes,
is like a sick person seeking a skilled doctor when already exhausted,
even with the expertise of Biǎn Què
or Yú Fū,
they still cannot be saved.
For the coming of calamity,
is born from people themselves;
the arrival of blessing,
is achieved by people themselves.
Calamity and blessing share the same gate,
benefit and harm are close neighbors,
unless one is a divine sage,
none can distinguish them.
In all human undertakings,
none do not first use their knowledge to plan and deliberate,
before daring to set their strategy.
Whether it brings benefit or harm,
this is what distinguishes the foolish from the wise.
Clearly considering oneself wise about the pivotal mechanisms of survival and demise,
the gateway to fortune and disaster,
yet acting on it and falling into difficulties,
such cases are innumerable.
If one knew the means to do what is right,
ensuring actions are feasible,
then there would be no impassable roads under heaven.
Therefore, knowledge and deliberation
are the gateway to fortune and disaster,
movement and stillness
are the pivotal mechanisms of benefit and harm.
The changes of all affairs,
the order or chaos of the state,
depend on them to be achieved.
Hence, those not drowned in difficulties succeed,
and thus one must be cautious.
Under heaven, there are three perils:
little virtue but much favor,
first peril;
low ability but high position,
second peril;
no great merit but generous salary,
third peril.
Thus, things may be diminished yet increased,
or increased yet diminished.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ had defeated Jìn between the Hé and
Yōng rivers,
and upon returning, he enfeoffed Sūnshū Áo.
Sūnshū Áo declined and did not accept,
and when he was ill and near death,
he said to his son:
"I am about to die,
and the king will surely enfeoff you.
You must decline the fertile and rich land,
and accept the sandy and stony land.
Between Chǔ and Yuè there is a place called Qǐnzhīqiū,
whose land is barren and whose name is ugly.
The people of Jīng believe in ghosts,
the people of Yuè practice jī rituals,
and no one finds it beneficial."
After Sūnshū Áo died,
the king indeed enfeoffed his son with fertile land,
but his son declined and did not accept,
requesting Qǐnzhīqiū instead.
According to Chǔ custom,
meritorious officials' titles and emoluments are reclaimed after two generations,
yet only Sūnshū Áo's line alone survived.
This is what is called losing to gain.
What is called gaining to lose?
In the past, Duke Lì of Jìn attacked Chǔ to the south,
attacked Qí to the east,
attacked Qín to the west,
and attacked Yān to the north.
His troops marched across the world without hindrance,
his might subdued the four directions without resistance,
and he then assembled the feudal lords at Jiālíng.
But with his spirit inflated and will arrogant,
indulging in excess without restraint,
he tyrannized the myriad people.
Internally, he had no ministers to assist and correct him;
externally, he had no support from the feudal lords.
He executed his high ministers,
and kept close to those who flattered him.
The following year, while traveling to Jiànglíshì,
Luán Shū
and Zhōngháng Yǎn seized and imprisoned him.
No feudal lord came to his rescue,
and none of the common people mourned for him;
he died after three months.
Now, to win in battle and capture cities,
to expand territory and elevate one's name,
this is what everyone under heaven desires,
yet it ended with his death and the state's destruction.
This is what is called gaining to lose.
Sūnshū Áo's request for Qǐnzhīqiū,
the sandy and stony land,
is why it remained unseized for generations.
Duke Lì of Jìn's assembly of feudal lords at Jiālíng
is why he met his death at Jiànglíshì.
Everyone knows to seek benefit and avoid harm,
but only the sage knows that harm can be benefit,
and benefit can be harm.
A tree that bears fruit twice will surely have its roots injured;
a family that unearths hidden treasure will surely suffer calamity—
this illustrates how great benefit can turn into harm.
Zhāng Wǔ advised Zhì Bó to seize the lands of Hán
and Wèi, yet he was captured at Jìnyáng,
while Shēnshū Shí advised King Zhuāng to enfeoff the descendants of the Chén family and he became hegemon over the world.
When Confucius read the Yìjīng, upon reaching "Diminishment"
and "Increase,"
he never failed to sigh and say:
"Increase and diminishment—
are they not the affairs of a true king!
Sometimes one intends to benefit something,
but ends up harming it;
sometimes one intends to harm something,
but instead benefits it.
The reversal of benefit and harm,
the gateway to fortune and misfortune,
must be carefully examined."
Yáng Hǔ caused turmoil in Lǔ,
and the ruler of Lǔ ordered the city gates closed to capture him,
offering a heavy reward for his capture,
and imposing a heavy penalty for his escape.
Surrounded three layers deep,
Yáng Hǔ was about to raise his sword to his own neck.
But a gatekeeper stopped him, saying,
"I will let you out."
Yáng Hǔ then broke through the encirclement and fled,
brandishing his sword and spear as he ran.
The gatekeeper let him out,
but Yáng Hǔ turned back and seized the one who had released him,
struck him with his spear,
and tore his sleeve, grazing his armpit.
The one who had released him complained:
"Did I not intentionally befriend you?
I risked death and crime for you,
yet you in turn injure me.
No wonder you have such misfortune!"
When the ruler of Lǔ heard that Yáng Hǔ had escaped,
he was furious,
inquired which gate he had exited from,
and ordered the officials to arrest those involved,
considering the injured as
those who had fought,
and the uninjured
as those who had let him escape.
The injured received heavy rewards,
while the uninjured suffered heavy penalties.
This is what is called harming but instead benefiting.
What is called intending to benefit but instead harming?
When King Gōng of Chǔ battled the people of Jìn at Yānlíng,
the fight was intense,
and King Gōng, wounded, called a halt.
Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn, thirsty, sought a drink,
and Shù Yánggǔ presented him with wine.
Zǐfǎn's nature
was such that he loved wine and found it sweet,
and he could not stop drinking,
so he became drunk and lay down.
King Gōng wished to resume battle,
and sent someone to summon Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn,
but Zǐfǎn pleaded a heart ailment.
The king rode to see him,
and upon entering the tent, smelled the stench of wine.
King Gōng angrily said:
"In today's battle,
I myself have been wounded;
what I relied on
was the Sīmǎ,
yet the Sīmǎ is in such a state.
This is to destroy the altars of Chǔ
and have no pity for my people.
I will not resume the battle!"
Thereupon, he withdrew the army and left,
and beheaded Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn as a punishment.
Thus, when Shù Yánggǔ offered the wine,
it was not to bring disaster upon Zǐfǎn,
but out of genuine affection and a desire to please him,
yet it sufficed to get him killed.
This is what is called intending to benefit but instead harming.
To force-feed one with a warm illness,
or give cold drinks to one with heatstroke,
is how the masses think to nourish,
but what a good physician considers causing illness.
What pleases the eye,
and delights the heart,
is what fools consider beneficial,
yet it is what the discerning avoid.
Thus, the sage first opposes and then unites,
while the masses first unite and then oppose.
To achieve merit
is what ministers strive for;
to incur guilt
is what ministers avoid.
Yet some with merit are suspected,
while some with guilt are trusted even more.
Why is this?
It is because those with merit may drift from kindness and duty,
while those with guilt dare not lose their humane heart.
When Yuè Yáng, a general of Wèi, attacked Zhōngshān,
his son was held in the city,
and the city hung his son out to show Yuè Yáng.
Yuè Yáng said:
"By the duty between ruler and minister,
I cannot act for private sake because of my son."
He attacked even more fiercely.
Zhōngshān then cooked his son
and sent him the cauldron of soup with his head,
Yuè Yáng stroked it and wept,
saying:
"This is my son."
He knelt before the messenger and drank three cups.
When the messenger returned and reported,
Zhōngshān said:
"This is one who adheres to covenant and dies for integrity;
we cannot withstand him."
So they surrendered to him.
He greatly expanded territory for Marquis Wén of Wèi,
achieving merit.
But after this,
he was increasingly distrusted.
This is what is called having merit but being suspected.
What is meant by "being trusted more despite having committed a fault"?
Mèngsūn caught a fawn while hunting,
and ordered Qín Xībā to take it home and cook it.
The fawn's mother followed, crying.
Qín Xībā could not bear it,
so he released the fawn and gave it back to its mother.
When Mèngsūn returned,
he asked where the fawn was.
Qín Xībā replied:
"Its mother followed, crying,
and I truly could not bear it,
so I secretly released it and gave it back."
Mèngsūn was angry,
and expelled Qín Xībā.
After a year had passed,
he appointed him as his son's tutor.
His attendants said:
"Qín Xībā was at fault before you,
yet now you appoint him as your son's tutor.
Why?"
Mèngsūn said:
"If he could not bear to harm a single fawn,
how much more would he care for people!"
This is what is called "being trusted more despite having committed a fault."
Therefore, one must be careful in choosing one's course of action.
This is why Gōngsūn Yāng was condemned in Qín,
and could not enter Wèi.
His achievements were not insignificant,
yet he had no place to stand securely,
because of his lack of righteousness.
Sometimes, by taking away, one ends up giving;
sometimes, by giving, one ends up taking away.
Zhì Bó sought territory from Wèi Xuānzǐ,
and Xuānzǐ was unwilling to give it.
Rén Déng said:
"Zhì Bó is powerful,
his might prevails throughout the realm.
If we refuse his request for land,
we will be the first among the feudal lords to suffer disaster.
It would be better to give it to him."
Xuānzǐ said:
"If he keeps demanding land,
what can we do?"
Rén Déng said:
"Give it to him,
make him pleased,
and he will surely seek more land from the other feudal lords.
The feudal lords will certainly prick up their ears.
Then we can unite with the realm to plot against him,
and what we gain from a united effort
will not be limited to just what we lost."
So Wèi Xuānzǐ divided his land and gave it to him.
Zhì Bó then sought land from Hán Kāngzǐ,
and Hán Kāngzǐ did not dare to refuse.
All the feudal lords were alarmed.
He also sought land from Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
but Xiāngzǐ refused.
Thereupon, Zhì Bó joined with Hán
and Wèi to besiege Xiāngzǐ in Jìnyáng.
The three states conspired together,
captured Zhì Bó, and divided his state into three.
This is what is called "taking from others only to be taken from in turn."
What is meant by "giving only to take away in return"?
Duke Xiàn of Jìn wanted to borrow a passage through Yú to attack Guó,
and presented the duke of Yú with the jade from Chuíjí and the steeds from Qūchǎn.
The duke of Yú was tempted by the jade and horses,
and intended to grant the passage.
Gōng Zhīqí admonished him:
"You must not!
The relationship between Yú and Guó
is like that of a carriage and its supporting boards.
The boards rely on the carriage,
and the carriage also relies on the boards.
Yú and Guó
are in a position of mutual dependence.
If we grant them passage,
then Guó will fall in the morning and Yú will follow by evening."
The duke of Yú did not listen,
and granted the passage.
Xún Xī attacked Guó
and conquered it.
On his return, he attacked Yú,
and captured it as well.
This is what is called "giving only to take away in return."
The sage kings spread virtue and bestowed blessings,
not seeking repayment from the people;
they performed suburban and ancestral sacrifices,
not seeking blessings from the spirits.
When a mountain reaches its height, clouds and rain gather there;
when water reaches its depth, dragons and serpents arise there;
when a gentleman attains the Way, fortune and prosperity come to him.
Those who accumulate hidden virtue will surely receive open reward;
those who practice unobserved goodness will surely achieve renowned fame.
In ancient times, when ditches and dikes were not maintained,
floods plagued the people.
Yǔ cut through the Lóngmén Mountains,
opened the Yīquē Gorge,
tamed the waters and leveled the land,
enabling the people to live on dry ground.
When the people were not affectionate,
and the five relationships were not respected,
Qì taught them the duties between ruler and subject,
the affection between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
and the order between elder and younger.
When the fields were not cultivated,
and the people had insufficient food,
Hòujì taught them to clear the land and plow the grass,
fertilize the soil and plant grain,
so that every household had enough.
Thus, the descendants of these three sovereigns
all became kings,
because they had accumulated hidden virtue.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
and ritual and righteousness were abandoned,
Kǒngzǐ taught the Way of the Three Dynasties to the world.
His lineage has continued unbroken to this day,
because he practiced unobserved goodness.
Qín King Zhào Zhèng annexed the world but perished;
Zhì Bó seized lands but was destroyed;
Shāng Yāng was torn apart;
Lǐ Sī was torn by chariots.
The Three Dynasties planted virtue and became kings;
Duke Huán of Qí restored broken lines and became hegemon.
Thus, those who sow millet do not reap rice;
those who sow enmity receive no kindness in return.
Long ago,
there was a man in Sòng who delighted in doing good,
and for three generations, this did not cease.
For no reason, his black cow gave birth to a white calf,
so he consulted a seer.
The seer said:
"This is auspicious,
offer it to the spirits."
After a year,
his father became blind for no reason.
The cow again gave birth to a white calf,
and his father again sent his son to consult the seer.
The son said:
"Last time we followed the seer's words, and he lost his sight.
Now we consult him again,
what is the use?"
The father said:
"The words of a sage
first contradict but later accord.
The matter is not yet concluded,
so try going to ask again."
The son went again to consult the seer,
and the seer said:
"This is auspicious,
again I advise offering it to the spirits."
Returning, he reported to his father,
who said:
"We shall follow the seer's words."
After a year,
the son also became blind for no reason.
Later, Chǔ attacked Sòng,
and besieged the city.
At that time,
people exchanged children to eat,
and split bones for fuel.
The able-bodied died,
while the old, sick, and children all went up the city walls,
holding firm and not surrendering.
The King of Chǔ was furious,
and when the city was breached,
he slaughtered all who had defended it.
Only because this father and son were blind
were they exempt from defending the walls.
When the army withdrew and the siege was lifted,
both father and son regained their sight.
Thus, misfortune and fortune revolve and generate each other,
their transformations are difficult to perceive.
Near the frontier there lived a man skilled in the arts of divination.
His horse wandered into the northern tribes for no reason,
and everyone consoled him.
His father said:
"How do we know this won't turn out to be a blessing?"
After several months,
his horse returned with fine steeds from the northern tribes,
and everyone congratulated him.
His father said:
"How do we know this won't turn out to be a misfortune?"
The household became rich with good horses,
and his son loved riding,
but fell and broke his thigh.
Everyone consoled him.
His father said:
"How do we know this won't turn out to be a blessing?"
After a year,
the northern tribes invaded the frontier in great force.
All able-bodied men took up bows to fight,
and of those near the frontier,
nine out of ten perished.
Only because of his lameness
did father and son preserve each other.
Thus misfortune may become blessing,
and blessing may become misfortune.
Their transformations have no limit,
their depths cannot be fathomed.
Some words are straightforward but not comprehensive in practice;
others offend the ear and contradict the heart yet accord with reality.
Gāoyáng Tuí was about to build a house,
and asked a craftsman.
The craftsman replied:
"It cannot be done yet.
The wood is still green;
if you apply plaster over it,
it will surely warp.
Using unseasoned timber to bear heavy plaster -
though it may hold together now,
will certainly fail later."
Gāoyáng Tuí said:
"Not so.
When wood dries it becomes stronger,
when plaster dries it becomes lighter.
With strong timber bearing light plaster,
though it seems poor now,
will certainly prove good later."
The craftsman was at a loss for words,
having no reply,
he received the order and built the house.
When first completed,
it appeared quite sound,
but eventually it indeed collapsed.
This is what is called straightforward in words but not comprehensive in practice.
What then means offending the ear
and contradicting the heart yet according with reality?
Jìngguō Jūn was about to fortify Xuē,
and many guests tried to stop him,
but he wouldn't listen.
Jìngguō Jūn told his usher:
"Do not announce any more guests."
A man from Qí requested an audience saying:
"I ask to speak but three words.
If I exceed three words,
I ask to be boiled alive."
Jìngguō Jūn heard this and received him.
The guest hurried forward,
bowed twice and rose,
then uttered:
"Sea big fish."
And turned to leave.
Jìngguō Jūn stopped him saying:
"I wish to hear your explanation."
The guest said:
"I dare not treat death as a game."
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"You have come this long distance, sir,
please explain for my sake!"
The guest said:
"A sea big fish -
nets cannot stop it,
hooks cannot pull it.
But if it drifts and loses water,
then even ants can have their way with it.
Now Qí -
is your deep pool.
If you lose Qí,
can Xuē preserve itself?"
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"Excellent."
And stopped fortifying Xuē.
This is what is called offending the ear,
contradicting the heart yet obtaining the reality of the matter.
Now using
"don't fortify Xuē"
to stop the fortification of Xuē -
in terms of persuasive effect,
is not as good as
"sea big fish."
Thus things may seem distant yet be near,
or seem near yet be distant;
some have their advice heard and plans approved yet become estranged,
others have their words unused
and plans unexecuted yet grow closer.
How to illustrate this?
Three states attacked Qí,
besieging Pínglù.
Kuòzǐ reported to Niúzǐ saying:
"The territories of the three states don't connect with ours;
they cross neighboring states to besiege Pínglù -
the gain isn't worth coveting.
Thus they seek reputation from us.
I suggest we send the Marquis of Qí there."
Niúzǐ thought this good.
As Kuòzǐ left,
Wúhàizǐ entered.
Niúzǐ told Wúhàizǐ what Kuòzǐ had said.
Wúhàizǐ said:
"This differs from what I have heard."
Niúzǐ said:
"When the state is in danger but not secured,
when troubles are knotted but not untied,
what use is valuing wisdom!"
Wúhàizǐ said:
"I have heard of splitting territory to secure the altars of state,
of sacrificing life and breaking family to preserve the country;
I have not heard of sending out one's ruler to protect the borders."
Niúzǐ didn't listen to Wúhàizǐ's words,
but used Kuòzǐ's plan.
The armies of the three states withdrew,
and the land of Pínglù was preserved.
After this,
Kuòzǐ became increasingly estranged,
while Wúhàizǐ became increasingly advanced.
Thus though he planned against trouble and the trouble was resolved,
though he schemed for the state and the state was preserved,
Kuòzǐ's wisdom succeeded.
Wúhàizǐ's considerations didn't hit upon the strategy,
his plans didn't benefit the state,
yet his heart harmonized with the ruler,
and he acted righteously.
Nowadays people wait for hats to adorn their heads,
wait for shoes to walk the ground.
Hats and shoes for people -
cannot warm against cold,
cannot block against wind,
cannot shelter against exposure,
yet people wear hats and put on shoes
because that is how they establish themselves.
Jiù Fàn achieved victory at Chéng Pú through battle,
while Yōng Jì had not the slightest merit in terms of military success,
yet Yōng Jì was rewarded first and Jiù Fàn only afterward.
This is because his words held greater value.
Thus, righteousness
is what the world esteems.
To speak a hundred words and have all be fitting
is not as good as choosing the right direction and acting with careful consideration.
Sometimes, one without merit is promoted first,
while another with merit is rewarded later.
How can this be illustrated?
Long ago, Duke Wén of Jìn was about to engage in battle with the Chǔ people at Chéng Pú,
and he asked Jiù Fàn,
"What should we do?"
Jiù Fàn replied,
"In matters of benevolence and righteousness,
one cannot have too much loyalty and trustworthiness;
in matters of warfare and strategy,
one cannot have too much deception and artifice.
Your Highness should simply employ deceit."
Duke Wén then took leave of Jiù Fàn
and asked Yōng Jì,
who responded,
"Burning a forest to hunt
may yield more game initially,
but in the end, there will be no more beasts.
To treat others with deception and artifice,
though it may bring greater immediate gain,
will ultimately lead to no further returns.
Your Highness should simply uphold what is right."
Thereupon, he did not heed Yōng Jì's advice
but followed Jiù Fàn's strategy,
engaged the Chǔ people in battle,
and routed them decisively.
Upon returning, he rewarded those with merit,
placing Yōng Jì first and Jiù Fàn afterward.
His attendants asked,
"The victory at Chéng Pú
was due to Jiù Fàn's strategy,
yet you reward Yōng Jì first;
why is that?"
Duke Wén said,
"Jiù Fàn's words
were a temporary expedient.
Yōng Jì's words
are of benefit for ten thousand generations.
How could I prioritize a temporary expedient
over the long-term benefit of ten thousand generations?"
Zhì Bó led the states of Hán
and Wèi to attack Zhào,
besieging Jìnyáng,
and diverted the Jìn River to flood it.
The people inside the city had to live in trees,
hanging their pots to cook.
Xiāng Zǐ said to Zhāng Mèngtán,
"Our strength in the city is exhausted,
provisions are depleted,
and the military officers are ill;
what should we do?"
Zhāng Mèngtán replied,
"If one cannot preserve what is lost,
or secure what is in peril,
then there is no use for wisdom.
I beg to attempt a covert journey
to meet the rulers of Hán
and Wèi and form an alliance with them."
He then went to see the rulers of Hán
and Wèi,
and persuaded them, saying,
"I have heard that
when the lips are gone, the teeth feel the cold.
Now Zhì Bó leads you two lords to attack Zhào,
and Zhào is about to perish.
Once Zhào falls,
you two will be next.
If you do not plan against this now,
disaster will befall you both."
The two rulers said,
"Zhì Bó, in his nature,
is coarse at heart and shows little affection.
If our plan is leaked,
we will surely fail.
What should we do?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said,
"The words come from your mouths
and enter my ears;
who else could know of them?
Moreover, those who share the same sentiment aid each other,
and those who share the same interests would die for one another;
I urge you to consider this!"
The two rulers then conspired secretly with Zhāng Mèngtán
and set a date with him.
Zhāng Mèngtán reported back to Xiāng Zǐ,
and on the appointed night,
the Zhào forces killed the officials guarding the dikes
and breached the waters to flood Zhì Bó's army.
Zhì Bó's troops were thrown into chaos as they tried to deal with the flood,
while Hán and Wèi attacked from the flanks,
and Xiāng Zǐ led his troops to assault them from the front.
They decisively defeated Zhì Bó's army,
killed him,
and divided his state into three parts.
After lifting the siege, Xiāng Zǐ rewarded those with merit,
and Gāo Hè was given the highest reward.
The ministers asked,
"The preservation of Jìnyáng
was due to Zhāng Mèngtán's merit.
Yet Hè receives the top reward;
why is that?"
Xiāng Zǐ said,
"During the siege of Jìnyáng,
my state was in peril,
the altars of soil and grain were endangered,
and all the ministers harbored arrogant and disrespectful hearts,
only Hè did not forsake the propriety between ruler and subject;
therefore, I reward him first."
From this, it can be seen that
righteousness
is the great foundation of humanity.
Even if one has the merit of winning battles or preserving the state,
it is not as noble as practicing righteousness.
Thus, Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Fine words can win respect,
and fine conduct can elevate others."
Sometimes, one who has committed a fault may be worthy of reward,
and sometimes, one who has achieved merit may be deserving of blame.
Xīmén Bào governed Yè,
yet the granaries held no stored grain,
the treasury had no reserve funds,
the armories contained no weapons or armor,
and the officials kept no accounts.
Several people reported his faults to Marquis Wén.
The Marquis personally visited the county
and found it exactly as described.
He said to Xīmén Bào,
"Dí Huáng recommended you to govern Yè,
yet it is in great disorder.
If you can change your methods, that is acceptable;
if not,
I will punish you."
Xīmén Bào replied,
"I have heard that
a kingly ruler enriches the people,
a hegemon enriches the military,
and a doomed state enriches its treasury.
Now, since you wish to be a hegemon or king,
I have therefore stored wealth among the people.
If you doubt this,
I ask to ascend the city wall and beat the drum;
armor, weapons, and grain will be ready at once."
Thereupon, he ascended the wall and beat the drum.
At the first beat,
the people donned armor, strung their arrows,
and came forth bearing weapons and crossbows.
At the second beat,
they hitched carts and brought loads of grain.
Marquis Wén said,
"Dismiss them!"
Xīmén Bào said,
"To build trust with the people
is not the work of a single day.
To deceive them in one move
would make them unreliable in the future.
Yān has often invaded eight cities of Wèi;
I ask to lead a northern campaign against them
to recover the lost territory."
He then raised troops to attack Yān,
regained the land, and returned.
This is an example of one who had faults but was worthy of reward.
Jiě Biǎn governed the eastern region,
and his annual report showed a threefold increase in revenue;
the officials requested that he be rewarded.
Marquis Wén said,
"Our land has not expanded,
nor have the people increased in number;
how then has revenue tripled?"
Jiě Biǎn replied,
"By felling trees in winter and storing them,
then floating them down the river in spring to sell."
Marquis Wén said,
"The people exert themselves in plowing in spring,
labor strenuously in weeding in summer,
and harvest in autumn.
In winter, when they have no work,
you have them cut down forests and store the wood,
then yoke them to float it down the river—
this does not allow the people to rest.
The people are exhausted;
even with a threefold increase in revenue,
what use is it?"
This is an example of one who had merit but was deserving of blame.
A wise ruler does not seek gains unscrupulously,
and a loyal minister does not pursue profits improperly.
How can this be demonstrated?
When Zhōngháng Mùbó attacked Gǔ,
he could not capture it.
Kuì Wénlún said:
"The steward of Gǔ,
I, Wénlún, know him.
Please do not tire our military officers,
and Gǔ can be obtained."
Mùbó did not respond.
His attendants said:
"Without breaking a single halberd,
without injuring a single soldier,
and Gǔ can be obtained,
why does my lord not send him?"
Mùbó said:
"Wénlún, as a person,
is cunning but unrighteous.
If I let Wénlún capture it,
can I avoid rewarding him?
If I reward him,
that would be rewarding a cunning person.
If a cunning person achieves his ambition,
it would cause the warriors of Jìn to abandon righteousness for cunning.
Even if we obtain Gǔ,
what use would it be!"
Those who attack cities
desire to expand their territory.
To obtain land but not take it
is to see the root and understand the branches.
When Qín Mùgōng sent Mèng Méng to lead troops in a surprise attack on Zhèng,
they passed through Zhōu to the east.
Zhèng's merchants Xián Gāo
and Jiǎn Tuō consulted together, saying:
"The army has marched several thousand miles,
crossing through the lands of various lords repeatedly,
their momentum must be aimed at a surprise attack on Zhèng.
Generally, those who launch surprise attacks on states
assume there is no preparation.
Now if we show that we know their true intent,
they surely will not dare to advance."
They then falsified an order from the Earl of Zhèng,
and presented twelve cattle to provision them.
The three commanders consulted together, saying:
"Generally, those who launch surprise attacks
assume the target is unaware.
Now that they are already aware,
their defenses must be solid,
and advancing would surely be fruitless."
They then turned the army around and returned.
Jìn's Xiān Zhěn led troops to attack them,
and decisively defeated them at Xiáo.
The Earl of Zhèng then offered a reward to Xián Gāo for saving the state,
but Xián Gāo declined, saying:
"If deceit is rewarded,
then Zhèng's trustworthiness will be abandoned.
To govern a state without trustworthiness
is to corrupt its customs.
To reward one person and ruin the state's customs
is something the righteous would not do.
To gain substantial reward through untrustworthiness
is something the principled would not do."
He then moved with his clan to the Eastern Yí,
and never returned for the rest of his life.
Thus, the righteous do not harm their nature with desires,
and the wise do not sacrifice principle for profit.
The thoughts of sages are cultivated,
while the thoughts of fools are flawed.
Loyal ministers strive to enhance their ruler's virtue,
while flattering ministers strive to expand their ruler's territory.
How can this be demonstrated?
When Chén's Xià Zhēngshū assassinated his ruler,
Chǔ Zhuāngwáng attacked him,
and the people of Chén obeyed the order.
After Zhuāngwáng had punished the guilty,
he dispatched troops to garrison Chén,
and all the ministers offered congratulations.
Shēn Shūshí, who had been on a mission to Qí,
returned without offering congratulations.
Zhuāngwáng said:
"Chén acted without principle,
I raised nine armies to punish them,
suppressed violence and chaos,
executed the guilty,
all my ministers congratulated me,
yet you alone do not congratulate me,
why?"
Shēn Shūshí said:
"Suppose a man leads his ox through another's field,
and the field owner kills the man and seizes the ox.
The man certainly had committed a fault,
but the punishment is too severe.
Now my king, considering Chén's lack of principle,
raised troops to attack it,
punished the guilty,
and dispatched troops to garrison Chén.
When the other lords hear of this,
they will think the king did not just punish the guilty,
but coveted Chén's territory.
I have heard that a nobleman does not abandon righteousness to seize profit."
The king said:
"Well said!"
He then withdrew the garrison from Chén,
and reestablished Chén's ruling line.
When the other lords heard of this,
they all came to pay homage to Chǔ.
This is an example of striving to enhance the ruler's virtue.
When Zhāng Wǔ advised Zhì Bó, saying:
"Of Jìn's six generals,
Zhōngháng Wénzǐ is the weakest,
and his superiors and subordinates are divided,
we can attack to expand our territory."
Thereupon they attacked Fàn
and Zhōngháng.
After destroying them,
he further advised Zhì Bó to demand land from Hán,
Wèi, and Zhào.
Hán and Wèi ceded land and offered it,
but the Zhào clan refused.
He then led Hán
and Wèi to attack Zhào,
besieging Jìnyáng for three years.
The three states secretly plotted together,
attacked the Zhì clan,
and annihilated them.
This is an example of striving to expand the ruler's territory.
Those who enhance the ruler's virtue become hegemons,
while those who expand the ruler's territory are destroyed.
Thus, a state of a thousand chariots
that practices civil virtue becomes kingly,
as with Tāng and Wǔ;
a state of ten thousand chariots
that loves to expand territory perishes,
as with Zhì Bó.
Do not undertake what is not your affair,
do not accept what is not your due name, (
do not dwell where fame comes without cause),
do not hold position without merit and wealth.
Those who claim others' names will be ruined,
those who undertake others' affairs will fail,
those who gain great profit without merit will later suffer harm.
It is like climbing a tall tree to look in all directions:
though one may find fleeting pleasure,
when a swift wind comes,
one cannot help but fear.
When calamity reaches one's person,
only then does one worry,
even with six thoroughbreds in pursuit,
one cannot catch up.
Therefore, when loyal ministers serve their ruler,
they accept rewards according to their achievements,
not for improper gains;
they accept office according to their abilities,
not coveting ranks and emoluments.
What they are capable of,
they accept without declining;
what they are not capable of,
they receive without joy.
To decline what one can do is to conceal one's ability,
to desire what one cannot do is delusion.
To decline what one cannot do and accept what one can do
then ensures a position without loss or decline,
and a responsibility that can be successfully borne.
In the past, Zhì Bó was arrogant,
attacked and defeated Fàn and Zhōngháng,
then coerced the rulers of Hán
and Wèi to cede their land.
Still not satisfied,
he raised troops to attack Zhào.
Hán and Wèi turned against him,
his army was defeated below Jìnyáng,
he died east of Gāoliáng,
his head was made into a drinking vessel,
his state was divided into three,
and he became a laughingstock of the world.
This is the calamity of not knowing satisfaction.
Lǎozǐ said:
"Knowing satisfaction avoids disgrace,
knowing when to stop avoids danger,
this ensures long-lasting preservation."
This is what it means.
Sometimes praising a person can precisely lead to their downfall,
while sometimes slandering a person may instead bring them success.
How do we know this is so?
Fèi Wújí reported to King Píng of Chǔ:
"The reason Jìn achieved hegemony
is because they are close to the central states.
The reason Chǔ cannot compete with them
is due to our remote location.
If Your Majesty wishes to lead the feudal lords,
it would be best to greatly fortify the city of Chéngfù,
and have Crown Prince Jiàn guard it,
thereby attracting support from the north,
while Your Majesty consolidates the south.
This is the way to gain the empire."
The King of Chǔ was pleased with this suggestion,
thus ordering Crown Prince Jiàn to guard Chéngfù,
with Wǔ Zǐshē as his tutor.
After one year,
Wǔ Zǐshē had someone speak to the king,
saying the Crown Prince was very benevolent and courageous,
capable of winning the people's hearts.
The king reported this to Fèi Wújí,
who said:
"I have long heard
that the Crown Prince internally comforts the common people,
externally forms alliances with feudal lords,
with Qí and Jìn assisting him—
all aimed at harming Chǔ.
The plot is already formed."
The king said:
"He is my crown prince—
what more could he want?"
Fèi replied:
"He resents you over the matter of the Qín princess."
The king then had Crown Prince Jiàn killed and executed Wǔ Zǐshē.
This is what is called 'praise that brings disaster'.
What is meant by 'slander that brings benefit'?
Tángzǐ spoke ill of Chén Piánzǐ to King Wēi of Qí.
King Wēi wanted to kill him,
so Chén Piánzǐ and his followers fled,
escaping to Xuē.
Lord Mèngcháng heard of this,
and sent a carriage to welcome him.
Upon arrival, he was provided with fine meats and grains of five flavors,
served three times daily.
In winter he wore fur and woolen garments,
in summer fine linen and hemp cloth;
when going out he rode in sturdy carriages
drawn by fine horses.
Lord Mèngcháng asked him:
"You were born in Qí,
and raised in Qí—
what do you miss about Qí?"
He replied:
"I miss that Tángzǐ."
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Isn't Tángzǐ
the one who slandered you?"
He answered:
"Yes."
Lord Mèngcháng asked:
"Why do you miss him?"
He replied:
"When I lived in Qí,
I ate coarse rice,
and soup of wild greens;
in winter I suffered cold and freezing,
in summer heat and sunstroke.
Since Tángzǐ slandered me,
I have found refuge with you,
eating fine meats,
dining on choice grains,
wearing light warm clothing,
riding in sturdy carriages with fine horses—
therefore I miss him."
This is what is called 'slander that brings benefit'.
Thus we can see that words of slander and praise
must be carefully examined.
Some who cling to life meet death,
while others who disregard death preserve life;
some who proceed slowly actually advance faster.
How do we know this is so?
A man from Lǔ who took revenge on someone from Qí for his father,
cut open the enemy's belly to see his heart,
then sat to adjust his cap,
rose to change his clothes,
walked slowly out the gate,
mounted his carriage and walked his horse,
without changing expression.
His driver wanted to whip the horses to speed,
but he calmed him and stopped him, saying:
"Today I went out to avenge my father expecting to die—
not to live.
Now that my task is accomplished,
why flee!"
The pursuers said:
"This is a man of principle and integrity—
we cannot kill him."
They lifted the siege and left.
Had he rushed out without fastening his clothes,
without adjusting his cap,
crawling and scrambling away,
mounting his carriage and galloping off,
he certainly wouldn't have escaped within ten paces.
But by sitting to adjust his cap,
rising to change his clothes,
walking slowly out the gate,
mounting his carriage and walking his horse,
without changing expression—
this composure that others would think meant certain death
instead enabled him to survive.
This is what is called 'slow but fast',
'delayed but swift'.
Running
is what people consider fast,
while walking
is what people consider slow.
But here what people consider slow
proved fast—
showing clear understanding of circumstances.
Those who understand that slowness can be speed,
that delay can be swift,
are close to the Way.
Thus when the Yellow Emperor lost his Dark Pearl,
he sent Lízhū
and Juèduō to search for it,
but they couldn't find it.
Then he sent Hūhuǎng,
who subsequently found it.
The sage respects the small and is cautious about the subtle,
acting never missing the right timing,
taking repeated precautions with utmost care—
thus disaster does not flourish.
When calculating blessings, don't count too much;
when considering disasters, overestimate them.
When the same day brings frost,
those under cover remain unharmed;
the foolish who are prepared
achieve the same success as the wise.
A torch flame in thin smoke
can be extinguished by one finger;
a leak in a dike like a mouse hole
can be blocked with one clod of earth.
But when fire spreads across Mèngzhū Marsh and blazes through Yúnmèng Marsh,
when floods burst through the Nine Rivers and inundate Jīngzhōu—
even mobilizing all three armies
cannot save the situation.
Accumulated kindness becomes blessing,
accumulated resentment becomes disaster.
Like a boil that must burst,
much will be soiled.
Zhūyù Yǎng reported to Duke Jiǎn:
"Chén Chéngcháng
and Zǎiyǔ—these two men
deeply hate each other.
I fear they will start conflict and endanger the state.
Your Highness should remove one of them."
Duke Jiǎn didn't listen.
Not long after,
Chén Chéngcháng indeed attacked Zǎiyǔ in the court,
and assassinated Duke Jiǎn in the court.
This resulted from not understanding the importance of respecting small matters.
The Jì clan of Lǔ and the Hòu clan held a cockfight.
The Hòu clan armored their cocks,
while the Jì clan fitted metal spurs to theirs.
When the Jì clan's cocks were defeated,
Jì Píngzǐ grew furious,
and proceeded to encroach upon the Hòu clan's estate, building on it.
Hòu Zhāobó was enraged,
and slandered them to Duke Zhāo of Lǔ, saying:
"At the sacrificial ceremony in the temple of Duke Xiāng,
only two dancers performed there,
while all the rest danced at the Jì clan's estate.
The Jì clan's lack of principle and disregard for superiors
has been long-standing.
If they are not eliminated,
they will surely endanger the state."
The duke was angered,
and reported this to Zǐjiā Jū.
Zǐjiā Jū said:
"The Jì clan has gained popular support;
the three great families are united as one.
Their virtue is profound,
their power formidable—
how can you, my lord, overcome them?"
Duke Zhāo would not listen,
and sent Hòu Zhāobó to lead troops and attack them.
The Zhòngsūn and
Shūsūn clans consulted together, saying:
"Without the Jì clan,
our own clans
would face imminent destruction."
Thereupon, they raised troops to rescue them.
Hòu Zhāobó was defeated and died,
and Duke Zhāo of Lǔ fled to Qí.
Thus, the origin of this calamity
began with the feet of cocks;
by the time it grew great,
it led to the loss of the state.
Thus, the Cài woman rocked the boat,
and the Qí army invaded Chǔ.
Two men bore grudges,
and Zǎi Yǔ was killed at court;
Duke Jiàn was murdered,
dying without an heir,
the Chén clan replaced him,
and Qí lost its Lǚ lineage.
Two families fought with cocks,
the Jì clan used metal spurs,
the Hòu clan raised a revolt,
and Duke Zhāo of Lǔ fled.
Thus, where armies tread,
thorns and brambles grow.
When calamity arises and is not swiftly extinguished,
it is like fire finding dry tinder,
or water meeting dampness—
it soaks and grows ever larger.
A boil may form on a finger,
yet the pain spreads throughout the body.
Thus, a worm's nibble can split a beam,
and gnats and horseflies can drive off oxen and sheep—
this is what is meant.
People all strive to prepare for rescuing from disaster,
yet none know how to prevent disasters from arising.
Preventing disasters from arising
is easier than rescuing from them,
yet none devote more effort to it—
such people cannot be spoken with about strategy.
When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn passed through Cáo,
the lord of Cáo wished to see his fused ribs,
and made him strip to catch fish.
Lí Fùjī劝阻ed him, saying:
"The prince
is no ordinary man.
Three of his followers
are all capable of assisting a hegemon or king.
To treat them with disrespect
will surely bring trouble to the state."
The lord would not listen.
When Chóng'ěr returned to his state,
he raised an army and attacked Cáo,
annihilating it.
The lord died at the hands of others,
his state became ruins,
all because of making him strip to catch fish.
Qí and Chǔ wished to save Cáo,
but could not preserve it.
Had he heeded Lí Fùjī's words,
there would have been no such ruinous disaster.
Now, if one does not strive to prevent disasters from arising,
but only rescues after they occur,
even with sage wisdom,
one cannot devise a plan.
Moreover, the ways by which calamities arise
are countless and without fixed direction.
Therefore, the sage dwells in seclusion to avoid disgrace,
and remains tranquil and patient, awaiting his time.
The petty man does not know the gateways of fortune and misfortune;
recklessly moving, he tangles in nets—
even if he exhaustively prepares,
how can it suffice to preserve himself!
It is like digging a pond after a fire has started,
or using a fan while wearing a fur coat.
If a pond has ten thousand holes,
and you block one of them,
how can the fish not find a way out?
If a house has a hundred doors,
and you close one of them,
how can a thief not find a way in?
A wall collapses because of a crack;
a sword breaks surely at a notch.
The sage perceives this early,
thus nothing in the world can harm him.
When Grand Steward Zǐ Zhū was attending Prime Minister Zǐ Guó at a meal,
Prime Minister Zǐ Guó found the soup hot,
and took a cup of water to cool it.
The next day,
Grand Steward Zǐ Zhū resigned his post and left.
His servant asked:
"The position of Grand Steward of Chǔ
is not easily obtained.
Why resign and leave,
what is the reason?"
Zǐ Zhū said:
"The Prime Minister acts lightly and neglects propriety;
he would not hesitate to humiliate others."
The following year,
he had a court official detained and flogged three hundred times.
Those who serve in high office first avoid harm and then seek benefit;
they first distance themselves from disgrace and then pursue fame.
Grand Steward Zǐ Zhū's insight into beginnings and ends was subtle indeed.
When the swan is still unhatched in the egg,
a single finger can crush it,
leaving it formless and dissolved;
but when its sinews and bones have fully formed,
and its wings and feathers are complete,
then it flaps its wings and shakes its pinions,
soaring above the floating clouds,
bearing the blue sky on its back,
brushing the crimson heavens with its breast,
hovering over the vast void,
darting among rainbows—
even with powerful crossbows,
sharp arrows and fine strings,
and the skill of Pú Jǔzǐ,
none can touch it.
When the River's waters first emerge from Mínshān,
one can lift his clothes and wade across;
but when it flows down to Dòngtíng,
races past Shíchéng,
passes through Dāntú,
and raises great waves,
a boat cannot cross it in a day.
Therefore, the sage
constantly acts in the realm beyond form,
and does not linger in thought over accomplished events—
thus calamity cannot harm him.
Someone once asked Confucius:
"What kind of person is Yán Huí?"
He said:
"A man of benevolence.
I am not his equal."
"What kind of person is Zǐgòng?"
He said:
"A man of eloquence.
I am not his equal."
"What kind of person is Zǐlù?"
He said:
"A man of courage.
I am not his equal."
The guest said:
"All three are worthy, yet they serve you.
Why is that?"
Confucius said:
"I can be benevolent yet firm,
eloquent yet reticent,
courageous yet cautious.
To exchange my one Way for the abilities of these three,
I would not do."
Confucius knew how to apply his qualities.
Qín Niúquē was traveling through the mountains when he encountered bandits.
They seized his carriage and horses,
emptied his bags and cases,
and stripped off his clothes and coverings.
The bandits looked back at him,
but he showed no sign of fear or distress,
instead appearing cheerful and self-satisfied.
The bandits then asked him:
"We have taken your possessions,
threatened you with swords,
yet your composure remains unshaken.
Why is that?"
Qín Niúquē replied:
"Carriages and horses are for carrying the body,
clothes and coverings for concealing the form.
A sage does not allow what sustains him to harm his true sustenance."
The bandits looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"One who does not injure life with desires,
nor burden the form with profit,
is a sage in this world.
If such a man were to appear before a king,
he would surely have us dealt with."
So they turned back and killed him.
This shows he could use knowledge to know,
but not use knowledge to not know;
he could be brave in daring,
but not brave in not daring.
All who possess the Way
respond to emergencies without being unprepared,
encounter difficulties yet can avoid harm,
thus the world values them.
Now, he knew how to act for himself,
but did not know how to act for others;
his understanding was not thorough.
If one can move from clarity into obscurity,
then one is close to the Way.
The Book of Songs says:
"There is a saying among people,
'No wise man is without folly.'"
This refers to this.
Sometimes doing something
precisely causes its failure;
sometimes preparing against something
precisely brings it about.
How do we know this is so?
The Qín emperor, possessing the prognostic charts,
saw the prophecy:
"What will destroy Qín is
the Hú."
Thereupon he dispatched five hundred thousand soldiers,
appointing Méng Gōng
and Yáng Wēngzǐ as commanders,
to build the long wall,
extending west to the Liúshā Desert,
north to the Liáo River,
east connecting to Cháoxiǎn,
with the interior provinces hauling supply carts to provision them.
Also coveting the Yuè region's rhinoceros horns,
elephant tusks,
kingfisher feathers,
and pearls,
he sent Commandant Tú Suī with five hundred thousand soldiers,
divided into five armies:
one army blocked the pass at Xúnchéng Ridge,
one guarded the Jiǔyí Fortress,
one stationed at the capital of Pānyú,
one defended the Nányě border,
one camped at the Yúgān River.
For three years they never removed armor or unstrung crossbows,
while Supervisor Lù transported supplies,
and soldiers dug a canal to open a grain route,
to fight the Yuè people,
killing the Xī'ōu chieftain Yì Xūsòng.
But the Yuè people all entered thick forests,
dwelling among birds and beasts,
refusing to be captured by Qín.
They appointed brave leaders as generals,
attacked the Qín forces at night,
greatly defeating them,
killing Commandant Tú Suī,
with corpses lying and blood flowing by the hundreds of thousands.
So Qín conscripted exiles for garrison duty.
At this time,
men could not tend their fields,
women could not spin hemp or weave thread,
the weak were forced into labor on the roads,
officials extorted taxes at crossroads,
the sick could not be cared for,
the dead could not be buried.
Then Chén Shèng rose up in Dàzé,
raising his arms and shouting,
the empire rolled up like a mat,
reaching as far as Xì.
Liú and Xiàng raised righteous troops following him,
and it was settled as easily as breaking dry twigs or shaking off dead leaves,
until Qín lost the empire.
The disaster lay in preparing against the Hú and coveting Yuè.
They knew building the long wall to prevent destruction,
but did not know that building the long wall would cause destruction;
they knew conscripting garrison troops to defend against Yuè,
but did not know the trouble would arise from within.
The magpies know beforehand when the year will be windy,
so they leave high trees to nest on lower branches.
Adults passing by then take their fledglings,
infants passing by then poke their eggs—
they prepare against distant dangers but forget nearby perils.
Thus Qín's defensive preparations
were like the magpie's wisdom.
Sometimes contending over gain instead strengthens it,
sometimes compliance instead stops it.
How do we know this is so?
Duke Āi of Lǔ wanted to expand his residence westward,
but the court historian opposed it,
considering westward expansion inauspicious.
The duke changed countenance and grew angry;
his attendants repeatedly admonished him without success,
so he asked his tutor Zǎi Zhésuī:
"I wish to expand my residence,
but the historian considers it inauspicious.
What do you think?"
Zǎi Zhésuī replied:
"There are three inauspicious things in the world, and westward expansion is not among them."
The duke was greatly pleased.
After a moment, he asked again:
"What are the three inauspicious things?"
The reply was:
"Not practicing ritual righteousness,
that is the first inauspicious thing;
having insatiable desires,
that is the second inauspicious thing;
not heeding strong admonitions,
that is the third inauspicious thing."
The duke fell silent, deeply reflecting,
resentful yet introspective,
and thus did not expand westward.
The historian thought opposition could stop it,
but did not know that not opposing would achieve it instead.
The wise diverge from the path yet find the Way,
the foolish stick to the path yet lose the way.
As for Ní Shuō's skill,
there was no knot he could not untie.
It was not that he could untie all knots,
but that he left the truly inextricable ones untied.
As for using non-untrying to untie them,
one can discuss this with those who understand.
Sometimes clarifying ritual righteousness
and expounding the Way's essence fails,
while deconstructing with wild words succeeds.
How to illustrate this?
When Confucius traveled through the eastern wilds,
his horse strayed
and ate a farmer's crops.
The rustic angrily took the horse and tied it up.
He sent Zǐgòng to persuade him,
but despite exhaustive arguments, he failed.
Confucius said:
"Using what people cannot comprehend to persuade them
is like offering the Tàiláo sacrifice to wild beasts,
or playing the Jiǔsháo music for flying birds.
The fault is mine,
not that man's error."
So he sent the horse groom to persuade him.
Arriving, the groom said to the rustic:
"You farm from the eastern sea
to the western sea.
My horse straying—
how could it not eat your seedlings?"
The rustic was greatly pleased,
untied the horse and gave it to him.
Persuasion so unorthodox
yet worked instead.
There are situations
where cleverness is inferior to simplicity;
thus the sage measures the mortise before shaping the tenon.
Singing the "Cǎilíng"
or performing the "Yáng'ē",
rustics listening
find them less harmonious than the "Yánlù"—
not that the singer is unskilled,
but that the listener is different.
Thus, when lines in a drawing don't connect,
or interlocked rings won't separate,
when things cannot be communicated,
the sage does not contend.
Benevolence is what the common people admire;
righteousness is what the masses esteem.
To embody what people admire
and practice what people esteem—
this is how a strict father teaches his son
and how a loyal minister serves his ruler.
Yet there are cases in the world where applying these leads to personal death and state destruction,
because they are not suited to the times.
In the past, King Yǎn of Xú was fond of practicing benevolence and righteousness,
and thirty-two states came to pay homage to him on land.
Wángsūn Lì said to King Zhuāng of Chǔ:
"If you do not attack Xú,
you will surely end up paying homage to Xú instead."
The king said:
"King Yǎn is a virtuous ruler
who delights in practicing benevolence and righteousness.
He cannot be attacked."
Wángsūn Lì said:
"I have heard that when large confronts small,
and strong confronts weak,
it is like stone striking an egg
or a tiger devouring a piglet.
What doubt can there be!
Moreover, to engage in civil virtues without being able to manifest one's moral power,
and to engage in martial affairs without being able to employ one's strength—
no disorder is greater than this."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent!"
Then he raised an army to attack Xú
and subsequently destroyed it.
This is an example of knowing benevolence and righteousness but not understanding the changes of the world.
Shēnshū and dùchǎi
are fragrances that beautiful women carry and wear,
but when steeped in foul water,
they cannot preserve their fragrance.
In ancient times,
the Five Emperors valued virtue,
the Three Kings employed righteousness,
and the Five Hegemons relied on force.
Now if we take the way of the emperors and kings
and apply it in the age of the hegemons,
it would be like riding a fine horse to chase someone through thickets
while wearing straw raincoat and hat.
If one sows grain when frost descends
and seeks harvest when ice melts,
it will be difficult to obtain food.
Therefore, the Yì Jīng says:
"The hidden dragon does not act"
—this means the time is not suitable for action.
Hence,
"The nobleman is vigilant throughout the day,
cautious as if in peril at night,
then there will be no blame."
Being vigilant throughout the day
means acting with yang energy;
being cautious as if in peril at night
means resting with yin energy.
Acting according to the day
and resting according to the night—
only those who possess the Way can practice this.
Now King Yǎn of Xú was destroyed for practicing righteousness,
Yān Zikuài perished for practicing benevolence,
Duke Āi was diminished for favoring Confucianism,
and the ruler of Dài was mutilated for practicing Mohism.
Destruction, demise, diminishment, and mutilation
are caused by violent disorder,
yet these four rulers alone are said to have perished because of benevolence, righteousness, Confucianism, and Mohism
because they encountered different exigencies of their times.
It is not that benevolence, righteousness, Confucianism, and Mohism are unworkable,
but if employed in the wrong era,
one becomes captive because of them.
The halberd is for attacking cities,
the mirror is for reflecting form.
If a palace attendant obtains a halberd, he uses it to cut mallows;
if a blind man obtains a mirror, he uses it to cover a wine vessel—
they do not know their proper applications.
Thus, goodness and baseness may be the same,
but censure and praise depend on custom;
pursuits and rejections may be the same,
but opposition and accord depend on the times.
Kuáng Jué refused salary and was executed,
Duàngàn Mù declined ministerial position and became illustrious—
their conduct was the same,
yet benefit and harm differed,
because the times made it so.
Therefore, even if a sage possesses his ambition,
if he does not encounter the right era,
he can barely secure his own preservation—
what achievement and fame could he possibly attain!
Knowing what Heaven does
and knowing what humans practice,
then one has means to navigate the world.
Knowing Heaven but not knowing humans,
then one has nothing with which to interact with customs;
knowing humans but not knowing Heaven,
then one has nothing with which to wander with the Way.
Shàn Bāo turned his back on the world and departed from customs,
dwelling in cliffs and drinking from valleys,
not wearing silk or hemp,
not eating the five grains.
Having lived to seventy years of age,
he still had the complexion of a child.
Suddenly he encountered a hungry tiger,
which killed and ate him.
Zhāng Yì was fond of respectfulness;
when passing palaces and temples, he would always hasten his steps;
seeing gates and crowds, he would always dismount.
Even servants and horse grooms
he treated with equal courtesy.
Yet he did not live out his lifespan,
dying from internal heat.
Bāo nurtured his interior but a tiger devoured his exterior;
Yì cultivated his exterior but illness attacked his interior.
Therefore, if one directly follows one's inclinations and indulges one's emotions,
then stubbornness harms them;
if one enslaves oneself to things,
then yin and yang consume them.
These are both cases of being burdened with pursuits and damaging one's harmony.
Those who have attained the Way
transform externally but do not transform internally.
External transformation
is how they enter into society;
internal non-transformation
is how they preserve
their
person.
Therefore, internally they have steadfast principles,
while externally they can bend and stretch,
expand and contract,
roll and unroll,
moving along with things.
Thus, even ten thousand actions will not trap them.
The reason we value sages
is because they can transform like the dragon.
Now those who rigidly cling to one principle
and push one course of action,
even if destroyed, shattered, and sunk,
still refuse to change—
these are people who perceive minor virtues
but are obstructed from the great Way.
Zhào Xuānmèng saved a starving man under a mulberry tree,
and the world praised his benevolence;
Jīng Cìfēi faced danger in the river,
yet did not lose his integrity,
and the world praised his courage;
thus, observing small actions allows one to discern greater principles.
Tián Zǐfāng went out,
saw an old horse on the road,
sighed with deep emotion,
and asked his driver:
"What horse is this?"
The driver replied:
"This was once a state-owned horse.
Now old and feeble, it is no longer of use,
so it has been sent out to be sold."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"To exploit its strength in youth
and abandon it in old age
is something a benevolent person would not do."
He used a bundle of silk to redeem it.
When weary warriors heard of this,
they knew where to place their loyalty.
Duke Zhuāng of Qí went hunting,
when an insect raised its leg to block his chariot wheel.
He asked his driver:
"What insect is this?"
The reply was:
"This is what is called a mantis.
As an insect,
it knows only to advance, not to retreat,
underestimating its strength and taking the enemy lightly."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"If this were a person,
they would surely be among the world's bravest warriors!"
Thereupon, he turned his chariot to avoid it.
When brave warriors heard of this,
they knew to devote themselves to the death.
Thus, Tián Zǐfāng's pity for an old horse won him the support of Wèi,
and Duke Zhuāng of Qí avoiding a mantis drew brave warriors to him.
Tāng taught the net-caster to spare prey,
and forty states came to pay homage;
King Wén buried the bones of the dead,
and the Jiǔyí tribes submitted;
King Wǔ sheltered a sunstroke victim under a tree,
holding him on his left and fanning him with his right,
and the world was moved;
King Gōujiàn of Yuè once wrongly decided a case,
took his sword Lóngyuān and cut his own thigh,
letting blood flow to his feet,
to punish himself,
and his warriors fought to the death,
touched by his grace.
Thus, when sages act in small matters,
they can influence great ones;
when they are careful with what is near,
they can win over what is far.
Sūn Shū'áo diverted the Qīsī River to irrigate the fields of Yūlóu,
and King Zhuāng knew he could be made prime minister.
Zǐfā distinguished between intense and light labor to equalize toil,
and Chǔ knew he could be made commander.
These are examples where small signs
reveal great understanding.
When sages undertake tasks,
they do not add unnecessary worry,
but examine the reasons behind them.
Now, if ten thousand people tune a bell,
it may not match the pitch;
but if one truly understands,
one person is enough.
The arguments of persuaders
are also like this.
If one truly grasps the method,
then there is no need for excess.
The reason a chariot can travel a thousand miles
lies in its key three-inch linchpin.
If urging someone does not move them,
or forbidding does not stop them,
it is because the approach lacks reason.
In the past,
the lord of Wèi paid homage to Wú,
and the king of Wú imprisoned him,
intending to exile him to the sea.
Persuaders came in endless streams,
but could not stop it.
When the lord of Lǔ heard,
he removed the bells and drums from their frames,
and held court in plain white mourning clothes.
Zhòngní entered and asked:
"Why does my lord look troubled?"
The lord of Lǔ said:
"Among lords, none are close kin,
yet I treat them as kin.
Among ministers, none form factions,
yet I treat them as allies.
Now the lord of Wèi paid homage to Wú,
and the king of Wú imprisoned him, intending to exile him to the sea.
Who would have thought such benevolence and righteousness would meet such misfortune!
I wish to save him but cannot—
what can be done?"
Zhòngní said:
"If you wish to save him,
then send Zǐgòng."
The lord of Lǔ summoned Zǐgòng,
and offered him the general's seal.
Zǐgòng declined, saying:
"Status does not help resolve crises;
it depends on the way it's done."
He set off humbly,
reached Wú,
and met Grand Steward Pǐ.
The Grand Steward was very pleased with him,
and wanted to recommend him to the king.
Zǐgòng said:
"If you cannot persuade the king yourself,
how can I rely on you?"
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"How do you know I cannot?"
Zǐgòng said:
"When the lord of Wèi came,
half of Wèi said
it was better to pay homage to Jìn;
the other half said
it was better to pay homage to Wú.
But the lord of Wèi believed Wú would allow him to return home in old age,
so he submitted willingly.
Now you receive him and imprison him,
and plan to exile him to the sea—
this rewards those who advocated paying homage to Jìn,
and punishes those who advocated Wú.
Moreover, when the lord of Wèi came,
the other lords saw it as an omen.
If paying homage to Wú brings harm,
they will all turn their hearts to Jìn.
Your desire to achieve hegemony—
will it not be difficult?"
Grand Steward Pǐ went in
and reported to the king.
The king ordered his officials:
"Within ten days,
anyone failing to prepare full honors for the lord of Wèi will die!"
Zǐgòng can be said to have known how to persuade.
Duke Āi of Lǔ built a large palace,
and Gōng Xuānzǐ admonished him:
"A large palace,
with many people, becomes noisy;
with few, it feels lonely.
I hope you will moderate it."
The duke said:
"I have heard your advice."
But construction continued.
Gōng Xuānzǐ saw him again:
"Our state is small, yet the palace is large;
the people will resent you,
and the lords will despise our state."
The lord of Lǔ said:
"I have heard your advice."
Construction continued.
Gōng Xuānzǐ saw him again:
"With Zhāo on the left and Mù on the right,
