building a great palace overlooking the temples of two former lords—
could this not harm your filial duty?"
The duke then ordered the work stopped and the planks removed.
The lord of Lǔ truly wanted to build the palace,
and Gōng Xuānzǐ was determined to stop him,
but of three attempts, only one worked—
because the other two were not the right way.
Fishing by the river,
one may not catch a single minnow all day—
not because the fish do not bite,
but because the bait is not what they desire.
But when a skilled angler casts his line,
and hooks them by the lips,
it is because he uses what they want.
Nothing is impossible to deal with;
only some people lack the means.
Lead and cinnabar,
different substances and colors,
yet can be made into elixir—
by knowing the method.
Thus, elaborate rhetoric
does not help persuasion;
what matters is examining the approach.
When things of similar kind rub against each other,
those that are close yet belong to different factions,
are numerous and hard to recognize.
Thus, some that appear similar are not,
while some that do not appear similar are;
some that seem to be so are not,
while some that are not seem to be so.
A proverb says:
"A kite dropped a rotten rat,
and the Yú family perished because of it."
What does this mean?
It is said: The Yú family
were great wealthy people of Liáng.
Their household was full and prosperous,
with immeasurable gold and coins,
and incalculable wealth and goods.
They ascended a high tower,
facing the main road,
set out music and laid out wine,
gathering gamblers above.
Knights-errant passed by in groups below the tower,
and the gamblers above shot dice,
hitting and flipping two with laughter,
when a flying kite happened to drop its rotten rat, hitting a knight-errant.
The knights-errant said to each other:
"The Yú family has enjoyed wealth and pleasure for too long,
and often have the intention to belittle others.
We dared not offend them,
yet they insult us with a rotten rat.
If we do not retaliate for this,
we cannot establish our dignity in the world.
Let us join forces with single purpose,
gather all our followers,
and surely destroy their household."
That night, they attacked the Yú family,
and utterly destroyed their household.
This is what is called appearing similar but not being so.
What is called not appearing similar but being so?
Qū Jiàn told Shí Qǐ:
"Bái Gōng Shèng is about to rebel."
Shí Qǐ said:
"Not so.
Bái Gōng Shèng humbles himself and treats scholars with respect,
not daring to be arrogant toward the worthy.
His household has no secure locks
or solid bolts.
He uses large measures to give out,
and light weights to take in.
To speak of him thus
is not appropriate."
Qū Jiàn said:
"This is precisely why he will rebel."
After three years,
Bái Gōng Shèng indeed rebelled,
killing Prime Minister Zǐ Jiāo
and Minister of War Zǐ Qī.
This is what is called not appearing similar but being so.
What is called seeming so but not being so?
Zǐ Fā was the magistrate of Shàngcài,
and a commoner committed a crime deserving punishment.
The case was decided and concluded,
and the sentence was carried out before the magistrate.
Zǐ Fā sighed with a sorrowful heart.
The criminal, after being punished, did not forget his kindness.
Later on,
Zǐ Fā offended King Wēi and fled.
The punished man then pursued the benefactor,
and the benefactor hid in a hut under the city wall.
When the pursuers arrived,
the punished man stamped his feet and angrily said:
"Zǐ Fā personally decided my crime and subjected me to punishment,
my hatred for him pierces to the marrow.
If I could get his flesh and eat it,
would that ever satisfy me!"
The pursuers all believed this and did not search inside,
thus saving Zǐ Fā.
This is what is called seeming so but not being so.
What is called not being so but seeming so?
In the past, King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè humbled himself before King Fū Chāi of Wú,
offering himself as a servant
and his wife as a concubine,
presenting sacrifices in all four seasons,
and submitting tributes in spring and autumn,
surrendering his state,
devoting his people's labor,
serving as a hidden shield in residence,
and fighting in the front lines in battle,
his etiquette extremely humble,
his words very submissive,
so that his intention to rebel seemed far away,
yet with three thousand armored soldiers, he captured Fū Chāi at Gūxū.
These four strategies
must be carefully considered.
The reason why matters are difficult to know
is because their clues are hidden and traces concealed,
establishing private interests within public affairs,
leaning evil upon righteousness,
thus using victory to confuse people's minds.
If what people harbor within
and what is seen without
were to match like tally slips,
then there would be no lost states or ruined families in the world.
When a fox preys on a pheasant,
it must first lower its body and smooth its fur,
waiting for the pheasant to approach.
The pheasant sees this and trusts it,
thus allowing itself to be caught.
If the fox were to widen its eyes and stare directly,
showing a determined intention to kill,
the pheasant would also know to fly far in alarm,
avoiding its wrath.
The mutual deception among humans
is not just the cunning schemes of beasts;
things that appear similar like this,
yet cannot be judged from the outside,
are numerous and hard to recognize,
therefore they must be carefully examined.
Some say:
"Non-action
is silent without sound,
still without movement,
pulling does not bring it,
pushing does not make it go.
Such a state
is the image of attaining the Way."
I believe this is not so.
I have once attempted to ask this question:
"As for Shénnóng,
Yáo,
Shùn,
Yǔ, and Tāng,
can they be called sage rulers?"
Any discussion must not dismiss them.
Observing these five sages,
it becomes clear that none achieved non-action.
In ancient times,
people ate grass and drank plain water,
gathered fruits from trees,
consumed the meat of snails and mussels,
often suffering from diseases and poisonous injuries.
Thereupon, Shénnóng began teaching people to sow the five grains,
assessing the suitability of land,
whether dry or wet, fertile or barren, high or low,
tasting the flavors of various herbs
and the sweetness or bitterness of spring waters,
enabling people to know what to avoid and what to pursue.
During this period,
he encountered seventy poisons in a single day.
Yáo established filial piety, compassion, and human kindness,
treating the people as his own children.
He spread teachings westward to the fertile lands,
eastward reaching the Black-Teeth territory,
northward pacifying Yōudū,
southward extending to Jiāozhǐ.
He exiled Huāndōu at Chóng Mountain,
banished the Sānmiáo to Sānwēi,
exiled Gōnggōng to Yōuzhōu,
and executed Gǔn at Yǔ Mountain.
Shùn built houses,
constructed walls and thatched roofs,
cleared land for planting grains,
teaching people to leave their caves
and establish their own homes.
At the beginning of his reign,
he marched south against the Sānmiáo,
and died on the way at Cāngwú.
Yǔ bathed in relentless rains,
combed his hair in strong winds,
dredged rivers and channeled waterways,
cut through the Dragon Gate,
opened the Yīquè pass,
repaired the embankments of Pénglí Lake,
riding on four types of vehicles,
following mountains and marking trees,
leveling the land and taming the waters,
pacifying eighteen hundred states.
Tāng rose early and retired late,
cultivating his intelligence;
he lightened taxes and reduced levies,
easing the burden on the people;
he spread virtue and bestowed favors,
relieving the impoverished;
he mourned the dead and cared for the sick,
supporting orphans and widows.
The people drew close to him,
his decrees were carried out smoothly,
then he marshaled troops at Míngtiáo,
besieged the Xià at Náncháo,
admonished them for their faults,
and banished them to Lì Mountain.
These five sages,
the illustrious rulers of the world,
exhausted their bodies and minds,
ceaselessly promoting benefits and eliminating harms for the people.
Holding a cup of wine,
one shows no change in complexion,
but lifting a heavy vessel makes one sweat profusely;
how much more so when bearing the worries of the world
and undertaking the affairs of the realm?
Their burden is far heavier than that vessel!
Moreover, the sage
is not ashamed of lowly status,
but regrets the failure to implement the Way;
does not worry about short life,
but grieves over the people's poverty.
Thus, Yǔ, tackling floods,
offered himself at Yángzhī's slope;
Tāng, distressed by drought,
prayed with his body in the Sānglín grove.
That sages care for the people
is so evident,
yet to claim
they practiced
"non-action"
—is that not contradictory?!
Furthermore, establishing emperors and kings in ancient times
was not to indulge their desires;
sages ascending the throne
was not for their own comfort and pleasure.
Because in the world, the strong overpower the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the cunning deceive the simple,
the brave bully the timid,
those with knowledge do not teach others,
those with accumulated wealth do not share it,
therefore, the Son of Heaven was established to unify them.
As one person's intelligence cannot illuminate the entire realm,
the three lords and nine ministers were set up to assist him.
Because distant lands with different customs,
remote and isolated places,
could not receive virtue and grace,
feudal lords were established to instruct them.
Thus, no land was left unused,
no season unutilized,
no official concealed affairs,
no state overlooked benefits.
This was to clothe the cold, feed the hungry,
nurture the old and weak, and relieve the weary.
If we observe commoners and ordinary men,
Yī Yǐn carried his cauldron to seek Tāng,
Lǚ Wàng wielded his knife to enter Zhōu,
Bó Lǐ Xī was sold and resold,
Guǎn Zhòng was bound in ropes,
Kǒngzǐ never had a soot-free stove,
Mòzǐ never warmed his mat.
Therefore, sages do not deem mountains too high,
nor rivers too wide,
enduring disgrace to appeal to worldly rulers,
not out of greed for salary or longing for position,
but wishing to promote the world's benefits and eradicate the people's harms.
I have heard it recorded in texts:
Shénnóng was haggard,
Yáo became emaciated,
Shùn turned dark and weathered,
Yǔ's hands and feet were calloused.
From this, we see
how deeply the sages worried and toiled for the people!
Hence, from the Son of Heaven above
down to the common people,
those who do not labor with their limbs,
do not employ their thoughts,
yet achieve orderly affairs and sufficient provisions—
such have never been heard of.
Now, the land's contour
makes water flow eastward,
but people must work at it,
then floods can follow the valleys.
Crops grow in spring,
but people must exert effort,
so the five grains can flourish.
If left to flow on their own,
left to grow naturally,
then Gǔn
and Yǔ's achievements would not exist,
and Hòu Jì's wisdom would be unused.
As for what I call
"non-action,"
it means personal whims cannot interfere with public principles,
desires cannot distort correct methods,
acting in accordance with reason,
achieving success based on resources,
following natural tendencies,
with no room for artificial schemes;
thus, affairs are accomplished without self-boasting,
merits are established without claiming fame,
not meaning unresponsive to stimuli,
or immobile when pushed.
As for using fire to dry a well,
or diverting the Huái River to irrigate a mountain,
this is acting based on oneself and opposing nature,
thus called forced action.
Whereas using boats on water,
sleds on sand,
carts in mud,
baskets in mountains,
digging channels in summer and building ponds in winter,
making mounds from high ground,
creating ponds from low land,
this is not what I call forced action.
When sages undertake tasks,
their methods differ yet accord with principle;
the paths they take vary but lead to the same destination.
They preserve the imperiled and stabilize the collapsing as one,
their minds never forgetting to benefit others.
How can this be demonstrated?
In the past,
when Chǔ intended to attack Sòng,
Mòzǐ heard of it and grieved,
hurrying from Lǔ to go there,
for ten days and ten nights,
his feet developing thick calluses without rest,
tearing his garments to wrap his feet,
until he reached Yǐng,
where he saw the King of Chǔ,
saying:
"I have heard that Your Majesty is raising troops to attack Sòng,
but have you calculated that you will certainly capture Sòng before attacking?
Or do you forget the suffering it will cause your masses and the toil of your people,
the wearing down of weapons and blunting of sharpness,
bearing the reputation of injustice throughout the world,
without gaining even a foot of land,
and still proceed to attack?"
The king said:
"If I certainly cannot capture Sòng,
and will moreover be unjust,
then why should I attack!"
Mòzǐ said:
"Excellent,
I see that Your Majesty would certainly harm righteousness and fail to capture Sòng."
The king said:
"Gōngshū Bān,
is the most skilled artisan in the world,
has created cloud-ladder devices to attack Sòng,
why should I not take it!"
Mòzǐ said:
"I request that Gōngshū Bān set up his attack,
and I will undertake the defense."
Thereupon Gōngshū Bān set up his devices to attack Sòng,
while Mòzǐ prepared the defenses for Sòng,
after nine attacks Mòzǐ repelled them nine times,
and they could not enter.
Thereupon they ceased military action,
and stopped attacking Sòng.
Duàngān Mù declined an official salary and lived at home,
and Marquis Wén of Wèi passed by his lane and leaned on his carriage rail in respect.
His servant said:
"Why does my lord lean on the rail?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Duàngān Mù is here,
therefore I lean on the rail."
His servant said:
"Duàngān Mù,
is a commoner scholar,
for my lord to lean on the rail at his lane,
is this not excessive?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Duàngān Mù does not chase after power and profit,
he embraces the way of the gentleman,
living in obscurity in a poor alley,
yet his reputation spreads for a thousand miles,
how dare I not lean on the rail!
Duàngān Mù is brilliant in virtue,
while I am brilliant in power;
Duàngān Mù is rich in righteousness,
while I am rich in wealth.
Power is not as honorable as virtue,
wealth is not as lofty as righteousness.
Even if Duàngān Mù were to exchange places with me,
he would not do it,
I am constantly ashamed when I see my shadow,
how can you belittle him!"
Later when Qín was about to raise troops to attack Wèi,
Sīmǎ Yǔ admonished:
"Duàngān Mù,
is a worthy man,
his lord treats him with respect,
there is no one in the world who doesn't know this,
no feudal lord who hasn't heard of it.
To raise troops to attack them,
would this not harm righteousness!"
Thereupon Qín ceased military action,
and stopped attacking Wèi.
Now Mòzǐ rushed a thousand miles with hurried steps,
to preserve Chǔ and
Sòng; Duàngān Mù stayed behind closed doors without going out,
to pacify Qín and
Wèi; though their actions of going and staying,
their circumstances were opposite,
yet both could preserve states,
this is what is called different paths leading to the same destination.
Consider those who fight fires,
they draw water and rush to the fire,
some use earthen jars,
some use basins or bowls,
their shapes square, round, pointed, or oval differ,
the containers for water vary,
but in putting out the fire,
they are equal.
Thus the songs of Qín,
Chǔ, Yān,
and Wèi,
have different melodies but all bring joy;
the weeping of the nine Yí and eight Dí tribes,
has different sounds but all express sorrow;
the principle is one.
Singing
is the expression of joy,
weeping
is the manifestation of sorrow.
What is felt within is expressed without,
thus it depends on what moves them.
The minds of sages,
day and night never forget their desire to benefit others,
the extent of their influence,
is also greatly effective.
When worldly customs decline and decay,
many criticize learning:
"Human nature has its own strengths and weaknesses,
like fish leaping,
or magpies having variegated feathers,
these are natural,
and cannot be increased or decreased."
I believe this is not so.
Fish leap,
magpies have variegated feathers,
just as humans are human,
horses are horses,
their sinews, bones, and physical forms,
are received from Heaven,
and cannot be changed.
To use this as an argument,
is not analogous.
When a horse is a young colt,
it jumps and kicks up its hooves,
raises its tail and runs,
humans cannot control it,
its biting is enough to pierce muscles and break bones,
its kicking enough to smash skulls and crush chests.
But when the stableman tames it,
and the skilled trainer teaches it,
covered with yoke and collar,
connected with reins and bit,
then even when passing through dangers and leaping over moats,
it does not dare refuse.
Thus its form as a horse,
cannot be transformed;
but that it can be harnessed and driven,
is the result of teaching.
Horses are dumb animals,
yet can communicate will and spirit,
still they require teaching to become useful,
how much more so humans!
Moreover, those with upright bodies and good natures,
who achieve through ardent dedication,
who become righteous through anxious exertion,
whose natures and destinies are agreeable,
who accord with the Way without awaiting study,
are Yáo, Shùn,
and King Wén;
those who are sunk in dissipation and indulgence,
who cannot be taught the Way,
who cannot be enlightened with virtue,
whom strict fathers cannot correct,
whom worthy teachers cannot transform,
are Dān Zhū
and Shāng Jūn.
Those with delicate cheeks and white teeth,
beautiful forms and excellent bones,
whose nature is agreeable without cosmetics or perfumes,
are Xī Shī
and Yángwén;
those with twisted lips and gaping mouths,
hunchbacked and deformed,
who cannot be made beautiful even with powder and paint,
are Mómǔ
and Pǐsuī.
Now those who are not equal to Yáo
and Shùn above, nor as bad as Shāng Jūn below,
not as beautiful as Xī Shī,
nor as ugly as Mómǔ,
these are whom teaching and instruction can enlighten,
and upon whom fragrances and cosmetics can be applied.
Moreover, though there are those who kill their fathers,
yet the world does not estrange all sons,
why?
Because those who love their fathers are many.
Though there are corrupt and deviant Confucians,
yet the Way of the former kings is not abandoned,
why?
Because those who practice it are many.
Now to criticize learning because some learners have faults,
this is like refusing to eat any grain
because of one choking incident;
like stopping walking
because of one stumbling difficulty;
this is delusion.
Today, a fine horse
does not need the whip and spur to run;
a nag cannot advance even with the whip and spur.
To drive without using the whip and spur for this reason
would be foolish.
A coward wielding a sharp sword
cannot cut when striking,
nor pierce when thrusting;
but when a brave warrior
swings it with a single blow,
he breaks ribs and injures torsos.
To discard Gānjiàng
and Mòyé swords and fight with bare hands for this reason
would be absurd.
What is said
aligns with the masses and conforms to common customs.
Now, if one does not speak of the highest peak of the nine heavens,
then speaks of the depths of the Yellow Springs,
this is an argument from two extremes,
how can it be considered a fair discussion?
Dínglì grows in winter,
yet people say winter is a time of death,
because death is prevalent;
jìwheat dies in summer,
yet people say summer is a time of life,
because life is abundant (
predominant).
Rivers twist and turn,
sometimes flowing north or south,
yet people say the Jiāng
and Hé rivers flow east;
Shètí, Zhènxīng, the sun, and the moon move eastward,
yet people say the stars, sun, and moon move westward:
this is based on the general rule.
Some Hú people are intelligent,
yet they are called stubborn;
some Yuè people are slow,
yet they are called hasty:
they are named after the majority.
As for Yáo, with his eight-colored eyebrows,
nine orifices fully open,
and impartial and selfless nature,
his one word unified all the people;
Shùn had double pupils,
which is called double brightness,
his actions set examples,
his words became texts;
Yǔ had triple-pierced ears,
which is called great penetration,
he promoted benefits and eliminated harms,
dredged rivers and opened channels;
King Wén had four breasts,
which is called great benevolence,
he was where the world turned to,
and the common people felt close to;
Gāoyáo had a horse's mouth,
which is called utmost trustworthiness,
he judged cases clearly,
and understood human sentiments;
Xiè was born from an egg,
Qǐ was born from a stone;
Shǐ Huáng could write as soon as he was born;
Yì had a long left arm and was skilled in archery.
Such nine worthies,
appearing once in a thousand years,
still followed one another in birth.
Now, without the heavenly endowments of the five sages,
or the rare talents of the four outstanding ones,
to abandon learning and follow one's nature
is (
as) to discard the boat and try to tread on water.
When Chúnjūn
and Yúcháng swords first come out of the mold,
they cannot cut when struck,
nor pierce when thrust;
but after being whetted on grindstones,
and their edges polished,
they can cut through dragon boats on water,
and slice rhinoceros hide on land.
When a bright mirror first leaves the mold,
it is dim and does not reflect images clearly;
but after being coated with black tin,
and polished with white felt,
even the finest hairs of the beard and eyebrows can be discerned.
Learning
is also the whetstone and polish for humans,
and to say that learning is useless
is a mistake in argument.
The shortcomings of the wise
are not as good as the strengths of the foolish;
the deficiencies of the worthy
are not as good as the surpluses of the ordinary.
How do we know this is so?
The paintings of Sòng and metalwork of Wú,
carved and engraved with intricate techniques,
their curves and details emerging in disorder,
achieve such subtlety
that even the sagehood of Yáo and Shùn cannot match.
Young girls of Cài,
tender maidens of Wèi,
weaving intricate patterns,
mixing rare colors,
suppressing black backgrounds,
highlighting red designs,
their skill cannot be reached by the wisdom of Yǔ and Tāng.
What heaven covers,
and earth supports,
encompassed within the six directions,
resting between the cosmos,
born from yīn and yáng,
the essence of blood and breath,
bearing fangs and horns,
with front claws and rear spurs,
flapping wings and seizing fiercely,
creeping and wriggling insects,
unite when pleased,
fight when angered,
approach for gain,
avoid harm,
their instincts are the same.
Although their likes and dislikes
do not differ from humans'.
Yet even with sharp claws and teeth,
strong tendons and bones,
they cannot avoid being controlled by humans,
because their knowledge cannot interconnect,
and their strengths cannot unite.
Each has its natural disposition,
without receiving shared efforts or achievements.
Wild geese fly with the wind
to conserve their energy,
carry reeds while soaring
to avoid arrows and nets;
ants know to build mounds,
badgers and raccoons dig winding burrows,
tigers and leopards have thick grass,
wild boars have qiúshāo
and cházhì,
digging interconnected hollows
resembling palaces,
shaded against rain,
sheltered from the sun:
this is how birds and beasts know to seek what benefits them.
Now, if a person is born in a remote and backward country,
grows up under a leaky roof in poverty,
without brothers in adulthood,
without parents in youth,
eyes never seeing rites and norms,
ears never hearing of ancient times,
alone in a solitary room without stepping outside,
even if their nature is not foolish,
their knowledge will certainly be meager.
In the past,
Cāngjié created writing,
Róngchéng devised the calendar,
Hú Cáo made clothing,
Hòujì farmed and cultivated,
Yí Dí brewed alcohol,
Xī Zhòng built carts.
These six individuals
all possessed divine understanding
and traces of sage wisdom,
so each contributed one thing to bequeath to later ages,
unable for one person to master all alone.
Each exhausted their knowledge,
valued what they wished to achieve,
thus providing for the world.
Now, if these six were to swap tasks,
why would they not be able to excel?
The myriad things are vast,
and knowledge cannot encompass them all.
After the Zhōu dynasty,
without the virtue of these six,
yet all continued their work;
people of the present,
without the talent of any one of them,
yet understand the ways of the six worthies: why?
Through teaching and continuity,
knowledge and ability can flow and spread.
From this perspective,
learning must not cease—
this is clear!
Now consider a blind person:
their eyes cannot distinguish day from night
or tell white from black,
yet when plucking the zither's strings,
coordinating multiple melodies and revisiting harmonics,
with swift plucking and gentle brushing,
their hands move like floating down,
never missing a single string.
But someone who has never played the zither,
even with Lí Zhū's keen sight
and nimble grasping skills,
still cannot flex their fingers properly.
Why is this?
It is the result of accumulated practice and familiarity.
Thus, a bow requires a straightener before it can be tuned,
and a sword needs whetting before it becomes sharp.
Jade, though hard and unmatched,
can be carved into beasts,
with head and tail taking shape,
thanks to the work of the grinding stone.
Wood straight as a guideline
is bent to form a wheel,
its curve matching the compass,
through the force of the straightening tool.
Even tough materials like turquoise,
can be engraved and carved
into useful vessels—
how much more so the mind and will!
Moreover, the spirit is subtle and fluid,
changing in an instant,
adapting with things,
like clouds rising and wind blowing,
ready to be applied.
If a noble person can refine and polish it,
honing their talents,
testing their own clarity,
observing the breadth of things,
penetrating their obstructions,
viewing the beginnings and ends,
perceiving the boundless realm,
they may wander freely within the formless,
stroll beyond the dust of the world,
transcending and standing alone,
eminently apart from the age—
this is how the sage lets their heart roam.
Yet people of later times cannot dwell in quiet contemplation,
playing the zither or reading books,
reflecting on antiquity,
befriending worthy scholars,
discussing and debating learning,
daily amusing themselves,
delving into worldly affairs,
distinguishing right from wrong,
calculating gains and losses,
observing fortune and misfortune,
establishing rituals and standards
that can serve as models,
exhausting the principles from root to branch,
probing the nature of events,
affirming the right and abolishing the wrong,
clearly showing later generations,
leaving a legacy after death,
and enjoying honor in life.
Such achievements
are within reach of human capability.
Yet few attain them,
due to idleness, neglect,
and having too much leisure.
People in barren lands often have determination—
because they labor;
those in fertile lands are often untalented—
because they are comfortable.
From this, we see
that a knowledgeable person who makes no effort
is不如 an ignorant one who loves learning.
From rulers and ministers down to commoners,
none who do not strive can achieve success—
this has never happened under heaven.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Daily progressing, monthly advancing,
through learning, one accumulates brightness unto illumination."
This refers to exactly that.
Fame can be diligently sought,
and merit can be forcefully achieved.
Thus, the noble person accumulates resolve and upholds integrity
to seek out enlightened teachers;
they strengthen their integrity and aim high
to transcend worldly customs.
How can this be illustrated?
In the past,
Nán Róng Chóu was ashamed that the sagely way alone was lost to him,
so he braved frost and dew,
tightened his gait and quickened his steps,
traversed mountains and rivers,
braved thorns and brambles,
with blistered feet over a hundred inns,
daring not to rest,
until he went south to see Lǎo Dān,
received a single teaching,
and his spirit became clear and cool,
dullness gave way to smooth understanding,
joyful as if after seven days without food
he feasted on the grand sacrifice,
thus illuminating the four seas,
his name extending to later ages,
comprehending the schemes of heaven and earth,
discerning the fine as autumn down,
praised in elegant words
that endure to this day.
This is what is meant by "fame can be diligently sought."
When Wú and Chǔ were at war,
Mò Xiāo Dà Xīn patted his charioteer's hand and said:
"Today we resist a powerful enemy,
face naked blades,
endure arrows and stones;
if I die in battle,
but victory is won and the people preserved,
then our state may perhaps survive!"
He then charged forth never to return,
with belly split and head severed,
dying without retreating a step.
Shēn Bāo Xū said:
"If I exhaust my strength against a formidable foe,
lying among corpses and blood,
I'd be no more than a common soldier's worth.
It's better to humble myself and speak modestly,
seeking aid from the nobles."
So he packed provisions and went barefoot,
journeying through valleys,
climbing steep mountains,
descending into deep gorges,
crossing rivers,
braving checkpoints,
pushing through thickets,
stumbling over sand and stones,
with soles worn to the knees,
layers of calluses and repeated blisters,
for seven days and seven nights,
until he reached the Qín court.
There, he stood like a crane without eating,
moaning by day and crying by night,
his face ashen,
complexion dark and haggard,
tears and snivel mingling,
until he was received by the Qín king,
and said:
"Wú is like a giant boar or long snake,
devouring the central states,
starting its tyranny with Chǔ.
My lord has lost his altars of land and grain,
and hides in the wilderness.
The people are scattered,
men and women with no time to rest.
He sends me, a humble servant, to report the urgency."
The Qín king then dispatched a thousand chariots,
seventy thousand foot soldiers,
under Zǐ Hǔ's command,
attacking Wú at the Turbid River,
and indeed crushed them decisively,
thus preserving the state of Chǔ.
His valor is enshrined in the temples,
recorded in the laws.
This is what is meant by "merit can be forcefully achieved."
The seven-foot-tall human form,
with a heart prone to worry and toil,
and skin that feels pain, illness, cold, and heat,
shares the same human nature.
The sage knows that time is hard to come by,
and that endeavors must be pursued;
thus, they toil their bodies and labor their forms,
burn with anxiety and tremble in their hearts,
not avoiding troubles and difficulties,
nor shunning danger and peril.
It is said that in the battles of Zǐ Fā,
his advance was like swift arrows,
his engagements like thunder and lightning,
his dispersals like wind and rain,
his circles conforming to the compass,
his squares fitting the ruler,
breaking enemy lines and storming formations,
none could block or resist him;
in marsh battles, he was sure to conquer,
in sieges, he was sure to capture.
He did not take his life lightly or delight in death;
his focus was on the task ahead,
leaving benefits for later,
thus his name stands firm and does not fall.
This is the result of self-strengthening and achieving success.
Therefore, if farmers do not strive,
their granaries will not be full;
if officials are not diligent,
their minds will not be sharp;
if generals and ministers do not exert themselves,
their achievements will not be accomplished;
if feudal lords and kings grow slack,
their posterity will have no renown.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"My horses are fine steeds,
the six reins like silk.
I drive and gallop,
everywhere seeking counsel."
This speaks of how people must have their pursuits.
Those who understand things cannot be startled by the strange;
those who comprehend the Way cannot be moved by the bizarre;
those who discern words cannot be dazzled by fame;
those who scrutinize forms cannot be deceived by appearances.
Common people of the world
often revere the past and belittle the present,
so those who expound the Way must attribute it to Shénnóng
and Huángdì before their teachings can be accepted.
In chaotic times and under dim-witted rulers,
they elevate the origins of such teachings,
and thus prize them.
Scholars,
blinded by theories, revere what they have heard,
sit solemnly together and praise it,
straighten their collars and recite it.
This shows the distinction between right and wrong is unclear.
Without compass and square,
even Xī Zhòng could not determine circles and squares;
without plumb line and marking cord,
even Lǔ Bān could not judge straight and curved.
Thus, when Zhǒng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá broke his zither and severed its strings,
knowing the world had none to appreciate it;
when Huì Shī died,
Zhuāngzǐ ceased his eloquent discourse,
seeing no one in the world to converse with.
Xiàng Tuó, at seven years old, became Confucius's teacher;
Confucius had reason to listen to his words.
But if, due to youth,
he spoke to village elders,
they would not even have time to save him from a beating—
how could they understand his Way!
In the past,
Xiè Zǐ appeared before King Huì of Qín,
and the king was pleased with him.
But when he asked Táng Gūliáng,
Táng Gūliáng said:
"Xiè Zǐ
is a debater from east of the mountains,
surely striving to win over the young ruler with his rhetoric."
King Huì then harbored anger and waited;
when Xiè Zǐ came again another day,
the king rejected him and would not listen.
It was not that his arguments had changed,
but the listener's mind had altered.
To mistake a minor note for a羽 note,
is not the fault of the string;
to take sweet for bitter,
is not the error of the taste.
A man of Chǔ cooked a monkey and invited his neighbor,
who thought it was dog stew and found it delicious.
Later, hearing it was monkey,
he knelt and vomited,
spewing out all he had eaten.
This is one who never truly knew taste.
A musician from Hándān composed a new melody,
attributing it to Lǐ Qí,
and everyone rushed to learn it.
Later, learning it was not his,
they all abandoned the tune.
This is one who never truly knew music.
A rustic found an uncarved jade,
delighted by its appearance,
thought it a treasure and stored it away.
Showing it to others,
they deemed it a stone,
so he discarded it.
This is one who never truly knew jade.
Thus, if one has an inner standard,
they value truth and align past and present;
without it to judge a discourse,
they prize it merely for its ancient origin.
This is why Hé Shì wept tears of blood beneath Jīng Shān.
Now, if a sword is chipped, worn, and notched,
with a bent and blunted blade,
yet labeled as King Qǐngxiāng's sword,
nobles will vie to wear it.
If a zither is warped and discordant,
with gaps and leaks in sound,
yet called King Zhuāng of Chǔ's zither,
concubines will compete to play it.
A blade from Miáo Shān,
or refined from yángtóu ore,
even if it cuts through dragon boats on water
and slices rhinoceros hide on land,
none will wear it.
A zither of mountain tong wood,
with a belly of valley zǐ wood,
even if its tones are pure, harmonious, and refined,
with Táng Yá's skill,
none will play it.
But the enlightened person is not so.
One who wields a sword seeks sharpness,
not necessarily Mò Yáng
or Mò Yé;
one who rides a horse seeks a thousand-mile runner,
not necessarily Huá Liú
or Lǜ Ěr;
one who plays a zither seeks clear, harmonious tones,
not necessarily Làn Xié
or Hào Zhōng;
one who recites the *Book of Songs*
and *Book of Documents* aims to understand the Way and grasp things,
not necessarily the "Hóng Fàn"
or "Shāng Sòng."
The sage perceives right and wrong
as clearly as the eye distinguishes black and white;
or the ear discerns clear and muddy sounds.
The multitude, however,
lack an inner master to receive it.
Like a posthumous child mourning at the grave mound,
crying ritually,
yet with no heart-felt grief.
Thus, of twin children who look alike,
only their mother can tell them apart;
of jade and stone that resemble each other,
only a skilled artisan can identify them;
of subtle writings and traditions,
only the sage can discuss them.
If today one takes a new sage's book
and attributes it to Confucius
or Mòzǐ, disciples will bow and receive it in droves.
Therefore, a beautiful person
need not be of Xī Shī's lineage;
an enlightened scholar
need not be of the Confucian
or Mohist kind.
Clearly, when the mind comprehends things,
one writes books to illustrate matters,
offering them to the wise.
If truly a clear-sighted scholar,
holding a mirror in the heart,
illuminates things with clarity,
not shifting intent for past or present,
can unfold the book and reveal its meaning to them,
even closing the coffin lid would bring no regret.
In the past, Duke Píng of Jìn ordered his artisans to cast a bell,
and when the bell was completed, he showed it to Shī Kuàng.
Shī Kuàng said:
"The bell's tone is not harmonious."
Duke Píng said:
"I showed it to the artisans,
and they all considered it harmonious.
Yet you consider it not harmonious,
why is that?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"If there are none in later ages who understand music, then so be it;
but if there are those who understand music,
they will surely know that the bell is not harmonious."
Thus, Shī Kuàng's desire to perfect the tuning of the bell
was for the sake of those in the future who would understand music.
The Three Dynasties and we share the same path,
the Five Hegemons and we share the same wisdom,
yet they alone possessed the substance of sagely knowledge,
while we have not even the reputation of a village lane
or the understanding of a poor alley—why is this?
They devoted themselves to establishing integrity,
while we are frivolous and negligent.
Now, Máo Qiáng
and Xī Shī
were the most beautiful women in the world,
but if they were made to hold a rotten rat in their mouths,
cover themselves with a hedgehog's skin,
wear a leopard-fur coat,
and gird themselves with a dead snake,
then even commoners in cloth garments and leather belts
would, upon passing by, without exception look askance and cover their noses.
But if they were to try applying fragrant oils,
adorning their delicate eyebrows,
setting hairpins and earrings,
wearing fine silks,
dragging Qí's thin silk,
powdering white and painting eyebrows black,
wearing jade pendants,
taking graceful steps,
mingled with zhǐ and ruò herbs,
with eyes veiled and dreamy,
with seductive smiles,
glances flowing,
lips slightly puckered,
exquisite teeth revealed,
dimples trembling,
then even kings, dukes, and great men
with stern wills and haughty conduct
would all feel their hearts stirred with delight and be pleased by their beauty.
Now, with the talent of an average person,
endowed with foolish and confused wisdom,
tainted by disgraceful conduct,
lacking a fundamental skill to cultivate
or an art to pursue,
how could they avoid the looks of disdain and covered noses?
Now, those who perform the drum dance,
coiling their bodies like a ring,
bending and scraping the ground,
leaning gracefully,
moving expressively and turning curvaceously,
elegantly imitating spirits,
their bodies like autumn herbs blown by the wind,
their hair like tied banners,
dashing swiftly as if startled;
those who perform tree dances,
lifting wú and jiǎ trees,
grasping bent branches,
swinging freely like apes,
fond of lush leaves.
Like dragons writhing elegantly,
like swallows perching on branches,
clutching abundant boughs,
dancing with spread foliage,
like dragons following and birds gathering,
grabbing, seizing, and stretching freely,
soaring and leaping lightly;
then the viewers all feel their hearts pained and feet sore,
yet they just begin to walk slowly and smile faintly,
adjusting their clothes and refining their gestures.
Those drum dancers are not inherently supple,
nor are the tree dancers innately agile and strong,
but gradual immersion and influence have made them so.
Therefore, the growth of a living tree
is unseen in its increase,
yet in time it becomes tall;
the grinding of a whetstone on a hard object
shows no visible loss,
yet in time it wears thin.
The growth of lí and diào weeds,
creeping slowly, adding inches daily,
cannot be used for roof beams;
the growth of pián, nán, and yùzhāng trees,
known only after seven years,
thus can be used for coffins and boats.
Things easily accomplished bring small fame,
while those difficult to achieve yield great merit.
The noble person cultivates beauty,
and though no benefit is yet seen,
fortune will arrive in time.
Thus, the Shī says:
"Daily accumulating, monthly progressing,
through learning, one gathers brightness unto illumination."
This refers to that.
Heaven established the sun and moon,
arrayed the stars,
harmonized yīn and yáng,
spread out the four seasons,
using the day to expose things,
the night to let them rest,
the wind to dry them,
rain and dew to moisten them.
In nurturing life,
none see how it is nourished, yet things grow;
in destroying life,
none see how it is lost, yet things perish,
this is called divine intelligence.
Sages emulate this,
thus when they bring about fortune,
none see its origin, yet fortune arises;
when they eliminate calamity,
none see the means, yet calamity is removed.
Distant, yet it feels near;
close, yet it feels remote;
examining it, one cannot grasp it,
observing it, it is not empty;
daily calculations show no tally,
yet yearly calculations show surplus.
When moisture arrives,
its form is unseen,
yet the charcoal has already grown heavy.
When the wind arrives,
its image is unseen,
yet the trees are already moving.
The sun's journey
shows no visible movement,
yet a qíjì horse running twice the sun's speed,
grasses and trees bow before it,
before the hanging torch has turned,
the sun is already ahead.
Thus, when Heaven is about to bring wind,
before the grasses and trees stir, birds are already soaring;
when it is about to rain,
before the gloomy clouds gather, fish are already gasping;
this is due to the interaction of yīn and yáng energies.
Thus, cold and heat, dryness and moisture,
follow each other by category;
sound and echo, speed and slowness,
respond to each other through tone.
Therefore, the Yì says:
"A calling crane in the shade,
its young ones answer it."
Gāozōng observed the mourning hut,
not speaking for three years;
within the four seas,
all was silent and without sound;
yet with one word resounding,
he greatly moved the world.
Thus, the heart of Heaven opens and closes,
so when its root moves once, all branches respond,
like spring rain irrigating all things,
flowing seamlessly,
pouring forth abundantly,
nowhere left unwatered,
nothing left unalive.
Thus, the sage embraces the heavenly heart,
and with silent potency can move and transform the world.
For when essence and sincerity stir within,
form and ether move in heaven,
then auspicious stars appear,
yellow dragons descend,
propitious phoenixes arrive,
sweet springs emerge,
fine grains grow,
rivers do not overflow,
seas do not surge with waves.
Therefore, the Book of Songs says:
"He pacifies all spirits,
and reaches to the rivers and lofty mountains."
But to oppose heaven and brutalize creatures,
then the sun and moon suffer eclipses,
the five planets stray from their courses,
the four seasons are thrown into discord,
daylight darkens and night glows,
mountains crumble and rivers run dry,
winter thunders and summer frosts.
The Book of Songs says:
"In the first month, heavy frost;
my heart is grieved and sorrowful."
Heaven and humanity are interconnected.
Thus, when a state is in peril and near ruin, celestial patterns change;
when the age is deluded and chaotic, rainbows appear;
all things are interconnected,
and essences and influences interact.
Therefore, affairs of the divine and luminous
cannot be achieved by cleverness or artifice,
nor can they be attained by physical strength.
What heaven and earth envelop,
what yīn and yáng breathe forth,
what rain and dew moisten—
gives birth to myriad varieties.
Kingfisher feathers and tortoise shell,
yáo jade, bì jade, jade pearls,
their patterns and colors bright and clear,
glossy and smooth as if moistened,
worn yet not degraded,
enduring without change—
Xī Zhòng could not replicate them,
Lǔ Bān could not create them.
This is called the great skill.
A man of Sòng used ivory to carve a mulberry leaf for his lord;
it took three years to complete.
Its stem, veins, and fine tips,
its sharp edges, hues, and luster—
when mixed among real mulberry leaves, it was indistinguishable.
Lièzǐ heard of it and said:
"If heaven and earth took three years to produce a single leaf,
then few things in the world would have leaves.
For heaven and earth in their transforming operations
breathe them forth to grow,
blow upon them to fall—
how could they be so laborious!"
Thus, all that can be measured
is small;
all that can be counted
is few.
The greatest
cannot be reached by measurement;
the most numerous
cannot be comprehended by counting.
Thus, the Nine Provinces cannot be gauged by the acre;
the Eight Extremes cannot be told by the mile;
Tài Shān cannot be measured by the foot;
rivers and seas cannot be contained by the bushel.
Therefore, the great person
aligns virtue with heaven and earth,
matches brightness with the sun and moon,
shares numinosity with ghosts and spirits,
and keeps faith with the four seasons.
Thus, the sage embraces heavenly ether,
holds the heavenly heart,
grasps centrality and harbors harmony,
and without leaving the ancestral temple, his influence spreads throughout the four seas,
transforming customs and changing habits,
so the people are reformed and turn to goodness
as if it were their innate nature,
able to accomplish this through spiritual transformation.
The Book of Songs says:
"The spirits listen to it,
ultimately harmonious and peaceful."
Now, ghosts and spirits are formless to look upon,
soundless to listen to,
yet we sacrifice to heaven,
worship mountains and rivers,
pray at shrines to seek blessings,
perform yú sacrifices to request rain,
use divination to decide matters.
The Book of Songs says:
"The coming of the spirits
cannot be fathomed;
how much less can they be disregarded!"
This refers to this.
Heaven achieves its height,
earth achieves its thickness,
the moon illuminates the night,
the sun illuminates the day,
the arrayed stars shine brightly,
yīn and yáng transform—
not through deliberate action,
but by aligning with the Dào, things occur naturally.
Thus, yīn, yáng, and the four seasons
do not exist to produce the myriad things;
rain and dew fall in season,
not to nurture plants and trees;
when spiritual luminosity connects,
yīn and yáng harmonize,
then the myriad things are born.
Thus, high mountains and deep forests
are not made for tigers and leopards;
great trees and lush branches
are not made for flying birds;
sources flowing a thousand miles,
deep abysses a hundred fathoms,
are not made for jiāo dragons;
they attain their loftiness and grandeur,
achieve their breadth and vastness,
and those dwelling in mountains, perching in trees,
nesting in branches, hiding in caves,
swimming in water, moving on land,
each find their place of peace.
For the great gives birth to the small,
the many gives birth to the few—
this is the way of heaven.
Thus, small mounds cannot generate clouds and rain;
puddles cannot breed fish and turtles—
because they are small.
The vapor of oxen and horses can generate lice and fleas,
but the vapor of lice and fleas cannot generate oxen and horses.
Thus, transformation arises from without,
not from within.
Now, the jiāo dragon lies hidden in the deep,
yet its eggs are laid on high grounds;
the téng snake, the male calling upwind,
the female calling downwind, take form through transformation—
such is the pinnacle of essence.
Therefore, in nurturing the heart, the sage
finds nothing better than sincerity,
for utmost sincerity can move and transform.
Now, those who possess the Dào
store essence within,
lodge spirit in the heart,
tranquil, serene, calm, and detached,
with harmony filling their breasts,
so that no perverse energy lingers or stagnates.
In their four limbs, joints, and tissues,
as pores steam and textures release,
then the pivotal mechanisms are regulated and smooth,
all vessels and nine orifices follow in harmony,
and the residing spirit finds its proper place—
how could this be achieved by merely tapping joints and stroking hairs!
When a sage ruler occupies the highest position,
he appears vast and formless,
silent and soundless.
The government offices seem as if without affairs,
the imperial court as if without people.
There are no reclusive scholars,
no displaced commoners,
no forced labor,
no unjust punishments.
Within the four seas, none fail to look up to the virtue of the sovereign,
following the ruler's direction.
Countries of barbarians arrive through multiple translations,
not because every household is persuaded and every family convinced,
but because his sincere heart is extended
and applied throughout the world.
The Book of Songs says:
"He benefits this central state,
thereby pacifying the four regions."
Thus, there is harmony within and peace without.
When King Dànyéfŭ dwelled in Bīn,
the Dí people attacked him.
He took his staff and departed,
while the common people carried their young and supported their aged,
bearing their cooking pots,
crossing Mount Liáng,
and established a state at Qízhōu.
This was not something commands could summon.
When Duke Mù of Qín was harmed by villagers eating his steed's meat,
he gave them fine wine to drink.
At the battle of Hán,
they repaid him with their utmost effort unto death,
which was not something a contract could demand.
When Mìzǐ governed Dànfǔ,
Wūmǎqī went to observe his transformation.
He saw a night fisherman release whatever small fish he caught,
which was not something punishments could prohibit.
When Confucius served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
no one picked up lost items on the road,
no merchants inflated prices in the market,
hunters and fishermen all yielded to their elders,
and the gray-haired carried no burdens.
This was not something laws could achieve.
The reason arrows can shoot far and pierce hard objects
is the power of the crossbow;
the reason they can hit the target and split fine hairs
is the human mind.
Rewarding good and punishing evil
is the function of government decrees;
the reason they can be implemented
lies in sincere devotion.
Thus, though the crossbow is strong, it cannot hit the target alone;
though decrees are clear, they cannot implement themselves.
There must be essential energy to apply the Way with them.
Therefore, when the Way is elaborated to cover the people,
yet the people do not follow,
it is because sincere heart is not applied.
Heaven, earth, and the four seasons
do not generate the myriad things;
when divine intelligence connects,
yin and yang harmonize,
then the myriad things are born.
When sages govern the world,
they do not change people's nature;
they follow what people possess and cleanse it,
thus following nature leads to greatness,
while forcing action leads to pettiness.
When Yǔ dredged the Dragon Gate,
opened the Yi Pass,
channeled the rivers and deepened the waterways,
directing them eastward to the sea,
he followed the flow of water.
When Hòujì cleared grasslands and opened wastelands,
fertilized the soil and planted grains,
making the five crops each suit their proper conditions,
he followed the lay of the land.
When Tāng and Wǔ led three hundred war chariots
and three thousand armored soldiers
to suppress tyrants and quell chaos,
subduing the Xià
and Shāng dynasties, they followed the people's desires.
Therefore, those who can follow nature
become invincible under heaven.
Things possess their inherent nature,
and only then can human affairs be properly ordered.
Thus, a skilled carpenter cannot carve metal,
a clever smith cannot melt wood,
for metal's nature cannot be carved,
and wood's character cannot be melted.
Kneading clay makes vessels,
hollowing wood makes boats,
smelting iron makes blades,
casting metal makes bells
by following what is possible.
Harnessing horses and yoking oxen,
making roosters announce the night,
making dogs guard gates
follows their inherent tendencies.
People have a nature of loving beauty,
hence there are the rites of grand marriage;
they have a nature of eating and drinking,
hence there are the ceremonies of great feasts;
they have a nature of joy and pleasure,
hence there is the music of bells, drums, pipes, and strings;
they have a nature of grief and sorrow,
hence there are the rituals of mourning garments, weeping, and stomping.
Thus, when ancient kings established laws,
they followed what people loved
to create regulated patterns.
Following the love of beauty, they established marriage rites,
thus distinguishing male and female;
following the enjoyment of music, they corrected the sounds of the "Yǎ"
and "Sòng" hymns,
thus preventing customs from degenerating;
following the desire for peaceful homes
and happy wives and children,
they taught obedience,
thus creating affection between father and son;
following the joy in friendship, they taught fraternal duty,
thus establishing order between elder and younger.
Then they cultivated court ceremonies to clarify nobility and baseness,
village drinking rituals and archery practice to clarify seniority,
seasonal hunts and military reviews to train in weaponry,
and entry into schools to cultivate human relationships.
All these stem from what people possess by nature,
and what sages expertly bring to completion.
Therefore, without the nature,
teaching is impossible;
with the nature
but without cultivation,
one cannot follow the Way.
The cocoon's nature is to become silk,
yet without a skilled girl boiling it in hot water and drawing out its threads,
it cannot become silk.
The egg transforms into a chick,
yet without a mother hen brooding warm and covering it,
accumulating days over time,
it cannot become a chick.
Human nature possesses the capacity for benevolence and righteousness,
yet without sage kings establishing models and teaching them,
they cannot be directed toward the proper path.
Thus, in the education of ancient kings,
they encouraged goodness by following what people loved,
and prohibited wickedness by following what people hated.
Hence punishments were unused yet authority flowed like water,
decrees were simple yet transformation shone like divinity.
Therefore, following human nature,
the world obeys and follows;
opposing human nature,
laws hang idle and unused.
In ancient times,
the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns, when administering governance and implementing teachings,
invariably employed the principles of three and five.
What are these three and five?
They looked upward to take symbols from heaven,
looked downward to take measures from earth,
and in the middle took models from humanity,
then established the court of the Bright Hall,
enacted the decrees of the Bright Hall,
to harmonize the energies of yīn and yáng,
and balance the nodes of the four seasons,
thereby warding off the calamities of disease and pestilence.
Looking down to observe terrestrial patterns,
they instituted standards and measurements,
examining the suitability of hills, plains, waters, marshes, fertile and lean, high and low lands,
establishing affairs and generating wealth,
to eliminate the troubles of hunger and cold.
Centrally examining human virtues,
they formulated rites and music,
practiced the way of benevolence and righteousness,
to govern human relations and remove the scourge of violence and chaos.
Then they clarified the natures of metal, water, wood, fire, and earth,
to establish the intimacy between father and son and form the family;
distinguished the clear and turbid of the five notes and the numbers of the six pitch-pipes' mutual generation,
to establish the righteousness between ruler and minister and form the state;
observed the sequence of the four seasons and their beginning and end months,
to establish the propriety between elder and younger and form the bureaucracy;
this is called the three.
Regulating the righteousness between ruler and minister,
the intimacy between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
the order between elder and younger,
and the interactions between friends,
this is called the five.
Then they divided the land into provinces,
assigned offices to govern them,
built cities for dwelling,
partitioned residences to differentiate them,
distributed wealth for food and clothing,
established the Great Academy to educate,
and rose early and retired late to labor diligently.
These are the guiding principles of governance.
Yet with the right person, they thrive;
without the right person, they decline.
Yáo governed the world,
his governance and teachings were equitable,
his virtue moistened and permeated all.
After seventy years on the throne,
he sought someone to inherit the rule of the world,
commanding the Four Peaks to promote the obscure and lowly.
The Four Peaks recommended Shùn to Yáo,
Yáo then gave him his two daughters in marriage,
to observe his inner qualities;
entrusted him with all officials,
to observe his external conduct;
after entering the great mountain forest,
he did not lose his way in fierce winds and thunderstorms,
then Yáo entrusted him with his nine sons,
bestowed upon him the Zhāohuá jade,
and passed the world to him.
Believing that although there were laws and measures,
Dānzhū could not uphold them.
Things never stretch without slackening,
or complete without destruction,
only the sage can prosper without decline,
be full without deficit.
When Shénnóng first created the qín,
it was to concentrate the spirit and curb excess; ,
returning to the heart of heaven.
When it declined,
it flowed without return,
indulged in lewdness and lust,
leading to the loss of the state.
When Kuí first created music,
it all harmonized with the six pitch-pipes and tuned the five notes,
to connect with the eight winds;
when it declined,
it led to drowning in excessive pleasure,
neglecting governance,
resulting in destruction.
When Cāngjié first created writing,
it was to distinguish and manage all officials,
oversee and order all affairs,
enabling the foolish not to forget,
the wise to record events;
when it declined,
it was used for crafty and forged documents,
to exonerate the guilty,
and kill the innocent.
When Tāng first established the hunting park,
it was to supply the temple with fresh sacrificial animals,
train soldiers,
practice archery and charioteering,
to prepare for unforeseen events;
when it declined,
it became about galloping and hunting,
depriving people of their farming time,
and exhausting their strength.
When Yáo promoted Yǔ,
Qì, Hòujì,
and Gāoyáo,
governance and teachings were equitable,
treachery ceased,
litigation stopped, and food and clothing were sufficient,
the worthy encouraged goodness and the unworthy embraced their virtue;
when it reached its end,
cliques formed and colluded,
each promoting their allies,
abandoning public duty for private gain,
inside and outside mutually recommending,
with villains in court and the worthy in seclusion. , , , , , (
The fault of the Spring and Autumn Annals is its criticism).
The way of heaven and earth
reaches its extreme and then reverses,
becomes full and then diminishes.
The five colors, though bright,
sometimes fade;
lush trees and abundant grass,
sometimes wither;
things have their rise and fall,
and cannot remain constant.
Therefore, when affairs reach an impasse, the sage changes his ways;
when laws become corrupt, he reforms the system,
not because he delights in altering antiquity and changing constants,
but to rescue from failure and support the declining,
eliminate excess and rectify wrongs,
to harmonize the energies of heaven and earth,
and accord with what is suitable for all things.
The sage is covered by heaven and supported by earth,
illuminated by the sun and moon,
harmonized by yin and yang,
transformed by the four seasons,
and though all things are different,
without the old or the new,
without the distant or the close,
thus they can emulate heaven.
Heaven does not have one season alone,
earth does not offer one benefit alone,
humans do not engage in one affair alone,
therefore endeavors must be multifaceted,
and pursuits must vary in direction.
The five elements have different energies but all harmonize,
the six arts are different disciplines but all interconnect.
Those gentle, kind, soft, and good
reflect the ethos of the Book of Songs;
those sincere, profound, earnest, and thick
embody the teachings of the Book of Documents;
those clear, bright, orderly, and penetrating
express the meaning of the Book of Changes;
those respectful, frugal, reverent, and yielding
are shaped by the rites;
those broad, generous, simple, and easy
are transformed by music;
those who criticize subtly and debate righteousness
follow the subtleties of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Thus, the Book of Changes may err toward the mystical,
Music may err toward excess,
the Book of Songs may err toward naivety,
the Book of Documents may err toward rigidity,
the rites may err toward obstinacy,
the Spring and Autumn Annals may err toward fault-finding.
These six,
the sage employs together and judiciously regulates.
Losing the root leads to chaos,
gaining the root leads to order.
Their beauty lies in harmony,
their flaw lies in imbalance.
Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grains,
different substances yet all are utilized,
compass, square, weight, balance, level, and line,
different forms yet all are applied,
cinnabar, azurite, glue, lacquer,
dissimilar yet all are used,
each has its appropriate place,
each thing has its suitability.
Wheels are round, carriages square,
shafts follow, crossbars are horizontal,
their arrangement is for convenience.
Outer horses desire to gallop,
central horses desire to walk,
belts do not disdain the new,
hooks do not disdain the old,
each suited to its position.
The "Guān Jū" arises from birds,
and the gentleman praises it,
for the male and female do not perch together improperly;
the "Lù Míng" arises from beasts,
and the gentleman esteems it,
taking that they call to each other when finding food.
In the battle of Hóng,
the army was defeated and the ruler captured,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals honors it,
taking that they did not attack before the enemy formed ranks;
Sòng Bó Jī sat and burned to death,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals honors her,
taking that she did not act beyond the rites.
Achieving success and establishing deeds,
how could it be enough to praise excessively?
It merely points to what is said,
and takes one principle from it.
Wáng Qiáo
and Chì Sōng departed from the realm of dust,
leaving behind the troubles of the crowd,
inhaling the harmony of yin and yang,
consuming the essence of heaven and earth,
exhaling to expel the old,
inhaling to take in the new,
treading lightly and rising effortlessly,
riding clouds and wandering through mist,
they may be called cultivators of nature,
but cannot be called filial sons.
The Duke of Zhōu executed Guǎn Shū
and Cài Shū,
to pacify the state and quell disorder,
he may be called a loyal minister,
but cannot be called a fraternal brother.
King Tāng exiled Jié,
King Wǔ executed Zhòu,
to rid the world of cruelty and villainy,
they may be called benevolent rulers,
but cannot be called loyal ministers.
Yuè Yáng attacked Zhōngshān,
but could not conquer it,
Zhōngshān cooked his son
and made him eat to demonstrate resolve,
he may be called a fine general,
but cannot be called a loving father.
Thus, what is acceptable is acceptable,
and what is unacceptable is unacceptable;
what is unacceptable is unacceptable,
and what is acceptable is acceptable.
Shùn
and Xǔ Yóu had different conducts but both were sagely,
Yī Yǐn
and Bó Yí had different ways but both were benevolent,
Jīzǐ
and Bǐ Gàn had different pursuits but both were worthy.
Therefore, in employing military forces,
some are light, some heavy,
some greedy, some廉洁,
these four are opposites yet none can be omitted.
The light desire to advance,
the heavy desire to halt,
the greedy desire to seize,
the廉洁 do not profit from what is not theirs.
Thus, the brave can be ordered to charge and fight,
but not to hold firm;
the heavy can be ordered to solidify defenses,
but not to assault the enemy;
the greedy can be ordered to advance and seize,
but not to guard duties;
the廉洁 can be ordered to uphold their lot,
but not to advance and seize;
the trustworthy can be ordered to keep agreements,
but not to adapt to changes.
These four are opposites,
yet the sage employs them together and judiciously uses them.
Heaven and earth do not encompass one thing alone,
yin and yang do not produce one kind alone.
The sea does not refuse streams and thus achieves its greatness,
mountains do not refuse earth and stones and thus achieve their height.
To hold one corner and neglect all others,
take one thing and discard the rest,
then what is gained is meager,
and what is governed is shallow.
Those governing greatly cannot use small ways,
those with vast lands cannot have narrow systems,
those in high positions cannot handle繁琐 affairs,
those with numerous people cannot impose harsh teachings.
Affairs that are fragmented
are hard to govern;
laws that are繁琐
are hard to implement;
demands that are excessive
are hard to satisfy.
Measuring by the inch,
to a zhang will surely err;
weighing by the zhu,
to a dan will surely exceed.
Weighing by the dan and measuring by the zhang,
direct and seldom mistaken;
counting silk threads and grains of rice,
繁琐 and unclear.
Thus, the grand overview is easy for wisdom,
intricate arguments are hard for insight.
Therefore, what does not benefit governance but adds to繁琐,
the sage does not do;
what does not benefit utility but increases waste,
the wise do not undertake.
Thus, achievements do not disdain simplicity,
affairs do not disdain conciseness,
demands do not disdain fewness.
Achievements simple
are easy to complete;
affairs concise
are easy to govern;
demands few
are easy to satisfy.
When the multitude finds it easy,
in employing people,
it is easy!
Confucius said:
"Petty arguments ruin speech,
petty profits ruin righteousness,
petty righteousness ruins the Way,
the Way petty does not reach far,
to reach far must be simple."
The river winds and meanders,
thus it can flow far;
the mountain rises lofty and vast,
thus it can stand high;
the Way is unhurried and serene,
thus it can transform.
To master one affair,
comprehend one phrase,
or scrutinize one skill
may allow for detailed explanation,
but cannot broadly respond to all.
When marsh herbs grow in rows,
and earthenware jars have bases,
weighing firewood to cook,
counting grains to prepare a meal
may suffice for managing small matters,
but not for governing great ones.
Round fits the compass,
square fits the square,
movements mimic beasts,
stillness forms patterns—
these may please in dance,
but cannot deploy an army.
Washing cups to eat,
cleansing vessels to drink,
bathing before offering food
may nourish a few,
but cannot feast a crowd.
Now, in sacrifices,
slaughtering, carving, cooking, and killing,
skinning dogs and roasting pigs,
balancing the five flavors
is the cook's role;
arranging the fǔguǐ vessels,
setting out zūn and zǔ stands,
placing the biān and dǒu containers
is the invoker's duty;
purified and in full attire,
silent and not speaking,
the one whom the spirits rely on
is the impersonator.
Though the steward and invoker may be incapable,
the impersonator does not overstep to take their place.
Thus, in tuning a sè,
the small strings are tight while the large are loose;
in establishing affairs,
the lowly toil and the noble rest.
Shùn as the Son of Heaven
played the five-stringed qín,
sang the "Ode of the South Wind,"
and the world was well-governed.
Zhōu Gōng had meats not cleared from before him,
bells and drums not taken down from their racks,
yet the four barbarians submitted.
Zhào Zhèng decided cases by day,
handled documents by night,
with couriers' carriages crowding the commanderies and counties,
reviewing and hastening, delaying and detaining,
garrisoning the Five Ridges to guard against Yuè,
building long walls to defend against the Hú,
yet treachery sprouted,
bandits gathered,
and the more he busied, the more chaos arose.
Thus, laws are
tools of governance,
not the means to govern.
Just as the bow and arrow
are tools for hitting the mark,
not the means to hit it.
Huángdì said:
"Vast and obscure,
relying on heaven's majesty,
share the same qì with the origin."
Thus, those who share the same qì become emperors,
those who share righteousness become kings,
those who share force become hegemons,
and those with none of these perish.
So when a ruler has ambitions to conquer a state,
village dogs howl in packs,
roosters crow at night,
arsenal weapons stir and warhorses startle;
but if he resolves grievances and halts warfare today,
elders sleep peacefully,
alleys hold no crowds,
and calamities do not arise.
This is not the response of laws,
but the movement of essential qì.
Thus, without speaking, there is trust;
without giving, there is benevolence;
without anger, there is authority—
these are transformations moved by the heart of heaven;
giving with benevolence,
speaking with trust,
anger with authority—
these are moved by sincere essence;
giving without benevolence,
speaking without trust,
anger without authority—
these are done through external appearance.
Therefore, with the Way to unify it,
even if laws are few,
they suffice to transform;
without the Way to implement it,
even if laws are numerous,
they suffice to cause chaos.
In cultivating the self,
the highest is to nurture the spirit,
the next is to nurture the form;
in governing a state,
the highest is to nurture transformation,
the next is to rectify laws.
A clear spirit and balanced will,
all joints at peace—
this is the root of nurturing nature;
fattening the skin and muscles,
filling the belly,
catering to desires—
this is the branch of nurturing life.
When people yield and contend to take the humble place,
relinquish profits and contend to accept less,
exert effort and contend to take on toil,
daily transforming upward toward goodness without knowing why—
this is the root of governance.
Lured by rewards to encourage goodness,
fearing penalties to avoid wrongdoing,
with laws decreed above and the people obeying below—
this is the branch of governance.
Ancient times nurtured the root, while later ages attend to the branch,
which is why great peace does not arise.
Rulers capable of governance do not appear every generation,
and ministers who can assist in governance are not one in ten thousand,
so seeking the rare ruler with the rare minister
is why they meet not once in a thousand years.
The nature of water
is soft and clear,
but in a stagnant valley pool,
it grows green algae,
not because its nature is altered.
Dig its flow to deepen it,
bank its breaks to heighten it,
let it follow the terrain,
ride the currents—
even with rotting carcasses and floating ice,
it cannot be polluted.
Its nature is not different;
it is about whether it is connected or not.
Customs are like this.
Truly guide their good intentions,
guard against their wicked thoughts,
open the path of goodness,
block the road of villainy,
leading them all along the same way—
then the people's nature can be good,
and customs can be beautified.
What makes Biǎn Què valuable
is not his adjusting medicine to the illness,
but his pressing to feel the pulse and blood,
knowing where the disease originates.
What makes a sage valuable
is not his meting out punishments for crimes,
but his knowing the source of chaos.
If one does not cultivate customs,
but allows depravity to spread,
then applying punishments afterward,
restraining with laws,
even if devastating the world,
cannot prohibit it.
Yǔ made Xià rule as king,
while Jié led Xià to ruin;
Tāng made Yīn rule as king,
while Zhòu led Yīn to ruin;
not that laws and measures did not exist,
but discipline was not upheld, and customs decayed.
The laws of the Three Dynasties remain intact,
yet the world is not well-governed,
because there is no wisdom of the Three Dynasties.
The six pitch pipes all exist,
but none can hear them,
because there is no ear like Shī Kuàng's.
Thus, although laws exist,
they must await sages to bring order;
although the pitch pipes are complete,
they must await ears to be heard.
Therefore, the reason a state survives
is not because it has laws,
but because it has worthy individuals;
the reason it perishes
is not because it lacks laws,
but because it lacks sages.
When Duke Xiàn of Jìn wished to attack Yú,
Gōng Zhī Qí was still there,
causing him to sleep restlessly,
eat without tasting his food,
and dare not send troops.
Bribed with precious jade and fine horses,
Gōng Zhī Qí remonstrated but was not heeded.
His words went unheeded,
so he crossed the border and left;
Xún Xī attacked Yú,
without staining a blade with blood,
and returned carrying the jade and leading the horses.
Thus, defense does not rely on moats to be secure,
nor attack on siege towers to succeed—
it is all about gaining or losing the worthy.
Hence, Zāng Wǔzhòng used his wisdom to preserve Lǔ,
and no one in the world could destroy it;
Qú Bóyù used his benevolence to pacify Wèi,
and no one in the world could endanger it.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
"He enlarges his house,
shadows his home,
peeps through his door,
and it is silent, with no one."
"No one"
does not mean there are no multitudes,
but that there is no sage to govern and manage them.
If the people lack integrity and shame,
they cannot be governed;
unless ritual and righteousness are cultivated,
integrity and shame will not be established.
If the people do not understand ritual and righteousness,
laws cannot correct them;
unless goodness is exalted and vice abolished,
they will not turn to ritual and righteousness.
Without laws, there can be no governance;
without understanding ritual and righteousness, laws cannot be implemented.
Laws can execute the unfilial,
but cannot make people act like Kǒngzǐ
or Zēngzǐ;
laws can punish thieves,
but cannot make people as incorruptible as Bó Yí.
Among Confucius' seventy disciples,
and his three thousand followers,
all were filial at home and respectful abroad,
their speech was eloquent,
their conduct exemplary—
this was the achievement of education.
Mòzǐ had a hundred and eighty followers,
all willing to tread fire and tread on blades,
dying without turning back—
this was the result of transformation.
To carve one's skin,
incise the flesh,
endure wounds and bleeding,
is extremely difficult,
yet the Yuè people do it
to seek honor.
When a sage king reigns above,
clearly showing likes and dislikes to the people,
guiding them with praise and blame,
drawing close to the worthy and promoting them,
disdaining the unworthy and dismissing them,
without the pain of wounds and bleeding,
but with the fame of high honor and esteem,
who among the people would not follow?
In ancient times, laws were established but not violated,
punishments were in place but not used—
not because they could punish but did not,
but because all officials were diligent,
all achievements flourished,
ritual and righteousness were cultivated, and the worthy were employed.
Thus, the most elevated in the world were raised to be the Three Dukes,
the most elevated in a state to be the Nine Ministers,
the most elevated in a county to be the twenty-seven Great Officers,
the most elevated in a village to be the eighty-one Exemplary Scholars.
Hence, one whose wisdom surpasses ten thousand is called an *yīng* (outstanding),
one who surpasses a thousand is called a *jùn* (brilliant),
one who surpasses a hundred is called a *háo* (heroic),
one who surpasses ten is called a *jié* (distinguished).
Understanding the way of heaven,
observing the principles of earth,
comprehending human feelings,
broad enough to embrace the multitude,
virtuous enough to attract the distant,
trustworthy enough to unify differences,
wise enough to understand expediency—
such a person is an *yīng* among men.
Virtuous enough to educate and transform,
conduct upright enough to uphold righteousness,
benevolent enough to win the multitude,
enlightened enough to illuminate those below—
such a person is a *jùn* among men.
Conduct exemplary enough to be a model,
wisdom sufficient to resolve doubts,
integrity to share wealth,
trustworthiness to keep agreements,
actions worthy of emulation,
words worthy of being followed—
such a person is a *háo* among men.
Diligent in duty without neglect,
upright in principle without bias,
facing difficulty without avoiding it,
facing gain without seizing it improperly—
such a person is a *jié* among men.
The *yīng*, *jùn*, *háo*, and *jié*,
each according to their ability, take their positions,
fitting appropriately,
from root to branch,
controlling the light with the heavy,
the ruler leads and the people harmonize,
the ruler acts and the subjects follow,
within the four seas,
all hearts turn as one,
turning from greed and baseness to benevolence and righteousness—
in transforming the people thus,
it is like the wind swaying grass and trees:
nothing fails to bend.
Now, if the foolish teach the wise,
if the unworthy oversee the worthy,
even with severe punishments,
the people will not follow—
for the small cannot control the great,
nor the weak command the strong.
Thus, a sage ruler promotes the worthy to achieve merit,
while an unworthy ruler promotes those like himself.
King Wén elevated Tàigōng Wàng
and Shào Gōng Shì to become kings;
Duke Huán employed Guǎn Zhòng
and Xí Péng to become hegemon—
these are examples of promoting the worthy to achieve merit.
Fū Chāi used Tàizǎi Pǐ and perished;
Qín employed Lǐ Sī
and Zhào Gāo and fell—
these are examples of promoting those like oneself.
Thus, observe whom they promote,
and order or chaos can be seen;
examine their factions,
and worthiness or unworthiness can be judged.
When sages bend,
it is to seek to stretch;
when they twist,
it is to seek straightness;
thus, even if they tread crooked paths,
walk in dark ways,
it is to elevate the great Way,
and achieve great merit.
It is like emerging from a forest without a straight path,
or saving a drowning person without getting one's feet wet.
Yī Yǐn worried about the world's disorder,
mastered the five flavors,
carried cauldron and stand on his journey,
five times approaching Jié,
five times approaching Tāng,
seeking to turn turbidity into clarity,
danger into peace.
The Duke of Zhōu supported the Zhōu house,
assisted King Chéng;
Guǎn Shū
and Cài Shū supported Prince Lù Fù and sought to rebel,
so the Duke of Zhōu executed them to stabilize the world—
compelled by necessity.
Guǎnzǐ worried about the decline of the Zhōu house,
the strife among feudal lords,
the invasion of the Yí Dí against the Central States,
and the people's lack of peace;
thus, he endured disgrace without dying,
seeking to alleviate the Yí Dí's threat,
and pacify their chaos.
Confucius wished to implement the kingly Way,
traveled east, west, south, and north, advocating seventy times without success,
so he sought to convey his Way through Lady of Wèi
and Mí Zǐxiá.
All these sought to level dangers and remove impurities,
moving from darkness to brightness,
acting with expediency and unified by goodness.
To observe those who chase after something, look at their return;
to observe those who act, look at their end.
Thus, Shùn exiled his younger brother,
and the Duke of Zhōu executed his elder brother,
yet they were still considered benevolent;
Wén Gōng planted rice,
and Zēngzǐ tethered a sheep,
yet they were still deemed wise.
In the current age,
the ugly invariably cloak themselves in goodness to justify their actions,
the wicked invariably disguise themselves with righteousness to excuse their deeds.
They travel without discussing the state,
