serve in office without choosing the right position,
act without avoiding corruption,
saying,
"This is the way of Yī Yǐn."
They quarrel over wealth,
sow discord among relatives and brothers,
and harm their own flesh and blood,
saying,
"This is the righteousness of the Duke of Zhōu."
They act without shame,
endure humiliation yet refuse to die,
saying,
"This is the conduct of Guǎn Zhòng."
They engage in bribery,
rush to powerful doors,
establish private interests while neglecting public good,
form cliques to gain favor,
saying,
"This is the method of Confucius."
This causes gentlemen and petty men to become confused and mixed,
with no one knowing right from wrong.
Thus, though a hundred streams flow together,
those that do not reach the sea are not true rivers;
though actions may vary and run in different directions,
those that do not lead to goodness are not those of a gentleman.
Therefore, good words must lead to feasible actions,
and good deeds must align with benevolence and righteousness.
Tián Zǐfāng
and Duàngān Mù despised rank and salary but valued their own persons,
not harming their lives with desires,
not burdening their bodies with profit,
while Lǐ Kè exhausted the strength of his limbs,
governed the officials,
and harmonized the myriad people,
ensuring that his ruler had no neglected affairs in life,
and no lingering worries in death.
These are different actions that lead to goodness.
Zhāng Yí
and Sū Qín had no fixed homes,
no steadfast lords,
formed alliances of vertical and horizontal schemes,
devised plans for overthrow,
threw the world into chaos,
confused the feudal lords,
causing the common people to have no peace in their lives,
sometimes aligning vertically, sometimes horizontally,
sometimes uniting the weak,
sometimes aiding the strong and wealthy.
These are different actions that lead to ugliness.
Thus, the faults of a gentleman,
like the eclipses of the sun and moon,
do no harm to their brightness!
The merits of a petty man,
like a dog barking by day,
or an owl seen at night,
contribute nothing to goodness!
The wise do not act recklessly,
the brave do not strike recklessly;
they choose what is good to do,
and consider righteousness in their actions.
Thus, their endeavors succeed and their achievements are reliable,
and upon their death, their names are worthy of praise.
Though one may have wisdom and ability,
they must be rooted in benevolence and righteousness,
and only then can they be established.
Wisdom and abilities may run in different directions,
and a hundred tasks may be undertaken simultaneously,
but the sage unifies them all with benevolence and righteousness as the standard.
Those who meet it are called gentlemen,
those who do not are called petty men.
Even in death,
the gentleman's name does not perish;
even if a petty man gains power,
his crimes are not forgiven.
If one were to hold the map of the world in the left hand and cut his own throat with the right,
no fool would do it,
for the body is more precious than the world.
Yet to die for the troubles of one's ruler or parents,
to regard death as a return home,
is because righteousness is heavier than the body.
The great benefit of the world,
compared to the body, is small;
the body is what we value,
but compared to righteousness, it is light;
righteousness is what we preserve.
The Book of Songs says:
"The genial and courteous gentleman,
seeks blessings without deviation."
This means to take trust and righteousness as the standard.
Those who can achieve the greatness of a hegemon or king
must be victors.
Those who can be victors
must be strong.
Those who can be strong
must employ the strength of others.
Those who can employ the strength of others
must win the hearts of the people.
Those who can win the hearts of the people
must first have mastery over themselves.
Thus, the heart is
the root of the body,
and the body is
the root of the state.
There has never been one who gained himself yet lost others,
nor one who lost himself yet gained others.
Therefore, the root of governance
lies in calming the people;
the root of calming the people
lies in sufficiency of resources;
the root of sufficiency of resources
lies in not disrupting the seasons;
the root of not disrupting the seasons
lies in reducing affairs;
the root of reducing affairs
lies in restraining desires;
the root of restraining desires
lies in returning to one's nature.
There has never been one who could shake the root yet calm the branches,
or muddy the source yet clear the flow.
Thus, those who understand the essence of nature
do not strive for what nature cannot achieve;
those who understand the essence of fate
do not worry about what fate cannot change.
Therefore, not building lofty palaces
is not out of love for wood;
not casting large bells and tripods
is not out of love for metal.
By following the true essence of life and nature,
institutions can serve as models for the myriad people.
Now, if the eyes delight in the five colors,
the mouth savors flavors,
the ears indulge in the five sounds,
and the seven apertures contend with each other,
harming one's nature,
daily drawing in evil desires and eroding one's heavenly harmony,
one cannot even govern oneself,
how then can one govern the world!
Thus, if self-cultivation is properly moderated,
then nurturing the people will win their hearts.
To possess the world does not mean
to tread a position of power,
receive registers and records,
or bear a noble title;
it means to mobilize the strength of the world
and win the hearts of the people.
King Zhòu's territory
stretched to the Eastern Sea on the left,
the Flowing Sands on the right,
Jiāozhǐ in the front,
and Yōudū in the rear.
His armies arose from Róng Pass,
reaching the Pǔ River,
with soldiers numbering over a hundred million,
yet they all turned their arrows to shoot backwards,
and fought with reversed halberds.
King Wǔ, holding a yellow battle-axe in his left hand
and a white banner in his right to command them,
caused them to disintegrate and flee,
collapsing like crumbling earth.
Zhòu had the name of facing south as ruler,
but not a single person praised him;
this is how one loses the world.
Thus, Jié and
Zhòu are not considered true kings,
while Tāng and Wǔ are not considered usurpers.
The Zhōu dwelling in Fēng
and Hào, with a territory of no more than a hundred li,
yet swore an oath against Zhòu in the wilds of Mù,
entered and occupied the state of Yīn,
paid respects at the temple of Chéng Tāng,
erected a marker at the lane of Shāng Róng,
built a mound over Bǐ Gān's tomb,
freed Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
then broke the drumsticks and destroyed the drums,
laid down the five weapons,
released the oxen and horses,
and with folded hands, received the homage of the world.
The common people sang and rejoiced,
the feudal lords brought gifts and paid court,
for they had won the people's hearts.
Hélǘ attacked Chǔ,
in five battles entered Yǐng,
burned the grain stores of Gāofǔ,
broke the Nine Dragon Bells,
whipped the tomb of Jīng Píng,
and lodged in King Zhāo's palace.
King Zhāo fled to Suí,
the common people, elders and youths carrying the young and supporting the old, followed him,
then vied with one another in bravery to confront the invaders,
all turning in their direction, baring their arms to fight for him.
At this time,
without commanders to array them in ranks,
each exerted himself to the death,
repelled the Wú troops,
and restored the land of Chǔ.
King Líng built the Zhānghuā Terrace,
launched the Gānxī campaign,
causing turmoil at home and abroad,
the people were exhausted and distressed,
Qìjí took advantage of the people's resentment and set up Prince Bǐ,
the people turned their backs and abandoned him,
he starved at Gānxī,
ate wild plants and drank plain water,
pillowed on a clod of earth and died.
The mountains and rivers of Chǔ did not change,
the land remained the same,
the nature of the people was no different,
yet for King Zhāo they vied to die for him,
while for King Líng they betrayed and left him,
such is the difference between gaining and losing the people's support.
Thus when the Son of Heaven possesses the Dào,
his defense lies with the four barbarian tribes;
when the Son of Heaven loses the Dào,
his defense lies with the feudal lords.
When the feudal lords possess the Dào,
their defense lies with the neighboring states;
when the feudal lords lose the Dào,
their defense lies within their own borders.
Thus Táng, dwelling in Bó with seventy lǐ,
and King Wén, dwelling in Fēng with a hundred lǐ,
both had their commands obeyed and prohibitions heeded throughout the realm.
When Zhōu declined,
the Róng attacked Fán Bó at Chǔqiū and took him captive.
Therefore, with the Dào, one can command the feudal lords with a hundred lǐ of land;
without the Dào, even with the vastness of the realm, one may fear a single province like Jìzhōu.
Hence it is said:
Do not rely on others not seizing from you,
rely on your being unseizable.
Practicing a way that can be seized,
yet condemning usurpation and regicide,
is of no benefit to holding the realm.
What sustains human life,
is clothing and food.
Now if one is imprisoned in a dark room,
even if nourished with fine meats,
clothed in embroidered silks,
one cannot be happy,
because the eyes see nothing,
the ears hear nothing.
Boring a small hole,
seeing rain fall,
then one laughs with joy;
how much more so when opening doors and windows,
moving from darkness into brightness!
From darkness to brightness,
one is already overjoyed and delighted,
how much more when leaving the room to sit in the hall,
seeing the sun and moon's light!
Seeing the sun and moon's light,
one is expansively happy,
how much more when ascending Tàishān,
treading the stone-fenced summit,
gazing over the eight wildernesses,
seeing the heavenly vault like a canopy,
the rivers like ribbons,
and all things in between!
Is not such joy immense!
Moreover, the deaf—
their ear structure is intact but they cannot hear;
the blind—
their eye structure remains but they cannot see.
Speech—
is how one communicates oneself to others;
hearing—
is how one receives others into oneself.
The mute cannot speak,
the deaf cannot hear,
being both mute and deaf,
human communication is blocked,
thus those with the ailments of muteness and deafness,
even if they bankrupt their family seeking treatment,
do not mind the expense.
Is it only the body that can be mute and deaf?
The mind and will can be so too.
When a finger is cramped,
none fail to strive to stretch it;
when the mind is blocked,
none know to strive to open it—
this is from not understanding categories.
To contemplate the breadth and loftiness of the Six Arts,
plumb the depths of the Dào and virtue,
reach the heights without limit,
descend to the depths without bottom,
move through the boundless,
soar in the formless,
broader than the four seas,
loftier than Tàishān,
richer than the rivers,
expansive and penetrating,
clear and bright,
with nothing in heaven and earth to obstruct or oppose,
the perspective it provides—
is it not immense!
What humans know is shallow,
yet the changes of things are endless,
what was unknown before is known now,
not because knowledge has increased,
but due to the accumulation of inquiry and learning.
Things often seen become recognized,
often done become mastered,
thus facing calamity, one devises preparations;
encountering difficulties, one gains expedience.
With the lifespan of one generation,
to observe the knowledge of a thousand years,
the discourses of past and present,
though one has not personally experienced them,
their principles are inherently present—
can this not be called having method!
When people wish to know height and depth but cannot,
teaching them the use of the water level pleases them;
wishing to know weight but having no means,
giving them scales and weights delights them;
wishing to know distance but unable to,
teaching them the sighting tube brings them joy;
how much more so for knowing responses without fixed patterns and inexhaustible!
Facing great difficulties without fear,
encountering perplexing complexities without confusion,
serene and self-possessed—
the joy it brings,
is it merely the pleasure of a single explanation!
The Dào—
all that has form is born from it,
as a parent, it is indeed intimate!
All who consume grains and breathe air receive from it,
as a ruler, it is indeed benevolent;
all who possess wisdom learn from it,
as a teacher, it is indeed broad.
An archer shooting multiple times without hitting,
if taught the proper method, is pleased;
how much more so for the source of that method!
None do not know that learning benefits themselves,
yet some fail to do so—
play and amusement hinder them.
Many people let the useless harm the useful,
hence knowledge is not broad and days feel insufficient.
If the effort spent digging ornamental ponds were used for farming,
then fields would surely be cultivated.
If the earth piled high for artificial mountains were used to repair dikes,
then water supply would surely be sufficient.
If the expense of feeding dogs, horses, swans, and geese were used to support scholars,
then reputation would surely flourish.
If the days spent on hunting and board games were used to recite the Shī and read the Shū,
then knowledge would surely be broad.
Thus, not learning compared to learning,
is like the mute and deaf compared to normal people.
All scholars who can distinguish between Heaven and humanity,
understand the root of order and chaos,
purify their minds and clarify their intentions to preserve it,
and perceive its beginning and end,
may be called knowledgeable in strategy.
What Heaven creates
are birds, beasts, plants, and trees;
what humanity creates
are rituals, rules, and institutions,
such as constructing palaces and dwellings,
and making boats and carriages.
The foundation of governance
is benevolence and righteousness,
while its branches
are laws and regulations.
What people use to serve the living
is fundamental,
while what they use to serve the dead
is secondary.
The root and branches
form one body,
and loving both
is human nature.
Putting the root before the branches defines a noble person,
while harming the root for the branches defines a petty person.
The nature of noble and petty persons is not different;
it lies only in what they prioritize.
In plants and trees,
the thick parts are the root,
while the thin parts are the branches.
In the nature of birds and beasts,
the large parts are the head,
while the small parts are the tail.
If the branches are larger than the root, they break;
if the tail is larger than the waist, it cannot wag.
Thus, feeding the mouth fattens all joints;
watering the root beautifies the leaves and branches.
Heaven and Earth, in their nature of creating things, have root and branches,
and in nurturing things, they have priorities.
Should humanity, in governance,
lack a sense of beginning and end?
Therefore, benevolence and righteousness
are the root of governance.
Now, not knowing to cultivate the root
but striving to manage the branches
is like neglecting the root to water the branches.
Moreover, laws are born
to assist benevolence and righteousness.
Now, emphasizing laws and abandoning benevolence and righteousness
is like valuing one's hat and shoes while forgetting one's head and feet.
Thus, benevolence and righteousness
form a solid foundation.
Not strengthening its depth but expanding its breadth leads to collapse;
not broadening its base but increasing its height leads to overthrow.
Zhào Zhèng did not enhance his virtue but piled up height,
thus he perished;
Zhì Bó did not practice benevolence and righteousness but sought to expand territory,
thus he fell.
The "Guóyǔ" says:
"Without enlarging the beam,
it cannot bear heavy loads.
Nothing is heavier than a state,
and no beam is greater than virtue."
The ruler's possession of the people
is like a wall having a foundation,
or a tree having roots.
Deep roots make the tree firm;
a fine foundation ensures stability above.
The ways of the Five Emperors and Three Kings
are the guiding principles of the world,
the model of governance.
Now, the policies of Shāng Yāng like "opening and blocking",
Shēn Zǐ's "three tallies",
Hán Fēi's "Solitary Indignation",
and the vertical and horizontal strategies of Zhāng Yí and Sū Qín
are all expedient measures,
temporary tactics,
not the great root of governance,
nor the constant norms of affairs,
fit to be widely adopted and passed down through generations.
Zǐ Náng's northern campaign preserved Chǔ,
but such extremity cannot be the norm;
Xián Gāo's deception saved Zhèng,
but deceit cannot be constant.
Now, the sounds of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng"
all arise from words,
rooted in emotion,
thus ruler and minister are harmonious,
father and son affectionate.
Hence, the music of "Sháo"
and "Xià"
soaks into metal and stone,
moistens plants and trees.
Now, if mournful and resentful tunes
are played on stringed instruments,
those who hear them
are either licentious or sorrowful.
Licentiousness blurs the distinction between men and women;
sorrow stirs the air of resentment.
Is this what is called music?
King Qiān of Zhào was exiled to Fánglíng,
longing for his homeland,
he composed the "Shānmù" lament;
none who heard it failed to shed tears.
When Jīng Kē went west to assassinate the King of Qín,
Gāo Jiànlí
and Sòng Yì played the zhù,
singing over the Yìshuǐ River;
none who heard it failed to glare with wide eyes,
their hair standing up and piercing their hats.
If such sounds are taken as music and used in ancestral temples,
is this what the ancients called music?
Thus, ceremonial caps and carriages
may be worn but not adored;
the blend of grand sacrifices
may be eaten but not craved;
vermilion strings and leaky flutes,
one chant with three sighs,
may be heard but not enjoyed.
Therefore, what is soundless
corrects the audible;
what is flavorless
perfects the tasteful.
Pleasing sounds clear to the ear,
mixed flavors delightful to the mouth,
are not what is noble.
Thus, affairs not rooted in the Dào and virtue
cannot be taken as models;
words not aligned with the ancient kings
cannot be considered the Way;
music not harmonized with the "Yǎ"
and "Sòng"
cannot be called proper music.
Therefore, the words of those five masters
serve expedient rhetoric and grabs for power,
not the universal principles of the world.
When sage kings establish governance and impart teachings,
they must examine the beginning and end;
when they promulgate laws and set models,
they must trace the root and branches,
not hastily preparing one thing for one purpose alone.
See its creation and ponder its effect;
observe its source and know its flow.
Thus, their broad bestowals never exhaust,
enduring long without soiling.
Water emerges from mountains and enters the sea;
grain grows in fields and stores in barns.
Sages see where things are born,
and thus know where they return.
Thus, Shǔn deeply hid gold in the Chányán Mountains,
to block greedy and base desires.
Yí Dí made wine,
Yǔ drank and found it sweet,
yet he distanced Yí Dí and abstained from excessive drink,
to curb the conduct of indulgence.
When Shī Yán played the music of the northern borders of Zhāogē for Duke Píng,
Shī Kuàng said:
"This is the music of a doomed state."
Sighing, he pressed the strings to stop it,
to prevent the winds of decadence.
Thus, when people know writing, virtue declines;
when they know calculation, kindness declines;
when they know contracts, trust declines;
when they know machinery, simplicity declines.
Cunning and deceit hidden in the breast
leave purity incomplete,
and spiritual virtue imperfect.
The sè does not sound itself,
yet its twenty-five strings each respond with their tone;
the axle does not turn itself,
yet its thirty spokes each exert their force swiftly.
Strings have slackness, tightness, largeness, and smallness, then they can form melodies;
a carriage has wear, ease, movement, and stillness, then it can reach afar.
What enables sound
is the soundless;
what reaches a thousand miles
is the motionless.
Thus, when superior and inferior follow different ways, there is order;
when they follow the same way, there is chaos.
High position with a great Way is followed;
great affairs with a small Way bring disaster.
Thus, petty pleasures harm righteousness,
petty cleverness harms the Way,
petty arguments harm governance,
harshness injures virtue.
Great governance is not perilous,
so the people are easily guided;
the highest rule is generous,
so subordinates do no harm;
the ultimate center returns to simplicity,
so the people have nothing to hide.
Shāng Yāng established the law of mutual responsibility in Qín,
yet the common people resented it;
Wú Qǐ promulgated the decree reducing noble ranks in Chǔ,
and the meritorious officials rebelled.
Shāng Yāng's establishment of laws,
Wú Qǐ's employment of troops,
were among the finest in the world.
However, Shāng Yāng caused Qín's demise through his laws,
being meticulous in the traces of legal documents,
but ignorant of the root of order and chaos.
Wú Qǐ weakened Chǔ with his military,
skilled in the affairs of battle formations,
but unaware of the strategies of temple warfare.
When Duke Xiàn of Jìn attacked Lí,
he obtained its princess,
which was not unpleasing,
yet Shǐ Sū sighed over it,
foreseeing the calamity that would befall four generations.
King Fūchāi of Wú defeated Qí at Àilíng,
and triumphed over Jìn at Huángchí,
which were not insignificant victories,
yet Zǐxū worried about them,
foreseeing his inevitable capture by Yuè.
Xiǎo Bái fled to Jǔ,
Chóng'ěr fled to Cáo,
which were not without hardship,
yet Bào Shū
and Jiù Fǎn followed and assisted them,
knowing they could achieve hegemony.
Gōu Jiàn dwelled on Kuàijī,
governing without respite,
planning without cease,
knowing misfortune could turn to blessing.
Xiāngzǐ had a worried expression after two victories,
fearing blessing could turn to misfortune.
Thus, Duke Huán of Qí lost the fields of Wènyáng yet became hegemon,
while Zhì Bó annexed the lands of the three Jìn states and perished.
The sage sees blessings within tightly closed doors,
and considers calamities beyond ninefold barriers.
Silkworms yielding two harvests a year,
is not unprofitable,
yet the king's laws forbid it,
because it damages mulberry trees.
Lí grass ripens before rice,
yet farmers weed it out,
not letting small gains harm the greater harvest.
The family elder eats different food,
uses special vessels for offerings,
daughters-in-law go barefoot to the hall,
kneel to serve soup,
which is not without cost,
yet cannot be omitted,
as it would harm righteousness.
Securing a matchmaker to arrange words,
betrothing and taking a wife,
dressing formally to fetch the bride,
is not without trouble,
yet cannot be changed,
as it prevents licentiousness.
Having neighbors monitor each other,
detecting crimes mutually,
to expose wickedness,
is not ineffective,
yet cannot be implemented,
as it injures harmonious hearts,
and builds enmity and resentment.
Thus, there are cases where chiseling one hole opens a hundred cracks,
planting one thing sprouts ten thousand leaves.
The chiseling does little for convenience,
yet the openings suffice for ruin;
the planting does little for profit,
yet the growth suffices for trouble.
Fools are deluded by small gains,
forgetting great harms,
and cannot be taken as models.
Cōngyáng repels fleas and lice,
yet people don't use it for mats,
as it attracts língqióng insects.
A cat catches mice,
but cannot be released in the courtyard,
as it also preys on chickens.
Thus, some deeds benefit the small but harm the great,
gain here but lose there.
So in playing checkers,
some take two pieces but end up trapped,
others sacrifice one and win.
Seeking petty gains is no proper conduct,
but wisdom and method can be models.
Thus, benevolence and wisdom
are the beauties of human talent.
What is called benevolence
is loving others;
what is called wisdom
is knowing others.
Loving others means no cruel punishments;
knowing others means no chaotic governance.
Governance through orderly principles,
then no absurdities occur;
punishments not excessive or abusive,
then no tyrannical acts arise.
Above, no vexatious governance;
below, no resentful hearts;
then all evils are eliminated and harmony prevails,
this is why the Three Dynasties flourished.
Thus the Shū says:
"Able to be wise and kind,
the common people cherish him.
Why worry about Huāndōu,
why banish the Yǒumiáo?"
Zhì Bó had five surpassing talents,
yet could not avoid dying by others' hands,
because he did not love others.
King Jiàn of Qí had three surpassing skills,
yet was captured by Qín,
because he did not know the worthy.
Thus, nothing is greater than loving others in benevolence,
nothing greater than knowing others in wisdom.
Without these two,
even with keen intelligence and quick skill,
toiling diligently and strenuously,
one cannot avoid chaos.
Those who compose books and discourses
do so to uphold morality,
order human affairs,
examining heaven above,
measuring earth below,
penetrating all principles in between.
Though unable to draw out the profoundest mysteries,
their richness suffices to observe beginnings and ends.
Summarizing essentials and outlining generalities,
if their words do not dissect simplicity,
nor disperse the great ancestor,
then people remain confused and unknowing;
hence they use many phrases,
broad explanations,
yet fear people may abandon root for branch.
Thus, speaking of the Way without speaking of affairs,
one cannot drift with the world;
speaking of affairs without speaking of the Way,
one cannot roam with transformation.
Therefore, I composed twenty chapters:
there is "Yuán Dào",
"Chù Zhēn",
"Tiānwén",
"Dìxíng",
"Shí Zé",
"Lǎn Míng",
"Jīngshén",
"Běn Jīng",
"Zhǔ Shù",
"Miù Chēng",
"Qí Sú",
"Dào Yìng",
"Fàn Lùn",
"Quán Yán",
"Bīng Lüè",
"Shuō Shān",
"Shuō Lín",
"Rén Jiān",
"Xiū Wù",
and "Tài Zú".
"Yuán Dào"
encompasses the six directions,
blends the myriad things,
images the form of the Great One,
probes the depths of obscurity,
to soar in the realm of nothingness.
Entrusting the small to embrace the large,
holding to simplicity to govern breadth,
it lets people know the sequence of fortune and misfortune,
the advantages and harms of action and stillness.
Sincerely comprehending its intent,
one can vastly observe with a noble spirit.
Wishing to awaken with one word,
then honor heaven and preserve authenticity;
wishing to penetrate with a second,
then disdain things and value the self;
wishing to exhaust with a third,
then externalize desires and return to nature.
Grasping its main points,
to internally harmonize the five viscera,
permeate skin and flesh,
clothe oneself in its rules,
and abide with it lifelong,
thus responding to all directions,
coupling with myriad changes,
like turning a pellet in the palm,
sufficient for self-contentment.
"Chù Zhēn" explores
the transformations from beginning to end exhaustively,
delves into the essence of existence and non-existence,
distinguishes the changes among all things,
harmonizes the forms of life and death,
enabling people to understand detachment from external matters and returning to oneself,
examine the nuances of benevolence and righteousness,
comprehend the principles of similarity and difference,
observe the system of supreme virtue,
know the laws of change and transformation,
discussing signs within the profound mysteries,
and penetrating the mother of creation.
"Tiān Wén" is
used to harmonize the energies of yin and yang,
regulate the light of the sun and moon,
moderate the times of opening and closing,
arrange the movements of the stars and constellations,
understand the variations of opposition and compliance,
avoid the calamities of taboos,
follow the responses of timely fortune,
emulate the constancy of the five spirits,
so that people can look up to heaven and comply with it,
without disturbing its normal order.
"Dì Xíng" is
used to exhaust the length from south to north,
reach the breadth from east to west,
map the shapes of mountains and hills,
demarcate the dwellings of rivers and valleys,
clarify the origins of all things,
know the multitude of living beings,
enumerate the counts of mountains and abysses,
plan the paths of far and near,
enabling people to be thorough and comprehensive,
unmoved by material things,
unstartled by the strange.
"Shí Zé" is
used to base on the timeliness of heaven above,
exhaust the resources of the earth below,
act appropriately according to measures,
align with human principles,
model the twelve nodes,
as a standard formula,
ending and beginning again,
revolving without limit,
following and imitating,
to understand fortune and misfortune,
handling choices of opening and closing,
each having its taboos,
issuing commands and decrees,
teaching and guiding in due time,
so that rulers know how to proceed.
"Lǎn Míng" is
used to speak of how the most refined penetrates the nine heavens,
the most subtle sinks into formlessness,
the pure enters the utmost clarity,
the bright communicates with the obscure.
It begins by gathering things and drawing analogies,
viewing and selecting,
immersing thoughts in subtle categories,
things that can illustrate ideas and forms,
thereby penetrating blockages,
clearing obstructions,
guiding human intentions,
connecting them to the infinite,
thus clarifying the感应 of categories of things,
the responses of shared energy,
the unions of yin and yang,
the signs of forms and boundaries,
to enable people to see far and broadly.
"Jīng Shén" is
used to trace the origin of human life,
and awaken to the form and nine orifices of the body,
taking images from heaven,
harmonizing its blood and energy,
with thunder, lightning, wind, and rain,
comparing joys and angers to day, night, cold, and heat,
examining the distinction between life and death,
differentiating the traces of similarity and difference,
moderating the dynamics of movement and stillness,
to return to the root of one's nature and destiny.
So that people cherish and nurture their spirit,
calm their soul,
not altering themselves for material things,
but firmly dwelling in emptiness and nothingness.
"Běn Jīng" is
used to illuminate the virtue of great sages,
penetrate the way of the primordial beginning,
outline the changes from ancient to modern in declining ages,
to praise the prosperity of former sages,
and criticize the corrupt governance of end times.
So that people renounce the keenness of ears and eyes,
calm the stirrings of the spirit,
restrain extravagant views,
moderate the harmony of nurturing life,
distinguish the conduct of emperors and kings,
and classify the differences between great and small.
"Zhǔ Shù" concerns
the affairs of ruling people,
utilizing appointments and oversight,
to make officials each fulfill their abilities.
Clarifying the grasp of power and control,
to manage subordinates,
matching names with reality,
examining through multiple checks,
so that the ruler holds methods and essentials,
without arbitrary joys or angers.
Its methods straightforwardly implement and correct deviations,
outwardly impartial and establishing public good,
making all officials communicate smoothly and converge like spokes,
each attending to their duties,
people contributing their achievements,
this is the clarity of rulership techniques.
"Miù Chēng" is
breaking down theories of Dao and virtue,
grading the distinctions of benevolence and righteousness,
briefly incorporating human affairs,
summarizing in accord with the virtue of the divine,
borrowing images for parallels,
to draw analogies,
cutting short to make sections,
to suit minor tools,
thus using detailed explanations to debate,
responding to感应 without exhaustion.
"Qí Sú" is
used to unify the short and long of all living beings,
harmonize the customs of the nine tribes,
connect ancient and modern discussions,
thread through the principles of all things,
tailor the appropriateness of rituals and righteousness,
and plan the beginning and end of human affairs.
"Dào Yìng" is
gathering traces of past events,
reviewing the footprints of antiquity,
observing the reversals of fortune, benefit, and harm,
testing the methods of Lǎo,
Zhuāng,
and aligning with the trends of gain and loss.
"Fàn Lùn" is
used to mend the gaps between fine details,
and fill the crevices of irregularities.
Connecting paths and straightforward application,
to trace back to original simplicity,
and foresee the changes of gain and loss,
the reversals of advantage and disadvantage,
so that people are not recklessly submerged in power and profit,
not deceived by circumstances,
aligning with verification,
while also examining the changes of the times,
and shifting with transformation.
"Quán Yán" is
used to analogize the aims of human affairs,
explain the essence of order and chaos.
Selecting the subtleties of profound words,
interpreting with the text of ultimate principles,
and mending the gaps of faults.
"Bīng Lüè" is
used to clarify the methods of victory in battle and conquest,
the situations of forms and opportunities,
the changes of deception and cunning,
embodying the way of following,
and holding the theory of restraint.
So that one knows that in battle formations and conflicts, without the Dao, they cannot proceed,
knows that in attack, conquest, firm defense, without virtue, they cannot strengthen.
Truly understanding its meaning,
advancing, retreating, left, right, without encountering danger,
riding the momentum as resource,
taking clarity and stillness as constant,
avoiding the solid and striking the weak,
like driving a flock of sheep,
this is what is said about military affairs.
"Shuō Shān"
and "Shuō Lín" are
used to bore through and penetrate the blockages of all matters,
and open up the obstructions of all things.
Borrowing analogies and taking images,
from different categories and varied forms,
to grasp the meaning of human principles,
loosening tangled knots,
explaining and selecting complexities,
thereby clarifying the patterns of events.
"Rénjiān" serves to observe the transformations of calamity and blessing,
examine the reversals of advantage and harm,
probe the traces of gain and loss,
and mark the boundaries of beginning and end.
It discriminates the subtleties of all affairs,
expounds the pivots of survival and demise,
enabling people to understand how calamity becomes blessing,
loss becomes gain,
success becomes failure,
and benefit becomes harm.
If one truly comprehends its profound meaning,
they can navigate through worldly affairs with flexibility,
remaining unharmed by slander, malice, or venom.
"Xiūwù" addresses those who have not yet immersed themselves in the Dào,
whose understanding remains shallow,
and who, upon encountering its writings,
mistakenly take clarity and tranquility as the norm,
and placid indifference as the foundation.
Consequently, they become lax in their studies,
indulge their desires, and follow their whims,
seeking only self-indulgence and ease,
thereby obstructing the great Dào.
Now, the mad have no worries,
and the sage has no worries.
The sage is without worry because of harmony with virtue;
the mad are without worry because they are ignorant of calamity and blessing.
Thus, the non-action of the enlightened and the non-action of the obstructed may appear the same,
but the reasons for their non-action differ.
Therefore, various explanations and discourses are provided to make them receptive,
encouraging scholars to strive diligently toward self-cultivation.
"Tàizú" spans the eight extremes,
reaches the heights of loftiness,
illuminates the three luminaries above,
and harmonizes water and earth below.
It threads the Dào of past and present,
orders the sequence of ethical principles,
gathers the pointers of all directions,
and returns them to a single root,
thereby weaving the fabric of governance
and structuring royal affairs.
It traces the workings of the mind,
regulates emotions and nature,
to harbor the spirit of clarity and peace,
purify the essence of divine intelligence,
and intimately engage with the harmony of Heaven.
Thus, it contemplates the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
who embraced the celestial energy,
held the heart of Heaven,
maintained central harmony within,
and embodied virtue internally,
thereby consolidating Heaven and Earth,
initiating yīn and yáng,
sequencing the four seasons,
rectifying the flow of directions,
calming what they pacified,
and moving what they propelled.
They molded and transformed all things,
guided and changed all living beings,
leading with voices that were followed,
acting with movements that were accompanied,
uniting all within the four seas with one heart and common purpose.
Hence, auspicious stars appeared,
propitious winds arrived,
yellow dragons descended,
phoenixes nested in rows of trees,
and qílins rested in the suburbs.
If virtue is not formed internally,
yet one enforces laws and regulations,
relying solely on institutions,
then the spirits will not respond,
fortune and auspiciousness will not come,
the four seas will not submit,
and the myriad people will not be transformed.
Therefore, virtue formed internally is the great foundation of governance.
This is the "Tàizú" of the "Hóngliè."
All writings are meant to glimpse the Dào and open blockages,
so that later generations may know the proper ways to act and choose,
externally engaging with things without confusion,
internally having means to settle the spirit and nurture the qì,
basking in the ultimate harmony,
and finding joy in what they have received from Heaven and Earth.
Thus, to speak of the Dào without clarifying beginning and end,
one would not know what to emulate;
to speak of beginning and end without illuminating Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons,
one would not know what to avoid;
to speak of Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons without drawing analogies and categories,
one would not recognize the subtle and refined;
to speak of the utmost refinement without tracing the human spirit and qì,
one would not know the key to nurturing life;
to trace human emotions without speaking of the virtue of the great sage,
one would not know the distinctions of the five elements;
to speak of the imperial Dào without discussing the affairs of rulers,
one would not know the gradations of great and small;
to speak of rulers' affairs without using comparisons,
one would not know the appropriateness of action and stillness;
to use comparisons without speaking of customs and changes,
one would not grasp the main intent of harmony and unity;
having spoken of customs and changes without mentioning past events,
one would not understand the responses of the Dào and virtue;
knowing the Dào and virtue but not the twists of the world,
one would have no means to correspond with all directions;
knowing broad discussions but not interpretive words,
one would have no means for composure;
understanding writings and texts but not the pointers of military strategy,
one would have no means to respond to emergencies;
knowing the general outline but not analogies and illustrations,
one would have no means to elucidate affairs;
knowing public principles but not the human world,
one would have no means to respond to calamity and blessing;
knowing the human world but not diligent effort,
one would have no means to encourage scholars to exert themselves.
Wanting to forcefully simplify the wording
and summarize the essentials,
without delving into details and nuances,
would be insufficient to exhaust the meaning of the Dào and virtue.
Therefore, writing these twenty books,
the principles of Heaven and Earth are thoroughly explored,
the affairs of the human world are connected,
and the Dào of emperors and kings is fully prepared.
Their words range from small to great,
from subtle to coarse,
with varying themes and volumes,
each serving its purpose.
Now, to speak solely of the Dào,
it is present everywhere,
yet only the sage can grasp the root and know the branches.
Today's scholars lack the sage's talent,
and if not provided with detailed explanations,
they will tumble forever in the murky chaos,
unaware of the path to awakening in clarity.
Now, the "Qián" and "Kūn" of the "Yì" suffice to exhaust the Dào and convey its meaning,
and the eight trigrams can discern fortune and misfortune,
know calamity and blessing,
yet Fúxī developed them into sixty-four variations,
and the Zhōu dynasty added the six lines,
to trace and measure the pure and clear Dào,
and gather the ancestors of all things.
The notes of the five tones
are no more than gōng,
shāng, jué,
zhǐ, and yǔ,
yet a five-stringed qín cannot be played;
there must be a blend of fine and broad,
harmony and driving force, to form a melody.
Now, if one draws a dragon's head,
observers will not know what beast it is;
but if the full form is provided,
there will be no doubt.
Now, to speak of the Dào is to speak much,
to speak of things is to speak little,
to speak of methods is to speak broadly,
to speak of affairs is to speak shallowly;
to extend this in discussion,
there would be nothing to say.
The purpose for scholars
is precisely to lead them to what is beyond words.
The discourse on the Dao is profoundly deep,
hence abundant words are employed to express its essence;
the myriad things are exceedingly numerous,
thus extensive explanations are made to comprehend their meanings.
Though the language may be winding and vast,
tangled and far-reaching,
it serves to purify and clarify the ultimate intent,
ensuring it remains unobstructed and unstagnant,
graspable yet not scattered.
The rotting carcasses in the Yangtze
and Yellow rivers are countless,
yet worshippers draw from them,
for they are vast.
A cup of sweet wine,
if a fly falls into it,
a common man will not drink it,
for it is small.
If one truly comprehends the discussions in these twenty chapters,
grasps the essentials and key points,
they can connect with the nine regions,
traverse the ten gates,
transcend heaven and earth,
and part mountains and rivers.
In roaming freely through this world,
shaping the forms of all things,
they will be at ease and unburdened.
Such a person,
embracing the sun and moon without being scorched,
nourishes all things without depletion.
Boundless and flowing,
it is sufficient to behold!
Vast and expansive,
limitless and open,
one may wander freely!
During King Wén's time,
Zhòu was the Son of Heaven,
levying taxes without restraint,
killing without end,
indulging in excess and dissipation,
turning the palace into a market,
inventing the punishment of the roasting pillar,
dismembering those who remonstrated,
and disemboweling pregnant women,
causing all under heaven to unite in suffering.
King Wén, through four generations of accumulated virtue,
cultivated moral conduct and righteousness,
residing between Qí and Zhōu,
with a territory no more than a hundred li,
yet two-thirds of the world turned to him.
King Wén sought to use humility and weakness to overcome violence,
to rid the world of cruelty and tyranny, establishing the Kingly Way,
thus giving rise to the strategies of Tàigōng.
King Wén laid the foundation but did not complete it,
so King Wǔ continued his enterprise,
employing Tàigōng's strategies,
mobilizing all resources with light taxes,
personally donning armor,
to attack the unprincipled and punish the unjust,
pledging his troops at Mùyě,
and ascending to the Son of Heaven's position.
Before the world was stabilized,
and the realm not yet pacified,
King Wǔ wished to glorify King Wén's virtuous legacy,
so that the Yí and Dí tribes would bring tribute according to their means,
but those from distant lands had not yet arrived,
so he observed a three-year mourning period,
placing King Wén's coffin between the pillars,
awaiting the distant regions.
King Wǔ reigned for three years before passing away,
and King Chéng was still in swaddling clothes,
unable to govern.
Cài Shū
and Guǎn Shū supported Prince Lùfù in plotting rebellion.
The Duke of Zhōu continued King Wén's enterprise,
holding the reins of the Son of Heaven's governance,
supporting the Zhōu house as its pillar,
and assisting King Chéng.
Fearing that the path of conflict would not be blocked,
and that ministers might endanger the ruler,
he released horses on Huàshān,
set oxen free in Táolín,
broke drums and snapped drumsticks,
and held court with tablets in hand,
to bring peace to the royal house,
and pacify the feudal lords.
When King Chéng came of age,
able to handle governance,
the Duke of Zhōu was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
using this to transform customs and practices.
Confucius cultivated the ways of King Chéng and King Kāng,
expounding the teachings of the Duke of Zhōu,
to instruct his seventy disciples,
having them wear the appropriate robes and caps,
and study the classical texts,
thus giving rise to the school of the Rúists.
Mòzǐ studied the Rúist traditions,
learning Confucius's methods,
but found their rituals cumbersome and impractical,
their lavish burials wasteful and impoverishing,
and prolonged mourning harmful to life and affairs,
so he turned away from the Zhōu way and adopted the governance of the Xià.
In Yǔ's time,
the world was flooded,
and Yǔ personally carried baskets and spades,
leading the people,
dredging rivers to create nine branches,
channeling the Yangtze to open nine routes,
and opening lakes to stabilize the Eastern Sea.
During this period,
there was no time to put out fires,
nor opportunity to dry wet clothes,
those dying on hills were buried on hills,
those dying in marshes were buried in marshes,
thus frugality with resources,
simple burials,
and plain mourning practices emerged.
During Duke Huán of Qí's time,
the Son of Heaven was weak,
feudal lords contended by force,
southern Yí and northern Dí tribes
alternately attacked the central states,
leaving the central plains hanging by a thread.
The territory of Qí,
bordered the sea to the east and the river to the north,
with limited land and few fields,
yet its people were clever and skilled.
Duke Huán worried about the central states' plight,
and suffered from the Yí and Dí disturbances,
seeking to preserve the perishing and revive the extinct,
honor the Son of Heaven's position,
and expand the enterprises of Kings Wén
and Wǔ,
thus giving rise to the book of Guǎnzǐ.
Duke Jǐng of Qí indulged in music and beauty within,
and delighted in dogs and horses without,
hunting and forgetting to return,
indiscriminate in his affections,
he built the Lùqǐn terrace,
cast a massive bell with his clan,
struck it in the courtyard,
causing pheasants in the suburbs to cry out,
and in one morning used three thousand zhōng of grain,
with Liángqiū Jù
and Zǐjiā Kuài guiding him by his side,
thus giving rise to Yànzǐ's remonstrances.
In later ages,
the feudal lords of the six states,
separated by different valleys and gorges,
divided by waters and mountains,
each governed their own territories,
guarded their allotted lands,
grasped their authority,
and controlled their administrations.
Below, there were no regional chiefs,
above, no Son of Heaven,
they contended for power by force,
with the victor taking precedence,
relying on alliances,
securing heavy pledges,
splitting tally tokens,
forging distant support,
to defend their states,
and maintain their altars of land and grain,
thus giving rise to the strategies of vertical and horizontal alliances.
Shěnzǐ was
an assistant to Hán Zhāolí,
Hán, a state separated from Jìn,
with arid land and contentious people,
sandwiched between great powers,
where Jìn's old rituals had not vanished,
and Hán's new laws repeatedly emerged,
former rulers' decrees not rescinded,
while new rulers' orders were issued,
creating contradictions between old and new,
and inconsistencies between past and present,
officials turned rebellious and chaotic,
uncertain of what to follow,
thus giving rise to the school of names and punishments.
The customs of Qín
were greedy, wolf-like, and forceful,
lacking righteousness and pursuing profit,
amenable to control by punishment,
but not transformable by goodness,
motivated by rewards,
but not inspired by reputation,
protected by perilous terrain and girded by rivers,
fortified on all sides,
with advantageous geography and convenient terrain,
and abundant accumulated wealth.
Duke Xiào desired to use this tiger-and-wolf momentum to devour the feudal lords,
thus giving rise to the laws of Shāng Yāng.
As for the works of the Liú clan,
they observe the phenomena of heaven and earth,
comprehend the discourses of past and present,
weigh circumstances to establish systems,
measure forms to apply what is fitting,
trace the heart of the Way and its virtue,
harmonize with the ethos of the Three Sovereigns,
in order to roam freely and expansively,
within the profound and subtle,
refining and discerning meticulously,
discarding what is tangled and chaotic,
sifting out what is gentle and tranquil,
so as to unify all under heaven,
order the myriad things,
respond to transformations and changes,
connect with diverse kinds,
not following a single track's path,
nor adhering to a corner's directive,
bound and entangled by things,
yet not shifting with the age,
thus placed in the ordinary without obstruction,
spread throughout the world without gaps.
